verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Would You Return to Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law says a divorced wife who has married another cannot go back to her first husband; You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? (v. 1). The bare heights show where she has been, and the rains have been withheld, yet you refuse to be ashamed (vv. 2-3). She still calls him My father, you are the friend of my youth and asks whether he will be angry forever, Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Affectionate words to God alongside unchanged behaviour are not repentance; and yet the impossible invitation to return is the one God makes.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man's wife, will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? declares the LORD. Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been ravished? By the waysides you have sat awaiting lovers like an Arab in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your vile whoredom. Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come; yet you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man's wife, will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? declares the LORD.

The chapter opens with a point of law. Under Deuteronomy, a man who divorced his wife could not take her back once she had married someone else: her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the LORD (Deut 24:4). The case is closed. The door is shut by God's own statute.

And then, in the same breath, God says: would you return to me?

That is the astonishing thing in this chapter, and everything else stands under it. What the law forbids, love offers. God is not pretending the marriage was undamaged or the adultery small — many lovers is his own phrase — and he still opens a door the law had bolted. How he can do this without ceasing to be just is the question the whole Bible answers at the cross.

Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been ravished? By the waysides you have sat awaiting lovers like an Arab in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your vile whoredom.

The invitation does not come with amnesia. Look up at the hilltops, God says: every one of them has a shrine, and you have been at all of them. The picture of sitting by the roadside waiting is worse than being seduced. It is initiative.

The simile is vivid: like an Arab in the wilderness — a desert raider crouched beside a caravan route, watching the road for whoever comes along. Israel is not pictured as a victim ambushed by temptation but as the one lying in wait for it.

Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come; yet you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed.

The drought was a message, and it was missed. The forehead of a whore is a face that has lost the capacity to blush. Shame is painful and it is a mercy; a conscience that can still be embarrassed is still alive. The danger point in any life is not doing wrong but reaching the stage of doing it without a flicker.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you not just now called to me, 'My father, you are the friend of my youth— will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end?' Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you not just now called to me, 'My father, you are the friend of my youth— will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end?' Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could."

And here is the most uncomfortable verse in the chapter, because the words are lovely. My father, you are the friend of my youth. Warm, intimate, theologically correct, and quite compatible with having done all the evil that you could. Religious language is not repentance. It is possible to call God Father in one breath and keep every arrangement he hates in the next, and this verse exists to stop us doing it comfortably.

And listen to the theology inside their question: will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end? It is true, and Scripture says it — He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever (Ps 103:9). But they are using it as a licence. God will say almost those words himself a few verses later, I will not be angry forever (v. 12), to people who return. The same truth is comfort to the penitent and presumption in the mouth of someone who has done all the evil that you could.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Faithless Israel and Treacherous Judah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Josiah's days God shows Jeremiah faithless Israel, who would not return, and her sister Judah who watched (vv. 6-7). Israel was sent away with a decree of divorce, and Judah still did not fear but played the whore too (vv. 8-9), returning not with her whole heart, but in pretense (v. 10). So Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah (v. 11), and northward goes the call: Return, faithless Israel, Only acknowledge your guilt (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Watching judgment fall on someone else and learning nothing is worse than the sin that brought it; and the way back is one honest admission.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what she did, that faithless one, Israel, how she went up on every high hill and under every green tree, and there played the whore? And I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me,' but she did not return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it. She saw that for all the adulteries of that faithless one, Israel, I had sent her away with a decree of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what she did, that faithless one, Israel, how she went up on every high hill and under every green tree, and there played the whore?

Now a history lesson with two sisters in it. Israel is the northern kingdom, which had already been destroyed by Assyria a century before Jeremiah preached. Judah is the southern kingdom, still standing, listening to this sermon.

And I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me,' but she did not return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it.

Two things to notice. First, God says, After she has done all this she will return to me — the language of a patient husband waiting at the window, which is how God describes his own long-suffering. Second, her treacherous sister Judah saw it. Judah had a front-row seat at her sister's funeral.

She saw that for all the adulteries of that faithless one, Israel, I had sent her away with a decree of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore.

Judah watched the exile of the north — the deportations, the ruined towns, the end of a nation — and drew no conclusion at all. Judah did not fear. There is no education in watching judgment fall on someone else if you have decided in advance that it cannot happen to you.

The decree of divorce is the legal image of verse 1 made concrete. Isaiah uses it the same way and asks the pointed question — Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away? — before giving the answer: for your transgressions your mother was sent away (Isa 50:1). The exile of the north was not God abandoning a faithful wife. It was the consequence of a marriage she had already left.

verseByVerse.quote: Because she took her whoredom lightly, she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and tree. Yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because she took her whoredom lightly, she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and tree. Yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD."

She took her whoredom lightly — that is how nations and people fall, not by deciding sin is good but by deciding it is small. And Judah's response is named exactly: she did return, but in pretense.

This is said in the days of King Josiah, during the great national reform: the idols were smashed, the temple repaired, the Passover kept. It was genuine at the top, and it never reached the heart of the people. A reformation of behaviour without a change of heart is what God calls pretence, and he can tell the difference.

The phrase to hold onto is with her whole heart. Isaiah describes the same condition exactly: this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me (Isa 29:13). And this book will later promise the cure that God himself supplies — I will give them a heart to know me, so that they shall return to me with their whole heart (24:7). What Judah could not produce under Josiah, God undertakes to give.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah. Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, "'Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful, declares the LORD; I will not be angry forever. Only acknowledge your guilt, that you rebelled against the LORD your God and scattered your favors among foreigners under every green tree, and that you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD said to me, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah.

A shocking verdict. The northern kingdom, whose name was a byword for apostasy, comes out better than Judah. Israel sinned with no warning example in front of her; Judah sinned having watched the consequences, while holding the temple, the law, the priesthood and the promises. Privilege raises the bar. The more light, the greater the guilt.

Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, "'Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful, declares the LORD; I will not be angry forever.

And then Jeremiah is told to face north — toward the people who are already gone, scattered a hundred years ago into Assyria, a lost cause by every reckoning — and preach to them. Return, faithless Israel.

The reasons given are all about God: I am merciful, I will not be angry forever. Not, you are not as bad as you think. The ground of the invitation is his character, which is the only ground any of us has.

Only acknowledge your guilt, that you rebelled against the LORD your God and scattered your favors among foreigners under every green tree, and that you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD.

And here is the whole requirement, in one word: Only acknowledge your guilt.

Only. Not make restitution first, not clean yourself up, not produce a period of good behaviour to prove you mean it. Say what is true. Chapter 2 ended with a people insisting I have not sinned (2:35); this is the exact reverse, and it is the door. Joel says it the same way: return to me with all your heart, rend your hearts and not your garments (Joel 2:12-13). Hosea gives the words to use: Take with you words and return to the LORD (Hos 14:2). And John says it to the church: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — Shepherds After My Own Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Return, O faithless children, for God is their master, and he will bring them to Zion one from a city and two from a family (v. 14), giving them shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding (v. 15). The ark will not be remembered or missed (v. 16); Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it (v. 17), and Judah and Israel will come home together (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration is small in its beginnings, pastoral in its care, and larger than Israel at its end.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion. "'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion.

The call is repeated, and the promise attached to it is deliberately modest: one from a city and two from a family. God is not predicting a national landslide. He is describing a remnant, gathered person by person out of places that will not come as a whole.

That is usually how it works. Revival is talked about in national terms; it arrives one person and two people at a time, and God calls that homecoming.

And the ground of the call is a claim: for I am your master. They had left, but they had not stopped being his. Their unfaithfulness did not cancel his right to them, and it is that right — not their merit — that gives him the standing to call them back.

"'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.

Chapter 2 exposed shepherds who transgressed against me (2:8). Here is the remedy: not better management but men whose hearts match God's, and whose work is feeding. The phrase echoes what God said of David, a man after my heart, who will do all my will (Acts 13:22). The risen Christ still gives the shepherds and teachers to his church (Eph 4:11), and behind every faithful one stands the good shepherd himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, in those days, declares the LORD, they shall no more say, "The ark of the covenant of the LORD." It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed; it shall not be made again. At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it, to the presence of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart. In those days the house of Judah shall join the house of Israel, and together they shall come from the land of the north to the land that I gave your fathers for a heritage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, in those days, declares the LORD, they shall no more say, "The ark of the covenant of the LORD." It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed; it shall not be made again.

The most sacred object in Israel's worship — the ark, the throne of God's presence, the centre of the holy of holies — will not be missed. Not destroyed and mourned; simply not needed, and not thought of.

That is not a downgrade but a promotion. A sign becomes unnecessary when the thing it signified has arrived in person. The next verse says what replaces it.

At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it, to the presence of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart. In those days the house of Judah shall join the house of Israel, and together they shall come from the land of the north to the land that I gave your fathers for a heritage.

Three enormous promises. The whole city becomes the throne room, not one gold box inside one room. All nations gather, not Israel alone. And the heart itself changes: they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart — which is exactly what chapter 31 will call the new covenant. The divided kingdoms come home together, the family reunited.

Isaiah saw the same gathering: all the nations shall flow to it, saying Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD (Isa 2:2-3). And the last pages of the Bible complete the thought about the ark. John sees the holy city and reports, I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev 21:22). The box that once marked God's throne is not missed, because God himself is present without one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me (v. 19), but Israel was treacherous as a wife who leaves (v. 20). Weeping is heard on the bare heights (v. 21), and God says, Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness (v. 22). The people answer that the hills were a delusion and salvation is in the LORD (vv. 23-24), and lie down in their shame: we have sinned against the LORD our God (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: God heals faithlessness rather than merely forgiving it, and the confession that follows is the evidence, not the condition.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me. Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"'I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me.

This is God speaking about his own hopes, and it is almost unbearable to read. How I would set you among my sons. He wanted to treat them as children, to give them the best land there was, to hear them call him Father.

Scripture is not embarrassed to show God like this. How can I give you up, O Ephraim?, he says through Hosea; My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender (Hos 11:8). Whatever else the judgment in this book is, it is not the cold act of a God who never wanted anything else.

Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.'"

And the sentence lands with the marriage image again. Not a tenant breaking a lease. A wife walking out. The offence is measured by the intimacy it violated, which is why sin against God is never merely rule-breaking.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice on the bare heights is heard, the weeping and pleading of Israel's sons because they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God. "Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness." "Behold, we come to you, for you are the LORD our God. Truly the hills are a delusion, the orgies on the mountains. Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A voice on the bare heights is heard, the weeping and pleading of Israel's sons because they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God.

The bare heights were the scene of the idolatry in verse 2. Now the same hills carry a different sound: weeping. The place of the sin becomes the place of the sorrow over it.

And the cause of the weeping is named in the right order: they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God. The crooked road is the symptom; the forgetting is the disease. Chapter 2 traced the whole apostasy to a question people stopped asking (2:6), and the grief here begins with remembering who they forgot.

"Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness."

Eight words that contain the gospel of this chapter. Notice what God promises to do. Not merely to forgive the faithlessness, but to heal it. He treats the disloyalty as a disease in his people rather than only a debt against himself, and he undertakes the cure.

That is the only reason anyone returns at all. If the invitation were simply "come back and do better", it would sink the very people it calls, who have already proved they cannot. The offer is that the God who is wronged will himself repair the capacity to love him.

"Behold, we come to you, for you are the LORD our God. Truly the hills are a delusion, the orgies on the mountains. Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.

And they answer. Behold, we come to you. The ESV notes that a delusion is in Hebrew "commotion": all that noise on the hilltops, all that energy, and nothing in it. Repentance always includes a revised opinion of what we left God for. They now see the shrines as they are.

And they relocate their hope: Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel. Not in the hills, not in the alliances, not in a better religious programme — in a person. It is the confession Jonah made from inside the fish, Salvation belongs to the LORD! (Jonah 2:9), and it is where every true return ends up.

verseByVerse.quote: "But from our youth the shameful thing has devoured all for which our fathers labored, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us. For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But from our youth the shameful thing has devoured all for which our fathers labored, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us. For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."

The confession is complete and it is costly. They add up what idolatry took: the livestock, the harvests, the children given to Molech — all for which our fathers labored. Sin is finally accounted for not as pleasure but as loss.

Let us lie down in our shame. Set that beside verse 3, where God said you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed. The capacity to blush has come back. In a returning people shame is not despair; it is the sign of a conscience coming back to life.

And they do not minimise: we have sinned, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day. No blaming the ancestors alone, no limiting it to a bad season. Compare chapter 2, where the same people said I am innocent (2:35). This is what the turn looks like, and it comes after the promise to heal, not before it. The kindness is what makes the confession possible.

3.title: Return, Faithless Israel: I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
3.overview:
The law says a wife who has left her husband for another cannot return, yet God asks his adulterous people, would you return to me? (v. 1). The hills show where they have been, the rains have been withheld, and they have lost the ability to blush (vv. 2-3). They still use affectionate words about God while doing all the evil they can (vv. 4-5).

In Josiah's days God contrasts two sisters: faithless Israel, whom he divorced and exiled, and treacherous Judah, who watched it happen, did the same, and returned only in pretence (vv. 6-10). So Israel is judged the more righteous of the two (v. 11), and the call goes north: Return, faithless Israel, on one condition — Only acknowledge your guilt (vv. 12-13).

God promises to gather a remnant one from a city and two from a family, to give shepherds after his own heart, to make the ark unnecessary, to make Jerusalem his throne with all nations gathered, and to reunite Israel and Judah (vv. 14-18). He speaks of how he longed to be called Father (vv. 19-20). Weeping is heard on the hills, God promises I will heal your faithlessness, and the people confess their sin from their youth until now (vv. 21-25).
3.theology:
The invitation to return goes beyond what the law allows (v. 1; Deut 24:1-4): grace opens a door justice had shut, at a cost only the cross explains. Religious language and partial reform are not repentance (vv. 4-5, 10).

Greater light brings greater accountability: Judah, who watched Israel's judgment, is more guilty than Israel (v. 11). The one condition of return is honest acknowledgement of guilt (v. 13; Joel 2:12-13; 1 John 1:9).

God gathers a remnant individually (v. 14), gives shepherds after his own heart (v. 15; Acts 13:22; Eph 4:11), and will make the ark unnecessary because the presence it signified has come (vv. 16-17), with the nations gathered and the stubborn heart changed — the new covenant of chapter 31. God promises to heal faithlessness, not merely pardon it (v. 22), and the confession of vv. 24-25 follows that promise rather than earning it.
3.examples:
A door the law bolted, opened by love.

A face that has lost the ability to blush.

Judah with a front-row seat at her sister's funeral, learning nothing.

Reform that is genuine at the top and never reaches the heart.

Revival arriving one from a city and two from a family.

A sacred box no longer missed, because the presence has come.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>"If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver,<sup>2</sup>and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory."<sup>3</sup>For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.<sup>4</sup>Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."<sup>5</sup>Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!'<sup>6</sup>Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction.<sup>7</sup>A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant.<sup>8</sup>For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."<sup>9</sup>"In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded."<sup>10</sup>Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life."<sup>11</sup>At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse,<sup>12</sup>a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them."<sup>13</sup>Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!<sup>14</sup>O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?<sup>15</sup>For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim.<sup>16</sup>Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah.<sup>17</sup>Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD.<sup>18</sup>Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war.<sup>20</sup>Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — If You Return, Return to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return, putting away detestable things and swearing truly, so that nations shall bless themselves in him (vv. 1-2). Then the command to Judah: Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns (v. 3), and Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, lest his wrath burn unquenched (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Real return is to a person, not to a programme, and it reaches the heart or it is not return at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver, and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver,

Chapter 3 ended with the people saying Behold, we come to you (3:22). Chapter 4 tests it. The sentence turns on a single phrase: to me you should return. Not to religion, not to the temple, not to better behaviour. To me.

It is possible to reform a life without returning to God, and the two look alike for a while. The conditions given are concrete: remove the idols, and do not waver — no half-return, no keeping the shrine in the garden in case.

and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory."

The oath formula As the LORD lives was the ordinary way to swear in Israel, and it was being said constantly by people serving other gods. God attaches three conditions: in truth, in justice, and in righteousness. His name on the lips of someone living a lie is not devotion; it is perjury. Integrity is what makes the confession honest.

And look where it leads. If Israel returns honestly, nations shall bless themselves in him. That is the promise made to Abraham surfacing in a sermon about repentance. A people genuinely right with God becomes the means of blessing to everyone else. The world has more at stake in the church's repentance than it knows.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.

Fallow ground is land that has been left unploughed so long it has hardened over. It is not barren; it is compacted. Seed thrown on it bounces. The command is not to sow harder but to break the ground first, and that is brutal work with an iron blade. Hosea said it too: Break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD (Hos 10:12).

Many people are trying to sow good seed on hard ground: more services, more resolutions, more reading, on a heart that has not been broken up in years. And sow not among thorns: clearing what chokes the seed is part of the work, as the parable of the sower says of cares and riches.

Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."

Circumcision was the covenant sign in the flesh, and every man in Judah had it. God says it has to happen somewhere else. The mark of belonging is worthless if the heart is untouched.

Now notice a difficulty the whole Bible answers. Here the people are commanded to circumcise their own hearts. In Deuteronomy God promises, the LORD your God will circumcise your heart (Deut 30:6), and in this book he will promise to write his law on it (31:33). Both are true: God commands what only he can give, and the command is how people come to ask him for it. Paul completes it: a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter (Rom 2:29), and it is done in Christ, a circumcision made without hands (Col 2:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The Alarm from the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The trumpet sounds and the people are told to flee to the fortified cities, for God brings disaster from the north and a destroyer of nations (vv. 5-8). Courage will fail king, officials, priests and prophets (v. 9), and Jeremiah protests that the people were told It shall be well with you (v. 10). A scorching wind comes, not to winnow or cleanse (vv. 11-13). Still the call stands: O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved (v. 14), while the besiegers close in and Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you (vv. 15-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is announced in detail, the false comfort is exposed, and in the middle of the siege the door is still open.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!' Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!' Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction.

The tone changes without warning. An air-raid siren goes off in the middle of a sermon. Blow the trumpet, raise the signal, run for the walled towns, do not stop to pack.

And the terrible clause in the middle of the panic: for I bring disaster from the north. The invasion is not an accident of history that God will use. He is bringing it.

This is the vision of Jeremiah's call arriving on schedule. As a young man he had been shown a boiling pot and told, Out of the north disaster shall be let loose upon all the inhabitants of the land (1:14). What was a picture then is a trumpet now. God's warnings are not decoration; they have dates attached.

verseByVerse.quote: A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant. For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant.

The enemy is described as a lion that has left its lair and is already on the road. Nebuchadnezzar is never named here; he is simply a destroyer of nations who has set out. The tense matters. This is not a threat about what might happen if things do not improve. It has started.

For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."

The right response to the news is not a strategy meeting but mourning. Sackcloth, lament, wailing. There is a kind of trouble that calls for grief before it calls for plans, and a church that has lost the ability to lament will meet such trouble with activity instead.

And notice the pronoun at the end: has not turned back from us. The prophet does not stand outside the verdict pointing. He counts himself among the people under it, and mourns as one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded." Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded."

The four groups again: king, officials, priests, prophets. Not one of them will have anything to say. The prophets, in particular, will be astounded — the men who had been predicting peace will be the most surprised people in the city.

Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life."

Jeremiah's protest is startling, and the Bible records it without softening it. He hears the message of the official prophets — It shall be well with you — and he lays the responsibility at God's door.

How should this be read? Not as Scripture teaching that God lies. God's own answer comes later in the book: he never sent those prophets, and they have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace (6:14). But there is a judicial reality here that the prophet feels: when people insist on comfortable preaching, God may let them have it, and the comfortable preaching becomes part of the judgment. The sermon you most want to hear may be the most dangerous one available.

Scripture shows that judicial reality elsewhere. When Ahab wanted only favourable prophets, Micaiah saw heaven's court decide it, and told the king, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets (1 Kgs 22:23). And Paul says of those who refuse the truth, God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false (2 Thess 2:11). God does not deceive the honest. He hands those who wanted to be deceived over to what they chose.

Notice too that Jeremiah says this to God, not about him behind his back. Honest protest addressed to God is a form of faith; the psalms are full of it.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse, a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them." Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse, a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them."

A farmer wants a light breeze to winnow grain, separating wheat from chaff. What is coming is the desert wind that strips the field bare: not to winnow or cleanse. This is not corrective discipline any more. It is judgment.

Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!

Dust on the horizon like a storm front, chariots like a whirlwind, horses faster than eagles — and then the voice of the people themselves, the first time they see it clearly: woe to us, for we are ruined!

Habakkuk describes the same army in the same terms — Their horses are swifter than leopards, and their horsemen fly like an eagle swift to devour (Hab 1:8). Two prophets watching one invasion from different vantage points, and neither sees any way to outrun it.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you? For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim. Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?

In the middle of the siege report, an invitation. The army is on the road and God is still saying that you may be saved. Mercy runs later into the story than anyone expects.

And the diagnosis is interior again: wash your heart, and the question, how long will wicked thoughts lodge within you? The word suggests a guest who has settled in. Sins that were once visitors become residents, and the difference is how long they were allowed to stay.

The call to wash echoes Isaiah's opening sermon — Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes (Isa 1:16) — and like every such command it drives the hearer to the one who can actually do it. Paul writes to converts who had been everything this chapter describes: But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Cor 6:11).

For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim. Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah.

Dan is the northern border; Ephraim is the hill country just above Jerusalem. The report is a relay of dispatches as the enemy moves south, and the distance is closing between sentences.

And Warn the nations that he is coming — the surrounding peoples are told too. What happens to Jerusalem is not a private family matter; the whole region is meant to learn from it what kind of God the God of Israel is.

verseByVerse.quote: Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD. Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. This is your doom, and it is bitter; it has reached your very heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD.

A quiet, awful image. Besieging armies ring the city the way watchmen sit around a field at harvest: patient, settled, waiting for what is inside to be ready.

Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. This is your doom, and it is bitter; it has reached your very heart."

The same verdict as 2:17, and it needs saying plainly, because people will do almost anything to avoid it. Not every disaster is deserved; Job exists to prevent that conclusion. But some are, and pretending otherwise makes repentance impossible. It has reached your very heart — the place the whole chapter has been pointing to.

Paul states the principle for the church without exception: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7). The bitterness in Judah's mouth was the taste of her own harvest.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly (v. 19). Crash follows hard on crash, and the prophet asks how long he must see the standard and hear the trumpet (vv. 20-21). God answers with the reason: my people are foolish; they know me not, clever at evil and ignorant of good (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who preaches the judgment is broken by it; God's word is never delivered from a safe distance.

verseByVerse.quote: My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war. Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are laid waste, my curtains in a moment. How long must I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?
verseByVerse.commentary:
My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war.

The voice changes, and this is why Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet. He is not reading a bulletin. He is doubled over. My anguish, my anguish! He can feel his own heartbeat; he cannot sit still or stay quiet.

Put this beside the message he has been given to preach. He announces the disaster, and the announcement tears him apart. There is no satisfaction in him at being proved right, no relish in the doom of people who have dismissed him for years.

That is the test of anyone who handles the severe parts of Scripture. Hell, judgment and wrath can be preached with a certain enjoyment, and when they are, something has gone badly wrong. The prophet who tells the truth about judgment should be the one most obviously wounded by it.

And that anguish points beyond Jeremiah. Six centuries later another man came down toward the same city under the same kind of sentence, and he wept over it, saying, Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! (Luke 19:41-42). The prophet's breaking heart was a preview of the heart of God made flesh.

Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are laid waste, my curtains in a moment. How long must I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?

The reports come in one after another, and he calls the ruined homes my tents, my curtains. These are not other people's losses to him. And then the cry every sufferer knows: How long?

verseByVerse.quote: "For my people are foolish; they know me not; they are stupid children; they have no understanding. They are 'wise'—in doing evil! But how to do good they know not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For my people are foolish; they know me not; they are stupid children; they have no understanding. They are 'wise'—in doing evil! But how to do good they know not."

God answers the How long with a diagnosis. The problem is not intelligence; it is that they know me not. And then the bitter irony: they are experts at evil and amateurs at good. Every culture has this shape — brilliant at what harms it, helpless at what would heal it.

Paul's hope for the Roman church is the precise reversal: I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil (Rom 16:19). Judah had it backwards — sophisticated in wrongdoing, naive about goodness — and the gospel does not simply make people cleverer. It turns their competence the right way round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — I Looked on the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four times he looks: the earth without form and void with no light (v. 23), mountains quaking (v. 24), no man and no birds (v. 25), the fruitful land a desert (v. 26). The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end (v. 27), for God has spoken and will not turn back (vv. 28-29). The city dresses in scarlet and paint, and her lovers seek her life (v. 30); the daughter of Zion cries like a woman in labour (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment is creation running backwards, and even there God sets a limit: not a full end.

verseByVerse.quote: I looked on the earth, and behold, it was without form and void; and to the heavens, and they had no light. I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking, and all the hills moved to and fro. I looked, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the air had fled. I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a desert, and all its cities were laid in ruins before the LORD, before his fierce anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I looked on the earth, and behold, it was without form and void; and to the heavens, and they had no light.

Four times Jeremiah says I looked, and what he sees is Genesis played backwards. The first phrase is quoted from the creation account: The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep (Gen 1:2). Then God said, let there be light. Here the light has gone out.

I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking, and all the hills moved to and fro.

Day three of creation gave dry land; here the land itself is unsteady. The earth staggers like a drunken man, says Isaiah of the same day (Isa 24:20).

I looked, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the air had fled.

Days five and six are undone: the birds gone, and humanity — the crown of the creation week — simply absent. There was no man.

I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a desert, and all its cities were laid in ruins before the LORD, before his fierce anger.

This passage is terrifying, and it makes a theological point that no amount of moralising could. Sin is not a private matter between a person and God with no wider consequence. It unmakes the world. Creation itself is dragged down by it, groaning, subjected to futility and waiting to be set free from its bondage to corruption (Rom 8:20-21).

Which is why salvation in the Bible is never merely the rescue of souls out of a doomed world. It is new heavens and a new earth, and the same God who spoke the first light will speak again.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, "The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end. "For this the earth shall mourn, and the heavens above be dark; for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD, "The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end.

Six words that keep this book from being despair: yet I will not make a full end. They will be repeated (5:10, 18). However far the judgment goes, God draws a line beyond which it will not go, and he draws it himself. A remnant will survive, and through it the promises will run on.

Jesus says the same of the worst days: if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short (Matt 24:22).

"For this the earth shall mourn, and the heavens above be dark; for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back."

Three verbs of settled intent: spoken, purposed, not relented. Elsewhere God does relent when people turn (18:7-8), which is exactly why this is so grave. The door in verse 14 is open, and the people are not walking through it.

verseByVerse.quote: At the noise of horseman and archer every city takes to flight; they enter thickets; they climb among rocks; all the cities are forsaken, and no man dwells in them. And you, O desolate one, what do you mean that you dress in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with ornaments of gold, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain you beautify yourself. Your lovers despise you; they seek your life. For I heard a cry as of a woman in labor, anguish as of one giving birth to her first child, the cry of the daughter of Zion gasping for breath, stretching out her hands, "Woe is me! I am fainting before murderers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the noise of horseman and archer every city takes to flight; they enter thickets; they climb among rocks; all the cities are forsaken, and no man dwells in them.

People in the bushes and up the crags, towns standing empty. The picture of refugees is ancient and current at once.

And you, O desolate one, what do you mean that you dress in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with ornaments of gold, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain you beautify yourself. Your lovers despise you; they seek your life.

And here is the saddest image of the chapter. With the army at the gates, the city is doing her make-up. Scarlet, gold, painted eyes — still trying to attract the very nations whose armies are coming. Your lovers despise you; they seek your life. The alliances she trusted have turned murderous, and she is still dressing for them.

People do this. Faced with ruin, we reach for the thing that ruined us, and go on presenting a face to a world that has no intention of saving us.

For I heard a cry as of a woman in labor, anguish as of one giving birth to her first child, the cry of the daughter of Zion gasping for breath, stretching out her hands, "Woe is me! I am fainting before murderers."

The chapter ends with the cry of a woman in her first labour: pain that cannot be postponed, and hands stretched out for help. In Scripture that image is not always the end — labour pains lead somewhere, and Paul uses the same picture for a creation in the pains of childbirth (Rom 8:22). But nothing of that comfort is offered here. The chapter closes on the cry, and leaves the reader inside it.

4.title: Break Up Your Fallow Ground
4.overview:
If Israel returns, it must be to God himself, putting away idols and swearing truly, so that the nations are blessed (vv. 1-2). Judah is told to break up hard ground rather than sow among thorns, and to circumcise their hearts (vv. 3-4).

Then the alarm: the trumpet, the flight to fortified cities, a lion and destroyer of nations coming from the north, and mourning (vv. 5-8). Courage will fail every leader, and Jeremiah protests at the message of peace the people were given (vv. 9-10). A scorching wind comes, not to winnow but to judge (vv. 11-13). Still God calls Jerusalem to wash her heart that she may be saved, even as the besiegers ring the city and her own deeds close in on her (vv. 14-18).

The prophet breaks down at what he must announce (vv. 19-21), and God names the cause: a people clever at evil who do not know him (v. 22). In four visions the creation is undone — formless earth, dark heavens, quaking mountains, no people, no birds, a desert where the fruitful land was (vv. 23-26). Yet God will not make a full end (v. 27). While the land empties, the city paints her face for lovers who seek her life, and the chapter closes on a cry like a woman in labour (vv. 28-31).
4.theology:
Repentance is return to God himself, not reform of behaviour (v. 1), and it must reach the heart: the command to circumcise the heart (v. 4) is what God elsewhere promises to do (Deut 30:6; 31:33) and does in Christ (Rom 2:29; Col 2:11).

God governs the invading army: he brings the disaster (v. 6). Comfortable preaching can itself be part of judgment (v. 10; 6:14). Mercy is still offered while judgment is arriving (v. 14), and honest protest may be addressed to God (v. 10).

Sin unmakes the world: judgment is creation running backwards (vv. 23-26; Gen 1:2; Rom 8:20-22), so salvation must include a renewed creation. And God limits his own judgment — yet I will not make a full end (v. 27; Matt 24:22).
4.examples:
Ground so hard that good seed simply bounces.

A covenant sign in the body and nothing in the heart.

The sermon you most want to hear being the most dangerous one available.

Wicked thoughts that arrive as visitors and become residents.

Besiegers sitting round a city like watchmen round a field.

A city doing her make-up while the army stands at the gate.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, look and take note! Search her squares to see if you can find a man, one who does justice and seeks truth, that I may pardon her.<sup>2</sup>Though they say, "As the LORD lives," yet they swear falsely.<sup>3</sup>O LORD, do not your eyes look for truth? You have struck them down, but they felt no anguish; you have consumed them, but they refused to take correction. They have made their faces harder than rock; they have refused to repent.<sup>4</sup>Then I said, "These are only the poor; they have no sense; for they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God.<sup>5</sup>I will go to the great and will speak to them, for they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God." But they all alike had broken the yoke; they had burst the bonds.<sup>6</sup>Therefore a lion from the forest shall strike them down; a wolf from the desert shall devastate them. A leopard is watching their cities; everyone who goes out of them shall be torn in pieces, because their transgressions are many, their apostasies are great.<sup>7</sup>"How can I pardon you? Your children have forsaken me and have sworn by those who are no gods. Thus shall it be done to them!'"<sup>14</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts: "Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them.<sup>15</sup>Behold, I am bringing against you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.
