verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah writes from Jerusalem to the deportees of 597 BC, sending the letter in a royal diplomatic pouch by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah (v. 3). God addresses them as all the exiles whom I have sent into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon (v. 4) — his act, not merely Nebuchadnezzar's. Then the orders: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce (v. 5), marry, raise families, multiply there, and do not decrease (v. 6). And the hardest line of all: But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Settle down in the place of judgment, and pray for the good of the city that burned yours.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the surviving elders of the exiles, and to the priests, the prophets, and all the people, whom Nebuchadnezzar had taken into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon. This was after King Jeconiah and the queen mother, the eunuchs, the officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the metal workers had departed from Jerusalem. The letter was sent by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. It said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the surviving elders of the exiles, and to the priests, the prophets, and all the people, whom Nebuchadnezzar had taken into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.

A letter. Not a sermon in a courtyard or a sign acted out in the street, but a document written to be carried a thousand kilometres and read aloud to people the prophet would never see again.

One word in the address carries a weight of grief: the surviving elders. Some who set out did not arrive. The community receiving this had already buried people on the road, and they are being written to as survivors.

This was after King Jeconiah and the queen mother, the eunuchs, the officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the metal workers had departed from Jerusalem.

These are the deportees of 597 BC — the good figs of chapter 24. The skilled and the well-connected, the people whose absence gutted the city, now sitting in settlements along the irrigation canals of Babylonia trying to work out what God was doing.

The letter was sent by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. It said:

Look at the postal arrangements, because God keeps using them. Zedekiah is sending an official delegation to his overlord, and Jeremiah's letter travels in the state pouch. One of the couriers is a son of Shaphan — the same family whose member Ahikam had saved Jeremiah's life (26:24). A royal errand and a faithful family together carry the word of God into exile, and none of the officials involved had any idea they were doing it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have sent into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters; take wives for your sons, and give your daughters in marriage, that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply there, and do not decrease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have sent into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon:

Before a single instruction, a correction of who did this. Nebuchadnezzar's army marched them out; God says whom I have sent into exile. The pagan empire was the instrument, and the hand on it was his.

That one clause changes what exile is. If Babylon is an accident of geopolitics, then the exiles are simply unlucky and their only sane response is to wait for better luck. If God sent them, then Babylon is an assignment, and there is something to do there.

Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters; take wives for your sons, and give your daughters in marriage, that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply there, and do not decrease.

These are the most ordinary commands imaginable, and in that setting they are radical. Build — not a tent, a house. Plant a garden, which means staying long enough to eat the fruit. Marry, and marry off your children, which means accepting that your grandchildren will be born in Babylon.

Every one of those instructions kills a hope the exiles were nursing, namely that this would be over soon. And every one of them refuses the alternative despair, the refusal to live because life is not what you wanted. God does not tell them to like Babylon. He tells them to live — to put down roots in the soil of a providence they did not choose.

The echo of Eden and of the ark is unmistakable: multiply there, and do not decrease. The covenant purpose is not suspended for the duration. It continues in captivity.

verseByVerse.quote: But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare.

And now the command that nobody could have predicted.

Babylon burned the temple, killed their relatives and marched them across a desert in chains. Psalm 137 is the honest sound of a heart in that city. And into that, God says: work for its good, and pray for it.

Welfare means the whole flourishing of a place, its peace and safety and prosperity together. Seek Babylon's welfare. Not merely tolerate it, not merely avoid trouble in it: seek its good actively, and take its needs to God in prayer.

This is the Old Testament seed of a hard command the Lord gives his people, that they love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them. It is asked here not of a victorious nation being magnanimous but of prisoners of war, about their captors' capital.

Notice too the promise attached: in its welfare you will find your welfare. God ties their good to the good of the pagan city. There is no separate, sealed-off prosperity for the people of God while the place around them rots.

Peter writes to Christians in exactly this key — elect exiles of the Dispersion (1 Pet 1:1), sojourners and exiles who are to Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable (1 Pet 2:11-12). The church is not to sulk in the culture or dissolve into it. Our citizenship is in heaven (Phil 3:20), and for that very reason we seek the welfare of the city we are passing through.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Seventy Years, and the Plans I Have for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The exiles have their own prophets promising a quick return, and God disowns them: it is a lie that they are prophesying to you in my name; I did not send them (v. 9). The truth is longer and better. When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise and bring you back to this place (v. 10), because I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope (v. 11). And the restoration runs through prayer: Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: A promise most of its first readers would die before seeing, and it was still the best news in Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Do not let your prophets and your diviners who are among you deceive you, and do not listen to the dreams that they dream, for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you in my name; I did not send them, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Do not let your prophets and your diviners who are among you deceive you, and do not listen to the dreams that they dream,

The false prophets were not left behind in Jerusalem. They were deported too, and they set up shop in the camps with the same product: it will be over soon.

The ESV's note here sharpens the accusation. The Hebrew behind the dreams that they dream reads "your dreams, which you cause to dream" — it is the people who cause the prophets to dream what they want to hear. The congregation supplies the longing; the preacher manufactures the vision to match. That is how the trade has always worked.

for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you in my name; I did not send them, declares the LORD.

The same verdict as chapter 27 and chapter 28, now posted to Babylon: I did not send them. Distance changed nothing. Wherever God's people are scattered, someone will be telling them what they want to hear in God's name, and the test does not change either.

And the cruelty of the comfortable lie shows up clearly here. If you believe the exile is nearly over, you will not build a house, plant a garden or raise a family. You will sit on your luggage for seventy years and waste your one life waiting for a boat that is not coming.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise and bring you back to this place. For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus says the LORD: When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise and bring you back to this place.

Here is the number, and it is brutal and kind at once. Seventy years is longer than most of the letter's readers had left. The old men weeping by the canals would die in Babylon; their grandchildren would make the journey home. God does not soften that.

But he fixes it. A sentence with an end is a different thing from a sentence without one, and the God who set the term will keep it — I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise. Decades later Daniel would sit with this very page open, having perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem, namely, seventy years (Dan 9:2), and begin to pray. And the chronicler records the outcome in the driest possible terms: it happened, to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah (2 Chr 36:21).

For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.

This verse turns up on mugs and graduation cards, and the setting is a prison camp. It is not a promise that your career will prosper or that the hard thing will be brief. It was given to people whose city was rubble, whose temple would burn within a decade, and who were being told to unpack.

Which makes it stronger, not weaker. The same English word, welfare, has come back from verse 7, and here the ESV notes it may be read as "peace": God's settled intention toward this people is their whole flourishing, and he is pursuing it through seventy years of Babylon rather than in spite of them. A future and a hope is not the absence of exile. It is God's guarantee that exile is not the end of the story he is telling.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart. I will be found by you, declares the LORD, and I will restore your fortunes and gather you from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you, declares the LORD, and I will bring you back to the place from which I sent you into exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart.

Notice where the restoration runs. Not through a rebellion, a lobbying campaign or a change in Babylonian politics, but through prayer — a people on their knees in a foreign country, calling on a God whose temple was in ruins.

And notice the order in the sentence. God announces what they will do before they do it. The seeking is promised, not demanded, which is the same grace as the heart he pledged to give them in the vision of the figs (24:7): God supplies the very response he requires.

The words come from Moses, spoken over the exile centuries before it happened: you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul (Deut 4:29). And they are taken onto the Lord's own lips in the plainest invitation he ever gave: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find (Matt 7:7).

I will be found by you, declares the LORD, and I will restore your fortunes and gather you from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you, declares the LORD, and I will bring you back to the place from which I sent you into exile.

The half-hearted search is the one that fails, and that is not a technicality about intensity. A man who wants God as one item among several has not yet wanted God. But hear what is actually promised to the whole-hearted: I will be found by you. God is not hiding. The exile was never a matter of his becoming unreachable, and the gathering will reach every place they were scattered to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — The Vile Figs Left Behind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The exiles are tempted to envy the people still at home, so God tells them what is coming to the king who sits on the throne of David and the kinsmen who did not go out with you into exile (v. 16). Sword, famine and pestilence are on their way, and the image is the one from the two baskets: I will make them like vile figs that are so rotten they cannot be eaten (v. 17). They will become a curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach among the nations (v. 18) — and the reason is given plainly: because they did not pay attention to my words, sent persistently by the prophets, but you would not listen (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who kept the address kept nothing; the ones in chains were the good figs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because you have said, 'The LORD has raised up prophets for us in Babylon,' thus says the LORD concerning the king who sits on the throne of David, and concerning all the people who dwell in this city, your kinsmen who did not go out with you into exile: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, behold, I am sending on them sword, famine, and pestilence, and I will make them like vile figs that are so rotten they cannot be eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Because you have said, 'The LORD has raised up prophets for us in Babylon,' thus says the LORD concerning the king who sits on the throne of David, and concerning all the people who dwell in this city, your kinsmen who did not go out with you into exile:

The exiles had a comparison running in their heads, and it was eating them. Our relatives are still at home. They have the city, the temple, a son of David on the throne, and prophets telling us we will soon join them.

So God answers the comparison directly, and the phrase your kinsmen who did not go out with you into exile names the envy precisely.

'Thus says the LORD of hosts, behold, I am sending on them sword, famine, and pestilence, and I will make them like vile figs that are so rotten they cannot be eaten.

And there is the image from the two baskets, sent to the people who were the good figs in that vision. They had been told it face to face in Jerusalem — Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten (24:8) — and now it is written to Babylon so the exiles can stop envying the wrong people.

The comfort in it is real, if uncomfortable. The ones who look blessed are not; the ones who lost everything are the objects of God's good intentions. That is a hard message to receive without bitterness, and the letter has already told them how: build, plant, pray for Babylon. Envy dies in a garden you are actually tending.

verseByVerse.quote: I will pursue them with sword, famine, and pestilence, and will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach among all the nations where I have driven them, because they did not pay attention to my words, declares the LORD, that I persistently sent to you by my servants the prophets, but you would not listen, declares the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will pursue them with sword, famine, and pestilence, and will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach among all the nations where I have driven them,

The verb is pursue. This is not a disaster they may outrun by staying put, which was the whole basis of their confidence. Judgment follows them into every country it drives them to.

Four words for what they become — a curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach — and the tragedy sits in the fact that this is the nation appointed to make God's name known among those same nations. The witness continues; only its content has inverted.

because they did not pay attention to my words, declares the LORD, that I persistently sent to you by my servants the prophets, but you would not listen, declares the LORD.'

The reason is given, and it is not obscure. God is not capricious here and there is no hidden decree to puzzle over: they did not pay attention to my words.

Weigh the adverb — persistently. Decades of prophets, sent again and again to a city that had every chance to listen and used none of them. Judgment in this book always arrives late, after a long patience that has been ignored, and that is why it can be announced without apology.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two named men are prophesying lies in Babylon, and their end will be public: God will hand Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah to Nebuchadnezzar, and he shall strike them down before your eyes (v. 21). Their names will pass into the exiles' own proverb: The LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire (v. 22). The charge joins two things people keep apart — they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, and they have spoken in my name lying words that I did not command them — and God closes it himself: I am the one who knows, and I am witness (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: The private life and the pulpit were never two separate files.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, all you exiles whom I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who are prophesying a lie to you in my name: Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall strike them down before your eyes. Because of them this curse shall be used by all the exiles from Judah in Babylon: "The LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire," because they have done an outrageous thing in Israel, they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, and they have spoken in my name lying words that I did not command them. I am the one who knows, and I am witness, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear the word of the LORD, all you exiles whom I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who are prophesying a lie to you in my name: Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall strike them down before your eyes.

Two men, named. The letter does not deal in generalities about false teaching; it identifies the individuals doing it, because the exiles had to know whose meetings to stop attending.

Their end is Nebuchadnezzar's doing — he will execute them, probably for the sedition their homeland-restoration preaching amounted to — and God claims it as his own sentence carried out by a pagan king who thought he was protecting his empire.

Because of them this curse shall be used by all the exiles from Judah in Babylon: "The LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire,"

Their names end up as a proverb for a horrible death. Men who had built careers on telling people what they wanted became the byword the same people used when they cursed.

because they have done an outrageous thing in Israel, they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, and they have spoken in my name lying words that I did not command them. I am the one who knows, and I am witness, declares the LORD.'

Two charges in one sentence, and Scripture will not separate them. Adultery with the neighbours' wives, and lying in God's name. The man who is willing to invent a message is the same man who is willing to betray a bed; a life that treats God's word as material to be shaped will treat other people the same way.

And then the quietest and most searching line in the chapter: I am the one who knows, and I am witness. They had done it where no one saw. Someone saw.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man among the exiles, Shemaiah of Nehelam, writes his own letters to Jerusalem, to the priest Zephaniah, whose job includes charge over every madman who prophesies, to put him in the stocks and neck irons (v. 26). His complaint is a question: Now why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth who is prophesying to you? (v. 27), quoting the offending line back — Your exile will be long; build houses and live in them (v. 28). Zephaniah's response is simply to read the letter aloud to Jeremiah (v. 29). The sentence on Shemaiah follows: he prophesied when I did not send him, and has made you trust in a lie (v. 31), and he shall not see the good that I will do to my people (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: He campaigned against the promise of restoration, and was excluded from it.

verseByVerse.quote: To Shemaiah of Nehelam you shall say: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have sent letters in your name to all the people who are in Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying, 'The LORD has made you priest instead of Jehoiada the priest, to have charge in the house of the LORD over every madman who prophesies, to put him in the stocks and neck irons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To Shemaiah of Nehelam you shall say: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have sent letters in your name to all the people who are in Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying,

Jeremiah's letter provoked a reply, and the reply went over his head. Shemaiah writes to Jerusalem — to the temple authorities, not to Jeremiah — to get him silenced.

The phrase in your name is the indictment in miniature. Jeremiah writes in the name of the LORD of hosts; Shemaiah writes in his own, and still expects the weight of God behind it.

'The LORD has made you priest instead of Jehoiada the priest, to have charge in the house of the LORD over every madman who prophesies, to put him in the stocks and neck irons.

He begins by reminding the priest of his job description, which includes policing anyone who prophesies — and he supplies the category in advance: every madman who prophesies. Call the man unbalanced and you need not answer him. It saves the trouble of weighing whether what he said was true.

The instruments named are specific — the stocks and neck irons — and Jeremiah had been in the stocks before, at the hands of Pashhur (20:2). Shemaiah knows exactly what he is asking for, and he is asking from a safe distance, in a letter, with his own name on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth who is prophesying to you? For he has sent to us in Babylon, saying, "Your exile will be long; build houses and live in them, and plant gardens and eat their produce."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth who is prophesying to you?

The question is designed to shame the priest into acting. Why have you not dealt with him? It is the standard move of a man who wants someone silenced and would rather another hand did it.

And the address is a sneer: Jeremiah of Anathoth. Not the prophet, not the man God sent — a villager from a small place, whose own townsmen had once plotted to kill him (11:21). Reduce a man to his postcode and you need not reckon with his message.

For he has sent to us in Babylon, saying, "Your exile will be long; build houses and live in them, and plant gardens and eat their produce."'"

Here is the charge sheet, and notice what finally provoked the campaign. Not a threat, not a curse. Shemaiah quotes back, accurately, the gentlest sentences in the letter: build houses, plant gardens.

That was the intolerable part. The instruction to live implied the timetable, and the timetable destroyed the hope he was selling. Men will forgive a preacher a great deal sooner than they will forgive him for taking away a comfortable expectation, and the offence here is not harshness but realism about how long the trouble will last.

verseByVerse.quote: Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet. Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Send to all the exiles, saying, 'Thus says the LORD concerning Shemaiah of Nehelam: Because Shemaiah had prophesied to you when I did not send him, and has made you trust in a lie, therefore thus says the LORD: Behold, I will punish Shemaiah of Nehelam and his descendants. He shall not have anyone living among this people, and he shall not see the good that I will do to my people, declares the LORD, for he has spoken rebellion against the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet.

One sentence, and a whole quiet mercy inside it. The priest who was being urged to put Jeremiah in irons instead took the letter to him and read it to him.

Nothing is said about Zephaniah's motives and he is given no speech. But this is how God has been protecting this prophet all along — Ahikam's hand at the trial, the officials who convened a proper court, and now a temple official who declines to act on a poisonous letter and quietly shows it to the man it targets.

Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Send to all the exiles, saying, 'Thus says the LORD concerning Shemaiah of Nehelam: Because Shemaiah had prophesied to you when I did not send him, and has made you trust in a lie,

The same two charges as Hananiah's, in the same words: not sent, and has made you trust in a lie (28:15). The offence is never merely that the man was wrong. It is that people rested their weight on what he said.

therefore thus says the LORD: Behold, I will punish Shemaiah of Nehelam and his descendants. He shall not have anyone living among this people, and he shall not see the good that I will do to my people, declares the LORD, for he has spoken rebellion against the LORD.'"

The sentence fits the crime with terrible precision. Shemaiah campaigned against the letter that promised a future and a hope, and the penalty is that he shall not see the good that I will do to my people. He argued the restoration away, and he is left outside it.

Yet look at what that sentence assumes, and let it be the last word of the chapter. There is good that I will do to my people. The letter that began by telling prisoners to unpack ends by taking that good for granted as the settled future of this battered congregation. God had sent them into exile and God would visit them there — and the visiting was not finished at Cyrus's decree. Peter tells scattered Christians to live so that their neighbours may glorify God on the day of visitation (1 Pet 2:12), because the Lord himself came into the far country to seek the welfare of the city that killed him, and prayed for it while it did. Every exile who builds, plants and prays for the place God has put him is living on the strength of that day.

29.title: The Letter to the Exiles
29.overview:
Jeremiah writes from Jerusalem to the deportees of 597 BC, sending the letter in the royal diplomatic pouch. God addresses them as the exiles he himself sent, and gives them ordinary orders that overturn all their expectations: build houses, plant gardens, marry and multiply, and seek the welfare of Babylon, praying to the LORD on its behalf (vv. 1-7).

They are not to listen to the prophets among them promising a quick return, for God did not send them. The truth is seventy years — and then God will visit his people and fulfil his promise, because his plans for them are for welfare and not evil, to give them a future and a hope. The restoration comes through prayer and whole-hearted seeking, and God pledges to be found (vv. 8-14).

Against their envy of the relatives left at home, God announces sword, famine and pestilence on the king and the city, making them like the vile figs of the two baskets, because they would not listen to the prophets he persistently sent (vv. 15-19).

Two named liars in Babylon, Ahab and Zedekiah, will be executed before the exiles' eyes and become a byword, charged with adultery and with speaking lies in God's name (vv. 20-23). Finally Shemaiah of Nehelam writes to Jerusalem demanding Jeremiah be put in the stocks; the priest Zephaniah reads the letter to Jeremiah instead, and Shemaiah is sentenced never to see the good God will do for his people (vv. 24-32).
29.theology:
Exile is an assignment, not an accident. God says he sent them, and that single clause turns captivity from bad luck into a place with work to do in it (vv. 4, 7).

The people of God are to seek the welfare of the city that holds them, praying for its good and tying their own welfare to it — the seed of loving enemies, and the pattern for the church as elect exiles (v. 7; 1 Pet 1:1; 2:11-12; Phil 3:20).

False comfort costs the hearer his life, not just his theology: believing the exile is nearly over means never building the house or planting the garden God commanded (vv. 8-9).

God's good purpose is not the absence of hardship but his settled intention through it. The plans for welfare were given to a prison camp with seventy years to run (vv. 10-11), and he kept the date to the letter (Dan 9:2; 2 Chr 36:21).

Grace precedes the search: God announces that they will call, pray and seek him with all their heart, as he promised to give the heart itself (vv. 12-13; 24:7; Deut 4:29; Matt 7:7).

Preaching and private life are one file. The men who invented messages were the men committing adultery, and God was the witness to both (v. 23).
29.examples:
A letter carried to Babylon in a king's diplomatic bag.

Planting a garden you will have to stay long enough to harvest.

Praying for the good of the city that burned yours.

Dreams the congregation supplies and the preacher manufactures.

A promise on a mug, first posted to a prison camp.

Daniel decades later, reading this page and starting to pray.

Envying relatives who kept the house and the throne.

Calling a man a madman so you need not answer him.

A priest who read the hostile letter aloud to its target.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Book, and a Day Like No Other
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Jeremiah to Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you (v. 2), because what follows is for people not yet born: days are coming when God will restore the fortunes of my people, Israel and Judah (v. 3). Then the tone drops into terror — a cry of panic, of terror, and no peace (v. 5), grown men doubled over like a woman in labor, every face pale (v. 6). And the verdict on that day holds both things at once: Alas! That day is so great there is none like it; it is a time of distress for Jacob; yet he shall be saved out of it (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The worst day in the story, and the promise of rescue is welded to it in the same sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you. For behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will restore the fortunes of my people, Israel and Judah, says the LORD, and I will bring them back to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall take possession of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you.

Forty years of preaching in the open air, and now: write it down.

The instruction marks a change of audience. Spoken words reach the people in front of you; a book reaches the ones who are not born yet. What follows in chapters 30 to 33 is largely promise, and promise needs to outlive the preacher — the generation that would need these pages most was the generation that would read them in Babylon, decades after Jeremiah was dead.

It is also how we have them. The reason a man in a besieged city could speak to the exiles, and to us, is that God told him to write it in a book.

For behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will restore the fortunes of my people, Israel and Judah, says the LORD, and I will bring them back to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall take possession of it."

Note who is included: Israel and Judah. Israel, the northern kingdom, had been gone for a century — deported by Assyria, its people scattered and assumed lost. Judah is about to follow. God names both halves of a broken nation and says he will restore the fortunes of both.

Hold that against every calculation of what is too far gone. The tribes nobody could find were still on God's list, and the promise is specific: they will come back, and they shall take possession of it — not visit, but hold.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words that the LORD spoke concerning Israel and Judah: "Thus says the LORD: We have heard a cry of panic, of terror, and no peace. Ask now, and see, can a man bear a child? Why then do I see every man with his hands on his stomach like a woman in labor? Why has every face turned pale?
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the words that the LORD spoke concerning Israel and Judah: "Thus says the LORD: We have heard a cry of panic, of terror, and no peace.

The Book of Consolation opens with screaming.

That is not a mistake in the arrangement. Before any comfort is offered, the trouble is described honestly, and the phrase no peace lands on the exact word the false prophets had been handing out for chapters. They said peace; God reports a cry of panic and terror. Real comfort never begins by understating the situation.

Ask now, and see, can a man bear a child? Why then do I see every man with his hands on his stomach like a woman in labor? Why has every face turned pale?

The image is deliberately grotesque, and it is the strongest picture of helplessness available. Soldiers — the men who were supposed to defend the city — are doubled over, hands clutching their bellies, in the posture of a woman in labour. Something is happening to them that they can neither stop nor escape, and they have no more control over it than a man could have over giving birth.

And labour is not an image of pointless agony. It is pain with an outcome, terrible and productive at once, which is precisely what this day will turn out to be for Jacob.

verseByVerse.quote: Alas! That day is so great there is none like it; it is a time of distress for Jacob; yet he shall be saved out of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alas! That day is so great there is none like it; it is a time of distress for Jacob; yet he shall be saved out of it.

One verse, and the whole book is in it.

Take the halves in order. That day is so great there is none like it — unequalled, off the scale of anything in the nation's memory, and the prophets use that language for the day of the LORD itself: A day of wrath is that day, a day of distress and anguish, a day of ruin and devastation (Zeph 1:15). The Lord borrows the same construction for the end — then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now (Matt 24:21) — so this verse looks at Babylon and past it.

Then it is a time of distress for Jacob. The name matters. Not Israel the prince, but Jacob the schemer, the man who limped away from a night of wrestling with God. The distress is his, and it is deserved.

And then the hinge of the chapter, one word: yet. Yet he shall be saved out of it. Not spared it, not diverted around it — saved out of the middle of it. God does not promise his people an easier day than the one that is coming. He promises that the day will not have the last word on them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — Fear Not, Jacob My Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In that day God will break his yoke from off your neck and burst the bonds (v. 8), and the people freed from foreign masters shall serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them (v. 9). So the word to a terrified people is fear not, O Jacob my servant (v. 10): God will save from far away, and Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. The reason is a presence, not a circumstance — For I am with you to save you (v. 11) — and the discipline has a limit: of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure.
verseByVerse.theology: The yoke this book has spent chapters fastening on is broken by the same hand that fastened it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass in that day, declares the LORD of hosts, that I will break his yoke from off your neck, and I will burst your bonds, and foreigners shall no more make a servant of him. But they shall serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And it shall come to pass in that day, declares the LORD of hosts, that I will break his yoke from off your neck, and I will burst your bonds, and foreigners shall no more make a servant of him.

The yoke again — the wood Jeremiah wore through the streets, the iron God said would replace it when Hananiah snapped the bars. Now the hand that put it on takes it off. Hananiah broke a yoke and died for it; God breaks this one, and the ESV notes that the closing clause may also be read "Or serve him", so that the sense is that foreigners will no longer make Israel serve them.

That order is the whole difference between rebellion and redemption. The same yoke, removed by the wrong hand at the wrong time, is a lie; removed by God in his day, it is salvation.

But they shall serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them.

Freedom here is not the absence of service but its transfer. They stop serving foreigners and start serving God — and a king.

David had been dead four hundred years. The promise is of a David God will raise up, and the other prophets say it in the same terms: I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David (Ezek 34:23); the people will seek the LORD their God, and David their king in the latter days (Hos 3:5). Zechariah sang when it finally happened, that God has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, nor be dismayed, O Israel; for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. For I am with you to save you, declares the LORD; I will make a full end of all the nations among whom I scattered you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, nor be dismayed, O Israel; for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid.

After the labour pains and the pale faces, two words: fear not.

And notice the title attached — Jacob my servant. This is the nation whose guilt was called great and whose sins were called flagrant a few verses later, addressed by God as his servant. The relationship is not suspended while the discipline runs.

The promise is domestic and small-scale, which is what frightened people actually need: quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. Not empire, not revenge. Sleep without fear.

For I am with you to save you, declares the LORD; I will make a full end of all the nations among whom I scattered you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished.

The ground of the comfort is a person: I am with you to save you. Not better circumstances, not a shorter exile — his presence.

Then a distinction the whole Bible runs on. The nations get a full end; his people do not. The difference is not that Judah sinned less, because the next verses say her guilt is great. The difference is covenant.

And the last clause refuses to make that soft: I will by no means leave you unpunished. God's people are not exempt from discipline; they are exempt from destruction. In just measure means the chastening is measured by a father, not unleashed by an enemy — which is exactly the difference between the two, and the reason sin in a believer's life is dealt with rather than overlooked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — No Healing for You, and I Will Heal You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The diagnosis is hopeless and God gives it himself: Your hurt is incurable, and your wound is grievous (v. 12), with no medicine for your wound, no healing for you (v. 13). The allies have gone, and the blow was God's own — I have dealt you the blow of an enemy — because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant (v. 14). Then, with nothing changed in the patient, the sentence turns: those who devoured her will be devoured, and For I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal, declares the LORD, and the reason given is the taunt of her enemies — It is Zion, for whom no one cares! (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: God pronounces the case terminal, and then heals it, for no reason found in the patient.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Your hurt is incurable, and your wound is grievous. There is none to uphold your cause, no medicine for your wound, no healing for you. All your lovers have forgotten you; they care nothing for you; for I have dealt you the blow of an enemy, the punishment of a merciless foe, because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus says the LORD: Your hurt is incurable, and your wound is grievous. There is none to uphold your cause, no medicine for your wound, no healing for you.

God gives the diagnosis, and it is terminal.

Read the list of what is unavailable: no advocate, no medicine, no healing. Earlier in the book Jeremiah had asked the question — Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? (8:22) — and here is the answer, spoken by God himself. Nothing in the pharmacy touches this.

This is the honesty that makes the gospel possible. Until a man believes his condition is beyond treatment, every offer of grace sounds like an optional extra. Judah's problem was never that she lacked good advice.

All your lovers have forgotten you; they care nothing for you; for I have dealt you the blow of an enemy, the punishment of a merciless foe, because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant.

The lovers are the allies she courted instead of trusting God — Egypt, Assyria, the whole diplomatic romance of chapter 2. They have moved on, as such lovers do.

And then the hardest sentence: I have dealt you the blow of an enemy. Not Babylon's blow. God's, and delivered with the force of a merciless foe. He does not hide behind secondary causes or blame the geopolitics. The reason is stated twice, without embarrassment — because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant — and a God who names the cause is a God who can be reasoned with about a cure.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you cry out over your hurt? Your pain is incurable. Because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant, I have done these things to you. Therefore all who devour you shall be devoured, and all your foes, every one of them, shall go into captivity; those who plunder you shall be plundered, and all who prey on you I will make a prey. For I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal, declares the LORD, because they have called you an outcast: 'It is Zion, for whom no one cares!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you cry out over your hurt? Your pain is incurable. Because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant, I have done these things to you.

The question has an edge to it. Why cry out, as though this were unjust or unforeseen? She had been told, persistently, for forty years.

Therefore all who devour you shall be devoured, and all your foes, every one of them, shall go into captivity; those who plunder you shall be plundered, and all who prey on you I will make a prey.

And then therefore, which is the last word anyone would expect after that accusation. Follow the logic and it does not work morally: your guilt is great, your sins are flagrant, therefore your enemies will be destroyed. Nothing in the patient has changed between verse 15 and verse 16.

The instruments God used are themselves judged. Babylon was employed, and being employed by God is no acquittal — a lesson the empire would learn when its own seventy years ran out.

For I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal, declares the LORD, because they have called you an outcast: 'It is Zion, for whom no one cares!'

The incurable is cured, by the only physician who was ever going to do it. And look at the stated reason: not her repentance, not her improvement, but the contempt of her enemies. They said nobody cares about Zion. God will not leave that sentence standing about his own people.

How he heals a wound he inflicted, without pretending the guilt away, is the question this chapter raises and does not answer. The answer comes from the wounds of another: he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isa 53:5). The blow of an enemy fell, in the end, on him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — The Prince Who Dares Draw Near
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rebuilding is domestic and detailed: tents restored, compassion on his dwellings, the city shall be rebuilt on its mound (v. 18), and out of it songs of thanksgiving, and the voices of those who celebrate (v. 19). Then a ruler: Their prince shall be one of themselves; their ruler shall come out from their midst; I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me — followed by the question that exposes the whole problem, for who would dare of himself to approach me? (v. 21). And the covenant formula closes it: And you shall be my people, and I will be your God (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: One of their own, brought near by God to do what no one would dare attempt on his own account.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD: Behold, I will restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob and have compassion on his dwellings; the city shall be rebuilt on its mound, and the palace shall stand where it used to be. Out of them shall come songs of thanksgiving, and the voices of those who celebrate. I will multiply them, and they shall not be few; I will make them honored, and they shall not be small.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD: Behold, I will restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob and have compassion on his dwellings; the city shall be rebuilt on its mound, and the palace shall stand where it used to be.

The promise gets specific and unglamorous: tents, dwellings, a city rebuilt on its mound — on the same rubble heap, on the old site. Not a better location. This one, restored.

And the word governing it is compassion. The God who dealt the blow of an enemy has compassion on the houses of the people he struck, which is a combination no other religion knows what to do with.

Out of them shall come songs of thanksgiving, and the voices of those who celebrate. I will multiply them, and they shall not be few; I will make them honored, and they shall not be small.

Out of the tents, singing. The last several chapters have been full of the sound of mourning, lament and the cry of panic; now the noise coming from the ruins is thanksgiving and celebration.

Both halves of each promise are stated, negative and positive: multiplied and not be few, honoured and not be small. God answers the diminishment directly. A remnant that felt like nothing is told it will not stay small.

verseByVerse.quote: Their children shall be as they were of old, and their congregation shall be established before me, and I will punish all who oppress them. Their prince shall be one of themselves; their ruler shall come out from their midst; I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me, for who would dare of himself to approach me? declares the LORD. And you shall be my people, and I will be your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their children shall be as they were of old, and their congregation shall be established before me, and I will punish all who oppress them.

As they were of old — restoration that reaches backwards, repairing what the generations had lost, and a congregation established before me, which is to say a worshipping people with access again.

Their prince shall be one of themselves; their ruler shall come out from their midst; I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me, for who would dare of himself to approach me? declares the LORD.

Here is the summit of the chapter. The ruler will not be a foreign governor but one of their own, and his defining act is not military or administrative. It is priestly: I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me.

Then God asks a question that stops every religious project in its tracks: who would dare of himself to approach me? Nobody. That is the honest answer, and Israel's whole system of curtains, courts and one annual entrance existed to say so. A prince who is both from among the people and able to approach God is a figure the Old Testament keeps sketching and never produces.

Hebrews names him. Since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near (Heb 10:19-22). One of ourselves, brought near by God, who is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (Heb 7:25). Nobody would dare of himself. He dared, and takes us in with him.

And you shall be my people, and I will be your God."

The covenant sentence, the thing all of it was for. It is not real estate or independence but belonging, and it is the sentence still being spoken at the end of the Bible: they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God (Rev 21:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–24 — The Storm of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends where it will not let the comfort go soft: Behold the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked (v. 23). The anger is not a mood that passes — The fierce anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind — and understanding is promised on a delay: In the latter days you will understand this (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Comfort that has a storm at the end of it is the only kind worth having.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked. The fierce anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind. In the latter days you will understand this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked.

And after all that comfort, a storm. It reads like an intrusion until you notice what it protects.

A promise of restoration that quietly dropped the subject of judgment would be a promise that evil simply stops mattering. Instead the chapter that healed an incurable wound insists in its last breath that wrath has gone forth and will burst upon the head of the wicked. The comfort is for people who needed rescuing from something real.

The fierce anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind. In the latter days you will understand this.

God's anger is not a temper that cools but a purpose that completes — it will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind. That is a fearful sentence about the wicked and a steadying one about everything else God intends, since the same resolve stands behind the promises in this chapter.

And the last line is a hand on the shoulder of anyone reading too early: In the latter days you will understand this. Not now. The generation holding this book in Babylon would not see how a wound God inflicted could be a wound God heals, or how a prince could walk in where nobody dares. Later, they would. We read it on the far side of a cross, and the storm and the healing turn out to have met in one place.

30.title: Write It in a Book: The Healing of an Incurable Wound
30.overview:
God tells Jeremiah to write his words in a book, because the promise is for a later generation: days are coming when he will restore the fortunes of Israel and Judah and bring them back to their land (vv. 1-3).

Then the terror is described without softening — a cry of panic and no peace, soldiers doubled over like women in labour, every face pale. That day is unequalled, a time of distress for Jacob, and yet he will be saved out of it (vv. 4-7). In that day God will break the yoke from their neck, and they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom he will raise up. So, fear not: God will save from far away, make a full end of the nations but not of his people, and discipline in just measure (vv. 8-11).

God then calls the wound incurable and says there is no medicine and no healing, that the blow was his own, and that the cause was great guilt and flagrant sin. With nothing changed in the patient he turns and promises that her devourers will be devoured and that he himself will restore her health — because her enemies called her an outcast nobody cared about (vv. 12-17).

The city will be rebuilt on its own mound, with thanksgiving coming out of the tents; their prince will be one of themselves, brought near by God to approach him, when no one would dare of himself; and they shall be his people and he their God (vv. 18-22). The chapter closes with the storm of the LORD bursting on the wicked, an anger that will not turn back until it has accomplished its purpose, and understanding promised for the latter days (vv. 23-24).
30.theology:
Written promise outlives the preacher. The comfort was recorded in a book for a generation not yet born (v. 2).

God does not promise his people an easier day than the one coming, but that the day will not have the last word: distress for Jacob, and yet saved out of it (v. 7).

Redemption is a transfer of service, not the end of it — freed from foreigners to serve the LORD and the David he will raise up (vv. 8-9; Ezek 34:23; Hos 3:5; Luke 1:69).

Covenant, not comparative innocence, is why the nations get a full end and Israel does not. God's people are exempt from destruction, never from discipline, and the measure is a father's (vv. 11).

God gives the terminal diagnosis himself and then cures it, with nothing altered in the patient and the reason found in his own honour rather than her repentance (vv. 12-17). How he heals a wound he inflicted is answered at Isa 53:5.

The one who draws near is one of ourselves, and he is brought near by God — the priestly king of Heb 7:25 and 10:19-22, answering the question no religion can (v. 21).

Comfort that drops the subject of wrath would mean evil no longer matters. The storm at the end guards the healing at the centre (vv. 23-24).
30.examples:
Forty years of open-air preaching, and now: write it down.

The Book of Consolation opening with screaming.

Soldiers doubled over in the posture of childbirth.

One word, yet, holding the whole book together.

A yoke broken by the hand that fastened it.

Sleep without fear, offered instead of empire.

No advocate, no medicine, no healing — from the physician's own mouth.

Therefore, arriving where no moral logic could put it.

A city rebuilt on the same rubble heap.

The question nobody can answer: who would dare approach?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Loved with an Everlasting Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God begins with the covenant sentence — I will be the God of all the clans of Israel, and they shall be my people (v. 1) — and grounds the whole chapter in something older than their failure: I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you (v. 3). So the ruined nation is told Again I will build you, and you shall be built, O virgin Israel! (v. 4), with tambourines, dancing and vineyards. He will gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, among them the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor (v. 8), leading them by brooks of water, for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn (v. 9). The God who scattered them keeps them as a shepherd keeps his flock (v. 10), and the result is a people radiant over the goodness of the LORD, whose life shall be like a watered garden (v. 12), with mourning turned into joy (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything promised here rests on a love that started before the ruin and did not depend on it ending.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time, declares the LORD, I will be the God of all the clans of Israel, and they shall be my people." Thus says the LORD: "The people who survived the sword found grace in the wilderness; when Israel sought for rest, the LORD appeared to him from far away. I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"At that time, declares the LORD, I will be the God of all the clans of Israel, and they shall be my people."

The chapter opens with the sentence the whole Bible is driving at, and it opens with all the clans — the ten tribes lost to Assyria a century before, written off by everyone as gone, included by name.

Thus says the LORD: "The people who survived the sword found grace in the wilderness; when Israel sought for rest, the LORD appeared to him from far away.

The picture reaches back to the exodus — survivors of the sword, out in the desert, finding grace there. That was the pattern once and it will be the pattern again: God meets his people in the wilderness, not after they have got themselves home.

The ESV notes that where the main text reads that the LORD appeared to him from far away, following the Septuagint, the Hebrew reads "me". Either way the striking thing stands: God appears, and the distance is crossed from his side.

I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you.

Here is the ground of everything that follows in this chapter, and it is not anything in them.

Weigh the word everlasting. A love with no beginning cannot have been started by anything Israel did, and a love with no end cannot be stopped by anything Israel did either. It was not switched on by her obedience in the wilderness and it was not switched off by her adultery in Canaan.

And then therefore. God's faithfulness is not the cause of his love but its consequence. He keeps on with this people because he loved them first — which is the only explanation the Bible ever gives for why any of us are still here.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I will build you, and you shall be built, O virgin Israel! Again you shall adorn yourself with tambourines and shall go forth in the dance of the merrymakers. Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; the planters shall plant and shall enjoy the fruit. For there shall be a day when watchmen will call in the hill country of Ephraim: 'Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again I will build you, and you shall be built, O virgin Israel! Again you shall adorn yourself with tambourines and shall go forth in the dance of the merrymakers.

Three times in three verses: Again. Again built, again dancing, again planting. The word is doing pastoral work, because the fear of a ruined people is not that God is unable but that the good days are simply over.

And notice what he calls her. O virgin Israel — spoken to the nation this book has called a prostitute, a faithless wife, a camel in heat. The name is not a polite fiction; it is what God intends to make her, and he uses the future name now.

The restoration is not solemn. It is tambourines and dancing, the noise of a village wedding.

Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; the planters shall plant and shall enjoy the fruit.

Samaria is the old northern capital, the heartland of the tribes everyone had given up on, and the promise is of vineyards there — a crop that takes years to bear, planted by people who expect to be around to drink the wine. The curse of sowing what others eat is lifted.

For there shall be a day when watchmen will call in the hill country of Ephraim: 'Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God.'"

And the most unlikely sentence yet. Watchmen in Ephraim — northern territory, where the rival shrines had stood for three centuries specifically so nobody would go up to Zion — now shouting at their own people to go and worship in Jerusalem. The schism that split the kingdom is healed from the northern side.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "Sing aloud with gladness for Jacob, and raise shouts for the chief of the nations; proclaim, give praise, and say, 'O LORD, save your people, the remnant of Israel.' Behold, I will bring them from the north country and gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, among them the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor, together; a great company, they shall return here. With weeping they shall come, and with pleas for mercy I will lead them back, I will make them walk by brooks of water, in a straight path in which they shall not stumble, for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD: "Sing aloud with gladness for Jacob, and raise shouts for the chief of the nations; proclaim, give praise, and say, 'O LORD, save your people, the remnant of Israel.'

They are told to sing the rescue before it happens, and to pray for it in the same breath. Praise and petition are not two stages here; the certainty of the promise is exactly what makes the asking confident.

Behold, I will bring them from the north country and gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, among them the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor, together; a great company, they shall return here.

Look at who is on this march. Not the fit and the useful, but the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor — the four categories any commander would leave behind, because a column moves at the pace of its slowest member.

God lists them deliberately. A rescue that quietly loses the weak on the road is not the rescue he is describing; nobody here is expendable, and the party travels at the speed of the woman in labour.

With weeping they shall come, and with pleas for mercy I will lead them back, I will make them walk by brooks of water, in a straight path in which they shall not stumble, for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.

They come home crying. The tears are not a failure of faith but the sound of repentance, and God leads a weeping people gently — brooks of water, level ground, a road chosen so the lame will not stumble on it.

And the reason is family: I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn. Ephraim, of all names — the tribe that led the rebellion, the shorthand for everything that went wrong in the north, called the firstborn son.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear the word of the LORD, O nations, and declare it in the coastlands far away; say, 'He who scattered Israel will gather him, and will keep him as a shepherd keeps his flock.' For the LORD has ransomed Jacob and has redeemed him from hands too strong for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Hear the word of the LORD, O nations, and declare it in the coastlands far away; say, 'He who scattered Israel will gather him, and will keep him as a shepherd keeps his flock.'

The nations are called as witnesses. They had watched the scattering and drawn the obvious conclusion — that Israel's God was weak, or finished — and now they are told to publish the correction as far as the coastlands reach.

The sentence they must carry holds the two halves together without flinching: He who scattered Israel will gather him. Not a rival power scattered them. The scatterer and the gatherer are the same person, and the hand that drove the flock apart is the hand that keeps it.

For the LORD has ransomed Jacob and has redeemed him from hands too strong for him.

Two words from the slave market and the family law court — ransomed, redeemed — and a phrase that explains why any of this had to be God's work: from hands too strong for him.

That is the honest assessment. Jacob was not held by something he could have shaken off with more effort. Babylon was stronger than him, and so was the sin that put him there. Self-rescue was never on the table, which is why the verb throughout this chapter is always in the first person: I will build, I will gather, I will lead, I have ransomed.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall come and sing aloud on the height of Zion, and they shall be radiant over the goodness of the LORD, over the grain, the wine, and the oil, and over the young of the flock and the herd; their life shall be like a watered garden, and they shall languish no more. Then shall the young women rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old shall be merry. I will turn their mourning into joy; I will comfort them, and give them gladness for sorrow. I will feast the soul of the priests with abundance, and my people shall be satisfied with my goodness, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall come and sing aloud on the height of Zion, and they shall be radiant over the goodness of the LORD, over the grain, the wine, and the oil, and over the young of the flock and the herd; their life shall be like a watered garden, and they shall languish no more.

Radiant over the goodness of the LORD. Their faces shine, and the thing they are shining about is named — grain, wine, oil, lambs, calves. Ordinary provision, received as goodness from a person.

The image of the watered garden would land hard on people who knew what a dry season did to a field. Everything in this book about drought, cracked cisterns and withered pasture is reversed in four words.

Then shall the young women rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old shall be merry. I will turn their mourning into joy; I will comfort them, and give them gladness for sorrow.

Three generations dancing in the same sentence — girls, young men, the old. The community that lost its future is given one with children in it.

And the verb is turn: I will turn their mourning into joy. Not replace the mourning with joy once it has run its course, but turn the thing itself. The grief is not deleted from their history; it is converted, which is a harder and better promise.

I will feast the soul of the priests with abundance, and my people shall be satisfied with my goodness, declares the LORD."

The word to end on is satisfied. This book opened with people digging broken cisterns that could hold no water, forsaking the fountain; it promises here that the thirst will finally be met, and met with God's own goodness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — Rachel's Tears and Ephraim's Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song stops for a mother's grief: A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping. Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted (v. 15). God does not scold the weeping; he answers it — there is a reward for your work, and There is hope for your future, and the children shall come back to their own country (vv. 16-17). Then he repeats a prayer he has overheard: Ephraim asking bring me back that I may be restored, for you are the LORD my God (v. 18), ashamed of the disgrace of his youth (v. 19). And God answers with the tenderest question in the book: Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child?... Therefore my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: God overhears a prayer for the very turning he commands, and answers it with yearning.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping. Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more." Thus says the LORD: "Keep your voice from weeping, and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, declares the LORD, and they shall come back from the land of the enemy. There is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children shall come back to their own country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping. Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more."

In the middle of the singing, someone is crying, and God stops the chapter to listen.

Rachel is Jacob's beloved wife, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and she died on the road near Ramah. Ramah is where the deportees were mustered in chains before the walk to Babylon. So the poem pictures the long-dead mother of the northern tribes waking to watch her descendants marched past her grave, and weeping — and she refuses to be comforted, which is not rebuked here. Some griefs should not be talked out of themselves too quickly.

Matthew heard this verse again on a night in Bethlehem when soldiers came for the children: A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more (Matt 2:18). The mothers of Bethlehem wept while the child who would end all such weeping was carried to safety in Egypt.

Thus says the LORD: "Keep your voice from weeping, and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, declares the LORD, and they shall come back from the land of the enemy. There is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children shall come back to their own country.

God does not answer the tears with an explanation. He answers them with a fact: they shall come back.

And he calls her grief your work, with a reward attached — the years of weeping over lost children counted as labour that will be paid. There is hope for your future is said to a woman in a graveyard, which is the only place that sentence ever needs saying.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard Ephraim grieving, 'You have disciplined me, and I was disciplined, like an untrained calf; bring me back that I may be restored, for you are the LORD my God. For after I had turned away, I relented, and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed, and I was confounded, because I bore the disgrace of my youth.' Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I do remember him still. Therefore my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have heard Ephraim grieving, 'You have disciplined me, and I was disciplined, like an untrained calf; bring me back that I may be restored, for you are the LORD my God.

God has been listening to his son talk to himself.

The image Ephraim reaches for is honest: like an untrained calf, a young animal that fights the yoke, bucks, and has to be broken to be any use. He does not dispute the discipline or ask for it to stop.

And then the prayer that lies at the heart of all true conversion: bring me back that I may be restored. He asks God to do the turning. He knows he cannot return under his own steam, and this is the answer to the question the book has pressed since the leopard and its spots — the return God commands is the return God must give.

For after I had turned away, I relented, and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed, and I was confounded, because I bore the disgrace of my youth.'

Striking the thigh is a gesture of grief at oneself. Notice the order in the sentence: the turning came first, then the instruction, then the shame. Real repentance is usually the last thing to arrive, not the first — shame here is the fruit of being brought back, not the fee for it.

Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I do remember him still. Therefore my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him, declares the LORD.

Two questions, and God answers them by the way he asks them. Even while pronouncing judgment — as often as I speak against him — he never stopped remembering him.

Where the ESV has my heart yearns for him, the note records that the Hebrew word is "bowels": the physical seat of feeling, the churn you feel in your stomach over someone you love. This is not benign divine goodwill. It is a father who cannot get his son out of his mind.

verseByVerse.quote: "Set up road markers for yourself; make yourself guideposts; consider well the highway, the road by which you went. Return, O virgin Israel, return to these your cities. How long will you waver, O faithless daughter? For the LORD has created a new thing on the earth: a woman encircles a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Set up road markers for yourself; make yourself guideposts; consider well the highway, the road by which you went. Return, O virgin Israel, return to these your cities.

A practical instruction for people about to be marched away: mark the route. Pile the stones, note the landmarks, pay attention to the road you are being taken along, because you are coming back down it.

It is a strange kind of comfort — plan your return journey while you are still going out — and it treats the promise as solid enough to survey.

How long will you waver, O faithless daughter? For the LORD has created a new thing on the earth: a woman encircles a man."

The rebuke is gentle and impatient at once: How long will you waver? The wavering is the old habit of hedging between God and the alternatives.

Then a line that has puzzled readers for as long as there have been readers, and it is better to say so than to pretend otherwise. The words are plain — a woman encircles a man — and the sense is not. What the verse does make clear is its frame: this is a new thing that the LORD has created, and created is the verb Genesis uses when God makes the heavens and the earth.

Something is coming that reverses the expected order, and it will be God's own creation rather than Israel's achievement. That is as far as the text takes us, and it is the same direction the rest of the chapter runs: the faithless daughter will be made new by an act of creation, not by finally pulling herself together.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–30 — Watching to Build and to Plant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah's towns will again say The LORD bless you, O habitation of righteousness, O holy hill! (v. 23), for God will satisfy the weary soul, and every languishing soul I will replenish (v. 25) — and the prophet wakes from the sweetest sleep he has had (v. 26). Days are coming when God will sow the land with people and cattle again, and the four destroying verbs of his call are answered: as I have watched over them to pluck up and break down, to overthrow, destroy, and bring harm, so I will watch over them to build and to plant (v. 28). The old fatalistic proverb about fathers eating sour grapes is retired, for everyone shall die for his own iniquity (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The same watchfulness that pulled the nation down is now set to building it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Once more they shall use these words in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore their fortunes: "'The LORD bless you, O habitation of righteousness, O holy hill!' And Judah and all its cities shall dwell there together, and the farmers and those who wander with their flocks. For I will satisfy the weary soul, and every languishing soul I will replenish." At this I awoke and looked, and my sleep was pleasant to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Once more they shall use these words in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore their fortunes: "'The LORD bless you, O habitation of righteousness, O holy hill!' And Judah and all its cities shall dwell there together, and the farmers and those who wander with their flocks.

An old blessing comes back into everyday use — the sort of thing neighbours say to each other in the street. And the name it uses for Jerusalem is habitation of righteousness, which is precisely what the city had stopped being.

The picture in the next line is of ordinary society knitted back together: settled farmers and wandering herdsmen living in the same land without preying on each other.

For I will satisfy the weary soul, and every languishing soul I will replenish."

Two words for exhaustion — weary and languishing — and two promises, to satisfy and to replenish. This is the pastoral centre of the chapter for anyone reading it tired.

At this I awoke and looked, and my sleep was pleasant to me.

And here the prophet himself appears, waking up.

Think of what this man's nights had been like: the boiling pot, the drought, the broken flask, the trial for his life, the stocks, the day he cursed his own birth. Now, after being shown all this, he wakes and records that his sleep had been sweet. It is the only moment of personal comfort he is given in the entire book, and it comes from having seen what God intends to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and the seed of beast. And it shall come to pass that as I have watched over them to pluck up and break down, to overthrow, destroy, and bring harm, so I will watch over them to build and to plant, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
