"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and the seed of beast.

The land that was emptied gets resown, and the metaphor is agricultural: God scatters people across it as a farmer scatters grain. Both houses again, and livestock with them — a country coming back to life at the level of herds.

And it shall come to pass that as I have watched over them to pluck up and break down, to overthrow, destroy, and bring harm, so I will watch over them to build and to plant, declares the LORD.

These are the six verbs of Jeremiah's commission, forty years on (1:10). For four decades he has been fulfilling the first four, and here the last two finally get their turn with the same divine attentiveness behind them.

The repeated word is watched over. God was not careless in the demolition and he will not be casual in the rebuilding. The same vigilance that saw every stage of the tearing down is now fixed on the building and planting — which means the ruin was never a loss of control, and the restoration will not be left to chance.

For a man who had spent his life announcing the first four verbs, it must have been something to be told that he had always been serving the last two.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days they shall no longer say: "'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.' But everyone shall die for his own iniquity. Each man who eats sour grapes, his teeth shall be set on edge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days they shall no longer say: "'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.'

The proverb was the popular theology of a defeated generation, and it was a complaint: our grandfathers sinned and we are the ones with our teeth on edge. There was something true in it — consequences do run downhill through families and nations — but as they used it, it was a way of saying that nothing they did mattered either way.

Ezekiel was told to stop the same saying among the exiles: this proverb shall no more be used by you in Israel (Ezek 18:3).

But everyone shall die for his own iniquity. Each man who eats sour grapes, his teeth shall be set on edge."

The answer is not that inherited consequence is a myth. It is that no one will be able to hide behind it. Everyone shall die for his own iniquity — each person dealt with by God directly, for what he himself has done.

That sounds severe until you see where it sits. It comes immediately before the new covenant, where God deals with each person individually in mercy — writing on this heart, knowing this man, forgetting these sins. The end of hiding behind your ancestors is also the end of being trapped by them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah (v. 31) — not like the one made at the exodus, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband (v. 32). The difference is location: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts, with the covenant formula attached (v. 33). Its members need no evangelising into it, for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, and underneath it all lies the reason any of it can stand: For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: The law moves from tablets to hearts, and the sins move out of God's memory.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah,

This is the sentence the rest of the Bible is built on, and the phrase new covenant is a rare one in the Old Testament — this is where it is given.

Consider who says it and when. A prophet standing in a doomed city, watching the old arrangement collapse around him, announces that God's answer is not a repair. It is a new covenant — and the promise is made to the same two houses that had just finished breaking the old one.

not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD.

The tenderness of the memory is startling: the day when I took them by the hand, like a father teaching a child to walk out of Egypt. That is how God remembers the exodus.

And then the failure, stated without excuse — my covenant that they broke — followed by four words that carry the ache of the whole book: though I was their husband. The problem with the old covenant was never its terms, which were holy, or its giver. It was that one party to a marriage kept the vows and the other did not.

Hebrews quotes this passage at length and draws the conclusion: God finds fault with them (Heb 8:8), not with the covenant. A law written on stone can tell you what to do and cannot make you want to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the LORD,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

The law does not change. Its address does.

The old covenant put God's commands on tablets outside the man, where they instructed him and condemned him and could not help him. The new one puts the same law within them and writes it on their hearts — which answers precisely the diagnosis this book has been making for thirty chapters: sin engraved on the tablet of the heart (17:1), a heart deceitful above all things (17:9), a people who could no more change than a leopard could change its spots (13:23). If the problem is the heart, only a new heart is a solution.

Paul saw it happen in his converts: a letter from Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Cor 3:3).

And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the LORD,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."

Under the old arrangement the covenant community was a mixed body — circumcised men who did not know God at all, which is why they had to be told to know him. In the new one, membership and knowing God are the same thing. Not that teaching ends, but that nobody inside this covenant needs to be introduced to its God. They shall all know me, from the least to the greatest — the child and the scholar on the same footing.

And then the foundation, introduced with For, because it is the reason the rest is possible: I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. Not overlook, not suspend. God puts his people's sin out of his own memory.

It cost him everything to be able to say it. On the last night, holding a cup, the Lord told his friends what would make this covenant new in fact and not only in promise: This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20). Hebrews, having quoted these verses twice, rests the whole assurance of a Christian on the final clause — I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more (Heb 10:17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 35–40 — As Fixed as the Sunrise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stakes Israel's future on the machinery of creation: the one who gives the sun for light by day and the fixed order of the moon and the stars for light by night (v. 35) says that only If this fixed order departs from before me will Israel's offspring cease (v. 36), and only if the heavens above can be measured will he cast them off (v. 37). Then the city is surveyed for rebuilding, gate by gate (vv. 38-39), and the last word falls on the worst ground in Jerusalem: The whole valley of the dead bodies and the ashes... shall be sacred to the LORD. It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: The rubbish tip where they burned their children is the last plot of land God claims as holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, who gives the sun for light by day and the fixed order of the moon and the stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar— the LORD of hosts is his name: "If this fixed order departs from before me, declares the LORD, then shall the offspring of Israel cease from being a nation before me forever." Thus says the LORD: "If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be explored, then I will cast off all the offspring of Israel for all that they have done, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD, who gives the sun for light by day and the fixed order of the moon and the stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar — the LORD of hosts is his name:

Before the guarantee, the credentials. The God about to make a promise is the one who runs the solar system and the tides.

"If this fixed order departs from before me, declares the LORD, then shall the offspring of Israel cease from being a nation before me forever."

The logic is a chain with a hinge: Israel's continuance is as secure as sunrise. Anyone doubting the promise is invited to test it against the evidence available every morning.

And this is said about a nation that was, at that moment, being dismantled. Its survival was not a projection from its circumstances. It was staked on the constancy of the God who keeps the moon in its course.

Thus says the LORD: "If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be explored, then I will cast off all the offspring of Israel for all that they have done, declares the LORD."

The second guarantee is built on immensity rather than regularity: measure the sky, survey the foundations of the earth, and then we can discuss rejection.

Note the honesty of the last clause — for all that they have done. God does not minimise the record. The guilt is real and it is not the deciding factor, because the question was never whether they deserved to be cast off. Paul was still resting on this when he wrote that God has not rejected his people (Rom 11:26-27).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when the city shall be rebuilt for the LORD from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. And the measuring line shall go out farther, straight to the hill Gareb, and shall then turn to Goah. The whole valley of the dead bodies and the ashes, and all the fields as far as the brook Kidron, to the corner of the Horse Gate toward the east, shall be sacred to the LORD. It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when the city shall be rebuilt for the LORD from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. And the measuring line shall go out farther, straight to the hill Gareb, and shall then turn to Goah.

The chapter ends with a survey. Named towers, named gates, a measuring line pulled across specific hills — the promise given as a plan an engineer could work from.

And the line goes farther than the old walls. The rebuilt city is larger than the one about to be destroyed.

The whole valley of the dead bodies and the ashes, and all the fields as far as the brook Kidron, to the corner of the Horse Gate toward the east, shall be sacred to the LORD. It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever."

Of every acre God could have chosen for the last word of this chapter, he takes the worst one.

The valley of the dead bodies and the ashes is the ravine below the city where the rubbish burned and the corpses went — the place Jeremiah had stood with a clay flask and called the Valley of Slaughter, where they had burned their own children to Baal (19:5-6). It was the most defiled ground in Israel, and its name became the New Testament's word for hell.

That valley, God says, shall be sacred to the LORD.

The book that began by measuring a nation's guilt ends this chapter by measuring a city that includes its own worst place inside the holy ground. This is what the new covenant does. It does not quarantine the shameful part of the record and build around it; it takes the ash heap into the city and calls it holy, and it fixes the boundary with a promise that has no expiry — It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever. The verbs of the demolition are used one last time, in the negative, and put beyond recall.

31.title: The New Covenant
31.overview:
God promises to be the God of all the clans of Israel, and grounds it in an everlasting love that explains his continued faithfulness. The ruined nation will be built again, dancing with tambourines and planting vineyards in Samaria, with watchmen in Ephraim calling people up to Zion. He will gather them from the ends of the earth — the blind, the lame and women in labour among them — leading them by brooks of water as a father, so that their life is like a watered garden and their mourning is turned into joy (vv. 1-14).

Rachel is heard weeping for her lost children and refusing comfort, and God answers her with a promise that they will come back. He repeats Ephraim's own prayer — bring me back that I may be restored — and responds with yearning and mercy. Israel is told to mark the road home, and a new thing is announced that God himself has created (vv. 15-22).

Judah's towns will bless Jerusalem again, the weary soul will be satisfied, and Jeremiah wakes from a sweet sleep. God will sow the land with people and beasts, and will watch over the building and planting as attentively as he watched over the tearing down; the proverb about sour grapes is retired, and each person will answer for himself (vv. 23-30).

Then the new covenant: not like the broken one made at the exodus, but with the law written on hearts, God as their God and they as his people, all of them knowing him from the least to the greatest, because he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more (vv. 31-34). Israel's future is staked on the fixed order of sun and moon and the unmeasurable heavens, and the city is surveyed for rebuilding — with even the valley of dead bodies and ashes declared sacred to the LORD, never to be overthrown again (vv. 35-40).
31.theology:
God's faithfulness is the consequence of his love, not its cause: an everlasting love has no beginning that Israel's obedience could supply and no end her sin could force (v. 3).

The scatterer and the gatherer are the same person, and the rescue was necessary because Jacob was held by hands too strong for him (vv. 10-11). The weakest travellers set the pace of the return (v. 8).

Repentance is asked for as a gift — bring me back that I may be restored — and shame follows the turning rather than purchasing it (vv. 18-19). God's compassion is visceral, not merely benign (v. 20).

The same divine watchfulness governs the demolition and the rebuilding, so the ruin was never loss of control (v. 28; 1:10).

The new covenant differs from the old not in its law but in where the law is written. If the heart is the problem (17:1, 9; 13:23), only a new heart is a solution; and because all its members know God, its membership and its reality are the same thing (vv. 33-34; 2 Cor 3:3; Heb 8:8-12).

Forgiveness is the foundation, not the reward: God puts his people's sin out of his own memory, sealed in the blood of Christ (v. 34; Luke 22:20; Heb 10:17).

Grace claims the worst ground. The valley where they burned their children is taken inside the holy city and put beyond overthrow forever (v. 40).
31.examples:
Again, again, again — the word spoken to people who thought the good days were over.

A nation called virgin Israel by the God who had called her faithless.

Watchmen in Ephraim shouting: let us go up to Zion.

A column that travels at the speed of the woman in labour.

A mother in a graveyard told there is hope for her future.

Asking God for the turning he has commanded.

A father who cannot get his son out of his mind.

Piling up road markers for a journey home you have not yet left on.

The one night in the book when Jeremiah slept well.

A law that moves from stone to the inside of a person.

Sins put out of God's memory.

The rubbish tip declared holy ground.

32.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar.<sup>2</sup>At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard that was in the palace of the king of Judah.<sup>3</sup>For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying, "Why do you prophesy and say, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall capture it;<sup>4</sup>Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye.<sup>5</sup>And he shall take Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain until I visit him, declares the LORD. Though you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall not succeed'?"<sup>6</sup>Jeremiah said, "The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>7</sup>Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you and say, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth, for the right of redemption by purchase is yours.'<sup>8</sup>Then Hanamel my cousin came to me in the court of the guard, in accordance with the word of the LORD, and said to me, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.' Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"And I bought the field at Anathoth from Hanamel my cousin, and weighed out the money to him, seventeen shekels of silver.<sup>10</sup>I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales.<sup>11</sup>Then I took the sealed deed of purchase, containing the terms and conditions and the open copy.<sup>12</sup>And I gave the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my cousin, in the presence of the witnesses who signed the deed of purchase, and in the presence of all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard.<sup>13</sup>I charged Baruch in their presence, saying,<sup>14</sup>'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these deeds, both this sealed deed of purchase and this open deed, and put them in an earthenware vessel, that they may last for a long time.<sup>15</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.'<sup>16</sup>"After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD, saying:<sup>17</sup>'Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you.<sup>18</sup>You show steadfast love to thousands, but you repay the guilt of fathers to their children after them, O great and mighty God, whose name is the LORD of hosts,<sup>19</sup>great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man, rewarding each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.<sup>20</sup>You have shown signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and to this day in Israel and among all mankind, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day.<sup>21</sup>You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and outstretched arm, and with great terror.<sup>22</sup>And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>23</sup>And they entered and took possession of it. But they did not obey your voice or walk in your law. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. Therefore you have made all this disaster come upon them.<sup>24</sup>Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city to take it, and because of sword and famine and pestilence the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it.<sup>25</sup>Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, "Buy the field for money and get witnesses"—though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans.'"<sup>26</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>27</sup>"Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?<sup>28</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall capture it.<sup>29</sup>The Chaldeans who are fighting against this city shall come and set this city on fire and burn it, with the houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods, to provoke me to anger.<sup>30</sup>For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The children of Israel have done nothing but provoke me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD.<sup>31</sup>This city has aroused my anger and wrath, from the day it was built to this day, so that I will remove it from my sight<sup>32</sup>because of all the evil of the children of Israel and the children of Judah that they did to provoke me to anger— their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>33</sup>They have turned to me their back and not their face. And though I have taught them persistently, they have not listened to receive instruction.<sup>34</sup>They set up their abominations in the house that is called by my name, to defile it.<sup>35</sup>They built the high places of Baal in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to offer up their sons and daughters to Molech, though I did not command them, nor did it enter into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.<sup>36</sup>"Now therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning this city of which you say, 'It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword, by famine, and by pestilence':<sup>37</sup>Behold, I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger and my wrath and in great indignation. I will bring them back to this place, and I will make them dwell in safety.<sup>38</sup>And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.<sup>39</sup>I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their own good and the good of their children after them.<sup>40</sup>I will make with them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from doing good to them. And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me.<sup>41</sup>I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul.<sup>42</sup>"For thus says the LORD: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them.<sup>43</sup>Fields shall be bought in this land of which you are saying, 'It is a desolation, without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.'<sup>44</sup>Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in the land of Benjamin, in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb; for I will restore their fortunes, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — A Field Bought in a Besieged City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Zedekiah's tenth year the Babylonian army is around Jerusalem and Jeremiah is shut up in the court of the guard for saying the city will fall (vv. 2-3). There God tells him his cousin will come with an offer, and Hanamel duly arrives: Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours (v. 8). Jeremiah buys it — seventeen shekels of silver, and he signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales (vv. 9-10) — then hands both copies to Baruch to be sealed in a jar, that they may last for a long time (v. 14). The reason is given last: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: A prisoner buys real estate in a country that is about to be confiscated, and has the paperwork witnessed.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard that was in the palace of the king of Judah. For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying, "Why do you prophesy and say, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall capture it; Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye. And he shall take Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain until I visit him, declares the LORD. Though you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall not succeed'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard that was in the palace of the king of Judah.

Fix the situation before reading the story, because everything in this chapter depends on it. It is 588 or 587 BC. The Babylonian army is camped around the walls. Food is running out. And the prophet is under arrest in the palace compound.

It is an unpromising moment for a property transaction.

For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying, "Why do you prophesy and say, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall capture it;

The king's question is almost plaintive. Not is it true, but why do you keep saying it. Zedekiah spends this whole book half-believing Jeremiah and never acting on it, and here he jails the man rather than answer him.

Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye. And he shall take Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain until I visit him, declares the LORD. Though you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall not succeed'?"

The detail about seeing Nebuchadnezzar eye to eye would be fulfilled with terrible precision: Zedekiah was brought before him at Riblah, watched his sons killed, and was then blinded. He saw the king of Babylon eye to eye, and the last thing those eyes saw was his own sons dying.

And even here a door is left open — until I visit him. The same verb that carried the promise to the exiles is attached to the man who imprisoned the prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said, "The word of the LORD came to me: Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you and say, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth, for the right of redemption by purchase is yours.' Then Hanamel my cousin came to me in the court of the guard, in accordance with the word of the LORD, and said to me, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.' Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah said, "The word of the LORD came to me: Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you and say, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth, for the right of redemption by purchase is yours.'

God tells him what is about to happen before it happens, and it is nothing spectacular: a relative is going to turn up with a business proposition.

The legal background is the law of redemption. When an Israelite fell into poverty and had to sell family land, the nearest kinsman had the right and duty to buy it, keeping the inheritance inside the family — his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold (Lev 25:25). It is the transaction Boaz performed at the gate, calling the town to witness that he had bought the inheritance of a dead man to keep his name alive (Ruth 4:9-10).

Then Hanamel my cousin came to me in the court of the guard, in accordance with the word of the LORD, and said to me, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.' Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.

Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD. The confirmation did not come by a vision or a voice. It came when a cousin walked into the guardhouse and said what God had said he would say.

Hanamel's motive is easy to guess and not held against him. Anathoth was three miles north of Jerusalem, in territory the Babylonians already controlled. The field was worthless and he wanted out. What he was selling was, commercially, a liability — and God had told his prophet to be the buyer.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I bought the field at Anathoth from Hanamel my cousin, and weighed out the money to him, seventeen shekels of silver. I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales. Then I took the sealed deed of purchase, containing the terms and conditions and the open copy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And I bought the field at Anathoth from Hanamel my cousin, and weighed out the money to him, seventeen shekels of silver.

He paid. That is the whole force of the sign, and it cost him real silver — seventeen shekels, recorded exactly, as a man records a sum he has genuinely parted with.

Faith here is not a feeling about the future. It is money leaving a purse for land the buyer will never walk on, in a district already under enemy control, paid by a man who had just been told the country was finished.

I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales.

Four verbs, and every one of them is ordinary conveyancing: signed, sealed, witnessed, weighed. God's prophet does not make a gesture; he completes a legally binding sale with the correct number of formalities in front of observers.

There is something bracing in that. An extravagant act of hope is carried out with paperwork. Faith that expects God to keep his word will generally look like something concrete and slightly inconvenient rather than like an inspiring mood.

Then I took the sealed deed of purchase, containing the terms and conditions and the open copy.

Two documents, which was the standard practice: a sealed copy that could not be tampered with, and an open copy for consultation. Both are kept, because the sale is meant to be verifiable generations later by people who will need to know exactly where the boundary ran.

verseByVerse.quote: And I gave the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my cousin, in the presence of the witnesses who signed the deed of purchase, and in the presence of all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard. I charged Baruch in their presence, saying, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these deeds, both this sealed deed of purchase and this open deed, and put them in an earthenware vessel, that they may last for a long time. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I gave the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my cousin, in the presence of the witnesses who signed the deed of purchase, and in the presence of all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard.

Baruch appears, the scribe who will carry this book into existence. And note the audience: the cousin, the official witnesses, and all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard — a yard full of prisoners and hangers-on, watching a man buy a field he could not reach.

The sign was performed publicly on purpose. In a city where everyone was calculating how long the food would last, here was a man behaving as though there would be a Judah in which to own land.

I charged Baruch in their presence, saying, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these deeds, both this sealed deed of purchase and this open deed, and put them in an earthenware vessel, that they may last for a long time.

An earthenware jar, that they may last for a long time. The instruction quietly concedes the whole tragedy: this will take decades. Jeremiah will not be redeeming anything himself; the jar is for somebody's grandchildren.

Storing documents in sealed pottery is how the ancient world preserved what mattered, and how the Dead Sea Scrolls survived two thousand years in the same region. Hope with a long timescale needs a container.

For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.'

And here is the interpretation, given after the act rather than before it. The point of the purchase was never the field. It was the sentence: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land — normal life, markets functioning, families buying property, in the country whose destruction had just been guaranteed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — Nothing Is Too Hard for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the deed handed over, Jeremiah prays — and the prayer starts in worship rather than complaint: Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you (v. 17). He rehearses the steadfast love shown to thousands (v. 18), the signs and wonders in Egypt (vv. 20-21), the land flowing with milk and honey (v. 22), and then the failure: they did not obey your voice or walk in your law (v. 23). He looks out of the window at the siege ramps and says What you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it (v. 24) — before laying his bewilderment down plainly: Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, "Buy the field for money and get witnesses" — though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: He obeyed first and asked his question afterwards, which is the right order.

verseByVerse.quote: "After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD, saying: 'Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD, saying:

Notice the sequence. He obeyed, completed the transaction, filed the deeds — and then prayed about it. The obedience was not waiting on the explanation.

'Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you.

The prayer opens with a sigh — Ah, Lord GOD! — the sound of a man who has done something he does not understand and has come to talk about it.

And then, before any question, he states what he knows: God made the heavens and the earth, and Nothing is too hard for you. That is the right foundation for a confused prayer. He does not begin with the problem; he begins with the Creator, and the problem gets measured against him rather than the other way round.

The words are borrowed. When Sarah laughed behind a tent flap at the idea of a baby, the LORD said to Abraham, Is anything too hard for the LORD? (Gen 18:14). The same question would be put to a girl in Nazareth in the plainest form: For nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37). A barren womb, a doomed city, a virgin — the question turns up at every point where God's promise looks physically ridiculous.

verseByVerse.quote: You show steadfast love to thousands, but you repay the guilt of fathers to their children after them, O great and mighty God, whose name is the LORD of hosts, great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man, rewarding each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You show steadfast love to thousands, but you repay the guilt of fathers to their children after them, O great and mighty God, whose name is the LORD of hosts,

Jeremiah holds two things together that we find easier to separate. Steadfast love to thousands, and guilt repaid into the next generation. He is quoting the words God used of himself at Sinai, and he does not edit them to make the prayer more comfortable.

Praying honestly means praying to the God who is actually there, including the parts of him that are currently battering your city.

The words come from the moment God proclaimed his own name to Moses: keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children (Exod 34:7). And notice the proportion inside that sentence. Love reaches thousands; the visiting of guilt reaches three or four generations. Even in the verse that warns, mercy is the larger number.

great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man, rewarding each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.

Two pairs, and they are the qualities a man in a besieged city most needs to believe. Great in counsel and mighty in deed — God both knows what he is doing and is able to do it; wisdom without power would be tragic, and power without wisdom would be terrifying.

Then whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man. Nothing in the siege, or in the guardhouse, or in the conduct of the men who put him there, is unobserved.

And the last clause is one God had already spoken about himself in this book: I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds (17:10). Jeremiah prays God's own words back to him. That is often the safest way to pray when a situation makes no sense — not with a theory, but with what God has said.

verseByVerse.quote: You have shown signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and to this day in Israel and among all mankind, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day. You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and outstretched arm, and with great terror. And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have shown signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and to this day in Israel and among all mankind, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day.

The prayer turns to history, which is where Israel always went for confidence. He does not reason from his circumstances to God's character; he reasons from what God has already done.

You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and outstretched arm, and with great terror.

The exodus, recited by a prisoner during a siege. And the phrase outstretched arm is the one he had already used in verse 17 of creation — the arm that made the world is the arm that emptied Egypt, and it has not shortened.

Praying through the record like this is not nostalgia. It is how a believer talks himself into hope: God has done the impossible before, with witnesses, and the account is public.

And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.

The land was a gift and an oath — which you swore to their fathers. That is precisely what makes the present moment so painful to pray about. The property Jeremiah has just bought is part of a gift God swore to give, and it is about to be taken away. He lays that contradiction in front of God rather than resolving it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And they entered and took possession of it. But they did not obey your voice or walk in your law. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. Therefore you have made all this disaster come upon them. Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city to take it, and because of sword and famine and pestilence the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it. Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, "Buy the field for money and get witnesses"—though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they entered and took possession of it. But they did not obey your voice or walk in your law. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. Therefore you have made all this disaster come upon them.

The prophet's prayer contains no defence of his people. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do, and the disaster is traced to its author without complaint: you have made all this disaster come upon them.

He is not asking God to be fair. He agrees with the verdict, which is the only honest place to pray from.

Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city to take it, and because of sword and famine and pestilence the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it.

He describes what is out of the window. Earth ramps rising against the wall, the three-fold judgment of the whole book arriving on schedule, and a flat acknowledgement: What you spoke has come to pass.

Forty years of being called a traitor for saying this, and there is no vindication in his tone at all.

Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, "Buy the field for money and get witnesses" — though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans.'"

And there is the question, finally, and it is left unfinished. Everything you said would happen is happening — Yet you told me to buy a field.

He does not accuse God of anything and he does not pretend to understand. He simply sets the command beside the circumstances and leaves them both in God's hands. That is what faithful bewilderment sounds like, and it is available to anyone who has obeyed something they could not explain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–35 — Is Anything Too Hard for Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers by handing the confession back as a question: Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me? (v. 27). Then he confirms the worst — the Chaldeans will take the city and burn it, houses and all, including the roofs where offerings were made to Baal (vv. 28-29). The indictment is total and historical: the city has aroused my anger and wrath, from the day it was built to this day (v. 31), through kings, officials, priests and prophets alike (v. 32). They have turned to me their back and not their face, and would not receive instruction though he taught them persistently (v. 33) — culminating at the high places of Baal where they offered their children, a thing God disowns entirely: he never commanded it, nor did it enter into my mind (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: The question that carries the promise is the same question that carries the judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?

God answers the prayer by quoting it.

Jeremiah had said Nothing is too hard for you; God replies Is anything too hard for me? It is the gentlest possible correction, and it is a real one. The prophet had stated the doctrine and then laid a difficulty beside it as though the two might not fit. God takes the man's own confession and turns it into the answer to his problem.

There is a great deal of pastoral help in that. What we mostly need in bewilderment is not new information but the application of what we already say we believe.

And the title God chooses is exact for the occasion: the God of all flesh. Not the God of Judah only, whose reach ends at a besieged wall, but of every living thing — including the Babylonian army, the cousin selling a field, and the generations who will one day open a clay jar.

Zechariah heard the same question asked after the exile, when the returned remnant thought the promised restoration too great to believe: If it is marvelous in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my sight? (Zech 8:6). What looks impossible to people standing in rubble does not look impossible from where God stands.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall capture it. The Chaldeans who are fighting against this city shall come and set this city on fire and burn it, with the houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods, to provoke me to anger. For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The children of Israel have done nothing but provoke me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall capture it.

Before the comfort, God confirms the catastrophe. He does not answer the hard question by softening the facts, and the first thing he says after Is anything too hard for me? is that the city will fall.

The Chaldeans who are fighting against this city shall come and set this city on fire and burn it, with the houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods, to provoke me to anger.

The detail about the roofs is precise and damning. Flat roofs were where families sat in the evening, and they had been using them as private altars. Those same houses are named as fuel.

For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The children of Israel have done nothing but provoke me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD.

The assessment is unrelieved, and it matters that it comes here rather than in a chapter of pure judgment. The restoration promised in a few verses is not going to rest on a reassessment of the nation's record. That record is being read out at full severity first.

verseByVerse.quote: This city has aroused my anger and wrath, from the day it was built to this day, so that I will remove it from my sight because of all the evil of the children of Israel and the children of Judah that they did to provoke me to anger— their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This city has aroused my anger and wrath, from the day it was built to this day, so that I will remove it from my sight

From the day it was built. Not since Manasseh, not since the monarchy went bad — from the beginning. God's review of Jerusalem's history finds no golden age to appeal to.

That is a sobering word about institutions and cities we are tempted to idealise, and it clears away any idea that the coming restoration is a return to an earlier, purer Jerusalem. There was never one.

Ezekiel said the same thing even more bluntly about the city's origins: Your origin and your birth are of the land of the Canaanites; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite (Ezek 16:3). Jerusalem had been a pagan city before David took it, and it never fully stopped being one. Whatever God does with it will be grace from the ground up, not a restoration of past merit.

because of all the evil of the children of Israel and the children of Judah that they did to provoke me to anger — their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

Six groups, and the list runs from the palace to the street. Kings, officials, priests, prophets, the men of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem — leadership and laity together, with no class exempted and nobody left to blame the others.

verseByVerse.quote: They have turned to me their back and not their face. And though I have taught them persistently, they have not listened to receive instruction. They set up their abominations in the house that is called by my name, to defile it. They built the high places of Baal in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to offer up their sons and daughters to Molech, though I did not command them, nor did it enter into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have turned to me their back and not their face. And though I have taught them persistently, they have not listened to receive instruction.

The image is domestic and wounding: a person who will not turn round. Not argument, not rival theology — the posture of someone who has decided not to look at you.

And though I have taught them persistently, which is the adverb of this whole book. God as the long-suffering teacher, sending prophet after prophet into a classroom whose pupils face the wall.

They set up their abominations in the house that is called by my name, to defile it.

Idols inside the temple. The building existed to display his name and was used to insult it.

They built the high places of Baal in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to offer up their sons and daughters to Molech, though I did not command them, nor did it enter into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.

The indictment ends at the bottom: the valley below the city where they burned their children.

And God adds a clause about himself that is almost unbearable to read — nor did it enter into my mind. The thing had never so much as occurred to him. Whatever the worshippers told themselves about devotion and cost, God disowns the whole idea as something that had never crossed his mind to want.

Remember where the previous chapter ended. This valley, this exact ground, is the plot God promised would be sacred to the LORD (31:40). The place named here as the floor of Judah's guilt is the place named there as holy, and between the two statements stands everything the gospel has to do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — One Heart and One Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now therefore (v. 36) turns the whole chapter. God will gather them from every country he drove them to, bring them back and make them dwell in safety (v. 37), and the covenant formula follows: And they shall be my people, and I will be their God (v. 38). He will give one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever (v. 39), make an everlasting covenant and put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me (v. 40). And then a sentence about God's own disposition: I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul (v. 41).
verseByVerse.theology: God secures the perseverance he requires, and says he will enjoy doing it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning this city of which you say, 'It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword, by famine, and by pestilence': Behold, I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger and my wrath and in great indignation. I will bring them back to this place, and I will make them dwell in safety. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Now therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning this city of which you say, 'It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword, by famine, and by pestilence':

Two words carry the weight of the chapter: Now therefore.

Read what precedes them — evil from the beginning, every class guilty, children burned in the valley, the city to be removed from God's sight. A therefore after that should introduce the sentence. Instead it introduces the promise. There is no logic in the world by which verse 37 follows verse 35, except the logic of grace.

Behold, I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger and my wrath and in great indignation. I will bring them back to this place, and I will make them dwell in safety.

The same hand appears on both ends of the action: he drove them, and he will gather them. The anger was real — God does not now describe the exile as a misunderstanding — and it is the same God who ends it.

And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.

The covenant sentence again, and in this setting it is the answer to everything in the indictment. Not a people who deserve him. A people who are his.

Hosea gave the same promise to a people who had been named for their rejection: I will say to Not My People, 'You are my people'; and he shall say, 'You are my God' (Hos 2:23). And Peter applies it to Gentile believers who had never belonged to Israel at all: Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy (1 Pet 2:10). The covenant sentence spoken to exiles in a doomed city is the sentence spoken over every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their own good and the good of their children after them. I will make with them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from doing good to them. And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me. I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their own good and the good of their children after them.

The gift is a heart, as it has been throughout this book — the heart to know him (24:7), the law written inside (31:33), and here one heart and one way. Ezekiel was given the same promise in almost the same words: I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them (Ezek 11:19).

One is doing real work. A divided heart was Judah's disease, wavering between the LORD and Baal, the temple and the roof altar. The cure is not more willpower but an undivided heart, given.

I will make with them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from doing good to them. And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me.

Two guarantees, one on each side of the relationship. God will not turn away from doing them good, and — this is the astonishing half — he will see to it that they do not turn away from him either. The covenant is secured at both ends by the same person. Hebrews calls it the eternal covenant and names the price: the blood of the great shepherd of the sheep (Heb 13:20).

I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul.

And then God says something about his own feelings. He will rejoice in doing them good, and he will do it with all my heart and all my soul — the phrase Israel was commanded to use about loving him, turned round and spoken by God about blessing them.

This is not a God who forgives reluctantly and blesses on sufferance. Zephaniah saw the same thing: he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing (Zeph 3:17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 42–44 — Deeds Signed and Sealed Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The argument closes with a symmetry: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them (v. 42). Fields will be bought in the land everyone is calling a desolation, without man or beast (v. 43), and the detail is deliberately clerical — Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in Benjamin, around Jerusalem, in the hill country, the Shephelah and the Negeb (v. 44).
verseByVerse.theology: The land registry will reopen, district by district, and that is the shape the hope takes.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them. Fields shall be bought in this land of which you are saying, 'It is a desolation, without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.' Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in the land of Benjamin, in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb; for I will restore their fortunes, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus says the LORD: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them.

The argument is an equation, and it is a practical sentence for anyone who has watched God keep a hard word.

They had just seen every threat land — siege mounds, famine, the city given over. Fine, says God: that same reliability is now working for you. The accuracy of the judgment is the evidence for the promise. A God whose warnings come true is a God whose assurances can be banked, and the logic runs the way Paul's does when he argues from the greater gift to the lesser (Rom 8:32).

Fields shall be bought in this land of which you are saying, 'It is a desolation, without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.'

God quotes the pessimism of the moment accurately — a desolation, without man or beast — and does not dispute it. That is exactly what the land is about to become. And in that land, fields will be bought.

Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in the land of Benjamin, in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb; for I will restore their fortunes, declares the LORD."

The chapter ends in a solicitor's office, and the vocabulary is the vocabulary of verse 10: bought for money, signed, sealed, witnessed. Jeremiah's private transaction in a prison yard turns out to be the first entry in a register that will reopen across five named districts — Benjamin, the area round Jerusalem, the hill country, the Shephelah, the Negeb.

That is how this hope is described: not as a vision or a feeling, but as ordinary people doing ordinary business in a country God had promised to empty and then promised to fill. And the man who bought the first field never saw it. He paid seventeen shekels, filed the deeds in a jar, and died elsewhere — which is the pattern for every believer who has ever acted on a promise whose fulfilment lay past his own lifetime.

32.title: The Field at Anathoth
32.overview:
In Zedekiah's tenth year, with Babylon besieging Jerusalem and Jeremiah imprisoned in the court of the guard for prophesying the city's fall, God tells him his cousin Hanamel will offer him the family field at Anathoth. Hanamel comes exactly as predicted, and Jeremiah buys it for seventeen shekels — signing, sealing, weighing the silver before witnesses — then has Baruch store both copies of the deed in an earthenware jar to last a long time, because houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (vv. 1-15).

Jeremiah then prays. He begins with the Creator and confesses that nothing is too hard for God, rehearses the exodus and the gift of the land, agrees that the present disaster is deserved and God-sent, describes the siege ramps outside, and lays down his bewilderment: yet you told me to buy a field (vv. 16-25).

God answers by returning the confession as a question — is anything too hard for me? — and then confirms the city's burning, with an indictment running from the day Jerusalem was built through every class of its people to the high places where they burned their children, a thing that never entered his mind (vv. 26-35).

Now therefore: God will gather them from every country he drove them to, bring them home in safety, be their God, and give them one heart and one way. He will make an everlasting covenant, put his fear in their hearts so they do not turn away, and rejoice in doing them good with all his heart and soul (vv. 36-41). Just as he brought the disaster, so he will bring the good: fields will be bought and deeds signed, sealed and witnessed across five named districts (vv. 42-44).
32.theology:
Faith acts before it understands. Jeremiah completed a binding purchase and prayed his question afterwards, and the obedience did not wait on the explanation (vv. 9-10, 16, 25).

Hope takes concrete and slightly inconvenient forms — silver weighed, deeds witnessed, documents sealed in a jar for a generation the buyer would never meet (vv. 10-14).

Jeremiah acts as kinsman-redeemer, buying back the family inheritance at the moment it is worthless (vv. 7-8; Lev 25:25; Ruth 4:9-10).

God answers bewilderment by applying what the believer already confesses, not by supplying new information (vv. 17, 27; Gen 18:14; Luke 1:37).

Grace does not rest on a reassessment of the record. The indictment is read at full severity — evil from the day the city was built, every class guilty — and then comes the therefore that introduces the promise (vv. 30-37).

The covenant is secured at both ends by God: he will not turn from doing them good, and he will put his fear in their hearts so that they do not turn from him (vv. 39-40; 24:7; Ezek 11:19; Heb 13:20).

God delights in blessing. He rejoices to do them good with all his heart and all his soul (v. 41; Zeph 3:17), and the threats that came true are the guarantee that the promises will (v. 42).
32.examples:
A prisoner buying farmland in a country under sentence.

A cousin arriving with a worthless field and a legal right.

Seventeen shekels, weighed on scales, in front of witnesses.

Deeds sealed in a clay jar for somebody's grandchildren.

Praying the doctrine first and the problem second.

Reciting the exodus from inside a besieged city.

Evening roofs used as private altars, named as fuel.

A therefore that should have introduced a sentence, introducing a promise.

God blessing with all his heart and all his soul.

A land registry reopening, district by district.
