They shall fear and tremble because of all the good and all the prosperity I provide for it.<sup>10</sup>"Thus says the LORD: In this place of which you say, 'It is a waste without man or beast,' in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man or inhabitant or beast, there shall be heard again<sup>11</sup>the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voices of those who sing, as they bring thank offerings to the house of the LORD: "'Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!' For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at first, says the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: In this place that is waste, without man or beast, and in all of its cities, there shall again be habitations of shepherds resting their flocks.<sup>13</sup>In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb, in the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.<sup>14</sup>"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the promise I made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah.<sup>15</sup>In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.<sup>16</sup>In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'<sup>17</sup>"For thus says the LORD: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,<sup>18</sup>and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to make sacrifices forever."<sup>19</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>20</sup>"Thus says the LORD: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time,<sup>21</sup>then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken, so that he shall not have a son to reign on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests my ministers.<sup>22</sup>As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levitical priests who minister to me."<sup>23</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>24</sup>"Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight.<sup>25</sup>Thus says the LORD: If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth,<sup>26</sup>then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second word comes to Jeremiah while he was still shut up in the court of the guard (v. 1), from the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it to establish it (v. 2), with an invitation: Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known (v. 3). The city's own houses have been demolished for rubble to plug the breaches (v. 4), and God has hidden my face from this city because of all their evil (v. 5). Then the turn: Behold, I will bring to it health and healing (v. 6), and beneath the healing, the reason the healing can stand at all — I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me, and I will forgive all the guilt of their sin and rebellion against me (v. 8). Said twice, with all both times.
verseByVerse.theology: God answers a man in prison by offering to tell him things he could not have worked out.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah a second time, while he was still shut up in the court of the guard: "Thus says the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it to establish it— the LORD is his name: Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah a second time, while he was still shut up in the court of the guard:

Two details, and both matter. A second time — God had not finished speaking after the field was bought. And still shut up in the court of the guard, with the siege tightening outside and the prophet no closer to release.

The circumstances have not improved by one degree between chapter 32 and chapter 33. What arrives instead is more revelation. God's answer to a faithful man in a bad situation is often not a change of situation but a further word about himself.

"Thus says the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it to establish it — the LORD is his name:

Before the promise, the credentials again: the God who made the earth and formed it to establish it. He built it to stand. The ESV notes that its wording here follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew simply has "it" — but the sense of a Creator who makes things in order to make them last is what the verse is for, and it is the ground of everything promised in the chapter.

Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.

Here is the invitation, and consider its recipient. A prisoner. A man whose preaching has failed by every visible measure, who has just spent silver on a field he will never see, and who prayed a bewildered prayer in the previous chapter.

God's reply to that prayer is to invite more of them. Call to me and I will answer you — not a rebuke for asking, but an offer of more. And what is promised is not a change of policy but disclosure: great and hidden things that you have not known. There are things about God's purposes that will not be worked out by looking at the siege ramps. They have to be told, and they are told to people who ask.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the houses of this city and the houses of the kings of Judah that were torn down to make a defense against the siege mounds and against the sword: They are coming in to fight against the Chaldeans and to fill them with the dead bodies of men whom I shall strike down in my anger and my wrath, for I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the houses of this city and the houses of the kings of Judah that were torn down to make a defense against the siege mounds and against the sword:

A picture of a city in its last weeks. They are pulling down their own homes — including royal buildings — for stone and timber to block the breaches where the Babylonian ramps are coming over the wall.

That is what the end looks like in practice: dismantling your own house to slow the enemy down for another afternoon. Every resource turned to a defence that cannot hold.

They are coming in to fight against the Chaldeans and to fill them with the dead bodies of men whom I shall strike down in my anger and my wrath, for I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil.

The ESV's note explains what gets filled with the dead: "That is, the torn-down houses". The improvised barricades become the morgue. The stones pulled from bedrooms end up packed with the bodies of the men who stacked them.

And underneath the military facts is the theological one: I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil. That is the real cause of the collapse. Not siege engineering, not the balance of power — the averted face of God. The worst thing that can happen to a people is not that their walls fail but that God looks away, and this verse names it as the reason the walls fail at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal them and reveal to them abundance of prosperity and security. I will restore the fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Israel, and rebuild them as they were at first. I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me, and I will forgive all the guilt of their sin and rebellion against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal them and reveal to them abundance of prosperity and security.

The same Behold that introduced the barricades full of corpses now introduces healing, in the same breath and about the same city.

This is the wound of chapter 30 again — the hurt God called incurable, with no medicine and no healing — and here is the physician arriving. Nothing has changed in the patient. What changes is that God announces he will do it himself.

I will restore the fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Israel, and rebuild them as they were at first.

Both houses again, the northern kingdom included a century after it vanished, and as they were at first — back to the beginning, with the damage of the intervening centuries undone.

I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me, and I will forgive all the guilt of their sin and rebellion against me.

And here is the foundation under the health, the prosperity and the security. Before any of that can stand, the guilt has to go — and notice how the sentence labours the point, saying it twice with all both times: cleansed from all the guilt, forgiven all the guilt of their sin and rebellion.

Cleansing and forgiveness are not quite the same thing, and both are needed. Forgiveness deals with the record; cleansing deals with the stain. A pardoned man who still feels filthy has only half of what God is promising here.

And the offence is named for what it is — sin against me, twice. Judah's problem was never merely social collapse or bad policy. It was personal, and so is the remedy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — The Voice of the Bridegroom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the place everyone is calling a waste without man or beast (v. 10) there will be heard again the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, and worshippers carrying thank offerings and singing the old refrain: Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever! (v. 11). Shepherds will rest their flocks there again (v. 12), and the promise is mapped district by district — hill country, Shephelah, Negeb, Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem — where flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Weddings, singing and a shepherd counting sheep: the restoration measured in ordinary noise.

verseByVerse.quote: And this city shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and a glory before all the nations of the earth who shall hear of all the good that I do for them. They shall fear and tremble because of all the good and all the prosperity I provide for it. "Thus says the LORD: In this place of which you say, 'It is a waste without man or beast,' in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man or inhabitant or beast, there shall be heard again the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voices of those who sing, as they bring thank offerings to the house of the LORD: "'Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!' For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at first, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this city shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and a glory before all the nations of the earth who shall hear of all the good that I do for them. They shall fear and tremble because of all the good and all the prosperity I provide for it.

The city that had become a curse and a byword among the nations becomes a name of joy, a praise and a glory — and the reversal is not in her reputation for strength but in what God does for her.

The odd phrase is the last one. The nations shall fear and tremble — not at judgment, but because of all the good. God's generosity is itself awe-inducing. Grace on that scale is not a comfortable thing to watch.

"Thus says the LORD: In this place of which you say, 'It is a waste without man or beast,' in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man or inhabitant or beast, there shall be heard again

God quotes the pessimism verbatim, as he did in the previous chapter, and grants every word of it. The place is a waste. Then: there shall be heard again.

the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voices of those who sing, as they bring thank offerings to the house of the LORD: "'Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!' For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at first, says the LORD.

Earlier in this book God had silenced exactly these sounds, promising to take away the voice of mirth and the voice of the bridegroom and bride (7:34; 16:9). Now he gives them back, item by item, in the same words — weddings in the streets, singing, people walking up to the temple with thank offerings.

And the song they sing is the one Israel had always sung, the refrain of Psalm 136: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever (Ps 136:1). It is sung by people who have watched the worst happen. They are not singing that nothing bad occurred; they are singing that his steadfast love outlasted it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: In this place that is waste, without man or beast, and in all of its cities, there shall again be habitations of shepherds resting their flocks. In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb, in the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD of hosts: In this place that is waste, without man or beast, and in all of its cities, there shall again be habitations of shepherds resting their flocks.

After the weddings, the sheep. The promise keeps getting more ordinary, which is how you can tell it is meant literally: shepherds with somewhere to settle, flocks lying down in country that had been emptied.

In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb, in the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.

The same five or six districts as the land-registry promise at the end of chapter 32, listed again — hill country, Shephelah, Negeb, Benjamin, the area round Jerusalem, the towns of Judah. God maps his promises.

And the closing image is a man counting sheep as they file past him under his hand. It is the smallest detail in the chapter and one of the most reassuring: flocks numerous enough to need counting, a shepherd unhurried enough to count them, and peace enough in the countryside for both. Nothing dramatic. Just a working farm in a land God had promised to empty and then promised to fill.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — A Righteous Branch, and a Name for the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, the days are coming when God will fulfil his promise to both houses (v. 14): I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land (v. 15). Then the name — and it has moved. Where chapter 23 gave it to the king, here it is the city that wears it: Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness' (v. 16). And two offices are guaranteed in perpetuity: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne (v. 17), and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer sacrifices forever (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The king's own name is handed to the people who live under him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the promise I made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the promise I made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah.

The verb is fulfill, and the object is a promise already made. God is not improvising a new plan to cope with the disaster; he is keeping an old word, and the disaster has not altered it.

In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.

The Branch returns. Ten chapters earlier, in the middle of an indictment of worthless shepherds, God had said Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land (23:5). Now the same promise is repeated to a man in prison in a city about to fall.

The image is agricultural and deliberately humble. A branch is what sprouts from a stump — which is what the house of David was about to become, with Zedekiah blinded and his sons dead. Out of that stump, a shoot. And spring up is the language of something growing quietly rather than being installed by force.

What he does when he comes is named in the plainest terms: justice and righteousness in the land. Not ceremony, not conquest. The two things chapter 22 said a king was for, and that the actual kings never delivered.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.' "For thus says the LORD: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'

Read this beside chapter 23 and you find one word changed, and it is a glorious change.

There, the name belonged to the king: this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness' (23:6). Here, the same name is given to the city — the name by which it will be called.

The king's name has passed to his people. What is true of him becomes the name over the place where they live, which is the whole doctrine of justification in a single editorial adjustment. His righteousness is not admired from a distance; it is worn by the community as its own address. Jerusalem is not renamed The City That Finally Got Its Act Together. It is called by his name, because the righteousness it lives on is his.

"For thus says the LORD: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,

This is the promise of 2 Samuel 7, restated at the moment of its apparent collapse: your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever (2 Sam 7:16).

Within a few years there would be no king in Jerusalem at all, and there never would be again in the old sense. The promise held anyway, and an angel told a girl in Nazareth how: the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32-33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — My Covenant with the Day and the Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stakes the throne and the altar on the sunrise: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time (v. 20), then the covenant with David and with the Levitical priests may be broken (v. 21). And rather than merely preserving them he promises increase in the terms sworn to Abraham: As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Anyone who wants the promise cancelled must first stop the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to make sacrifices forever." The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
verseByVerse.commentary:
and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to make sacrifices forever."

Alongside the endless throne, an endless altar. The temple was weeks from being burned and its priesthood scattered, and God promises that there will never be a moment without a priest in my presence making offerings.

Taken literally that promise failed twice over — the sacrifices stopped in 586, resumed, and stopped again in AD 70, this time for good. So either the word was broken, or it was pointing at a priesthood that does not depend on mortal men.

Hebrews takes the second view and explains what was always wrong with the Levitical arrangement: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Heb 7:23-24). The reason Israel needed a succession of priests was that each one kept dying. A priest who does not die needs no successor — and there has not been an hour since the cross when God has lacked a man in his presence offering, because he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb 7:25).

The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:

A new word begins, and the formula itself says something in a chapter about permanence. God keeps speaking to this prisoner, paragraph after paragraph, while the city burns down around him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time, then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken, so that he shall not have a son to reign on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests my ministers. As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levitical priests who minister to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time,

God offers a test anybody can attempt. Stop tomorrow morning from arriving.

Calling the sunrise a covenant is a striking way to describe creation's regularity. Day and night are not mere physics; they are God keeping an appointment he made, every twelve hours, without fail, in front of everyone.

then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken, so that he shall not have a son to reign on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests my ministers.

The logic is a chain with one hinge. Break the sunrise and you may argue about the throne; until then, the argument is closed.

And the man hearing this could see the Babylonian army from the courtyard. His own eyes told him the Davidic line was finished. God does not dispute the evidence of his eyes; he gives him a better one, available every morning.

As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levitical priests who minister to me."

Not merely preserved — multiplied, and in the exact terms of the oath to Abraham: I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Gen 22:17).

That is a promise of a royal family and a priesthood beyond counting, spoken over a dynasty about to lose its last king. It is hard to read it, on this side of the cross, without thinking of a kingdom of priests too many to number from every tribe and tongue.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — The Two Clans He Chose
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has heard what people are saying: The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose (v. 24) — a verdict that has left his people despised, no longer a nation in their sight. The answer runs on the same foundation as before: only If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth (v. 25) would he reject the offspring of Jacob and David. And the last words of the Book of Consolation are not argument but mercy: For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: The rumour was that God had finished with them; the reply ends in mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight. Thus says the LORD: If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight.

God has been listening to the talk, and he repeats it back. The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose — Israel and Judah, both apparently finished, and the conclusion drawn everywhere that God had changed his mind about his own election.

Notice the consequence: his people are despised and no longer a nation in their sight. When God's people are visibly defeated, the watching world does not usually conclude that God is disciplining them. It concludes that he has dropped them, or was never there.

Thus says the LORD: If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The same argument as before, now aimed at the rumour rather than at the prophet's doubt. God answers gossip about his faithfulness the way he answered his servant's confusion — by pointing at the sky.

And the name-stacking at the end is deliberate: Jacob, David, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob again. Every layer of the promise is named, so that rejecting this people would mean breaking all of it at once.

For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them."

And so the Book of Consolation ends, not with an argument won but with mercy.

Weigh where these four chapters have come from. They were written by a man in custody, in a city eating itself, under a king who would be blinded, about a temple that would be ash within months — and they contain the new covenant, the everlasting love, the sins remembered no more, the healed wound, the field bought in faith, the Branch, and this last word of mercy. The circumstances never improved while he wrote. The revelation simply got better.

That is the answer to the invitation at the head of the chapter. He called, and God told him great and hidden things he had not known — and the greatest of them was a name he would not live to hear anyone use, given first to a king and then handed to his people: The LORD is our righteousness.

33.title: Call to Me and I Will Answer You
33.overview:
A second word comes to Jeremiah while he is still imprisoned in the court of the guard, from the God who made the earth and formed it to stand, with an invitation to call on him and be told great and hidden things he does not know (vv. 1-3).

The city is pulling down its own houses for rubble against the siege ramps, and those barricades will be filled with the dead, because God has hidden his face from the city for its evil. Then he promises health and healing, the restoration of both Judah and Israel as they were at first, and cleansing and forgiveness of all the guilt of their sin and rebellion — until the city becomes a name of joy and a praise before all the nations, who will tremble at the good God does for it (vv. 4-9).

In the place everyone calls a waste there will again be the voice of mirth and gladness, of bridegroom and bride, and worshippers singing that his steadfast love endures forever; shepherds will rest their flocks across the hill country, the Shephelah, the Negeb, Benjamin and Judah, and flocks will pass again under the hand of the one who counts them (vv. 10-13).

God will fulfil his promise: a righteous Branch for David who executes justice and righteousness, Judah saved and Jerusalem secure — and the city itself will be called The LORD is our righteousness. David will never lack a man on the throne, nor the Levitical priests a man in God's presence (vv. 14-18). All of it is staked on the covenant with day and night: break the sunrise and the throne may be broken too, and instead of merely surviving, David's offspring will be multiplied like the stars and the sand (vv. 19-22). To those saying the LORD has rejected the two clans he chose, the same answer is given, and the Book of Consolation ends in mercy (vv. 23-26).
33.theology:
God's answer to a faithful man in a bad situation is often not a changed situation but a further word about himself — and he invites the bewildered to ask for more (vv. 1-3).

The real cause of a city's collapse is the hidden face of God, not the engineering of its enemies (v. 5).

Forgiveness and cleansing are both promised and both needed: one deals with the record, the other with the stain, and the offence is personal — sin against me (v. 8).

Grace on this scale is itself awe-inducing; the nations tremble at the good God does (v. 9).

The sounds God once silenced he gives back item by item, and the song of the restored is sung by people who watched the worst happen (v. 11; 7:34; 16:9; Ps 136:1).

The Branch springs from a stump, and the king's own name passes to his people: what chapter 23 gave to him, this chapter gives to the city (vv. 15-16; 23:5-6). That is justification in one editorial change.

The endless priesthood could not be kept by mortal priests, who kept dying; it is kept by one who does not (v. 18; Heb 7:23-25). And the throne promised at 2 Sam 7:16 was fulfilled past the end of the monarchy (Luke 1:32-33).

God answers both private doubt and public rumour the same way: by pointing at the sunrise he keeps as a covenant (vv. 20, 25).
33.examples:
A second sermon delivered to a man still in the same cell.

Tearing down your own bedroom to plug a breach for one more afternoon.

Barricades that end up packed with the men who built them.

All the guilt, said twice, in one verse.

Nations trembling at God's generosity rather than his judgment.

Wedding voices returned to streets where God had silenced them.

A shepherd unhurried enough to count his sheep.

A branch out of a stump, weeks before the stump was cut.

The king's name written over the city's gate.

Stop tomorrow morning from arriving, and then we will talk.

And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With Nebuchadnezzar's army and all the kingdoms of the earth under his dominion attacking Jerusalem (v. 1), Jeremiah is sent to the king with a message that gives and takes in the same breath. The city will be burned and Zedekiah captured — You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face (v. 3) — and yet: You shall not die by the sword. You shall die in peace, with spices burned and mourners crying Alas, lord! as for the kings before him (vv. 4-5). Jeremiah delivers it while the army is reducing the last fortified towns, Lachish and Azekah (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A promise of an honourable funeral, offered to a king who will be blinded first.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army and all the kingdoms of the earth under his dominion and all the peoples were fighting against Jerusalem and all of its cities: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire. You shall not escape from his hand but shall surely be captured and delivered into his hand. You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face. And you shall go to Babylon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army and all the kingdoms of the earth under his dominion and all the peoples were fighting against Jerusalem and all of its cities:

The scale is spelled out to make the odds plain: not merely Babylon but every vassal nation in the empire, conscripted into the siege lines. Jerusalem is facing the known world.

"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.

And the prophet is sent to the palace with it. Not a written note — Go and speak to Zedekiah, face to face, the man who had already imprisoned him for saying this.

You shall not escape from his hand but shall surely be captured and delivered into his hand. You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face. And you shall go to Babylon.'

The phrase eye to eye had been used of this king before (32:4), and its fulfilment was exact in a way nobody would have wanted. Zedekiah was brought before Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, made to watch his sons executed, and then blinded. He did meet him eye to eye, and it was the last thing he ever saw.

God's words come true in their detail, and the detail is not always the comfort we imagined when we heard them.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah! Thus says the LORD concerning you: 'You shall not die by the sword. You shall die in peace. And as spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so people shall burn spices for you and lament for you, saying, "Alas, lord!"' For I have spoken the word, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah! Thus says the LORD concerning you: 'You shall not die by the sword.

Yet. After the sentence, a concession — and it is addressed to him personally, by name and title, with an urgency that reads almost like pleading.

You shall die in peace. And as spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so people shall burn spices for you and lament for you, saying, "Alas, lord!"' For I have spoken the word, declares the LORD."

What is offered is a decent death and a proper funeral: the royal spices, the formal lament, the cry Alas, lord! that had been denied to Jehoiakim, who was promised the burial of a donkey (22:18-19).

It is a strange mercy. Zedekiah will lose his city, his sons and his sight, and be told he will die in his bed with mourners at the door. But weigh it against the alternative he was courting, and against the treatment his brother received, and it is real. God keeps a kindness back even for a weak and faithless king.

And the guarantee is the same one attached to every threat in this book: For I have spoken the word. The promise of the funeral rests on exactly the authority as the promise of the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah, in Jerusalem, when the army of the king of Babylon was fighting against Jerusalem and against all the cities of Judah that were left, Lachish and Azekah, for these were the only fortified cities of Judah that remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah, in Jerusalem,

All these words. He delivered the funeral and the fire, the concession and the sentence, without editing either half to suit the audience. It is the same obedience as chapter 26: do not hold back a word.

when the army of the king of Babylon was fighting against Jerusalem and against all the cities of Judah that were left, Lachish and Azekah, for these were the only fortified cities of Judah that remained.

Two names, and they date the scene precisely. Lachish and Azekah were the last strongpoints in the Judean lowlands, and archaeologists digging at Lachish found a guardroom of ostraca — letters written on pottery by officers in these very weeks. One of them reports that the signal fires of Azekah could no longer be seen.

That is the situation in which the next paragraph happens. The kingdom has been reduced to a capital and two garrisons, the beacons are going out one by one, and in that atmosphere the king of Judah decides to do something religious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — The Proclamation and the Reversal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah makes a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to make a proclamation of liberty to them (v. 8), freeing every Hebrew slave, so that no one should enslave a Jew, his brother (v. 9). And it works — They obeyed and set them free (v. 10). Then, in one of the ugliest sentences in the book, But afterward they turned around and took back the male and female slaves they had set free (v. 11). God answers by citing the law they were keeping for a week: he had commanded release every seventh year when he brought them out of the house of slavery (vv. 13-14). They had recently repented and did what was right in my eyes — and then turned around and profaned my name (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The reform lasted exactly as long as the siege did.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to make a proclamation of liberty to them, that everyone should set free his Hebrew slaves, male and female, so that no one should enslave a Jew, his brother. And they obeyed, all the officials and all the people who had entered into the covenant that everyone would set free his slave, male or female, so that they would not be enslaved again. They obeyed and set them free. But afterward they turned around and took back the male and female slaves they had set free, and brought them into subjection as slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to make a proclamation of liberty to them, that everyone should set free his Hebrew slaves, male and female, so that no one should enslave a Jew, his brother.

And for one moment, Judah does the right thing.

This is a genuine reform, formally covenanted, and its wording is beautiful: no one should enslave a Jew, his brother. The word brother is the argument. A fellow Israelite is not labour to be owned; he is family.

The motive was almost certainly the siege. With the enemy at the wall, freeing slaves put more men on the ramparts and fewer mouths in private households, and a public act of obedience might move God to relent. Repentance under pressure is still repentance, and God takes it at face value in verse 15.

And they obeyed, all the officials and all the people who had entered into the covenant that everyone would set free his slave, male or female, so that they would not be enslaved again. They obeyed and set them free.

The verse says They obeyed twice. In a book where nobody obeys anything, the narrator lingers on it. For a few days in the last months of Judah, the law of Moses was actually kept in Jerusalem.

But afterward they turned around and took back the male and female slaves they had set free, and brought them into subjection as slaves.

And then the sentence that ruins it.

Read what it describes. Men and women who had been told they were free — who had walked out of their owners' houses, perhaps found family, started to plan a life — were rounded up and put back. Somebody had to go and fetch them. It is one thing never to free a slave; it is another to free him, watch him taste it, and then take it back.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I myself made a covenant with your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, saying, 'At the end of seven years each of you must set free the fellow Hebrew who has been sold to you and has served you six years; you must set him free from your service.' But your fathers did not listen to me or incline their ears to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I myself made a covenant with your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, saying,

God's answer begins with the exodus, and the phrase he chooses is the knife: out of the house of slavery. He is talking to slave-owners who have just re-enslaved their brothers, and he identifies himself as the God who empties houses of slavery.

Everything Israel possessed came out of that rescue. To hold a fellow Hebrew in bondage was to contradict the event that made them a people at all.

'At the end of seven years each of you must set free the fellow Hebrew who has been sold to you and has served you six years; you must set him free from your service.' But your fathers did not listen to me or incline their ears to me.

The law being quoted is Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 — six years of service, release in the seventh, he shall go out free, for nothing (Exod 21:2). It was not an obscure statute. It was one of the first ordinances given after Sinai, designed precisely so that poverty could never become a permanent status in Israel.

And it had been ignored for centuries — your fathers did not listen to me or incline their ears to me. Zedekiah's proclamation was not an innovation but the overdue obedience of generations, which makes its reversal worse. They restored a law their ancestors had let lapse, and then let it lapse again within the month.

verseByVerse.quote: You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes by proclaiming liberty, each to his neighbor, and you made a covenant before me in the house that is called by my name, but then you turned around and profaned my name when each of you took back his male and female slaves, whom you had set free according to their desire, and you brought them into subjection to be your slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes by proclaiming liberty, each to his neighbor, and you made a covenant before me in the house that is called by my name,

God gives them full credit for it. You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes — he does not dismiss the reform as insincere theatre, even though the timing was self-interested. It was right, and he says so.

And the setting is noted: the covenant was made in the house that is called by my name, in the temple, with God as witness to a promise about other people's freedom.

but then you turned around and profaned my name when each of you took back his male and female slaves, whom you had set free according to their desire, and you brought them into subjection to be your slaves.

The charge is profaned my name. Not merely broke a promise, not merely wronged the poor — dragged God's reputation through it, because his name had been invoked over the transaction.

That is what makes a broken religious commitment different in kind from a broken private one. When a vow is made before God and then reversed, the watching world learns something false about God.

And notice the small phrase according to their desire. The freed slaves wanted their freedom. Of course they did. The masters knew it, and took it away anyway.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sentence is built from their own word. You have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty, God says, so behold, I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine (v. 17). And the men who broke the covenant are handed the ceremony they used to ratify it: I will make them like the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts (v. 18) — officials, eunuchs, priests and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: They walked between the halves of a dead animal to seal their promise, and became the animal.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, thus says the LORD: You have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother and to his neighbor; behold, I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine, declares the LORD. I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth. And the men who transgressed my covenant and did not keep the terms of the covenant that they made before me, I will make them like the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts— the officials of Judah, the officials of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore, thus says the LORD: You have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother and to his neighbor; behold, I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine, declares the LORD. I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.

God takes their own word and turns it round, and the result is one of the grimmest lines in Scripture. You would not proclaim liberty, so I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine.

The sword, plague and famine are given their freedom. The three judgments that have stalked this book are released into the city like slaves let out of a house — the only emancipation Jerusalem will get, because it refused the one it had promised.

Sin is answered in its own coin here. Refuse to release, and something else gets released.

And the men who transgressed my covenant and did not keep the terms of the covenant that they made before me, I will make them like the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts —

Now we learn how the ceremony had been conducted. They had cut a calf in half, laid the two halves apart, and walked between them — the oldest and most graphic form of covenant-making, whose meaning is unmistakable: may this be done to me if I break my word. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is more compressed than the English here, lacking "them like", which leaves the identification even starker.

It is the ceremony of Genesis 15. Abram cut the animals and laid the halves against each other (Gen 15:10), and then, in the dark, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces (Gen 15:17) — God walking the path alone, taking the curse of the covenant on himself while Abram slept.

the officials of Judah, the officials of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf.

The list names everyone who took that walk, and the sentence is simply that the oath be honoured. They asked for it in the temple, in front of witnesses, with a dead animal at their feet.

And this is where the chapter turns toward the gospel, because there are only two ways the curse of a broken covenant can fall. It can fall on the one who broke it, as here. Or it can fall on someone who walks the bloody path alone in the dark on his behalf — which is what God did for Abram, and what he did at the cross for covenant-breakers who have taken back every freedom they ever promised.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The Army That Withdrew Will Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Their bodies will be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth (v. 20), and Zedekiah and his officials will be given to the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you (v. 21) — the detail that explains the whole chapter. God will recall it: Behold, I will command, declares the LORD, and will bring them back to this city. And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The relief that made them confident enough to re-enslave their brothers was temporary.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give them into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives. Their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth. And Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives, into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you. Behold, I will command, declares the LORD, and will bring them back to this city. And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I will give them into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives. Their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth.

No burial. The men who had denied their brothers a life will be denied a grave, left in the open for scavengers — the ancient world's picture of total disgrace.

Set it beside verse 5, where the king is promised spices and mourners. God distinguishes between people, and the difference here is not rank.

And Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives, into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you.

And there, at last, is the explanation of the whole chapter: the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you.

The siege had lifted. Egypt had marched north, and Nebuchadnezzar pulled back to deal with it, and suddenly the pressure was off. That is when the slaves were taken back. The covenant had been made when the ramps were rising; it was revoked when the dust cleared and the fields were safe to work again.

It is a devastating diagnosis of a certain kind of religion — sincere while frightened, and no longer required once the danger passes. The vow made in the hospital corridor, forgotten in the car park. Peter described the pattern without mercy: the last state has become worse for them than the first (2 Pet 2:20).

Behold, I will command, declares the LORD, and will bring them back to this city. And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant."

God recalls the army. I will command — Nebuchadnezzar will think he is choosing his moment, and he will be answering an order he never heard.

And the chapter ends by leaving the word liberty ringing. Judah proclaimed it, took it back, and lost everything. Centuries later a man stood up in a synagogue in Nazareth, read that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him to proclaim liberty to the captives, and told the room it was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:18). He proclaimed it and did not take it back. For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery (Gal 5:1) — which is the one warning this chapter exists to give.

34.title: Liberty Proclaimed and Taken Back
34.overview:
While Nebuchadnezzar and every nation under his rule are besieging Jerusalem, Jeremiah is sent to Zedekiah in person: the city will be burned and the king captured and taken to Babylon, seeing Nebuchadnezzar eye to eye. Yet he will not die by the sword but in peace, with royal spices burned and mourners lamenting for him. Jeremiah delivers it all while Lachish and Azekah, the last fortified cities, are still holding (vv. 1-7).

Zedekiah then makes a covenant in the temple with all the people to proclaim liberty, freeing every Hebrew slave so that no one should enslave his brother — and they obey and set them free. Afterward they turn round and take the freed slaves back into subjection (vv. 8-11).

God answers by recalling the exodus from the house of slavery and the law of release in the seventh year, which their fathers had ignored. He credits them with genuine repentance in proclaiming liberty, and then charges them with profaning his name by reversing it (vv. 12-16).

Since they would not proclaim liberty, God proclaims liberty to the sword, pestilence and famine, and makes the covenant-breakers like the calf they cut in two and walked between — officials, eunuchs, priests and people alike, their bodies left unburied (vv. 17-20). Zedekiah and his officials will be handed to the Babylonian army that has withdrawn; God will command it back to take the city and burn it (vv. 21-22).
34.theology:
God's word comes true in its detail, and the detail is not always the comfort we assumed: Zedekiah did meet Nebuchadnezzar eye to eye, and was then blinded (v. 3).

God keeps a kindness back even for a weak and faithless king, and the promise of a decent funeral rests on the same authority as the promise of the fire (vv. 4-5).

Repentance under pressure is still repentance, and God credits it honestly (v. 15). But a vow made in God's name and then reversed profanes that name, because the watching world learns something false about him (v. 16).

Sin is answered in its own coin. Refuse to release, and God releases sword, famine and pestilence instead (v. 17).

The curse of a broken covenant falls either on the breaker or on a substitute. They became the calf they walked between; God himself walked that path alone for Abram in the dark, and again at the cross (vv. 18-19; Gen 15:10, 17).

Religion that is sincere only while the danger lasts is exposed the moment the siege lifts (v. 21; 2 Pet 2:20).

Liberty proclaimed and withdrawn by Judah is proclaimed and never withdrawn by Christ (Isa 61:1; Luke 4:18; Gal 5:1).
34.examples:
Every nation in the empire drafted into one siege line.

Spices and mourners promised to a king who will be blinded.

Officers at Lachish writing that Azekah's signal fires had gone out.

They obeyed — said twice, in a book where nobody obeys.

Somebody had to go and fetch the freed slaves back.

Freedom taken away from people who plainly wanted it.

Liberty granted to the sword, the plague and the famine.

Walking between the halves of a calf, and becoming it.

A vow made in the hospital corridor and forgotten in the car park.

An emperor obeying an order he never heard.

35.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:<sup>2</sup>"Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them and bring them to the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers; then offer them wine to drink."<sup>3</sup>So I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah and his brothers and all his sons and the whole house of the Rechabites.<sup>4</sup>I brought them to the house of the LORD into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was near the chamber of the officials, above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, keeper of the threshold.<sup>5</sup>Then I set before the Rechabites pitchers full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, "Drink wine."<sup>6</sup>But they answered, "We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, 'You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons forever.<sup>7</sup>You shall not build a house; you shall not sow seed; you shall not plant or have a vineyard; but you shall live in tents all your days, that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn.'<sup>8</sup>We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us, to drink no wine all our days, ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters,<sup>9</sup>and not to build houses to dwell in. We have no vineyard or field or seed,<sup>10</sup>but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us.<sup>11</sup>But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, 'Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians.' So we are living in Jerusalem."<sup>12</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>13</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Go and say to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? declares the LORD.<sup>14</sup>The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command. I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.<sup>15</sup>I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, saying, 'Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, and do not go after other gods to serve them, and then you shall dwell in the land that I gave to you and your fathers.' But you did not incline your ear or listen to me.<sup>16</sup>The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have kept the command that their father gave them, but this people has not obeyed me.<sup>17</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered."<sup>18</sup>But to the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you,<sup>19</sup>therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Wine Set Before the Rechabites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Jehoiakim's reign God gives Jeremiah an odd instruction: Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them and bring them to the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers; then offer them wine to drink (v. 2). He fetches Jaazaniah and the whole clan and brings them into a room in the temple complex — the chamber of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, next to the officials' chamber and above that of the keeper of the threshold (v. 4). Then the staging is complete: Then I set before the Rechabites pitchers full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, "Drink wine." (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet sets out drinks in the temple and presses them on men he knows will refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them and bring them to the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers; then offer them wine to drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:

The date takes us back. Jehoiakim died in 598, so this episode belongs years before the siege chapters on either side of it. The book is arranged by theme here rather than by calendar, and this chapter has been placed next to the broken covenant of chapter 34 for a reason: there, men who promised obedience to God reneged within weeks; here, men who never promised God anything have kept their word for generations.

"Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them and bring them to the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers; then offer them wine to drink."

It is one of the strangest commands given to any prophet. Fetch a particular family, take them into the temple, and put wine in front of them.

God knows exactly what will happen. This is not a test of the Rechabites, who are in no danger of failing it; it is a piece of theatre with an audience in mind, and the audience is Judah. Jeremiah has smashed a flask and worn a yoke; now the visual aid is a group of teetotal nomads and a tray of drinks.

verseByVerse.quote: So I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah and his brothers and all his sons and the whole house of the Rechabites. I brought them to the house of the LORD into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was near the chamber of the officials, above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, keeper of the threshold. Then I set before the Rechabites pitchers full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, "Drink wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah and his brothers and all his sons and the whole house of the Rechabites.

Names, and a whole household — brothers, sons, the entire clan. Their head happens to share the prophet's name, which is a coincidence the narrator lets stand.

Who were they? Descendants of Jonadab son of Rechab, and that man appears once elsewhere in Scripture, riding in Jehu's chariot during the purge of Baal worship. Jehu asked him, Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?, and then said Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD (2 Kgs 10:15-16). So the family's founder was a man known for his allegiance, two and a half centuries before this scene.

I brought them to the house of the LORD into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was near the chamber of the officials, above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, keeper of the threshold.

The address is given with a surveyor's precision — whose room, next to which, above which. The point of the detail is that this happened somewhere real, with officials in the adjoining rooms who could look in.

Then I set before the Rechabites pitchers full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, "Drink wine."

Not a token glass. Pitchers full of wine, and cups, laid out properly, with a prophet of the LORD in the temple of the LORD telling them to help themselves.

Every pressure in the scene runs one way. The setting is sacred, the host is a man of God, the invitation is direct, and refusing would look rude and possibly impious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — We Will Drink No Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They decline, and give their reason: We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us — no wine ever, and further, You shall not build a house; you shall not sow seed; you shall not plant or have a vineyard; but you shall live in tents all your days (vv. 6-7). Their account of themselves is simple: We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us (v. 8); We have no vineyard or field or seed (v. 9); but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us (v. 10). And one honest exception: they came inside the walls for fear of the army of the Chaldeans, so we are living in Jerusalem (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Two and a half centuries of obedience to a man none of them had ever met.

verseByVerse.quote: But they answered, "We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, 'You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons forever. You shall not build a house; you shall not sow seed; you shall not plant or have a vineyard; but you shall live in tents all your days, that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they answered, "We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, 'You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons forever.

They do not hesitate and they do not argue. They simply cite their father.

Notice what they do not say. They do not claim wine is evil, or that God forbade it, or that they are holier for abstaining. Their whole reason is that Jonadab told them not to. Their obedience does not need a justification beyond the person who gave the command.

You shall not build a house; you shall not sow seed; you shall not plant or have a vineyard; but you shall live in tents all your days, that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn.'

The rule is wider than drink. No houses, no crops, no vineyards, tents only. It is a deliberate refusal of settled life, and the likeliest reason is spiritual: Canaanite religion was bound up with agriculture, with Baal as the god of rain and harvest, and a family that owned no fields had less to be tempted by. The tents kept them strangers.

And a purpose is attached — that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn. Even the word sojourn concedes that the land was not theirs. The Rechabites were resident aliens who had made peace with never settling down.

It must be said plainly that God nowhere commanded this. It is a family rule, not a law of Moses. Scripture does record a God-given abstinence — the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD, in which a man shall separate himself from wine and strong drink (Num 6:2-3) — but that was voluntary, usually temporary, and instituted by God. Nothing here is being held up as a standard for Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us, to drink no wine all our days, ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters, and not to build houses to dwell in. We have no vineyard or field or seed, but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us. But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, 'Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians.' So we are living in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us, to drink no wine all our days, ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters, and not to build houses to dwell in. We have no vineyard or field or seed,

The report is in the plural and covers everybody — wives, sons, daughters. This was not one impressive individual but a culture, handed down until it was simply how the family lived.

And it cost them. We have no vineyard or field or seed is a statement of poverty. Generation after generation watched their neighbours plant, harvest, build and inherit, and stayed in tents.

but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us.

The verb obeyed appears again, and it is the word the whole chapter turns on. In a book where Judah has not obeyed anything, here is a family whose summary of two and a half centuries is: we did what we were told.

But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, 'Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians.' So we are living in Jerusalem."

And here they volunteer the exception, which is the most attractive thing about them. They are not in a tent as they speak; they are inside city walls, in a room in the temple, because an army was in the countryside.

They do not pretend otherwise and God does not reproach them for it. Their obedience was intelligent rather than wooden: the rule existed to keep them separate from Canaan's settled religion, not to get them killed by Babylonian cavalry. That distinction — between the purpose of a command and its letter — is one the people next door in the temple had never learned to make in either direction.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Will You Not Receive Instruction?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the sermon the whole scene was arranged for: Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? (v. 13). Jonadab's command about wine has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command — and then the contrast, in the adverb that runs through this book: I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me (v. 14). God sent all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, with a simple message — Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds — and you did not incline your ear or listen to me (v. 15). So the disaster comes, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: A dead man's house rule was kept for centuries; the living God's word was not kept for a generation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Go and say to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? declares the LORD. The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command. I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Go and say to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? declares the LORD.

The demonstration is over and the sermon begins, and it turns out the Rechabites were never the subject. They were the exhibit.

Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? The question is put to Judah with the tray of untouched wine still in the room.

The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command. I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.

Set the two halves of that verse side by side, because the comparison is the whole point.

On one side: a command from a man long dead, about a matter of no moral weight, with no sanction attached, kept for eight or nine generations. On the other: the word of the living God, on matters of life and death, backed by every warning and every mercy, delivered persistently by prophet after prophet — and ignored.

The argument is not that the Rechabites were righteous. It is that Judah cannot plead difficulty. Obedience across centuries is evidently possible, because a family of nomads managed it over wine. What Judah lacked was not capacity but willingness, and the untouched pitchers proved it in front of witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, saying, 'Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, and do not go after other gods to serve them, and then you shall dwell in the land that I gave to you and your fathers.' But you did not incline your ear or listen to me. The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have kept the command that their father gave them, but this people has not obeyed me. Therefore, thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, saying, 'Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, and do not go after other gods to serve them, and then you shall dwell in the land that I gave to you and your fathers.' But you did not incline your ear or listen to me.

Notice how reasonable the message had been. Not a demand for tents or abstinence — Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, with the promise of keeping the land attached. God asked less of Judah than Jonadab asked of his sons, and offered more for compliance.

And the word persistently appears a second time in three verses. This is the pathos of the whole book: God as the sender who will not stop sending.

The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have kept the command that their father gave them, but this people has not obeyed me.

The comparison is stated once more, stripped to its bones, and the pronoun at the end lands hard. The charge is not that they failed to keep a code, but that this people has not obeyed me. Disobedience in this book is always personal.

Therefore, thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered."

The sentence is grounded in a conversation that never happened. I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered. Two attempts, two silences.

God does not list idols or injustices here, though the book has catalogued both. The charge at the end is simply that he kept speaking and they never replied.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–19 — Never Lack a Man to Stand Before Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last word is a blessing on the visual aid. Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you (v. 18), God promises: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The same promise given to David's throne and Levi's altar, handed to a clan from outside the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you, therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But to the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you,

And before the chapter closes God turns to the men who had been used as an illustration, and speaks to them for their own sake.

They had been brought to the temple to make a point and had not asked for any of this. God gives them a word of their own, and it begins with a full recital of what they did right.

therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me."

Weigh that promise against the one given two chapters earlier. David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne, and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence (33:17-18). The formula is identical, and here it is given to a clan that was not one of the twelve tribes at all — a family of Kenite outsiders, attached to Israel but not descended from Jacob.

And to stand before me is priestly language, the posture of a servant in the sanctuary. Outsiders are promised a permanent place in God's presence in the same breath that insiders are told their city will burn. The book has been moving this way for a while, and it is where the gospel goes: a household with no tribal claim, blessed for faithfulness, given standing before God.

Their tents turn out to have been preaching all along. Abraham had lived the same way, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, because he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Heb 11:9-10). Men who refused to build houses were saying, for two hundred and fifty years, that they were not home yet.

And a last word so nobody mistakes the lesson. This chapter is not a call to abstinence or to canvas. God never issued the Rechabite rule, and the Lord himself warned about the trick of treating human tradition as divine command: So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God (Matt 15:6). He came eating and drinking and was slandered for it, while John came eating no bread and drinking no wine and was called demon-possessed (Luke 7:33-34) — the same crowd finding fault either way. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17). The pitchers were only ever a mirror, and the question they asked was never about wine: he has spoken to you persistently. Have you answered?

35.title: The Rechabites
35.overview:
Back in the days of Jehoiakim, God sends Jeremiah to fetch the whole clan of the Rechabites, bring them into a chamber of the temple, set pitchers of wine and cups before them, and tell them to drink (vv. 1-5).

They refuse, citing their ancestor Jonadab son of Rechab, who had commanded his descendants never to drink wine, never to build houses, sow seed or plant vineyards, but to live in tents. They report that they have kept all of it — no vineyard, no field, no seed — for generations, with one honest exception: they are currently inside Jerusalem because of the Babylonian and Syrian armies (vv. 6-11).

Then comes the sermon the demonstration was arranged for. A dead man's rule about wine has been kept for centuries, while God has spoken to Judah persistently and sent prophet after prophet with a far more reasonable message — turn from your evil way and amend your deeds, and keep the land — and Judah did not incline its ear. So all the disaster God pronounced is coming, because he spoke and they did not listen, he called and they did not answer (vv. 12-17).

Finally God speaks to the Rechabites for their own sake, and because they obeyed their father's command he promises that Jonadab son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before him (vv. 18-19).
35.theology:
The chapter is comparative, not prescriptive. God never gave the Rechabite rule, and it is held up as an example of constancy rather than a standard of holiness (vv. 6-7; Num 6:2-3; Matt 15:6; Rom 14:17).

Judah cannot plead difficulty. Sustained obedience is demonstrably possible, and God asked less of Judah than Jonadab asked of his sons while offering more for compliance (vv. 14-15).

Obedience can be intelligent without being slack: the Rechabites came inside the walls during a war, and God does not reproach them, because they understood what the rule was for (v. 11).

Disobedience is personal. The charge is not that they broke a code but that this people has not obeyed me, and that God spoke and called while they neither listened nor answered (vv. 16-17).

Outsiders are promised standing in God's presence in the same breath that insiders are told their city will burn. The formula given to David's throne and Levi's altar is given to a Kenite household (v. 19; 33:17-18).
