Tents preach. A family that refused to build houses was saying for centuries that it was not home yet, which is exactly what Abraham's tents meant (Heb 11:9-10).
35.examples:
Pitchers and cups laid out in the temple by a prophet who knew they would not be touched.

A founder remembered for one ride in Jehu's chariot.

Obeying a man none of them had ever met.

Watching the neighbours plant vineyards for two hundred and fifty years.

Admitting they were in a house, not a tent, and why.

A rule about wine kept longer than a covenant about God.

God asking less than Jonadab and being refused.

Two attempts, two silences.

The promise of David's throne handed to outsiders.

36.text: <sup>1</sup>In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD:<sup>2</sup>"Take a scroll and write on it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah until today.<sup>3</sup>It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin."<sup>4</sup>Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD that he had spoken to him.<sup>5</sup>And Jeremiah ordered Baruch, saying, "I am banned from going to the house of the LORD,<sup>6</sup>so you are to go, and on a day of fasting in the hearing of all the people in the LORD's house you shall read the words of the LORD from the scroll that you have written at my dictation. You shall read them also in the hearing of all the men of Judah who come out of their cities.<sup>7</sup>It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the LORD has pronounced against this people."<sup>8</sup>And Baruch the son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him about reading from the scroll the words of the LORD in the LORD's house.<sup>9</sup>In the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem proclaimed a fast before the LORD.<sup>10</sup>Then, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the scroll, in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the secretary, which was in the upper court, at the entry of the New Gate of the LORD's house.<sup>11</sup>When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,<sup>12</sup>he went down to the king's house, into the secretary's chamber, and all the officials were sitting there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the officials.<sup>13</sup>And Micaiah told them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the scroll in the hearing of the people.<sup>14</sup>Then all the officials sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi, to say to Baruch, "Take in your hand the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come." So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.<sup>15</sup>And they said to him, "Sit down and read it." So Baruch read it to them.<sup>16</sup>When they heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear. And they said to Baruch, "We must report all these words to the king."<sup>17</sup>Then they asked Baruch, "Tell us, please, how did you write all these words? Was it at his dictation?"<sup>18</sup>Baruch answered them, "He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll."<sup>19</sup>Then the officials said to Baruch, "Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are."<sup>20</sup>So they went into the court to the king, having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the secretary, and they reported all the words to the king.<sup>21</sup>Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the secretary. And Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who stood beside the king.<sup>22</sup>It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him.<sup>23</sup>As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the fire pot.<sup>24</sup>Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.<sup>25</sup>Even when Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them.<sup>26</sup>And the king commanded Jerahmeel the king's son and Seraiah the son of Azriel and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet, but the LORD hid them.<sup>27</sup>Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>28</sup>"Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.<sup>29</sup>And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, 'Thus says the LORD, You have burned this scroll, saying, "Why have you written in it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cut off from it man and beast?"<sup>30</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night.<sup>31</sup>And I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring upon them and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem and upon the people of Judah all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, but they would not hear.'"<sup>32</sup>Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote on it at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Write It on a Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Jehoiakim's fourth year God tells Jeremiah to Take a scroll and write on it all the words that I have spoken to you, twenty-three years of preaching (v. 2), with a stated hope: It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin (v. 3). Baruch writes it at Jeremiah's dictation (v. 4), and since the prophet is banned from going to the house of the LORD (v. 5), Baruch must read it publicly — again in hope that every one will turn from his evil way (v. 7). And he does it (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-three years of sermons copied out, on the chance that somebody might still repent.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Take a scroll and write on it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah until today. It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Take a scroll and write on it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah until today.

The fourth year of Jehoiakim is 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar beat Egypt at Carchemish and became the fact everyone had to live with. And Jeremiah is told to make a book.

Count the span: from the days of Josiah until today. He had begun in Josiah's thirteenth year, so this is twenty-three years of preaching to be collected into one document — the sermons nobody acted on, gathered up and written down.

It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin."

And here is why God wanted it written, in words that should govern how the whole book is read: It may be.

The scroll is not an archive for the record, or evidence for the prosecution. It is an attempt. The aim is that they might turn, and the goal beyond that is forgiveness — that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin. Every threat in the collection exists to make the pardon possible.

Twenty-three years of being ignored had not changed God's purpose in speaking. He was still trying.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD that he had spoken to him. And Jeremiah ordered Baruch, saying, "I am banned from going to the house of the LORD,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD that he had spoken to him.

Baruch takes his place in the story, and the mechanics are stated plainly: Jeremiah spoke, Baruch wrote. Two men and a great deal of ink.

Something quietly important is happening in this verse. The prophetic word is moving from air into text, where it can be carried, copied, read in rooms the prophet cannot enter, and survive him. This chapter is the Bible describing its own production.

And Jeremiah ordered Baruch, saying, "I am banned from going to the house of the LORD,

The reason for the arrangement is a restraining order. The prophet is barred from the temple — presumably since the trial of chapter 26, or the confrontation of chapter 20.

So the man with the message cannot reach the place where the crowds are. And God's response to that obstacle is not to remove it but to route around it: if the preacher is banned, send the book.

verseByVerse.quote: so you are to go, and on a day of fasting in the hearing of all the people in the LORD's house you shall read the words of the LORD from the scroll that you have written at my dictation. You shall read them also in the hearing of all the men of Judah who come out of their cities. It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the LORD has pronounced against this people." And Baruch the son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him about reading from the scroll the words of the LORD in the LORD's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so you are to go, and on a day of fasting in the hearing of all the people in the LORD's house you shall read the words of the LORD from the scroll that you have written at my dictation. You shall read them also in the hearing of all the men of Judah who come out of their cities.

The instructions are strategic. A fast day, when the temple is full and the mood is already serious, and an audience including country people up from the towns. Maximum hearing for one reading.

And notice what is asked of Baruch. He is to stand in the temple and read aloud a document predicting national ruin, in the name of a man the king has banned, to a crowd that has beaten and imprisoned that man before. The scribe is taking the prophet's risk with none of the prophet's calling.

It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the LORD has pronounced against this people."

It may be, a second time, now on Jeremiah's own lips. He had no illusions left about his audience and he still would not close the door.

That hope and the sentence in the same breath — great is the anger and wrath — is the whole posture of faithful preaching. The severity is exactly what makes the appeal urgent.

And Baruch the son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him about reading from the scroll the words of the LORD in the LORD's house.

One flat sentence of obedience. He did all of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — Read It to the Officials
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On a fast day in the fifth year Baruch reads the scroll in the temple, in Gemariah's chamber at the entry of the New Gate (v. 10). Gemariah's son Micaiah carries word to the palace, where the officials are sitting (vv. 11-12), and they send for Baruch: Sit down and read it (v. 15). Their reaction is the opposite of their king's — they turned one to another in fear, and said We must report all these words to the king (v. 16). They ask how it was written, and Baruch tells them: He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll (v. 18). Then they do the decent thing: Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The civil servants were frightened by the book, and warned the men who wrote it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem proclaimed a fast before the LORD. Then, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the scroll, in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the secretary, which was in the upper court, at the entry of the New Gate of the LORD's house. When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem proclaimed a fast before the LORD.

A year has passed between the command and the reading — the scroll took time to write, and the right day had to come. The fast in the ninth month was probably called because of Babylon; fear makes people religious, as chapter 34 showed.

Then, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the scroll, in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the secretary, which was in the upper court, at the entry of the New Gate of the LORD's house.

The location is given exactly, and two details in it carry weight. The chamber belongs to a son of Shaphan — that family again, whose members keep turning up on the right side of this story, as Ahikam did when he saved Jeremiah's life (26:24). Somebody sympathetic lent Baruch a room.

And it stands at the entry of the New Gate, which is where the officials had convened the court that acquitted Jeremiah (26:10). The book is being read at the spot where its author was once tried.

When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,

Three generations of the same family are named across these verses — Shaphan, Gemariah, Micaiah — and the young man who hears the reading does not shrug it off. He goes to tell the government.

verseByVerse.quote: he went down to the king's house, into the secretary's chamber, and all the officials were sitting there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the officials. And Micaiah told them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the scroll in the hearing of the people. Then all the officials sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi, to say to Baruch, "Take in your hand the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come." So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
he went down to the king's house, into the secretary's chamber, and all the officials were sitting there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the officials.

A cabinet meeting, with the members listed by name. These lists are not padding; they are the marks of testimony written by someone who was there and knew who sat where.

One name should stop us: Elnathan the son of Achbor. He is the man Jehoiakim sent to Egypt to extradite the prophet Uriah, who was brought back and executed (26:22-23). In a few verses he will be one of three men urging the king not to burn this scroll. People are not always consistent, and God uses them at the point where they are willing.

And Micaiah told them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the scroll in the hearing of the people.

Then all the officials sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi, to say to Baruch, "Take in your hand the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come." So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.

A summons from the government, and Baruch goes, carrying the evidence against himself in his own hand. He could have hidden it or left it behind. He takes it to the palace because he was asked for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, "Sit down and read it." So Baruch read it to them. When they heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear. And they said to Baruch, "We must report all these words to the king." Then they asked Baruch, "Tell us, please, how did you write all these words? Was it at his dictation?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they said to him, "Sit down and read it." So Baruch read it to them.

Sit down and read it. They want to hear the whole thing, not a summary, and they give the scribe a chair. It is the second public reading of the day.

When they heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear. And they said to Baruch, "We must report all these words to the king."

And this is the reaction the book has been waiting twenty-three years to record. They turned one to another in fear. Not agreement necessarily, not repentance yet, but men visibly shaken by what they have heard, looking at each other because it is too much to absorb alone.

Their instinct is that the king must hear it. They are not trying to suppress the document; they think the head of state needs to know what is in it. Ordinary officials doing their job well, and God's word making its way up through a bureaucracy.

Then they asked Baruch, "Tell us, please, how did you write all these words? Was it at his dictation?"

The question is the mark of serious men. How did you write all these words? They want to know the provenance — is this really Jeremiah's, and how did it get onto the page?

verseByVerse.quote: Baruch answered them, "He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll." Then the officials said to Baruch, "Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baruch answered them, "He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll."

The answer is unglamorous and precise: he spoke, I wrote, with ink.

There is a doctrine sitting in that sentence. The words are God's, given to a prophet, spoken to a scribe, and fixed in ink by an ordinary man doing careful work — and the humanity of the process takes nothing away from the divinity of the words. All Scripture is breathed out by God (2 Tim 3:16), and this chapter shows what that looked like from the inside: a voice, a pen, a bottle of ink, a long afternoon.

Then the officials said to Baruch, "Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are."

They know their king. Before they walk into his presence with this, they tell the two men to disappear — and they tell them properly: hide, and let no one know where you are, so that no official, under pressure, can give them away.

It is a small act of courage from men with careers to protect, and it belongs with Ahikam's hand and Zephaniah's reading of the hostile letter. God's care for his servants keeps arriving in this book through people who decide to act decently at some cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — A Penknife and a Fire Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The officials report to the king, having left the scroll behind (v. 20), and Jehoiakim sends for it. It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him (v. 22). Then the coldest sentence in the book: As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed (v. 23). And the verdict on the room: Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments (v. 24). Three men urge him not to, and he would not listen (v. 25); he sends men to arrest Baruch and Jeremiah, but the LORD hid them (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: He listened to three or four columns at a time, and only long enough to know what to cut off.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went into the court to the king, having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the secretary, and they reported all the words to the king. Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the secretary. And Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who stood beside the king. It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they went into the court to the king, having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the secretary, and they reported all the words to the king.

They leave the scroll behind in a side room — perhaps hoping a verbal report would be enough, and the document itself might survive.

Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the secretary. And Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who stood beside the king.

Jehoiakim will not have it second-hand. He sends for the scroll and has it read aloud, and the detail that the officials stood beside the king while he sat is the small print of a court: everyone else on their feet, the king in his chair by the fire.

It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him.

The scene is set with a novelist's economy. December, the winter palace, a brazier of coals at the king's feet, and a man standing in front of him unrolling the word of God.

Everything needed for what happens next is already in the room, and the narrator lets us notice the fire before the king uses it.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the fire pot. Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the fire pot.

Read the tense carefully — would cut them off. This was not one hot-blooded gesture. It was a rhythm, repeated the length of a long document: listen to three or four columns, slice them off with the scribe's own penknife, feed them to the coals, listen again.

He heard every word. He simply destroyed each section as soon as he had heard it. There is a kind of attention paid here that is worse than not listening at all — the deliberate, unhurried, methodical disposal of God's word by a man warm and comfortable in his winter room.

And the tool is the detail that stings. A scribe's knife, made for trimming pens and repairing scrolls, used to dismember one.

Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.

Now set this against the officials in Elishama's chamber, who turned one to another in fear. Same words, opposite response.

And set it against his father. Twenty-two years earlier a scroll had been found in this same temple and read to King Josiah, and When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes (2 Kgs 22:11). That tearing began the last reformation Judah ever had.

Josiah tore his robe at the word of God. His son took a knife to the word of God and kept his robe intact. The two men are father and son, the two scrolls were read in the same city, and everything that follows in the history of Judah runs out of that difference.

verseByVerse.quote: Even when Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them. And the king commanded Jerahmeel the king's son and Seraiah the son of Azriel and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet, but the LORD hid them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even when Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them.

Three men speak up, and they are named so that we know somebody in that room tried. Elnathan, who had once been the instrument of a prophet's death; Delaiah; Gemariah, in whose son's hearing the scroll had first been read.

He would not listen to them. It is the verdict of the whole book, applied here to a man refusing not a prophet but his own advisers. By this point Jehoiakim will not hear God, will not hear Jeremiah, and will not hear the officials he appointed.

And the king commanded Jerahmeel the king's son and Seraiah the son of Azriel and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet, but the LORD hid them.

Burning the book is not enough; he wants the men. A royal prince and two officers are detailed to find them — the same energy that once sent an extradition party to Egypt after Uriah.

And then four words end the paragraph: but the LORD hid them. No angel, no miracle described, no method given. The officials had said go and hide; the narrator says God hid them. Both are true, and that is usually how providence looks — sensible advice taken, a friend's back room, and behind it all a hand the searchers never see.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's answer is immediate: Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned (v. 28). The king's own question is quoted back at him (v. 29), and sentence passed: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night (v. 30), for they would not hear (v. 31). So Baruch writes it again — And many similar words were added to them (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The book came back longer than the one he burned.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned. And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, 'Thus says the LORD, You have burned this scroll, saying, "Why have you written in it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cut off from it man and beast?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:

The king destroys the words, and the word comes again. That sequence is the point of the chapter, and the narrator does not even pause over it.

"Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.

The instruction is almost dismissive in its simplicity. Write it again.

A book can be burned; the word it carries cannot. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:8), and the Lord said the same of his own: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matt 24:35). Every regime that has since burned Bibles has been doing what Jehoiakim did in a warm room in December, with the same result.

And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, 'Thus says the LORD, You have burned this scroll, saying, "Why have you written in it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cut off from it man and beast?"

God quotes the king's objection back at him, and notice what the offence actually was. Not the moral demands, not the accusations of injustice — the prediction about Babylon. He burned the scroll because of its politics.

Burning a forecast does not alter the weather.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night. And I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring upon them and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem and upon the people of Judah all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, but they would not hear.'" Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote on it at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night.

The sentence answers the crime in kind. He fed the scroll to the fire in his warm room; his own body will lie out in the open, in the heat by day and the frost by night.

Both halves had been announced before. Jeremiah had already said of this king that With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem (22:19), and that his line was finished: none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David (22:30). His son Jehoiachin reigned three months and was deported, and that was the end of it.

And I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring upon them and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem and upon the people of Judah all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, but they would not hear.'"

The last clause is the epitaph of the whole reign: but they would not hear. Everything else in the verse is consequence; this is the cause.

Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote on it at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.

So they sat down and did it all over again — the same long labour, voice and pen and ink, with a price now on both their heads.

And the final clause is the quiet triumph of the chapter: And many similar words were added to them. The second edition was longer. Everything Jehoiakim had cut off came back, and more with it, including the paragraph about his own corpse that only exists because he burned the first one. He could not even succeed in making the book shorter.

What he held in his hands that December was the book we are reading. It survived him, outlasted his dynasty, outlasted Babylon, and is still being read aloud in rooms full of people — which is what it was written for in the first place: It may be that someone will hear, and turn, and be forgiven.

36.title: The Scroll Burned and Rewritten
36.overview:
In Jehoiakim's fourth year God tells Jeremiah to collect twenty-three years of preaching onto a scroll, in the hope that Judah will hear it, turn from evil, and be forgiven. Baruch writes it at his dictation, and because Jeremiah is banned from the temple, Baruch is sent to read it publicly on a fast day — which he does (vv. 1-8).

A year later he reads it to the crowds in a chamber at the New Gate. Gemariah's son Micaiah reports it to the officials in the palace, who summon Baruch and have him read it again. They are visibly shaken, decide the king must hear it, ask how it was written, and then tell Baruch and Jeremiah to go into hiding (vv. 9-19).

The officials report to the king, leaving the scroll in a side room, but Jehoiakim sends for it. Sitting by a brazier in his winter house, he listens to three or four columns at a time, cuts each section off with a knife and burns it, until the whole scroll is gone. Neither he nor his servants were afraid or tore their garments. Three officials urge him not to and he will not listen; he orders the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, but the LORD hides them (vv. 20-26).

God tells Jeremiah to take another scroll and write it all again, and passes sentence on Jehoiakim: no heir on David's throne, and his body cast out to the heat and frost, because they would not hear. Baruch rewrites the whole book at Jeremiah's dictation, and many similar words are added to it (vv. 27-32).
36.theology:
God's purpose in writing down the threats is repentance and pardon, not record-keeping: it may be that they will turn, and that I may forgive (vv. 3, 7). Twenty-three years of refusal had not changed that aim.

When the preacher is barred, God sends the book. The word moves from air into ink so that it can enter rooms the prophet cannot and outlive the men who carry it (vv. 4-6, 18; 2 Tim 3:16).

Attention is not the same as obedience. Jehoiakim heard every column and destroyed each one as he heard it, which is worse than never listening (v. 23).

The same words produced fear in the officials and none in the king (vv. 16, 24), and the sharpest contrast is domestic: Josiah tore his clothes at a scroll, and his son took a knife to one (2 Kgs 22:11).

Providence works through decent people and remains God's doing: the officials said hide, and the narrator says the LORD hid them (vv. 19, 26).

A book can be burned; the word cannot. The second scroll came back longer, including the sentence that exists only because the first was burned (vv. 28, 32; Isa 40:8; Matt 24:35).
36.examples:
Twenty-three years of ignored sermons, copied out by hand.

A banned preacher sending a scribe in his place.

Carrying the evidence against yourself to the palace because you were asked.

Sit down and read it — the whole thing, not a summary.

Officials turning to look at each other, too shaken to speak.

He spoke, I wrote, with ink.

A brazier at the king's feet, noticed before he used it.

A scribe's penknife, made for mending scrolls, used to cut one up.

A father who tore his robe, a son who kept his intact.

Burning a forecast to change the weather.

A second edition, longer than the one he burned.

37.text: <sup>1</sup>Zedekiah the son of Josiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah, reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim.<sup>2</sup>But neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of the LORD that he spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.<sup>3</sup>King Zedekiah sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "Please pray for us to the LORD our God."<sup>4</sup>Now Jeremiah was still going in and out among the people, for he had not yet been put in prison.<sup>5</sup>The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt. And when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news about them, they withdrew from Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet:<sup>7</sup>"Thus says the LORD, God of Israel: Thus shall you say to the king of Judah who sent you to me to inquire of me, 'Behold, Pharaoh's army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt, to its own land.<sup>8</sup>And the Chaldeans shall come back and fight against this city. They shall capture it and burn it with fire.<sup>9</sup>Thus says the LORD, Do not deceive yourselves, saying, "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us," for they will not go away.<sup>10</sup>For even if you should defeat the whole army of Chaldeans who are fighting against you, and there remained of them only wounded men, every man in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire.'"<sup>11</sup>Now when the Chaldean army had withdrawn from Jerusalem at the approach of Pharaoh's army,<sup>12</sup>Jeremiah set out from Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to receive his portion there among the people.<sup>13</sup>When he was at the Benjamin Gate, a sentry there named Irijah the son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah, seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans."<sup>14</sup>And Jeremiah said, "It is a lie; I am not deserting to the Chaldeans." But Irijah would not listen to him, and seized Jeremiah and brought him to the officials.<sup>15</sup>And the officials were enraged at Jeremiah, and they beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary, for it had been made a prison.<sup>16</sup>When Jeremiah had come to the dungeon cells and remained there many days,<sup>17</sup>King Zedekiah sent for him and received him. The king questioned him secretly in his house and said, "Is there any word from the LORD?" Jeremiah said, "There is." Then he said, "You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon."<sup>18</sup>Jeremiah also said to King Zedekiah, "What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison?<sup>19</sup>Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon will not come against you and against this land'?<sup>20</sup>Now hear, please, O my lord the king: let my humble plea come before you and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there."<sup>21</sup>So King Zedekiah gave orders, and they committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. And a loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah reigns as Babylon's appointee in Coniah's place (v. 1), and the verdict on his reign comes first: neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of the LORD (v. 2). Yet he sends Jehucal and Zephaniah the priest to the prophet with a request — Please pray for us to the LORD our God (v. 3) — while Jeremiah is still going in and out among the people, for he had not yet been put in prison (v. 4). And the reason for the sudden piety is in the next line: The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt, and hearing of it, the Chaldeans withdrew from Jerusalem (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: They will not hear a word he says, and they would like him to pray for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah the son of Josiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah, reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim. But neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of the LORD that he spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zedekiah the son of Josiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah, reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim.

The sentence tells you everything about his position. He is Josiah's son, so the blood is right, but he sits on the throne because a foreign emperor put him there, in place of a nephew who was deported. Every day of his reign he is somebody else's arrangement.

That is the man the rest of this chapter shows us: a king with a title and no authority, frightened of his own officials, frightened of Babylon, and half-persuaded that Jeremiah is right.

But neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of the LORD that he spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.

Before a single event is narrated, the narrator gives the verdict, and it covers the whole society — the king, the civil service, and the ordinary population. Nobody listened.

Put that verse beside what happens next and the chapter's real subject appears. This is a study of what religion looks like in people who have settled the question of obedience in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "Please pray for us to the LORD our God." Now Jeremiah was still going in and out among the people, for he had not yet been put in prison. The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt. And when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news about them, they withdrew from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Zedekiah sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "Please pray for us to the LORD our God."

A royal delegation, politely worded, asking for intercession. And it comes one verse after we were told that this king does not listen to anything the prophet says.

Weigh the phrase the LORD our God. They claim him as theirs while ignoring his word, and they want his power without his instruction — prayer treated as a service the prophet provides, detached from the message the prophet brings.

Both messengers have histories. Zephaniah son of Maaseiah had come on this same errand once before, when Zedekiah sent to say Inquire of the LORD for us (21:2), and he was the priest who read Shemaiah's hostile letter aloud to Jeremiah rather than acting on it (29:29). Jehucal will shortly stand in front of the king demanding this prophet's death, on the ground that he is weakening the hands of the soldiers (38:4). The man who carries the prayer request is the man who will call for the execution.

Now Jeremiah was still going in and out among the people, for he had not yet been put in prison.

A quiet note of foreboding. Not yet. The narrator lets us know where this is heading while the prophet is still a free man walking the streets.

The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt. And when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news about them, they withdrew from Jerusalem.

And here is why the palace suddenly wants prayer, and also why it is about to stop wanting it. Pharaoh Hophra has marched north, Nebuchadnezzar has broken off the siege to deal with him, and the pressure is off.

This is the same withdrawal named three chapters earlier — the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you (34:21) — the breathing space in which the slave-owners of Jerusalem went and fetched back the people they had just freed. Chapter 34 and this chapter are one moment seen from two angles: the same lifted siege that produced the broken covenant produced this request for prayer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer is unwelcome. Pharaoh's army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt, to its own land (v. 7), and the Chaldeans shall come back and fight against this city. They shall capture it and burn it with fire (v. 8). So the warning is against the comfort everyone is drawing: Do not deceive yourselves, saying, "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us," for they will not go away (v. 9). And the point is pressed to its limit — even if Judah beat the whole Babylonian army and there remained of them only wounded men, every man in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The outcome was never a military calculation, so a lifted siege proves nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet: "Thus says the LORD, God of Israel: Thus shall you say to the king of Judah who sent you to me to inquire of me, 'Behold, Pharaoh's army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt, to its own land. And the Chaldeans shall come back and fight against this city. They shall capture it and burn it with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet: "Thus says the LORD, God of Israel: Thus shall you say to the king of Judah who sent you to me to inquire of me, 'Behold, Pharaoh's army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt, to its own land.

God answers the request, and the answer is not what was ordered.

They asked for prayer; they get a word. And it begins by dismantling the very thing that had raised their spirits: the relieving army is going home. Not defeated in a great battle, just about to return — the help everyone was counting on will simply turn around and leave.

Judah's reliance on Egypt was an old sickness. Isaiah had named it a century before: men who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt (Isa 30:2), and who would find that the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame (Isa 30:3).

And the Chaldeans shall come back and fight against this city. They shall capture it and burn it with fire.

Three plain verbs: come back, capture, burn. The empty siege lines outside the walls are a pause, not a deliverance, and God says so before anyone has time to build a theology out of the good news.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, Do not deceive yourselves, saying, "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us," for they will not go away. For even if you should defeat the whole army of Chaldeans who are fighting against you, and there remained of them only wounded men, every man in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD, Do not deceive yourselves, saying, "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us," for they will not go away.

The command is about the inside of their heads: Do not deceive yourselves.

Nobody was lying to them here. They were doing it themselves, and they were doing it with evidence — the army really had gone, the fields really were passable again, the relief was real. Self-deception rarely needs false facts; it only needs true facts read the way we want them read.

God even supplies the sentence they were saying to each other, in quotation marks. He knows the exact form the wish had taken, and answers it directly: for they will not go away.

For even if you should defeat the whole army of Chaldeans who are fighting against you, and there remained of them only wounded men, every man in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire.'"

The picture is deliberately extreme, and it settles what kind of situation this is. Suppose you won. Suppose the entire Babylonian army lay wounded in their tents. Those men would get up and burn Jerusalem anyway.

That is not a comment on Babylonian toughness. It is a statement that the fall of this city is God's decision, and therefore not available to be overturned by force of arms. The question in this war was never military.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: During the withdrawal Jeremiah leaves for his home district to receive his portion there among the people (v. 12). At the Benjamin Gate a sentry named Irijah seizes him: You are deserting to the Chaldeans (v. 13). The denial is flat — It is a lie; I am not deserting to the Chaldeans — But Irijah would not listen to him (v. 14). Then the officials were enraged at Jeremiah, and they beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary (v. 15), where he came to the dungeon cells and remained there many days (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Forty years of being called a traitor, and when the charge is finally laid it is false.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Chaldean army had withdrawn from Jerusalem at the approach of Pharaoh's army, Jeremiah set out from Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to receive his portion there among the people. When he was at the Benjamin Gate, a sentry there named Irijah the son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah, seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans." And Jeremiah said, "It is a lie; I am not deserting to the Chaldeans." But Irijah would not listen to him, and seized Jeremiah and brought him to the officials.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the Chaldean army had withdrawn from Jerusalem at the approach of Pharaoh's army, Jeremiah set out from Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to receive his portion there among the people.

With the roads briefly open, the prophet goes home to Anathoth on family business — to receive his portion there among the people, some matter of inherited land, quite possibly connected with the field he had bought from his cousin.

It is an ordinary errand, and that is what makes what follows so bitter.

When he was at the Benjamin Gate, a sentry there named Irijah the son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah, seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans."

A sentry with a name and a grandfather, doing what sentries do in a war. And the charge was not absurd on its face: Jeremiah had publicly advised the city to surrender, telling them that whoever went out to the Chaldeans would live (21:9). A man with those views, walking out of the north gate during a lull, looked exactly like a defector.

And Jeremiah said, "It is a lie; I am not deserting to the Chaldeans." But Irijah would not listen to him, and seized Jeremiah and brought him to the officials.

The denial is blunt and it is true. It is a lie. For forty years he had been called a traitor for telling Judah what God said, and when an actual charge of treason was finally laid against him it was false. He had urged surrender because God had spoken, and he was not slipping away himself.

And then the phrase that has echoed through the whole book, now from a soldier at a gate: Irijah would not listen to him. Nobody in this chapter listens to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: And the officials were enraged at Jeremiah, and they beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary, for it had been made a prison. When Jeremiah had come to the dungeon cells and remained there many days,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the officials were enraged at Jeremiah, and they beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary, for it had been made a prison.

These are not the officials of chapter 26 who convened a fair court, nor those of chapter 36 who trembled at the scroll and told Baruch to hide. A different generation is in office now, and they are enraged.

He is beaten and locked in a private house converted into a jail. There is no trial mentioned, no hearing, no examination of the sentry's claim. The man who had just been asked to pray for the king is flogged by the king's officials.

When Jeremiah had come to the dungeon cells and remained there many days,

Two details, and they are the whole cost of his obedience in this chapter: dungeon cells, and many days.

The narrator does not dwell on it and gives us no lament from the prophet. But this is the same man who had written that God's word was a fire in his bones he could not hold in, and here is where holding it in would have kept him out of — a cellar, for weeks, with no prospect of release and a fair expectation of dying there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — Is There Any Word from the LORD?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king sends for him and questioned him secretly in his house: Is there any word from the LORD? Jeremiah's answer is two words and then the same sentence that had him beaten — There is, and You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon (v. 17). Only then does he plead his own case: What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison? (v. 18), and Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon will not come against you'? (v. 19). He asks not to be sent back, lest I die there (v. 20), and is moved to the court of the guard with a loaf of bread... daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: He answers honestly first and asks for mercy second, in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent for him and received him. The king questioned him secretly in his house and said, "Is there any word from the LORD?" Jeremiah said, "There is." Then he said, "You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon." Jeremiah also said to King Zedekiah, "What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison? Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon will not come against you and against this land'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Zedekiah sent for him and received him. The king questioned him secretly in his house and said, "Is there any word from the LORD?" Jeremiah said, "There is." Then he said, "You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon."

Everything about this interview is furtive. The king has the prophet brought up from the cells and questions him secretly in his house, because he dare not be seen consulting the man his officials have just beaten.

His question is one of the saddest in Scripture: Is there any word from the LORD? He has heard the word for years, refused it, imprisoned the man who brought it, and now asks in a private room whether there is any more of it. He wants a different answer, and he asks the one person guaranteed not to give him one.

And consider Jeremiah's position as he replies. He is standing in front of the only man who can release him, bruised from a beating, expecting to die in a cellar. One softened sentence would have helped his case enormously.

What he says is There is — and then the same sentence that put him where he is: You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon. No hedging, no trading. The message did not change because the prophet's circumstances had.

Six hundred years later another prisoner stood in front of another frightened ruler who kept asking questions in private, and there the answer was different: he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed (Matt 27:14). Jeremiah spoke the word and was spared; the Word himself was silent, and was not.

Jeremiah also said to King Zedekiah, "What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison? Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon will not come against you and against this land'?

Only after delivering the word does he speak for himself, and both questions are fair.

The first is the protest of an innocent man: What wrong have I done? The second is unanswerable: Where are your prophets, the ones who promised Babylon would never come? They had been believed and he had been beaten, and now the Babylonians were camped in the fields and the optimists had nothing to say.

verseByVerse.quote: Now hear, please, O my lord the king: let my humble plea come before you and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there." So King Zedekiah gave orders, and they committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. And a loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now hear, please, O my lord the king: let my humble plea come before you and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there."

And here the iron prophet asks for something, courteously and without pretence. Let my humble plea come before you.

He does not ask for vindication, or for his accusers to be punished, or even for freedom. He asks not to be sent back to that particular cellar, and he says plainly why: lest I die there. There is no false bravery in this. He was afraid of dying in a hole, he said so, and asking a weak king for a small mercy was not beneath him.

So King Zedekiah gave orders, and they committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. And a loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.

The king does the one decent thing within his power. Not release — he has not the courage for that — but a transfer to the court of the guard, and a daily loaf.

Compare the rations another prophet was promised for telling a king the truth: Put this fellow in prison and feed him meager rations of bread and water (1 Kgs 22:27). Jeremiah gets a loaf a day from the bakers' street, and it comes through the frightened man who had him beaten.

Then the clause that quietly measures the whole siege: until all the bread of the city was gone. His provision lasted exactly as long as there was any bread in Jerusalem to be had. God kept him alive on the last supplies of a starving city, one loaf at a time, in a courtyard — and it was in that courtyard, on that daily bread, that he bought the field at Anathoth and was given the new covenant to write down.

Which is the answer to Zedekiah's question, though he never grasped it. Is there any word from the LORD? There was, and the chapters we have just read are it — dictated by a beaten man on a bread ration, about an everlasting love and sins remembered no more.

37.title: Arrested at the Benjamin Gate
37.overview:
Zedekiah reigns as Nebuchadnezzar's appointee in place of the deported Coniah, and neither he nor his officials nor the people listen to the word of the LORD through Jeremiah. Even so he sends Jehucal and Zephaniah the priest to ask the prophet to pray for them — because Pharaoh's army has marched out of Egypt and the Babylonians have lifted the siege (vv. 1-5).

God's answer is that the Egyptian army is going home, the Chaldeans will return, capture the city and burn it. They are not to deceive themselves that the enemy has gone for good: even if Judah defeated the whole Babylonian army and only wounded men were left in their tents, those men would rise and burn Jerusalem (vv. 6-10).

During the lull Jeremiah sets out for Benjamin on family business and is seized at the Benjamin Gate by a sentry who accuses him of deserting. He denies it flatly, but is not listened to; the officials are enraged, beat him, and shut him in a converted house, where he stays in the dungeon cells many days (vv. 11-16).

Zedekiah has him brought up and questions him secretly: is there any word from the LORD? There is — the same word, unchanged: you will be handed to the king of Babylon. Jeremiah then asks what wrong he has done, and where the prophets are who promised Babylon would not come, and pleads not to be returned to that cellar lest he die there. The king transfers him to the court of the guard with a daily loaf, until all the bread of the city was gone (vv. 17-21).
37.theology:
People who have settled the question of obedience in advance will still want the benefits of prayer. They claim the LORD as our God while ignoring his word, treating intercession as a service detached from the message (vv. 2-3).

Self-deception rarely needs false facts, only true facts read as we wish. The siege really had lifted, and the conclusion drawn from it was still a lie (v. 9).

The fall of the city was God's decision, not a military calculation, which is why even a defeated enemy would rise to finish it (v. 10).

Faithfulness does not trade the message for better treatment. Beaten and expecting to die, Jeremiah gave the king the same sentence that had imprisoned him (v. 17).

Asking for mercy is not a failure of courage. He spoke the word first and pleaded for himself second, admitting plainly that he was afraid to die in that cellar (vv. 17-20).

God's provision can come through the hand of a frightened man who wronged you, and it can be exactly sufficient — a loaf a day, lasting as long as the city had bread (v. 21).
37.examples:
A king who is somebody else's arrangement.

Asking for prayer from a man whose words you have decided to ignore.

The messenger carrying the prayer request who will later call for the execution.

Not yet put in prison — the narrator's quiet warning.

An empty siege line read as deliverance.

Wounded men rising from their tents to finish the job.

A family errand that ends in a beating.

The one true charge of treason in his life, and it was false.

A king consulting his prisoner in a back room.

One loaf a day, for as long as there was bread in the city.

38.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Shephatiah the son of Mattan, Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchiah heard the words that Jeremiah was saying to all the people:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD: He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live. He shall have his life as a prize of war, and live.<sup>3</sup>Thus says the LORD: This city shall surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon and be taken."<sup>4</sup>Then the officials said to the king, "Let this man be put to death, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers who are left in this city, and the hands of all the people, by speaking such words to them. For this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm."<sup>5</sup>King Zedekiah said, "Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you."<sup>6</sup>So they took Jeremiah and cast him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king's son, which was in the court of the guard, letting Jeremiah down by ropes. And there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud.<sup>7</sup>When Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern—the king was sitting in the Benjamin Gate—<sup>8</sup>Ebed-melech went from the king's house and said to the king,<sup>9</sup>"My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah the prophet by casting him into the cistern, and he will die there of hunger, for there is no bread left in the city."<sup>10</sup>Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, "Take thirty men with you from here, and lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies."<sup>11</sup>So Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the house of the king, to a wardrobe in the storehouse, and took from there old rags and worn-out clothes, which he let down to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes.<sup>12</sup>Then Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, "Put the rags and clothes between your armpits and the ropes." Jeremiah did so.<sup>13</sup>Then they drew Jeremiah up with ropes and lifted him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.<sup>14</sup>King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and received him at the third entrance of the temple of the LORD. The king said to Jeremiah, "I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me."<sup>15</sup>Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "If I tell you, will you not surely put me to death? And if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me."<sup>16</sup>Then King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, "As the LORD lives, who made our souls, I will not put you to death or deliver you into the hand of these men who seek your life."<sup>17</sup>Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "Thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: If you will surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then your life shall be spared, and this city shall not be burned with fire, and you and your house shall live.<sup>18</sup>But if you do not surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then this city shall be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and you shall not escape from their hand."<sup>19</sup>King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans, lest I be handed over to them and they deal cruelly with me."<sup>20</sup>Jeremiah said, "You shall not be given to them. Obey now the voice of the LORD in what I say to you, and it shall be well with you, and your life shall be spared.<sup>21</sup>But if you refuse to surrender, this is the vision which the LORD has shown to me:<sup>22</sup>Behold, all the women left in the house of the king of Judah were being led out to the officials of the king of Babylon and were saying, "'Your trusted friends have deceived you and prevailed against you; now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you.'<sup>23</sup>All your wives and your sons shall be led out to the Chaldeans, and you yourself shall not escape from their hand, but shall be seized by the king of Babylon, and this city shall be burned with fire."<sup>24</sup>Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "Let no one know of these words, and you shall not die.<sup>25</sup>If the officials hear that I have spoken with you and come to you and say to you, 'Tell us what you said to the king and what the king said to you; hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death,'<sup>26</sup>then you shall say to them, 'I made a humble plea to the king that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan to die there.'"<sup>27</sup>Then all the officials came to Jeremiah and asked him, and he answered them as the king had instructed him. So they stopped speaking with him, for the conversation had not been overheard.<sup>28</sup>And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Is in Your Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four officials hear Jeremiah repeating his message — He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live (v. 2) — and go to the king: Let this man be put to death, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers, since this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm (v. 4). Zedekiah's reply gives away his whole reign: Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A king who cannot say no, and hands over a man he believes to be a prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Shephatiah the son of Mattan, Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchiah heard the words that Jeremiah was saying to all the people: "Thus says the LORD: He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live. He shall have his life as a prize of war, and live. Thus says the LORD: This city shall surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon and be taken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Shephatiah the son of Mattan, Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchiah heard the words that Jeremiah was saying to all the people:

Four men, each named with his father, and one of them we have met. Jucal son of Shelemiah is the Jehucal who carried the king's request for prayer to this same prophet one chapter ago (37:3). The man sent to ask for intercession now appears at the head of the party demanding an execution.

Notice also where Jeremiah is and what he is doing. He is confined to the court of the guard, and he is still preaching to all the people. A prison in the middle of a palace compound turned out to be a pulpit.

"Thus says the LORD: He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live. He shall have his life as a prize of war, and live.

This is the word that made him hated, and it pays to be clear about what it actually offered. It was not propaganda for Babylon. It was an escape route: stay and die, go out and live, and live — repeated, as if to make sure nobody missed the offer inside the threat.

Thus says the LORD: This city shall surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon and be taken."

And the ground of the offer is the certainty of the outcome. Because the city will fall, leaving is life. Everything depends on whether the announced future is true, which is precisely what his hearers would not grant.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officials said to the king, "Let this man be put to death, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers who are left in this city, and the hands of all the people, by speaking such words to them. For this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm." King Zedekiah said, "Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the officials said to the king, "Let this man be put to death, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers who are left in this city, and the hands of all the people, by speaking such words to them. For this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm."

The charge is morale, and on its own terms it is not stupid. A man telling the garrison that the city will fall and they should surrender is, militarily, a liability. Any war cabinet in history would have said the same.

But listen to the last clause, because it is the exact inversion of the truth: this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm. This is the prophet who had written to the exiles telling them to seek the welfare of the city and pray for it (29:7), who had pleaded with Judah for forty years to turn and live, and who was at that moment offering the only survivable course available. The men who were marching the city into a furnace accused him of wanting its harm.

That accusation has a long life. The person who tells an uncomfortable truth is charged with wishing the harm his warning is trying to prevent.

King Zedekiah said, "Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you."

And there is the most pitiful sentence in the book. The king says he has no power.

It is not true, as the next paragraph proves — he will overrule these same men within hours when someone asks him to. What he lacks is not authority but nerve. He hands over a man he believes to be a prophet, to men he is afraid of, and consoles himself with the fiction that he had no choice. The fear of man lays a snare (Prov 29:25).

Another ruler would one day say the same thing with water and a basin, knowing the prisoner was innocent, and give him up because the crowd was louder than his conscience (John 19:12-16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Cast Into the Mud, and Lifted Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They lower the prophet by ropes into the cistern of Malchiah, where there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud (v. 6). Then one man acts. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house (v. 7), goes straight to Zedekiah and calls it what it is: these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah the prophet, and he will die of hunger, for there is no bread left in the city (v. 9). The king, asked plainly, agrees plainly (v. 10). And then the detail that makes the rescue memorable: Ebed-melech fetches old rags and worn-out clothes from a palace storeroom and lets them down first, telling him, Put the rags and clothes between your armpits and the ropes (vv. 11-12). Only then do they draw him up.
verseByVerse.theology: A foreigner and a eunuch, thinking about how the ropes would cut.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took Jeremiah and cast him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king's son, which was in the court of the guard, letting Jeremiah down by ropes. And there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud. When Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern—the king was sitting in the Benjamin Gate— Ebed-melech went from the king's house and said to the king,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they took Jeremiah and cast him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king's son, which was in the court of the guard, letting Jeremiah down by ropes. And there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud.

A cistern is a bottle-shaped pit cut into rock, narrow at the neck and wide below, designed to hold rainwater. This one was empty because the city was under siege and the rain had not come.

So they lowered him into a stone jar in the ground, in the dark, and he sank in the mud. There is no way out of such a hole without help from above: the walls curve inward and the floor gives way beneath you. They did not need to kill him; they only needed to leave him.

Hold the image, because a psalm turns it into the picture of salvation itself: He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure (Ps 40:2). That is exactly what is about to happen to Jeremiah, and it is what God does for sinners — not advice shouted down the shaft, but someone coming to haul us out.

When Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern — the king was sitting in the Benjamin Gate — Ebed-melech went from the king's house and said to the king,

And the rescuer is introduced with three details that in that society were all disqualifications: a foreigner, from Ethiopia, and a eunuch. His name means servant of the king.

Every Judean official in this chapter behaves badly. The one man who moves is a black African court servant who could never enter the assembly of Israel, and he moves immediately — heard, and then went. No committee, no delay.

verseByVerse.quote: "My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah the prophet by casting him into the cistern, and he will die there of hunger, for there is no bread left in the city." Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, "Take thirty men with you from here, and lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah the prophet by casting him into the cistern, and he will die there of hunger, for there is no bread left in the city."

He says it to the king's face, in public at the Benjamin Gate, with the officials' faction in power and his own position entirely dependent on royal favour: these men have done evil.

No diplomacy, no softening, and he calls Jeremiah what the officials would not — the prophet.

And his argument is practical and humane: the man will starve down there, because there is no bread left in the city. The daily loaf of the previous chapter has run out, which dates this scene to the last weeks of the siege.

Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, "Take thirty men with you from here, and lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies."

And Zedekiah, who an hour before can do nothing, immediately orders a rescue party of thirty men.

The comparison is merciless. The king could act all along. What he needed was someone to ask him, and the whole difference between a prophet dying in mud and a prophet drawn out of it was one man willing to speak up. Thirty men were available the moment somebody requested them.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the house of the king, to a wardrobe in the storehouse, and took from there old rags and worn-out clothes, which he let down to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes. Then Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, "Put the rags and clothes between your armpits and the ropes." Jeremiah did so. Then they drew Jeremiah up with ropes and lifted him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the house of the king, to a wardrobe in the storehouse, and took from there old rags and worn-out clothes, which he let down to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes.

He had his authorisation and thirty men, and before he pulled, he went looking for rags.

Think about what that means. He detoured to a palace storeroom, found old rags and worn-out clothes, and lowered them down the shaft first — because a man hauled out of a pit on bare ropes, by thirty men pulling hard, would have the rope cut into his armpits.

Then Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, "Put the rags and clothes between your armpits and the ropes." Jeremiah did so.

He even explains the padding to the exhausted man below, telling him exactly where to place it.

Scripture spends three verses on this. It could have said they pulled him out. Instead it records the wardrobe, the old clothes, the instruction about the armpits — because God takes notice of kindness that troubles itself over details. Anyone can want a man rescued. This is what it looks like to actually care whether the rescue hurts.

Then they drew Jeremiah up with ropes and lifted him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.

Out of the mud and back to the courtyard — still a prisoner, but alive and above ground.

Ebed-melech is not finished in this book. When the city falls, God sends a private word to him: I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me (39:18). The same phrase offered to anyone who would leave the city is given personally to the man who pulled the prophet out — and the reason given is not his courage but his trust.

And there is a promise made for men in exactly his position. Isaiah had said: let not the eunuch say, "Behold, I am a dry tree", for God would give such men a monument and a name better than sons and daughters... an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isa 56:3-5). A childless foreign slave has his name written in Scripture, remembered for one afternoon's decency, long after the officials who outranked him are recalled only as the men who did evil.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king smuggles Jeremiah to a third entrance of the temple: I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me (v. 14). Jeremiah names the futility first — if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me (v. 15) — and Zedekiah swears secretly by the LORD lives, who made our souls not to kill him (v. 16). The offer is then set out twice over: surrender and your life shall be spared, and this city shall not be burned with fire (v. 17); refuse, and the city burns and you shall not escape from their hand (v. 18). The king's objection is fear of the deserters (v. 19), and the vision answers it — palace women led out chanting, now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Obedience was offered to the end, and refused for fear of the wrong people.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and received him at the third entrance of the temple of the LORD. The king said to Jeremiah, "I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me." Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "If I tell you, will you not surely put me to death? And if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me."
