Then King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, "As the LORD lives, who made our souls, I will not put you to death or deliver you into the hand of these men who seek your life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and received him at the third entrance of the temple of the LORD. The king said to Jeremiah, "I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me."

Another secret meeting, in a discreet corner of the temple. The king who let him be thrown in a pit wants a private consultation, and he opens with a demand for total honesty from a man he has failed to protect.

Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "If I tell you, will you not surely put me to death? And if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me."

The prophet's reply is two accusations, and both are accurate.

The first is about his own safety; he had just been left to die and had every reason to expect it again. The second is sadder and sharper: if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me. He has read the man. There is no point in advising someone who has already decided that advice will not move him, and Jeremiah says so before he speaks.

Then King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, "As the LORD lives, who made our souls, I will not put you to death or deliver you into the hand of these men who seek your life."

The oath is solemn and beautifully phrased — As the LORD lives, who made our souls — and it is sworn secretly. A king who dares not be seen keeping faith with a prophet swears by the God who made them both, in a side entrance, where nobody will hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "Thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: If you will surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then your life shall be spared, and this city shall not be burned with fire, and you and your house shall live. But if you do not surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then this city shall be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and you shall not escape from their hand." King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans, lest I be handed over to them and they deal cruelly with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "Thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: If you will surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then your life shall be spared, and this city shall not be burned with fire, and you and your house shall live.

And here, in the final weeks, with the walls about to break, God is still making an offer.

Read what is on the table: the king's life, his household, and this city shall not be burned with fire. Jerusalem could still have been spared. The temple need not have burned. Everything depended on one man walking out of a gate.

But if you do not surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then this city shall be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and you shall not escape from their hand."

Two roads, stated plainly, with nothing hidden — exactly what the king had asked for. This is the same structure as the whole book: repent and live, refuse and perish, and the choice genuinely open until the last hour.

King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans, lest I be handed over to them and they deal cruelly with me."

And this is his answer to the offer of his city's survival: he is worried about being mocked.

The men who had already defected — following Jeremiah's advice — would jeer at the king who arrived last. That is the calculation. Weigh it: Jerusalem burned, the temple destroyed, his sons killed, his own eyes put out, thousands dead of famine, because a frightened man could not bear the humiliation of walking out to people who had gone before him.

Fear of man does this. It will accept enormous real disaster to avoid a small loss of face, and it always presents itself as prudence.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said, "You shall not be given to them. Obey now the voice of the LORD in what I say to you, and it shall be well with you, and your life shall be spared. But if you refuse to surrender, this is the vision which the LORD has shown to me: Behold, all the women left in the house of the king of Judah were being led out to the officials of the king of Babylon and were saying, "'Your trusted friends have deceived you and prevailed against you; now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you.' All your wives and your sons shall be led out to the Chaldeans, and you yourself shall not escape from their hand, but shall be seized by the king of Babylon, and this city shall be burned with fire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah said, "You shall not be given to them. Obey now the voice of the LORD in what I say to you, and it shall be well with you, and your life shall be spared.

The prophet answers the actual fear directly — You shall not be given to them — and then presses the one thing needed: Obey now the voice of the LORD.

Note the pastoral patience of it. He does not lecture the king on cowardice. He removes the objection, promises that it shall be well with you, and asks for obedience today.

But if you refuse to surrender, this is the vision which the LORD has shown to me:

Behold, all the women left in the house of the king of Judah were being led out to the officials of the king of Babylon and were saying, "'Your trusted friends have deceived you and prevailed against you; now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you.'

The vision is of the royal harem being marched out of the palace, and the words God gives them are a taunt in verse — the sort of thing that would be sung about him afterwards.

And look at the image they use. Now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you. The king who left a prophet to sink in mud will himself be stuck in it, abandoned by the officials he was too frightened to cross. Jeremiah was pulled out by a foreigner with rags; nobody will come down for Zedekiah.

His trusted friends — the men whose approval cost him his city — will be the ones who prevailed against you and then walked away. That is the standing testimony of every idol: it demands everything, and abandons you when you need it.

All your wives and your sons shall be led out to the Chaldeans, and you yourself shall not escape from their hand, but shall be seized by the king of Babylon, and this city shall be burned with fire."

The last word of the appeal is the list of what refusal will cost: wives, sons, his own capture, the city burned. Every item arrived exactly as stated.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah's last concern is management: Let no one know of these words, and you shall not die (v. 24). He coaches the prophet on what to tell the officials — repeat the plea about not being sent back to the house of Jonathan to die there (v. 26). The officials come and ask, and he answered them as the king had instructed him, so they stop questioning him, for the conversation had not been overheard (v. 27). And the chapter closes: And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The king protected the secret of the conversation and not the city it was about.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "Let no one know of these words, and you shall not die. If the officials hear that I have spoken with you and come to you and say to you, 'Tell us what you said to the king and what the king said to you; hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death,' then you shall say to them, 'I made a humble plea to the king that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan to die there.'" Then all the officials came to Jeremiah and asked him, and he answered them as the king had instructed him. So they stopped speaking with him, for the conversation had not been overheard. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "Let no one know of these words, and you shall not die.

The offer of life for his city has just been laid before him, along with the vision of his wives led away. His response is to worry about who might find out that they had spoken.

If the officials hear that I have spoken with you and come to you and say to you, 'Tell us what you said to the king and what the king said to you; hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death,' then you shall say to them, 'I made a humble plea to the king that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan to die there.'"

He scripts the answer, and the line he supplies is a real one — it is word for word what Jeremiah had said to him at their last meeting: do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there (37:20). The king is telling him to give a true statement about an earlier conversation instead of the subject of this one.

Notice too that the officials will offer Jeremiah the same bargain the king just did — tell us everything and we will not kill you. Everyone in this palace negotiates with a man's life as the currency.

Then all the officials came to Jeremiah and asked him, and he answered them as the king had instructed him. So they stopped speaking with him, for the conversation had not been overheard.

They came, exactly as the king predicted, and Jeremiah answered as instructed. The interrogation stopped because nobody could contradict him.

And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken.

One sentence for the rest of the siege. He stayed in the courtyard while the food ran out and the walls were undermined, and the city fell around a man nobody would listen to.

Set the two figures of this chapter side by side, because that is how it is arranged. A king of David's line, with armies, officials and the word of God delivered privately into his hand, who could do nothing — and an African eunuch with no rights at all, who heard about an injustice, walked to the gate, said so, fetched rags, and saved a prophet's life. God's verdict on them is already recorded: one lost his sons, his sight and his city; the other was told, because you have put your trust in me (39:18).

And the mud is the picture to keep. A man sinking in a pit with curved walls, who could not climb out and did not get advice shouted down the shaft, but ropes, padding and hands — He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock (Ps 40:2). That is the gospel in a cistern, and the one who came down for us was not embarrassed to be seen doing it.

38.title: The Cistern and the Ethiopian
38.overview:
Four officials hear Jeremiah telling the people that those who stay in the city will die and those who surrender will live, and they ask the king for his death, saying he is weakening the soldiers' morale and seeking the people's harm. Zedekiah answers that the king can do nothing against them, and they lower Jeremiah by ropes into an empty cistern, where he sinks in the mud (vv. 1-6).

Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch of the palace, goes to the king at the Benjamin Gate, tells him plainly that these men have done evil and that Jeremiah will starve because there is no bread left in the city. The king at once gives him thirty men. Ebed-melech fetches old rags from a palace storeroom, lowers them first, and tells Jeremiah to put them between his armpits and the ropes before they haul him up (vv. 7-13).

Zedekiah then meets him secretly and demands total honesty. Jeremiah says the king will not listen, and is given a solemn oath of protection. The offer is put twice: surrender and your life is spared and the city is not burned; refuse and it burns and you will not escape. The king objects that he fears the deserters' mockery, and Jeremiah answers the fear, urges obedience, and describes the vision of the palace women led out chanting that his trusted friends have abandoned him now that his feet are sunk in the mud (vv. 14-23).

The king's final concern is secrecy. He scripts what Jeremiah is to tell the officials — the true but irrelevant plea about not being returned to Jonathan's house — and Jeremiah answers as instructed, so the questioning stops. He remained in the court of the guard until the day Jerusalem was taken (vv. 24-28).
38.theology:
The message that made him hated was an escape route: stay and die, go out and live. The offer sat inside the threat, and it stayed open until the final weeks (vv. 2, 17).

Those marching a city into ruin accused the one man trying to save it of seeking its harm — the exact inversion of what he had commanded the exiles to do (v. 4; 29:7).

Fear of man is a snare that disguises itself as helplessness. Zedekiah said the king can do nothing, then ordered thirty men the moment somebody asked him; he lost city, sons and sight rather than face being mocked (vv. 5, 10, 19; Prov 29:25; John 19:12-16).

God notices kindness that troubles itself over details. Scripture spends three verses on a wardrobe and some old rags because the rescuer thought about how the ropes would cut (vv. 11-12).

The outsider with no standing is the one commended. A foreign eunuch is given a personal oracle and a name in Scripture, and the reason stated is his trust, not his courage (39:18; Isa 56:3-5).

The mud is the picture of salvation: walls that curve inward, a floor that gives way, and no way out but hands from above (vv. 6, 22; Ps 40:2).
38.examples:
The man who brought the prayer request, now asking for an execution.

A prison in a palace courtyard used as a pulpit.

Accused of wanting the harm his warning was trying to prevent.

A king explaining that he has no power, hours before ordering thirty men.

A cistern with inward-curving walls and mud for a floor.

Heard, and then went — with no committee in between.

A detour to a storeroom for rags, so the ropes would not cut.

An oath by the God who made our souls, sworn where nobody could hear.

A city burned because a man could not bear being laughed at.

Trusted friends who prevail against you and then turn away.

39.text: <sup>1</sup>In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem and besieged it.<sup>2</sup>In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city.<sup>3</sup>Then all the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the middle gate: Nergal-sar-ezer of Samgar, Nebu-sar-sekim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, with all the rest of the officers of the king of Babylon.<sup>4</sup>When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them, they fled, going out of the city at night by way of the king's garden through the gate between the two walls; and they went toward the Arabah.<sup>5</sup>But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. And when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, at Riblah, in the land of Hamath; and he passed sentence on him.<sup>6</sup>The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah.<sup>7</sup>He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.<sup>8</sup>The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the house of the people, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained.<sup>10</sup>Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.<sup>11</sup>Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you."<sup>13</sup>So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon<sup>14</sup>sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard. They entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, that he should take him home. So he lived among the people.<sup>15</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard:<sup>16</sup>"Go, and say to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day.<sup>17</sup>But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid.<sup>18</sup>For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Breach Was Made in the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The siege runs from the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year until, in the eleventh year, a breach was made in the city (v. 2) — eighteen months of famine in one line. Babylonian officers take their seats in the middle gate (v. 3), and the king runs: out at night by way of the king's garden through the gate between the two walls toward the Arabah (v. 4). They overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho and bring him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah (v. 5). There the sentence falls in the order that makes it unbearable: The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes (v. 6), and then He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The last thing he ever saw was what his refusal cost his own children.

verseByVerse.quote: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem and besieged it. In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city. Then all the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the middle gate: Nergal-sar-ezer of Samgar, Nebu-sar-sekim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, with all the rest of the officers of the king of Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem and besieged it. In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city.

Two dates, and thirty months between them.

The narrator gives the siege no adjectives. Everything that happened inside those walls — the bread running out, the cistern, the last loaf from the bakers' street, the things Lamentations says mothers did — sits compressed into the gap between one month and another. Then five words: a breach was made in the city.

This is the sentence the whole book has been walking toward. Forty years of warning, and when it arrives it is reported like a line in a chronicle.

Then all the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the middle gate: Nergal-sar-ezer of Samgar, Nebu-sar-sekim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, with all the rest of the officers of the king of Babylon.

Foreign officers sit down in the gate, and the detail is precise in a way that carries real weight: these are Babylonian names and Babylonian titles, one of which — Rab-saris, chief officer — has turned up on a clay tablet from Nebuchadnezzar's court bearing a name very like Nebu-sar-sekim's.

And the gate is the point. The gate was where Israel's elders sat to judge, where Boaz called witnesses, where the officials had once acquitted Jeremiah. Now other men sit there, and their language is not Hebrew. The seat of justice in Jerusalem has changed occupants.

verseByVerse.quote: When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them, they fled, going out of the city at night by way of the king's garden through the gate between the two walls; and they went toward the Arabah. But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. And when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, at Riblah, in the land of Hamath; and he passed sentence on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them, they fled, going out of the city at night by way of the king's garden through the gate between the two walls; and they went toward the Arabah.

He had been told, twice and plainly, that if he walked out to the Babylonians his life would be spared and the city would not burn (38:17). He would not do it in daylight as an act of obedience.

So here he goes out anyway — at night, by a garden gate, through a gap in the walls, running for the Jordan valley. The same feet that would not carry him out in surrender carry him out in flight. What obedience would have cost him was his dignity; what disobedience cost him is in the next three verses.

But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. And when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, at Riblah, in the land of Hamath; and he passed sentence on him.

They catch him on the flat ground near Jericho — where Israel had first entered the land, the same plains Joshua crossed into. The story of the possession of Canaan ends where it began, with the last king of Judah taken prisoner.

And he is brought to Riblah, a hundred and fifty miles north, to have sentence passed on him. He is tried as a rebel vassal, because that is what he was: Nebuchadnezzar had put him on the throne and he had broken his oath.

verseByVerse.quote: The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah. He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah.

Read the order of events, because it is deliberate and it is the fulfilment of a specific word.

His sons are killed in front of him. The Davidic line running through him is ended while he watches, and the nobles with them. The parallel accounts record it identically — The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes (52:10), They slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes (2 Kgs 25:7).

He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.

And then they blind him.

God had told him, through the man he left in a cistern, that he would see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face (32:4), and that he would go to Babylon. Every clause came true, and not one of them the way he would have imagined it when he heard it. He met Nebuchadnezzar eye to eye at Riblah. He went to Babylon. And the last image his eyes ever held was his children dying because he had been afraid of being laughed at.

God's words are not riddles, but they are not tame either. Zedekiah had heard this sentence for years and treated it as a bargaining position. It was a description.

And there is a mercy buried here that is easy to miss: he was told in chapter 34 that he would not die by the sword but in peace, with mourners and spices (34:4-5). Blinded, in chains, in Babylon — and God kept even that small kindness to a king who had earned none.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Chaldeans burn the palace and the houses and break down the walls (v. 8), and Nebuzaradan deports the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained (v. 9). Then one sentence that nobody in Jerusalem would have predicted: he left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The people with nothing to lose ended the day owning land.

verseByVerse.quote: The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the house of the people, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem. Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the house of the people, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem.

The palace, the houses, the walls. Everything Judah had trusted in — dynasty, city, defences — dismantled in one verse, exactly as had been said of the scroll Jehoiakim burned: the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land (36:29).

The temple is not mentioned here. Chapter 52 will supply that detail, and perhaps this account cannot bring itself to say it yet.

Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained.

Three groups, all deported: those who held out, those who defected, and the remainder. Even the deserters go, which shows that surrendering was never a trick to avoid exile — it was how to stay alive. Jeremiah had promised life as a prize of war, not a comfortable outcome.

Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.

And then this, which has no business being in a chapter about catastrophe.

The people left in the land are the poor people who owned nothing, and a pagan general hands them vineyards and fields. The landless get land on the day the landowners lose everything. Men who had been at the bottom of every list in Judah — who had been cheated by the officials of chapter 34, sold and re-enslaved, denied their wages by the house-builders of chapter 22 — wake up as freeholders.

Nobody planned this as justice. Nebuzaradan was solving an administrative problem: keep the countryside producing, deport anyone who could organise a revolt. But the effect is a reversal so exact that it reads like a verdict, and the New Testament says out loud what this verse only does: has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom (Jas 2:5). Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth (Matt 5:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Deal With Him As He Tells You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nebuchadnezzar himself gives orders about the prophet: Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you (v. 12). So the chief officers of Babylon sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard (v. 14) and entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, to take him home — So he lived among the people.
verseByVerse.theology: The emperor's standing order for one prisoner: do whatever he asks.

verseByVerse.quote: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying, "Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you." So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard. They entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, that he should take him home. So he lived among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying, "Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you."

The emperor of the world has one named prisoner on his mind, and the instruction is extraordinary: protect him, harm him in no way, and deal with him as he tells you. Do what he asks.

Weigh the irony without missing the providence. For forty years the kings of Judah imprisoned this man, beat him, banned him from the temple, burned his book and dropped him in a pit. The pagan king who destroyed the city gave orders that he was to be treated well and have his own way.

Presumably the Babylonians knew he had urged surrender and counted him useful. God's protection of his servants routinely arrives through people acting for their own reasons.

So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard.

The full list of titles again, and the whole senior staff of the occupying army is involved in fetching one old man out of a courtyard.

They entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, that he should take him home. So he lived among the people.

And the name at the end of the chain is a gift. Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan — the son of the man whose hand had been with Jeremiah when the priests wanted him dead: But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah so that he was not given over to the people to be put to death (26:24).

Ahikam protected him at a trial decades earlier; Ahikam's son takes him home after the city falls. Shaphan's family has turned up at every hinge of this book — reading the law to Josiah, lending Baruch a room, carrying the letter to Babylon, and now this. Faithfulness across generations does not make headlines, and it keeps quietly holding things up.

So he lived among the people. After the stocks, the cistern, the dungeon cells and the court of the guard, the prophet ends the chapter a free man living among ordinary Judeans.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Because You Have Put Your Trust in Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes by reaching back into the siege, to a word given while he was still shut up in the court of the guard (v. 15), for Ebed-melech: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day (v. 16). But I will deliver you on that day, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid (v. 17). And the ground of it is named last: you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who fetched the rags is told why he will live, and it is not because of the rags.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard: "Go, and say to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day. But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid. For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard:

The narrator now goes back in time. This word was given before the walls broke, while Jeremiah was still a prisoner — placed here, out of sequence, so that it lands after the catastrophe it was spoken into.

"Go, and say to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day.

God sends a personal message to the man who fetched the rags.

And he begins by telling him the truth about what is coming: the city will fall, and Ebed-melech will watch it happen — they shall be accomplished before you on that day. No promise that he will be spared the sight. He will see the palace he worked in burn.

But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid.

The men of whom you are afraid. God names the fear without rebuking it. Ebed-melech had walked up to the king at a public gate and accused four powerful officials of evil, and he had been frightened of them ever since — as well he might be, since they had just shown what they did to people who crossed them.

Courage, in this book, is not the absence of fear. It is what Ebed-melech did while afraid, and God's answer is not that his fear was foolish but that those men will never have him.

For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.'"

The phrase your life as a prize of war is the one Jeremiah had shouted to the whole city: go out to the Chaldeans and you shall have his life as a prize of war, and live (38:2). What was offered publicly to everyone is now guaranteed personally to one man.

And notice the reason God gives. Not because you rescued my prophet. Not because you were brave, or kind, or fetched padding for the ropes — because you have put your trust in me.

That is the verdict of the chapter, and it sorts everyone in it. A king of David's line, who had the promises, the temple and the prophet's private counsel, lost his sons and his sight because he trusted the opinion of men he was afraid of. A foreign eunuch with no tribe, no children and no rights was saved because he trusted God — and his trusting showed itself, as it always does, in what he did about a man sinking in mud.

The city fell, and the promise held: God knew the name of the one servant in Jerusalem who believed him, and had a word addressed to him by name before the first stone came down.

39.title: The City Falls
39.overview:
After a siege of some thirty months the wall of Jerusalem is breached, and the officers of Babylon take their seats in the middle gate. Zedekiah and his soldiers escape by night through a garden gate, but the Chaldeans overtake him in the plains of Jericho and bring him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah for sentence. His sons are slaughtered before his eyes, along with the nobles of Judah, and then his eyes are put out and he is taken to Babylon in chains (vv. 1-7).

The Chaldeans burn the palace and the houses and break down the walls, and Nebuzaradan deports those who held out, those who deserted, and the rest — but leaves in the land some of the poor who owned nothing, giving them vineyards and fields (vv. 8-10).

Nebuchadnezzar gives orders that Jeremiah is to be taken, looked after well, not harmed, and dealt with as he asks. The senior officers fetch him from the court of the guard and entrust him to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, to take him home, and he lives among the people (vv. 11-14).

The chapter then reaches back to a word given during the siege, for Ebed-melech the Ethiopian: the city will fall before his eyes, but God will deliver him and he will not be handed to the men he fears; he will have his life as a prize of war, because he has put his trust in God (vv. 15-18).
39.theology:
God's words are descriptions, not bargaining positions. Zedekiah did see the king of Babylon eye to eye, exactly as promised, and was blinded immediately afterwards (vv. 5-7; 32:4; 34:3).

What obedience would have cost him was his dignity; refusing cost him his sons, his sight and his city — and he still went out of Jerusalem in the end, only by night and in flight (v. 4; 38:17-19).

Even to a king who earned nothing, God kept the small kindness he had promised: not death by the sword (v. 7; 34:4-5).

The landless inherit on the day the landowners lose everything, arranged by a pagan general for administrative reasons and reading like a verdict (v. 10; Jas 2:5; Matt 5:5).

God's care for his servants arrives through people acting for their own motives — an emperor's standing order, and a family that had been faithful for three generations (vv. 12, 14; 26:24).

Courage is not the absence of fear. God names the men Ebed-melech was afraid of without rebuking him for it, and the reason given for saving him is trust, not bravery or service (vv. 17-18).
39.examples:
Thirty months of famine, compressed into the gap between two dates.

Foreign officers sitting in the gate where Israel's elders gave judgment.

Walking out of the city at night, after refusing to walk out by day.

Caught on the plains where Joshua came in.

The last thing his eyes were allowed to see.

Men who owned nothing, handed vineyards.

An emperor's order: do whatever he asks.

Ahikam's hand at the trial, and Ahikam's son at the fall.

A private letter from God, delivered by name, to a palace servant.

Saved not for the rags, but for the trust.

40.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he took him bound in chains along with all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon.<sup>2</sup>The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, "The LORD your God pronounced this disaster against this place.<sup>3</sup>The LORD has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you.<sup>4</sup>Now, behold, I release you today from the chains on your hands. If it seems good to you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will look after you well, but if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, do not come. See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go.<sup>5</sup>If you remain, then return to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor of the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people. Or go wherever you think it right to go." So the captain of the guard gave him an allowance of food and a present, and let him go.<sup>6</sup>Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.<sup>7</sup>When all the captains of the forces in the open country and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land and had committed to him men, women, and children, those of the poorest of the land who had not been taken into exile to Babylon,<sup>8</sup>they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah— Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.<sup>9</sup>Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you.<sup>10</sup>As for me, I will dwell at Mizpah, to represent you before the Chaldeans who will come to us. But as for you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken."<sup>11</sup>Likewise, when all the Judeans who were in Moab and among the Ammonites and in Edom and in other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over them,<sup>12</sup>then all the Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance.<sup>13</sup>Now Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces in the open country came to Gedaliah at Mizpah<sup>14</sup>and said to him, "Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.<sup>15</sup>Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "Please let me go and strike down Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no one will know it. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish?"<sup>16</sup>But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, "You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Whole Land Is Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is found bound in chains along with all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon (v. 1), and the Babylonian captain of the guard preaches Judah's own theology to him: The LORD your God pronounced this disaster against this place. The LORD has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you (vv. 2-3). Then the chains come off and the choice is his: come to Babylon and be looked after, or See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go (v. 4). He is given an allowance of food and a present (v. 5), and he goes to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: A pagan officer with better theology than Judah's kings, handing a prophet his freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he took him bound in chains along with all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon. The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, "The LORD your God pronounced this disaster against this place. The LORD has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he took him bound in chains along with all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon.

Something has gone wrong between chapters, and the narrator does not hide it. The emperor had ordered that this man be looked after and given his own way (39:12), and here he is bound in chains in a column of deportees at Ramah, the staging camp where the prisoners were mustered.

Ramah is where Rachel was heard weeping for her children (31:15). The prophet who wrote that verse is now standing in the very place, chained, among the people it was about.

Orders get lost. Somebody in the chain of command did not know, or did not care, and the protected man was processed with everyone else. God's promises to his servants are not always administered smoothly by the people carrying them.

The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, "The LORD your God pronounced this disaster against this place.

The LORD has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you.

Read that again and notice who is speaking. A Babylonian general, an idolater, summarising the theology of Jeremiah's entire ministry in three sentences — and getting it right.

He names the agent: The LORD has brought it about. Not Babylonian siege engineering. He names the reliability: has done as he said. He names the cause: Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice.

Forty years of preaching that to Judah had produced a beating, a cistern and a burned scroll. The occupying officer worked it out from the outside, and said it to the one man in the country who had been saying it all along.

It is a strange, bleak vindication. The nations understood what Judah would not, and there is a warning in that for anyone who has grown deaf inside the church while outsiders can see plainly what God is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, behold, I release you today from the chains on your hands. If it seems good to you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will look after you well, but if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, do not come. See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go. If you remain, then return to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor of the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people. Or go wherever you think it right to go." So the captain of the guard gave him an allowance of food and a present, and let him go. Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, behold, I release you today from the chains on your hands. If it seems good to you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will look after you well, but if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, do not come. See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go."

The chains come off, and the old man is handed something he has not had in decades: a choice.

And look at the two options. Babylon means comfort, safety and status — the deportees included the skilled and the well-connected, and a prophet with a record of urging surrender would have been honoured there. Judah means rubble, poverty and a wrecked community.

See, the whole land is before you. The phrase would echo for any Israelite; it is the language of Abraham and Lot looking over Canaan. Except that the land before him now is ash.

If you remain, then return to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor of the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people. Or go wherever you think it right to go." So the captain of the guard gave him an allowance of food and a present, and let him go.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew of the phrase about the allowance and the present is uncertain, its rendering here following the Syriac — "Syriac; the meaning of the Hebrew phrase is uncertain". What is clear is the kindness: rations and a gift, from the man who burned the temple, to the prophet who said it would burn.

Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.

He stays. Offered Babylon, with a pension and a hearing, he chooses the ruined country and the poor people in it.

That decision is the last great act of his ministry and it is entirely consistent with the first. He had wept for this people for forty years while they hated him; now that they are broken and leaderless he will not leave them. A man who had every reason to shake the dust off his feet went and lived among them instead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Gather Wine and Summer Fruits
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The captains still at large come in to Gedaliah at Mizpah (vv. 7-8), and he puts them under oath with a promise: Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you (v. 9). He will handle the occupiers himself; their business is ordinary life — gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities (v. 10). Word spreads to the Judeans scattered in Moab, Ammon and Edom (v. 11), and they come home: And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: A harvest in the year the city burned.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the captains of the forces in the open country and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land and had committed to him men, women, and children, those of the poorest of the land who had not been taken into exile to Babylon, they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah— Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When all the captains of the forces in the open country and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land and had committed to him men, women, and children, those of the poorest of the land who had not been taken into exile to Babylon,

Judah is now a province run by a Judean governor, and its population is described without flattery: the poorest of the land. The people Nebuzaradan gave vineyards to (39:10) are the nation now.

Out in the countryside are armed bands — officers whose units survived by staying out of the city. They come in when they hear there is a government again.

they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah — Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.

Five commanders, named. The first of them, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, will murder the governor within months; the second, Johanan the son of Kareah, will try to prevent it and then lead the survivors into the mistake of chapter 42.

The narrator lists them flatly, the assassin first, and lets us discover later which was which. That is how it looked at the time: a group of loyal officers reporting to the new administration.

verseByVerse.quote: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you. As for me, I will dwell at Mizpah, to represent you before the Chaldeans who will come to us. But as for you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you.

Gedaliah's inaugural policy is Jeremiah's sermon turned into government.

Compare what the prophet had been saying for years: bring your neck under the yoke of Babylon and serve him and his people and live (27:12), and it shall be well with you. Gedaliah says the same three things — do not be afraid, serve Babylon, dwell in the land — and adds an oath to guarantee it.

This is what it looks like when someone finally believes the prophet. And it is no accident that the man doing it is Ahikam's son. He grew up in a house where Jeremiah was taken seriously.

As for me, I will dwell at Mizpah, to represent you before the Chaldeans who will come to us. But as for you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken."

He takes the unpleasant job himself — to represent you before the Chaldeans, standing between his people and the occupiers — and gives everyone else the ordinary work: pick the grapes, gather the summer fruit, press the oil, fill the jars, live in your towns.

It is the same instruction God had sent to the exiles in Babylon: build houses, plant gardens, live (29:5). After catastrophe, the path back is not a grand project but harvest, storage and settled homes. Leaders who take the hard conversations on themselves and leave their people free to get on with ordinary faithful life are doing something very close to pastoral work.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, when all the Judeans who were in Moab and among the Ammonites and in Edom and in other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over them, then all the Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, when all the Judeans who were in Moab and among the Ammonites and in Edom and in other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over them,

The refugees hear. Judeans had scattered into Moab, Ammon, Edom and further during the invasion, and news reaches them that there is a remnant and a governor.

then all the Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance.

They come home, and the year produces a harvest in great abundance.

Sit with that for a moment, because it is a real mercy and the book does not oversell it. In the year Jerusalem burned, with the temple gone and the king blinded, the vines and the fruit trees of Judah bore heavily, and scattered people came back from four countries to pick them. God had said he would gather them from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you (29:14), and here is a first small instalment, small enough to miss and real enough to eat.

Mercies after judgment often look like this. Not a restored temple — a good grape harvest and somewhere to put it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — He Would Not Believe Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Johanan and the other commanders bring a warning: Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life? — and Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them (v. 14). Johanan presses privately, offering to kill Ishmael quietly, with the stakes named exactly: Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish? (v. 15). Gedaliah refuses: You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: A good man's refusal to think ill of anyone, and the remnant paid for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces in the open country came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and said to him, "Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces in the open country came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and said to him, "Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?"

The intelligence is specific: a named foreign king, a named agent, a named target. Baalis of Ammon wants the Babylonian settlement destabilised, and Ishmael — who, chapter 41 tells us, was of the royal family — has a claim of his own to resent a commoner governing Judah.

It is brought by several commanders together, not by one grudge-bearer, and it was true.

But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.

Six words, and the remnant of Judah turns on them.

Why would he not believe it? Everything we know of him suggests a generous man: he had sheltered Jeremiah, he had sworn oaths of safety to these very officers, his policy was trust and ordinary life. A man like that finds it hard to credit that someone who eats at his table is planning to kill him.

And that is the uncomfortable point of the paragraph. This is not the failure of a fool or a cynic. It is a good man's charity applied where discernment was needed, and Scripture records it as a disaster rather than a virtue. Refusing to think ill of anyone is not the same as wisdom, and leaders who will not hear a warning about a colleague can be as destructive as leaders who trust nobody.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "Please let me go and strike down Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no one will know it. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, "You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "Please let me go and strike down Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no one will know it. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish?"

Johanan tries again in private, and his proposal is ugly: let me kill him quietly, and no one will know it. A secret assassination to prevent an assassination.

Gedaliah was right to refuse that. There is no warrant for murdering a man on intelligence, however good, and the governor who had just sworn oaths of safety could hardly begin with a private killing.

But look at the reasoning Johanan attaches, because he had seen further than anyone: Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish? He understood that everything now rested on one man's survival. Kill Gedaliah and the harvest, the returning refugees, the whole fragile settlement come apart.

He was exactly right, and he was proposing the wrong remedy. Sound analysis and a sinful solution frequently arrive together.

But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, "You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael."

And there is the sentence that ends the chapter, and very nearly ends the remnant. He does not merely decline the murder; he calls the warning a lie. You are speaking falsely of Ishmael.

He could have refused the assassination and still taken precautions — kept Ishmael at a distance, declined to dine with him, posted a guard. Instead he accused the men telling him the truth of slander, and took no measures at all. Within months Ishmael came to Mizpah with ten men, and as they ate bread together there they rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword (41:1-2).

So the last good governor of Judah, from the family that had protected the prophet for three generations, was murdered at his own table by a man he refused to suspect — and the remnant scattered exactly as Johanan had said. The book gives him no rebuke and no eulogy. It simply records that he would not believe them, and lets the next chapter say what it cost.

Judah's story does not end with a Babylonian army but with a dinner party and a knife, which is a sober word about how communities that have survived catastrophe are usually lost. Not to the great enemy outside, but to one of their own, welcomed at the table, while a warning went unheeded.

40.title: Released at Ramah
40.overview:
Jeremiah is discovered in chains at Ramah among the deportees, despite Nebuchadnezzar's order that he be protected. The Babylonian captain of the guard states Judah's own theology back to him — the LORD brought this about, has done as he said, because you sinned and did not obey his voice — then releases him, offers him Babylon with care and comfort or the freedom of the whole land, gives him rations and a present, and lets him go. He chooses to stay, going to Gedaliah at Mizpah to live among the people left in the land (vv. 1-6).

The surviving captains come in to Gedaliah, who swears to them that they need not fear the Chaldeans: dwell in the land, serve Babylon, and it will be well. He will deal with the occupiers himself while they gather wine, summer fruits and oil and live in their towns. Judeans scattered in Moab, Ammon, Edom and elsewhere hear of the remnant and come home, and the harvest is abundant (vv. 7-12).

Johanan and the other commanders warn Gedaliah that Baalis king of Ammon has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to kill him, and he will not believe them. Johanan presses privately for permission to kill Ishmael first, naming what is at stake — the Judeans scattered, the remnant perishing — and Gedaliah refuses, telling him he is speaking falsely of Ishmael (vv. 13-16).
40.theology:
God's promises to his servants are not always smoothly administered by the people carrying them: the man the emperor ordered protected was processed in chains with everyone else (v. 1; 39:12).

An outsider can state plainly what those inside the covenant refuse to hear. A Babylonian officer summarised Jeremiah's whole message and got it right (vv. 2-3).

Offered comfort in Babylon or ruin in Judah, the prophet chose his broken people, which is the shape of his entire ministry (vv. 4-6).

After catastrophe the way back is not a grand project but harvest, storage and settled homes — the same counsel sent to the exiles (vv. 9-10; 27:12; 29:5). Mercy often looks like a good grape harvest rather than a restored temple (v. 12).

Refusing to think ill of anyone is not wisdom. A generous man called a true warning slander, took no precautions, and the remnant paid for it (vv. 14, 16; 41:1-2).

Sound analysis and a sinful remedy often arrive together: Johanan read the situation correctly and proposed a secret murder (v. 15).
40.examples:
A protected man processed in chains anyway, at Ramah of all places.

An idolater with better theology than Judah's kings.

A pension in Babylon or rubble at home, and he chose the rubble.

Rations and a gift, from the man who burned the temple.

Five commanders listed flatly, the assassin first.

A governor who took the hard conversations and left his people the harvest.

Grapes and summer fruit in the year the city burned.

Six words: he would not believe them.

Calling the men who told you the truth slanderers.

A nation lost at a dinner table rather than to an army.

41.text: <sup>1</sup>In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there at Mizpah,<sup>2</sup>Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land.<sup>3</sup>Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there.<sup>4</sup>On the day after the murder of Gedaliah, before anyone knew of it,<sup>5</sup>eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah came out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he came. As he met them, he said to them, "Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam."<sup>7</sup>When they came into the city, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern.<sup>8</sup>But there were ten men among them who said to Ishmael, "Do not put us to death, for we have stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields." So he refrained and did not put them to death with their companions.<sup>9</sup>Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men whom he had struck down along with Gedaliah was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.<sup>10</sup>Then Ishmael took captive all the rest of the people who were in Mizpah, the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.<sup>11</sup>But when Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done,<sup>12</sup>they took all their men and went to fight against Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon.<sup>13</sup>And when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him, they rejoiced.<sup>14</sup>So all the people whom Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.<sup>15</sup>But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites.<sup>16</sup>Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the rest of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, after he had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon.<sup>17</sup>And they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt<sup>18</sup>because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — As They Ate Bread Together
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah — of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king — comes to Mizpah with ten men (v. 1). The horror is in the setting: As they ate bread together there at Mizpah, they rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him (v. 2). Then the killing widens: Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: A guest at the governor's table, with a sword under the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there at Mizpah, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land. Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there at Mizpah,

Two months after the harvest of chapter 40, the assassin arrives — and now we learn who he was. Of the royal family, and one of the chief officers of the king. A prince of David's line, and Gedaliah was a commoner appointed by Babylon.

That is motive enough without Ammonite money. A man with royal blood watching a scribe's grandson govern Judah, in a country where the throne had just been emptied.

And then the clause that makes this more than politics: As they ate bread together there at Mizpah. He came with ten men, was received as a guest, was given a meal, and drew his sword across the table.

In the ancient world a shared meal was a bond. To eat a man's bread was to place yourself under obligation to him, which is why a psalm reaches for exactly this image to describe the deepest wound available: Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps 41:9).

The Lord took that verse onto his own lips in an upper room, of a man sitting at his table with the money already counted: He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me (John 13:18). And there is a difference between the two tables that is the whole gospel. Gedaliah did not know, and had refused to be told. Jesus knew exactly who was reaching for the dish, and passed him the bread anyway.

Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land.

The full genealogy is given as an epitaph: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan. Shaphan read the law to Josiah; Ahikam's hand saved Jeremiah's life at his trial; Gedaliah took the prophet home when the city fell. Three generations of quiet faithfulness, and the line ends at a dinner table.

Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there.

The Chaldean garrison dies too, and with them any hope that Babylon will treat this as an internal matter. Ishmael has not merely killed a governor; he has guaranteed a reprisal, which is what drives the rest of the book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Eighty Pilgrims and a Cistern
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Next day, before anyone knew of it (v. 4), eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD (v. 5). Ishmael goes out weeping as he came and invites them in — Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam (v. 6) — then slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern (v. 7). Ten buy their lives with stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields (v. 8). And the pit was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael filled it with the slain (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief counterfeited at the gate, and a reservoir built to save life packed with the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day after the murder of Gedaliah, before anyone knew of it, eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day after the murder of Gedaliah, before anyone knew of it,

The news has not travelled. For one day Mizpah looks like a functioning provincial capital with a governor in it, and Ishmael is still inside pretending it is.

eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD.

Look carefully at these eighty men, because they are one of the saddest details in the book.

They come from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria — the old northern kingdom, whose people had been deported by Assyria a century and a half before. These are the descendants of those left behind, and they are still walking south with offerings for the God of Israel.

They are in mourning for Jerusalem: beards shaved, clothes torn, bodies cut. And two of those three were expressly forbidden. You shall not make any cuts on your body for the dead (Lev 19:28); You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead (Deut 14:1). Their grief was genuine and their practice was pagan, learned from neighbours over generations without the law to correct it.

And they are carrying grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD — to a temple that had been ash for two months. Either they had not heard, or they were going to the site anyway to lay offerings in the ruins.

It would be easy to be superior about them, and it would be wrong. Eighty men walked forty miles through occupied country, disfigured with grief, to bring flour and incense to a God whose house was rubble. Their theology was muddled and their hearts were not. God's people are often more sincere than they are well-taught, and the answer to that is teaching, not contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah came out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he came. As he met them, he said to them, "Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam." When they came into the city, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah came out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he came. As he met them, he said to them, "Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam."

Weeping as he came. He had murdered the governor the day before and he comes out onto the road in tears.

The tears were the trap. These men were in mourning, and the one sure way into their confidence was shared grief. So he wept with them over the city he had just made worse, and then said the name of a dead man as an invitation: Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam.

This is what hypocrisy is for. Not self-deception, but a tool — the borrowing of the forms of godliness and sorrow in order to get close enough to do harm. Wolves come in sheep's clothing because the clothing works.

When they came into the city, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern.

Eleven men killed eighty pilgrims inside the walls, and the bodies went into a water pit.

Hold the cistern beside the one three chapters ago. Jeremiah had been lowered into a cistern with no water in the cistern, but only mud (38:6), and a foreigner came with ropes and old rags and drew him out. Here the same kind of pit is used to hide a massacre. The identical feature of the identical landscape: in one, a man is hauled up to live; in the other, eighty worshippers are thrown down. What differs is not the hole but the hand.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were ten men among them who said to Ishmael, "Do not put us to death, for we have stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields." So he refrained and did not put them to death with their companions. Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men whom he had struck down along with Gedaliah was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But there were ten men among them who said to Ishmael, "Do not put us to death, for we have stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields." So he refrained and did not put them to death with their companions.

Ten men live because they knew where food was buried.

The detail tells you what a country looks like after a siege. Wheat, barley, oil and honey hidden in the open country, because anything kept in a house was taken. And it tells you what Ishmael valued: seventy-eight murders were nothing to him, and a cache of grain was enough to stay his hand.

There is no comment on the ten. They bought their lives with the location of their food, which is the kind of bargain famine forces on people, and Scripture records it without either praise or blame.

Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men whom he had struck down along with Gedaliah was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.

The narrator stops to tell us who dug the hole, and the ESV notes that where the English reads that these men were struck down along with Gedaliah, the Hebrew has "by the hand of" — the bodies of the men killed by Gedaliah's side, in his company.

Three hundred years earlier King Asa had fortified Mizpah against the northern kingdom, carrying away the stones of Ramah to build it (1 Kgs 15:22). The cistern was part of that work: a reservoir to keep a garrison alive through a siege. It was engineering in the service of survival.

And a prince of Asa's own line filled it with the slain. Things built by good men to preserve life get used by later men for atrocity — the institution intact, the purpose inverted. Judah's story is full of it: a temple built for God's name used to house idols, a covenant ceremony used to seal a lie, and now a waterworks made into a grave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — Recovered at the Pool of Gibeon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ishmael takes the rest captive — the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah — and set out to cross over to the Ammonites (v. 10). Johanan and the commanders hear of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done (v. 11) and pursue: They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon (v. 12). When the captives see the rescue party they rejoiced (v. 13), and turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The one glad moment in the chapter: prisoners seeing who has come for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ishmael took captive all the rest of the people who were in Mizpah, the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Ishmael took captive all the rest of the people who were in Mizpah, the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.

One verse, and it contains the whole remnant of Judah walking east in ropes.

The king's daughters are mentioned, and it is a small shock to find them here. Zedekiah's sons were killed at Riblah; his daughters survived the fall of the city, were left behind as no threat to anybody, and are now being driven toward Ammon as spoil by a man of their own royal house.

Note also whose charge these people were: whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. They had been formally entrusted to him. The Babylonians left them in his care, and the man who murdered him is now stealing them.

And the destination is the point. Ishmael is taking them to the Ammonites — to the king whose money had bought the assassination (40:14). This was never a bid for the throne of Judah. It was a foreign operation, and the remnant were the payment.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done, they took all their men and went to fight against Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon. And when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him, they rejoiced. So all the people whom Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done, they took all their men and went to fight against Ishmael the son of Nethaniah.

But. The first good word in the chapter.

And it is Johanan — the man who brought the warning Gedaliah would not believe, and who had asked permission to deal with Ishmael quietly and been told he was a liar (40:14-16). He had every excuse to say he had told them so. Instead he raised his men and went after the column.

Being disbelieved is a real injury, and the test of a man is what he does for people who dismissed him once they are in trouble. Johanan passes it.
