They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon.

The place is named because everyone knew it — the great pool at Gibeon, where Joab's and Abner's men had once fought a murderous tournament in David's day. Old ground, and more Israelite blood about to be spilled on it.

And when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him, they rejoiced.

They rejoiced. It is the only gladness in the chapter, and it is the gladness of prisoners who look up and see who has come over the hill.

Notice that the captives had been with Ishmael for at least a day's march, and their loyalty was never his. The moment there was an alternative, it was obvious where they stood — which is usually true of people held by force, and it is easy to forget when strength looks like consent.

So all the people whom Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.

No battle is described. The hostages simply turned around and walked to the rescue party, and Ishmael's operation collapsed because the thing he was carrying had legs of its own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Intending to Go to Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ishmael escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites (v. 15) — no justice, at least here. Johanan gathers the recovered remnant, soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon (v. 16), and they camp at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt (v. 17) — because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, since Gedaliah, Babylon's own appointee, had been killed (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Frightened people walking back toward the country God had brought them out of.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites. Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the rest of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, after he had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon. And they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites.

He gets away.

Two of his eleven are unaccounted for; the rest reach Ammon with him, where his paymaster is. He murdered a governor, eighty pilgrims and a garrison, and the chapter simply records that he escaped. There is no execution, no capture, no word of judgment pronounced over him in this book at all.

Scripture is honest about this. Wickedness frequently walks away from the scene, and the person who wants the ledger balanced on the page will not always find it there. What we are given instead is the assurance that the accounts are kept elsewhere by someone who said I am the one who knows, and I am witness (29:23).

Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the rest of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, after he had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam — soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon.

Read the list slowly: soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs. This is what was left of the people of God in the land of promise. Not a nation — a column of survivors on a road, with their governor dead behind them.

And they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.

They camp near Bethlehem, and their reasoning is stated plainly and it is not stupid. Babylon's appointed governor has been murdered along with Babylonian soldiers. A reprisal is coming, and nobody will stop to ask who was responsible. So: Egypt.

Every word of that is sound risk assessment, and it points them at the one direction God had forbidden. Egypt is where the story of this people began, and the whole shape of their existence is that God brought them out of it. To walk back in is to unpick the exodus.

And fear is what does it. Not appetite, not idolatry in any obvious form — fear, with a plausible case attached. Gedaliah would not believe a warning and died of it; these men believe the evidence of their eyes and are about to make a worse mistake. Between credulity and calculation there is a third thing, and the next chapter is them asking for it: that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do (42:3).

It is the right question, asked by men who have already decided the answer. And the last picture the chapter leaves is a company of refugees encamped beside Bethlehem, facing south, afraid — which is where, six centuries later, the answer to all of it would be born, and where a young family would also be told to go down into Egypt for a while and then come home.

41.title: Murder at Mizpah
41.overview:
In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah, a prince of the royal house, comes to Mizpah with ten men, and while they are eating together he and his men kill Gedaliah, along with the Judeans present and the Chaldean garrison (vv. 1-3).

The next day, before the news has spread, eighty pilgrims arrive from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria in mourning — beards shaved, clothes torn, bodies gashed — carrying grain offerings and incense for a temple that no longer stands. Ishmael goes out weeping, invites them in to Gedaliah, and slaughters them, throwing the bodies into a cistern. Ten buy their lives by revealing hidden stores of food. The pit was the large cistern King Asa had dug to defend Mizpah, and Ishmael filled it with the slain (vv. 4-9).

He takes the rest of the people captive, including the king's daughters, and sets out for Ammon. Johanan and the commanders hear of it, pursue him, and catch him at the great pool in Gibeon, where the captives rejoice at the sight of the rescue party and simply turn around and walk back to Johanan (vv. 10-14).

Ishmael escapes to the Ammonites with eight men. Johanan gathers the recovered remnant — soldiers, women, children and eunuchs — and camps at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go down to Egypt, because they are afraid of Babylonian reprisal for the murder of Babylon's own governor (vv. 15-18).
41.theology:
The bond of a shared meal makes betrayal at table the deepest wound there is; the Lord applied that psalm to Judas, with one difference — Gedaliah did not know and had refused to be told, while Jesus knew and passed him the bread anyway (vv. 1-2; Ps 41:9; John 13:18).

Sincerity and sound practice are not the same thing. Eighty men walked forty miles through occupied country to a ruined temple, disfigured by rites the law forbade, and the answer to that is teaching rather than contempt (v. 5; Lev 19:28; Deut 14:1).

Hypocrisy is a tool, not merely a self-deception: the tears were how he got near enough to kill (v. 6).

What differs between the cistern a man is lifted out of and the cistern filled with the dead is not the hole but the hand (v. 7; 38:6). Things built by good men to preserve life are repurposed by later men for atrocity (v. 9; 1 Kgs 15:22).

Scripture is honest that wickedness often escapes on the page, and leaves the accounting to the one who said he is the witness (v. 15; 29:23).

Fear with a plausible case attached is what turns God's people back toward Egypt and undoes their own exodus (vv. 17-18).
41.examples:
A guest received at the governor's table, with a sword under the meal.

Three generations of faithfulness ending at a dinner.

Eighty men carrying flour and incense to a temple of ashes.

Weeping on the road as a way of getting through the gate.

One cistern a man is drawn out of, another packed with the slain.

Ten lives bought with the location of buried grain.

A reservoir dug to keep a garrison alive, used as a grave.

The king's daughters driven east as payment.

The man who was called a liar, raising his men for the people who called him one.

Prisoners who simply turned around and walked back.

Refugees camped beside Bethlehem, facing south, afraid.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Whether It Is Good or Bad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole remnant, from the least to the greatest, comes to Jeremiah with a request that could not be better worded: pray to the LORD your God for us, for all this remnant, that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do (vv. 2-3). He promises total honesty — whatever the LORD answers you I will tell you. I will keep nothing back from you (v. 4). And they bind themselves by oath: May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to all the word (v. 5), Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: A perfect prayer and a total oath, from people who have already decided where they are going.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the commanders of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, came near and said to Jeremiah the prophet, "Let our plea for mercy come before you, and pray to the LORD your God for us, for all this remnant— because we are left with but a few, as your eyes see us— that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then all the commanders of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, came near

Everyone comes. Not a delegation this time — the commanders, the officers, and all the people from the least to the greatest. After Mizpah there is nobody left who can afford to be indifferent.

and said to Jeremiah the prophet, "Let our plea for mercy come before you, and pray to the LORD your God for us, for all this remnant — because we are left with but a few, as your eyes see us —

The request is beautifully put, and every part of it is right. They ask for prayer, they plead for mercy, they name their condition honestly — we are left with but a few — and they appeal to what the prophet can see with his own eyes.

One phrase is a small warning light: the LORD your God. Not ours. It is the same wording Zedekiah's messengers used (37:3), and men who keep God at one remove in their grammar are often keeping him at one remove elsewhere.

that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do."

And there is the question, and it is the right question. Which way, and what to do. You could not improve on it as a prayer for guidance, and the tragedy of the chapter is that it was asked by men with their bags already packed.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah the prophet said to them, "I have heard you. Behold, I will pray to the LORD your God according to your request, and whatever the LORD answers you I will tell you. I will keep nothing back from you." Then they said to Jeremiah, "May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to all the word with which the LORD your God sends you to us. Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you, that it may be well with us when we obey the voice of the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah the prophet said to them, "I have heard you. Behold, I will pray to the LORD your God according to your request, and whatever the LORD answers you I will tell you. I will keep nothing back from you."

He agrees at once, and then makes one promise about himself: I will keep nothing back from you.

Forty years of ministry stand behind that sentence. He had been beaten, put in stocks, dropped in a cistern and had his book burned for keeping nothing back, and he was too old and too tested to start editing now. A preacher who tells his people in advance that he will not trim the answer has given them the most useful thing he has.

Then they said to Jeremiah, "May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to all the word with which the LORD your God sends you to us.

They swear an oath, and they invite God to be the witness against them if they break it. This is not a casual undertaking; it is the most solemn form of commitment available to them.

Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you, that it may be well with us when we obey the voice of the LORD our God."

Whether it is good or bad. They anticipate the possibility of an unwelcome answer and pledge obedience anyway. And notice the grammar has improved: twice now it is the LORD our God.

Every word is correct and the whole thing is hollow, as chapter 43 will show within a day. There is a way of praying for guidance that is really a search for endorsement, and it can produce sincere-sounding oaths. The test of whether we meant whether it is good or bad only comes when the answer is bad.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — If You Will Remain in This Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the end of ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah (v. 7), and he calls them all together (v. 8). The answer is the four verbs of his own commission, with only the constructive pair used: If you will remain in this land, then I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you, and not pluck you up; for I relent of the disaster that I did to you (v. 10). Their fear is named and answered twice: Do not fear the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Do not fear him, declares the LORD, for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand (v. 11), and I will grant you mercy, that he may have mercy on you and let you remain in your own land (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Stay, and God will build and plant — and handle Nebuchadnezzar himself.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah. Then he summoned Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest, and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your plea for mercy before him:
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah.

Ten days of nothing.

The prophet prayed and God did not answer for a week and a half, with a frightened camp waiting outside and a Babylonian reprisal expected any day. Jeremiah had to go out each morning with nothing to report.

God is not on call. He answers according to his own timetable even when the request is urgent and the people are genuinely afraid, and the delay is not indifference. Ten days also gave the remnant ten days to examine what they actually wanted, and gave the oath time to be more than a mood.

Then he summoned Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest,

He calls the same crowd back — all the people from the least to the greatest — because the answer belongs to everyone who asked, not to the leadership alone. There will be no private briefing and no managed release.

and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your plea for mercy before him:

He begins by reminding them that this was their idea. To whom you sent me. Whatever follows, they asked for it.

verseByVerse.quote: If you will remain in this land, then I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you, and not pluck you up; for I relent of the disaster that I did to you. Do not fear the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Do not fear him, declares the LORD, for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand. I will grant you mercy, that he may have mercy on you and let you remain in your own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you will remain in this land, then I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you, and not pluck you up; for I relent of the disaster that I did to you.

Listen to the verbs, because they are the verbs of Jeremiah's ordination. He was appointed to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant (1:10), and for forty years the first four had done the work. Here only the last two are used, with the destructive pair explicitly refused: built up and not pulled down, planted and not plucked up.

And the reason given is staggering: for I relent of the disaster that I did to you. God says he is sorry over the harm — not that he was wrong to send it, but that he takes no pleasure in it and is ready to reverse his posture the moment they will stay put.

The whole offer turns on one condition, and it is not a religious programme. It is geography: If you will remain in this land. Stay where God has put you.

Do not fear the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Do not fear him, declares the LORD, for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand.

God names the fear precisely — the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid — and then says the same thing twice: do not fear him, do not fear him. He knows that a frightened man needs the sentence repeated.

And the ground offered is not a change in Nebuchadnezzar's plans but a presence: for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand.

I will grant you mercy, that he may have mercy on you and let you remain in your own land.

Follow the chain. God will show them mercy, and the effect will be that the emperor shows them mercy. The disposition of the most powerful man alive is treated as something God adjusts in order to keep a promise to a few hundred refugees.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alternative is quoted in their own voice: No, we will go to the land of Egypt, where we shall not see war or hear the sound of the trumpet or be hungry for bread, and we will dwell there (v. 14). And the answer turns their reasoning inside out: then the sword that you fear shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you to Egypt, and there you shall die (v. 16). All who set their faces to go shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, with no remnant or survivor (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The two things they were running from were waiting at the destination.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you say, 'We will not remain in this land,' disobeying the voice of the LORD your God and saying, 'No, we will go to the land of Egypt, where we shall not see war or hear the sound of the trumpet or be hungry for bread, and we will dwell there,' then hear the word of the LORD, O remnant of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: If you set your faces to enter Egypt and go to live there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you say, 'We will not remain in this land,' disobeying the voice of the LORD your God

God quotes the sentence before they say it, and labels it: saying We will not remain in this land is disobeying the voice of the LORD your God. There will be no room afterwards to present the move as prudence rather than rebellion.

and saying, 'No, we will go to the land of Egypt, where we shall not see war or hear the sound of the trumpet or be hungry for bread, and we will dwell there,'

Here is their case, in their own words, and it is a good one. Egypt means no war, no alarm trumpet, no hunger. After thirty months of siege, a murdered governor and a country of ashes, who would not want that?

Which is what makes this passage searching. The sin is not a craving for something wicked. It is a craving for peace and bread in a place God had forbidden. Their instincts were humane and their destination was disobedient.

And Egypt was forbidden by name. The law had said of the king that he must not cause the people to return to Egypt, because You shall never return that way again (Deut 17:16), and Isaiah had pronounced Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help (Isa 31:1). Egypt is the house of slavery they were brought out of. Walking back is not a change of address; it is a reversal of the exodus.

then hear the word of the LORD, O remnant of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: If you set your faces to enter Egypt and go to live there,

The phrase set your faces carries the whole problem. This is not drifting; it is a deliberate turning of the head in a chosen direction.

verseByVerse.quote: then the sword that you fear shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you to Egypt, and there you shall die. All the men who set their faces to go to Egypt to live there shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. They shall have no remnant or survivor from the disaster that I will bring upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
then the sword that you fear shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you to Egypt, and there you shall die.

The answer takes their two reasons and hands them back.

They were going to Egypt to escape war and hunger. God says the sword they fear will overtake them there, and the famine they dread will follow close after them — a picture of two pursuers outrunning a column on the road.

There is no safe country. What a man flees from is not escaped by distance if the thing he is fleeing was sent, and the only refuge available was obedience in a ruined land. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death (Prov 14:12).

All the men who set their faces to go to Egypt to live there shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. They shall have no remnant or survivor from the disaster that I will bring upon them.

The three-fold sentence of the whole book falls one last time, now on the survivors of it. And the closing phrase is the bitterest thing in the chapter: no remnant or survivor.

These people are the remnant. The word had been their identity and their comfort for two chapters. If they go down to Egypt, the remnant will have no remnant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — You Shall See This Place No More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wrath poured out on Jerusalem will be poured out on them in Egypt; they will become an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt, and You shall see this place no more (v. 18). The warning is made formal: Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day (v. 19), that you have gone astray at the cost of your lives (v. 20). Their own oath is read back to them (v. 20), and the verdict follows: you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in anything that he sent me to tell you (v. 21), so you shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence in the place where you desire to go to live (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The last words of the oracle are the place where you desire to go.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you go to Egypt. You shall become an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. You shall see this place no more. The LORD has said to you, O remnant of Judah, 'Do not go to Egypt.' Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you go to Egypt. You shall become an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. You shall see this place no more.

The comparison is exact and it should have ended the discussion: As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you. They had just watched what that looked like. The smoke was barely gone.

Then four words for their reputation — an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt — the same list pronounced over Jerusalem, now transferred to the refugees.

And a short sentence that would fall hardest on anyone who loved the country: You shall see this place no more. Go, and you will never come back.

The LORD has said to you, O remnant of Judah, 'Do not go to Egypt.' Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day

The instruction is reduced to four words so that nobody can claim it was ambiguous: Do not go to Egypt.

And Jeremiah puts his own testimony on record — Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day. He is establishing that the warning was given, plainly, on a particular day, in front of everyone. A faithful minister makes sure that if his people go wrong they cannot say they were not told.

verseByVerse.quote: that you have gone astray at the cost of your lives. For you sent me to the LORD your God, saying, 'Pray for us to the LORD our God, and whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it.' And I have this day declared it to you, but you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in anything that he sent me to tell you. Now therefore know for a certainty that you shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence in the place where you desire to go to live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
that you have gone astray at the cost of your lives. For you sent me to the LORD your God, saying, 'Pray for us to the LORD our God, and whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it.'

Their oath is read back to them, and the tense is the sting. You have gone astray — already, before a single step south. God treats the decision as taken, because it was taken before they ever asked.

And he quotes their promise with the possessive they had used: whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it. They had called him theirs and pledged obedience in advance. The words are now evidence.

And I have this day declared it to you, but you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in anything that he sent me to tell you.

Jeremiah has kept his side exactly: I have this day declared it to you, nothing held back, as promised in verse 4. And the charge against them is total — not obedient in anything.

Weigh what that means about the ten days. The delay was not the problem and the clarity was not the problem. They received a specific, urgent, gracious answer to the exact question they had asked, sworn in advance to obey, and obeyed none of it.

Now therefore know for a certainty that you shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence in the place where you desire to go to live."

And the oracle ends on six words that diagnose the whole human problem: the place where you desire to go to live.

That is where they will die. Not in the place they feared — in the place they wanted. The destination chosen for safety, bread and quiet turns out to be the grave, and it is chosen freely, with a warning ringing in their ears and an oath still warm on their lips.

Which is why this chapter is more than a piece of sixth-century politics. God gave them a plain word, named their fear, promised his presence, offered to build and plant them, and undertook to manage the emperor himself — and they preferred a country of their own choosing. The offer was If you will remain in this land, and remaining is generally harder than moving, because it requires trusting a person rather than changing a circumstance.

42.title: Whether It Is Good or Bad
42.overview:
The whole remnant, from the least to the greatest, comes to Jeremiah and asks him to pray that God will show them the way they should go and what they should do. He promises to keep nothing back, and they swear a solemn oath, calling God as witness against them, that they will obey whatever comes — whether it is good or bad (vv. 1-6).

Ten days later the word comes, and Jeremiah calls them all together. If they remain in the land, God will build them up and not pull them down, plant them and not pluck them up, for he relents of the disaster he sent. They need not fear the king of Babylon, for God is with them to save them, and will grant them mercy so that Nebuchadnezzar shows them mercy and lets them stay (vv. 7-12).

But if they refuse and say they will go to Egypt, where there is no war, no trumpet and no hunger, then the sword they fear will overtake them there and the famine they dread will follow close after them, and they will die — by sword, famine and pestilence, with no remnant or survivor (vv. 13-17).

God's wrath, poured out on Jerusalem, will be poured out on them in Egypt; they will become an execration, a horror, a curse and a taunt, and will never see this place again. The command is four words — do not go to Egypt — and Jeremiah puts the warning formally on record, reads their own oath back to them, and states that they have not obeyed in anything, so they will die in the place where they desire to go to live (vv. 18-22).
42.theology:
There is a way of asking for guidance that is really a search for endorsement, and it can produce faultless prayers and sincere oaths. The test of whether we meant whether it is good or bad comes only when the answer is bad (vv. 3, 6).

God answers on his own timetable. Ten days of silence with a reprisal expected was not indifference, and it gave the oath time to be more than a mood (v. 7).

The constructive verbs of the call stand alone here, with the destructive pair refused, and God says he relents of the disaster he sent — not that it was unjust, but that he takes no pleasure in it (v. 10; 1:10).

The ground offered against fear is not a change in the enemy's plans but God's presence, and the emperor's disposition is something God adjusts to keep a promise to a few hundred refugees (vv. 11-12).

The sin here is not appetite for evil but a craving for peace and bread in a place God forbade. Egypt is the house of slavery; going back reverses the exodus (vv. 14-15; Deut 17:16; Isa 31:1).

What is fled from is not escaped by distance when it was sent. They die not in the place they feared but in the place they wanted (vv. 16, 22; Prov 14:12).
42.examples:
A faultless prayer for guidance, offered with the bags already packed.

I will keep nothing back from you — from a man who had been beaten for that.

Ten mornings of going out with nothing to report.

Build and plant, with pull down and pluck up expressly refused.

Do not fear him — said twice, because frightened people need it twice.

No war, no trumpet, no hunger: a good case for a forbidden country.

Two pursuers outrunning a column on the road.

The remnant told it would have no remnant.

An oath read back as evidence.

Dying in the place you chose for safety.

43.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them,<sup>2</sup>Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and Johanan the son of Kareah and all the insolent men said to Jeremiah, "You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,'<sup>3</sup>but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may kill us or take us into exile in Babylon."<sup>4</sup>So Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah.<sup>5</sup>But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven—<sup>6</sup>the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan; also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah.<sup>7</sup>And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.<sup>8</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes:<sup>9</sup>"Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah,<sup>10</sup>and say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.<sup>11</sup>He shall come and strike the land of Egypt, giving over to the pestilence those who are doomed to the pestilence, to captivity those who are doomed to captivity, and to the sword those who are doomed to the sword.<sup>12</sup>I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive. And he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin, and he shall go away from there in peace.<sup>13</sup>He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis, which is in the land of Egypt, and the temples of the gods of Egypt he shall burn with fire.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — You Are Telling a Lie
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The moment Jeremiah finishes, the answer comes back: You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,' (v. 2). And they supply an explanation — but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans (v. 3). So the verdict is recorded plainly: Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah (v. 4), and they gather all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Ten days waiting for an answer, and one day to decide it was a forgery.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them, Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and Johanan the son of Kareah and all the insolent men said to Jeremiah, "You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,' but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may kill us or take us into exile in Babylon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them,

The narrator labours the point before anyone speaks. These were all these words of the LORD their God, and God had sent him with them. Twice in one verse: the LORD their God. Whatever the people are about to claim, the record is set straight first.

Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and Johanan the son of Kareah and all the insolent men said to Jeremiah, "You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,'

Ten days they waited for this answer. They swore an oath to obey it whether it is good or bad. And within a day of hearing it they call the prophet a liar.

Look at how the denial is framed. They do not say the message is hard, or ask for time, or admit they are afraid. They say God did not send it. When obedience becomes unbearable, the tempting move is not open rebellion but reclassification: decide the word was never really God's, and the problem dissolves.

And Johanan is among them. The man who brought the true warning to Gedaliah and was called a liar for it (40:16), and who rescued the captives at Gibeon, is now doing to Jeremiah exactly what was done to him.

but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may kill us or take us into exile in Babylon."

Then the conspiracy theory, and it is aimed at the scribe. Baruch is the pro-Babylonian influence; the old prophet has been captured by his secretary; the oracle is really policy.

It is an efficient slander because it need not deny that Jeremiah is godly — only that he is being handled. A word you cannot refute can still be neutralised by explaining where it came from, and forty years of proven ministry were set aside with one accusation about the man holding the pen.

verseByVerse.quote: So Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah. But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven—
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah.

The narrator will not let the euphemism stand. They had called it a lie; he calls it what it is — did not obey the voice of the LORD — and he names the specific command they broke: to remain in the land of Judah.

Notice that the sin is stated as a failure to stay. Nothing was required of them but to remain where God had put them and let him build and plant them there.

But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven —

And here is the detail that turns the paragraph tragic. These were the people who had returned. They had come home from Moab, Ammon, Edom and elsewhere when they heard there was a governor and a harvest (40:11-12). God had begun gathering them, in a small and real way, exactly as he promised.

Now they are taken out again, in the opposite direction, by their own leaders. The gathering is undone by the people it had gathered.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list of who went down is given in full — the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah — and at the end of it, also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah (v. 6). And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The two men who told them not to go were carried along with them.

verseByVerse.quote: the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan; also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah. And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan; also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah.

The inventory is complete and it is heartbreaking: men, women, children, the royal daughters, and every single person the Babylonians had entrusted to Gedaliah. Whatever was left of Judah in Judah is on this road.

And then, at the end of the list, as if incidental: also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah. The two men who had just been called a liar and a manipulator are taken along.

He had been offered Babylon with a pension and had chosen his ruined country to stay with these people (40:4-6). This is what that choice cost him. He is somewhere past seventy, and the last journey of his life is a forced march into the one country his whole message had warned against, in the company of men who had just disowned his ministry.

There is no lament recorded. He does not protest, and the text gives him no speech. He simply goes with them, which is the shape of his entire life: tied to a people who would not hear him and would not let him go.

And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.

The reason is stated a third time in four verses — for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. The narrator is making sure no future reader mistakes this for migration.

Tahpanhes was a frontier garrison town in the eastern delta, the first substantial place on the road in. And the geography is the theology: the people God took out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm walked back in of their own accord.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Tahpanhes the word comes again, with an errand: Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah (v. 9). Then the meaning: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: A foundation laid in Pharaoh's forecourt for a throne that is coming anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes: "Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah, and say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes:

God speaks to him in Egypt.

That is not a small thing. Jeremiah had been dragged into a country of forbidden refuge by men who denied his commission, and the word of the LORD arrives there as it always had. He was disobedient in nothing, and God does not treat him as though he were — he remains a prophet on the wrong side of a border he never wanted to cross.

"Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah,

One more acted sign, and after the yoke, the flask and the field, this one is characteristically odd: bury large stones in the wet mortar of the pavement outside Pharaoh's palace, and do it in the sight of the men of Judah.

He is an old man on his knees in a foreign forecourt, pushing stones into mortar while his countrymen watch. The stones will be invisible within a day, which is the point — they are hidden, and they are still there.

and say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.

And the meaning lands hard. They came to Egypt to get away from Nebuchadnezzar, and God says he will set the man's throne on this very pavement, with his canopy spread over the spot. The buried stones are a foundation stone for a Babylonian dais in Pharaoh's own doorway.

Twice more the title appears that has run through this book: my servant (25:9; 27:6). The emperor is still an instrument, and the God who moves him is the God these refugees were running from — I will send and take him.

There is no hiding place from providence. You may cross a border to escape a man, and find that the one who commands him was waiting at the destination.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — As a Shepherd Cleans His Cloak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Egypt itself is sentenced. Nebuchadnezzar shall come and strike the land of Egypt, dealing out pestilence, captivity and the sword to those doomed to each (v. 11). I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive, and he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin (v. 12). The obelisks of Heliopolis will be broken and the temples burned (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The refuge they chose gets the same treatment as the city they left.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall come and strike the land of Egypt, giving over to the pestilence those who are doomed to the pestilence, to captivity those who are doomed to captivity, and to the sword those who are doomed to the sword. I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive. And he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin, and he shall go away from there in peace. He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis, which is in the land of Egypt, and the temples of the gods of Egypt he shall burn with fire.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He shall come and strike the land of Egypt, giving over to the pestilence those who are doomed to the pestilence, to captivity those who are doomed to captivity, and to the sword those who are doomed to the sword.

Egypt gets the sentence of Judah. The three-fold judgment follows them across the frontier, sorted with the same grim precision, and the refuge turns out to be under the same verdict as the place they left.

I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive. And he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin, and he shall go away from there in peace.

Note who lights the fire: I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt. God says he will do it, and Nebuchadnezzar will carry it out. The gods that Judah had gone down to live among will be burned and carted off as loot by an army God sends.

And then an image of startling contempt: he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin. A shepherd sitting in the sun picking lice out of his coat and flicking them away. That is the sack of the greatest of the old civilisations, described as delousing a garment — and the shepherd walks off afterwards in peace, unhurried, having lost nothing.

He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis, which is in the land of Egypt, and the temples of the gods of Egypt he shall burn with fire.'"

The last thing named is the obelisks of Heliopolis — the sun-god's city, whose pillars were the most permanent objects in the world these people had fled into. Stone that had stood for a thousand years, broken.

So the chapter ends where it began, with buried stones and standing ones. The obelisks that looked eternal come down; the stones an old prophet pushed into mortar mark where an emperor's throne will stand. What is visible is temporary, and what God has hidden is the thing that holds.

And this is not the last word on Egypt in Scripture. Six centuries later an angel would tell a carpenter to take a child down into Egypt to keep him alive from a king who wanted him dead, and then to bring him home again, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: Out of Egypt I called my son (Matt 2:15; Hos 11:1). Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience and did not come back. The true Son went down in obedience, and came out — and made the road home for everyone who had taken the wrong one.

43.title: Down Into Egypt
43.overview:
As soon as Jeremiah finishes delivering God's answer, Azariah, Johanan and the insolent men tell him he is lying: the LORD did not send him to say do not go to Egypt. They explain the oracle away as Baruch's doing, a plot to hand them to the Chaldeans. So the commanders and all the people disobey the command to remain in the land of Judah, and gather up the whole remnant — including those who had only just returned from the surrounding nations (vv. 1-5).

The list of those taken down is complete: men, women, children, the princesses, everyone Nebuzaradan had entrusted to Gedaliah — and Jeremiah and Baruch with them. They come into Egypt because they did not obey the voice of the LORD, and arrive at Tahpanhes (vv. 6-7).

There the word comes again. Jeremiah is to bury large stones in the mortar of the pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace, in full view of his countrymen, and announce that God will bring Nebuchadnezzar, his servant, and set his throne above those very stones and spread his canopy over them (vv. 8-10).

Nebuchadnezzar will strike Egypt, dealing out pestilence, captivity and sword; God will kindle fire in the temples of Egypt's gods and their images will be carried off; he will clean the land as a shepherd picks vermin from his cloak and go away in peace; and the obelisks of Heliopolis will be broken (vv. 11-13).
43.theology:
When obedience becomes unbearable, the tempting move is not open rebellion but reclassification — deciding the word was never really God's (v. 2).

A word that cannot be refuted can still be neutralised by explaining where it came from. Forty years of proven ministry were set aside with one accusation about the man holding the pen (v. 3).

The sin is named as a failure to stay. Nothing was asked but to remain where God had put them (v. 4; 42:10).

God's gathering can be undone by the people it gathered: those who had come home from the nations were marched out again by their own leaders (v. 5; 40:11-12).

The word of the LORD reaches his servant in a country he never chose, and God does not treat the obedient man as though he shared the guilt of those who carried him there (vv. 6, 8).

There is no hiding place from providence: you may cross a border to escape a man and find that the one who commands him was waiting at the destination (v. 10; 25:9; 27:6).

What is visible is temporary and what God has hidden is what holds — obelisks broken, buried stones marking a throne (vv. 9, 13). Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience and never returned; the true Son went down in obedience and was called out (Hos 11:1; Matt 2:15).
43.examples:
Ten days waiting for an answer, one day to call it a forgery.

The man who was called a liar, now calling the prophet one.

Blaming the secretary for the sermon.

People who had just come home, marched out again.

Also Jeremiah the prophet — at the end of the list, as if incidental.

An old man on his knees pushing stones into wet mortar.

A throne set up on the pavement you fled to.

An empire deloused like a shepherd's coat.

Thousand-year obelisks broken; hidden stones still in place.

44.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans who lived in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros,<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah. Behold, this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them,<sup>3</sup>because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, in that they went to make offerings and serve other gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.<sup>4</sup>Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!'<sup>5</sup>But they did not listen or incline their ear, to turn from their evil and make no offerings to other gods.<sup>6</sup>Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a waste and a desolation, as at this day.<sup>7</sup>And now thus says the LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant?<sup>8</sup>Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live, so that you may be cut off and become a curse and a taunt among all the nations of the earth?<sup>9</sup>Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers, the evil of the kings of Judah, the evil of their wives, your own evil, and the evil of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?<sup>10</sup>They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.<sup>11</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah.<sup>12</sup>I will take the remnant of Judah who have set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live, and they shall all be consumed. In the land of Egypt they shall fall; by the sword and by famine they shall be consumed. From the least to the greatest, they shall die by the sword and by famine, and they shall become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a taunt.<sup>13</sup>I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence,<sup>14</sup>so that none of the remnant of Judah who have come to live in the land of Egypt shall escape or survive or return to the land of Judah, to which they desire to return to dwell there. For they shall not return, except some fugitives."<sup>15</sup>Then all the men who knew that their wives had made offerings to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, all the people who lived in Pathros in the land of Egypt, answered Jeremiah:<sup>16</sup>"As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you.<sup>17</sup>But we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, both we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster.<sup>18</sup>But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by the sword and by famine."<sup>19</sup>And the women said, "When we made offerings to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands' approval that we made cakes for her bearing her image and poured out drink offerings to her?"<sup>20</sup>Then Jeremiah said to all the people, men and women, all the people who had given him this answer:<sup>21</sup>"As for the offerings that you offered in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land, did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind?<sup>22</sup>The LORD could no longer bear your evil deeds and the abominations that you committed. Therefore your land has become a desolation and a waste and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is this day.<sup>23</sup>It is because you made offerings and because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD or walk in his law and in his statutes and in his testimonies that this disaster has happened to you, as at this day."<sup>24</sup>Jeremiah said to all the people and all the women, "Hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt.<sup>25</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You and your wives have declared with your mouths, and have fulfilled it with your hands, saying, 'We will surely perform our vows that we have made, to make offerings to the queen of heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her.' Then confirm your vows and perform your vows!<sup>26</sup>Therefore hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the LORD, that my name shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, 'As the Lord GOD lives.'<sup>27</sup>Behold, I am watching over them for disaster and not for good. All the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by famine, until there is an end of them.<sup>28</sup>And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live, shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.<sup>29</sup>This shall be the sign to you, declares the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, in order that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for harm:<sup>30</sup>Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Have Seen All the Disaster
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word comes to the Judeans now scattered across Egypt — at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros (v. 1) — and it begins with evidence they cannot dispute: You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem, and this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them (v. 2). The cause is named — offerings to gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers (v. 3) — and so is God's patience: Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!' (v. 4). But they did not listen or incline their ear (v. 5), and the wrath was poured out as at this day (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The argument opens with a ruin they had walked through themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans who lived in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah. Behold, this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them, because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, in that they went to make offerings and serve other gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans who lived in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros,

Four place names, and they tell a story on their own. The company that arrived together at Tahpanhes has spread — north to Migdol on the frontier, south to Memphis, and up the Nile into Pathros, which is upper Egypt. They are settling in, scattering through the country, making lives.

"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah. Behold, this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them,

God begins with what is not in dispute. You have seen — not heard, not been told. These people had walked out through the rubble. Whatever else is arguable, the ruin is a fact they carry in their own memories.

And he claims it: the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem. Not Babylon's achievement.

because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, in that they went to make offerings and serve other gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.

The cause is stated in one word — idolatry — and there is a small devastating clause attached: gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.

These were not ancestral deities with a long claim on the family. They were novelties, picked up from neighbours, unknown to the generations that had actually seen God act. A nation abandoned the God who brought it out of Egypt for gods it had only recently met.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!' But they did not listen or incline their ear, to turn from their evil and make no offerings to other gods. Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a waste and a desolation, as at this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!'

There is the adverb of the whole book again — persistently — and this time it carries an interjection that sounds like nothing else in Jeremiah.

Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate! That is not the language of a statute. It is the cry of someone trying to stop a person he loves from doing something that will destroy them, and God puts it in his own mouth as the summary of four centuries of prophetic preaching. Forty generations of warning, distilled to a single Oh.

But they did not listen or incline their ear, to turn from their evil and make no offerings to other gods.

Two verbs of refusal, and they are the epitaph of the kingdom: did not listen, did not incline their ear. The second is worse than the first. To incline the ear is to lean in; they would not even turn their heads toward it.

Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a waste and a desolation, as at this day.

And as at this day is the hinge of the argument. The evidence is present tense. God is not asking them to accept a theory about judgment; he is pointing at a country they can still see from where they stand, and asking them to read it correctly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Why Do You Commit This Great Evil Against Yourselves?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The question is put as self-harm: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant? (v. 7). They are doing it again, now in Egypt, with the works of your hands (v. 8). Then five kinds of evil are listed as a single inheritance — of their fathers, the kings of Judah, the kings' wives, their own, and their wives' (v. 9) — and the verdict on all of it: They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin described from God's side as a wound the sinner opens in his own household.

verseByVerse.quote: And now thus says the LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant? Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live, so that you may be cut off and become a curse and a taunt among all the nations of the earth? Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers, the evil of the kings of Judah, the evil of their wives, your own evil, and the evil of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now thus says the LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant?

Notice how God describes their sin: against yourselves.

It is the truest thing said about idolatry anywhere in the chapter. He has already told them it provokes him to anger, and here he frames it as self-mutilation — a knife taken to man and woman, infant and child, cutting away their own future. Sin is treason against God and suicide in the family, and the second is often what finally gets a person's attention.

Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live, so that you may be cut off and become a curse and a taunt among all the nations of the earth?

The works of your hands. They made the thing they are worshipping. Paul's summary of the same exchange runs the same way: men who exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals (Rom 1:23).

And note where you have come to live. They had gone to Egypt for safety and immediately resumed the practice that had cost them their own country. A change of address does nothing to the heart that made the move.

Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers, the evil of the kings of Judah, the evil of their wives, your own evil, and the evil of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?

Five generations and classes of evil in one sentence, and the ESV notes that where the English has the plural, the Hebrew reads "his" — the kings' wives spoken of in the singular. Either way the list is comprehensive: fathers, kings, royal wives, the hearers themselves, their own wives. Nobody in the assembly is outside it, and the wives are named twice, which prepares for verse 19.

verseByVerse.quote: They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.

One verse, three failures, and a phrase that should stop any reader: even to this day.

Consider what this day contains. The city burned. The temple gone. The king blinded after watching his sons die. Thirty months of famine, a governor murdered at his table, eighty pilgrims in a cistern, and a forced march into Egypt. If catastrophe by itself produced humility, these would be the humblest people alive.

They are not. They have not humbled themselves, nor have they feared. Suffering does not soften a heart on its own; it only reveals what the heart already was. The same fire hardens clay and melts wax, and Judah in Egypt is the proof.

And the third failure is the plainest: they have not walked in my law and my statutes. God had not asked for an emotion. He had given instructions, set before them and before their fathers, and the charge is simply that nobody did them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — They Shall All Be Consumed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah (v. 11). Those who set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live will be consumed there, From the least to the greatest, becoming an oath, a horror, a curse, and a taunt (v. 12). Egypt will be punished as Jerusalem was, with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence (v. 13), so that none shall escape or survive or return to the land of Judah, to which they desire to return to dwell there — and then one crack of light: except some fugitives (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: They wanted Egypt for a while and Judah in the end, and are told they will have neither.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah. I will take the remnant of Judah who have set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live, and they shall all be consumed. In the land of Egypt they shall fall; by the sword and by famine they shall be consumed. From the least to the greatest, they shall die by the sword and by famine, and they shall become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, so that none of the remnant of Judah who have come to live in the land of Egypt shall escape or survive or return to the land of Judah, to which they desire to return to dwell there. For they shall not return, except some fugitives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah.

I will set my face against you. Earlier in this book God had hidden his face from the city (33:5); here he turns it toward these people, and it is worse. An averted face means abandonment; a set face means deliberate opposition.

I will take the remnant of Judah who have set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live, and they shall all be consumed. In the land of Egypt they shall fall; by the sword and by famine they shall be consumed. From the least to the greatest, they shall die by the sword and by famine, and they shall become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a taunt.

The phrase is answered exactly. They set their faces toward Egypt (42:15), and God set my face against them. Two settings of the face in opposite directions, and only one of them can hold.

And From the least to the greatest is the phrase used of the crowd that came asking for guidance and swore to obey (42:1, 8). The whole company that took the oath is the whole company under the sentence.

I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence,

The comparison is the argument: as I have punished Jerusalem. They had seen what that looked like. Egypt will not be an exception clause.

so that none of the remnant of Judah who have come to live in the land of Egypt shall escape or survive or return to the land of Judah, to which they desire to return to dwell there. For they shall not return, except some fugitives."

Here is the hidden assumption of the whole migration, exposed in one clause: to which they desire to return to dwell there. They never meant to stay in Egypt. The plan was to sit out the danger and go home afterwards — the reasoning of everyone who intends a short detour away from obedience and fully expects to come back.

They will not come back. And then, at the very end, four words that refuse to close the door completely: except some fugitives. A handful will straggle home. Even in this sentence God keeps a remnant of a remnant, and it matters that he says so, because the chapter is about to record the most direct refusal in the book and this clause is spoken before it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — We Will Not Listen to You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer is given by a great assembly, men and women together: As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you (v. 16). Instead they will keep their vows to the queen of heaven, and their reasoning is economic — then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster (v. 17), whereas since they stopped, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by the sword and by famine (v. 18). And the women add their own defence: was it without our husbands' approval that we made cakes for her bearing her image? (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: They read the ruin of Jerusalem as evidence that they had not sinned enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men who knew that their wives had made offerings to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, all the people who lived in Pathros in the land of Egypt, answered Jeremiah: "As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you. But we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, both we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then all the men who knew that their wives had made offerings to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, all the people who lived in Pathros in the land of Egypt, answered Jeremiah:

The description is careful. The men knew what their wives were doing; the women are standing there; it is a great assembly. This is not a faction muttering. It is a congregation, organised, with the households aligned.

"As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you.

And there it is, said out loud at last.

For forty years this people had not listened, but they had always said something else — that Jeremiah was a traitor, or mad, or Baruch's puppet, or that the LORD had not sent him. Here the pretence is dropped. They grant the premise — the word was spoken in the name of the LORD — and refuse it anyway: we will not listen to you.

It is the plainest sentence of unbelief in the Old Testament, and it is not the speech of ignorant people. It is informed, deliberate and corporate.

But we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, both we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster.

The queen of heaven is a goddess of fertility and provision, and this cult is not new. Jeremiah had described it decades earlier in Jerusalem: The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven (7:18). A whole family working together at it — which is exactly what is happening again here.

And the argument they give is economic. When we served her, we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster. It is the reasoning of a woman in Hosea: I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink (Hos 2:5) — and God's answer there is the answer here: she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil (Hos 2:8).

verseByVerse.quote: But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by the sword and by famine." And the women said, "When we made offerings to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands' approval that we made cakes for her bearing her image and poured out drink offerings to her?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by the sword and by famine."

This is the sentence to sit with, because it is a reading of history and it is exactly upside down.

What they are describing is Josiah's reformation. The idols were cleared out, the high places pulled down, the queen of heaven's cakes went off the family table — and then came Megiddo, Egypt, Babylon, the siege, the famine and the fall. They have drawn the obvious conclusion from the sequence: the trouble started when the reform did.

The facts are not in dispute; the causation is inverted. And they are so nearly right that it is frightening. There is a way of reading providence that is careful, empirical, and completely wrong, because it leaves out the four centuries of patience that preceded the reform and the fact that the reform was too late and never reached the heart.

People still argue this way. Things went badly after I began to take God seriously, therefore taking God seriously was the mistake. The timeline is accurate and the verdict is a lie.

And the women said, "When we made offerings to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands' approval that we made cakes for her bearing her image and poured out drink offerings to her?"

The women speak for themselves, and the ESV notes that the introduction here follows the Syriac — "Compare Syriac; Hebrew lacks And the women said" — so in the Hebrew the voice simply continues.

Their point is legal. Under the law a husband who heard his wife's vow and said nothing had confirmed it, and only by opposing it on the day he heard could he annul it (Num 30:6-8). So: our husbands knew, and never once forbade us. That is unanswerable as far as it goes, and it is an indictment of the men standing beside them, who had known all along (v. 15).

But look at what they are actually doing with the argument. They are not asking forgiveness or pleading pressure; they are establishing that the guilt is shared, as a reason to carry on. Spreading the blame feels like a defence and functions as a confession — and Jeremiah's reply goes, deliberately, to all the people, men and women (v. 20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah answers that God did remember those offerings: did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind? (v. 21), and The LORD could no longer bear your evil deeds (v. 22). Their own vow is handed back as a sentence — Then confirm your vows and perform your vows! (v. 25) — and God swears by my great name that it shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt (v. 26). He is watching over them for disaster and not for good (v. 27), and the survivors will know whose word will stand, mine or theirs (v. 28). The sign is Pharaoh Hophra, handed to his enemies as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: Two words were on offer in this book, and the end of it is finding out which one holds.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah said to all the people, men and women, all the people who had given him this answer: "As for the offerings that you offered in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land, did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind? The LORD could no longer bear your evil deeds and the abominations that you committed. Therefore your land has become a desolation and a waste and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is this day. It is because you made offerings and because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD or walk in his law and in his statutes and in his testimonies that this disaster has happened to you, as at this day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jeremiah said to all the people, men and women, all the people who had given him this answer:

He accepts their own framing. They had argued that everybody was in it together, so he addresses everybody together.

"As for the offerings that you offered in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land, did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind?

Two questions, and they go straight at the hole in the argument. They had said that in the days of the cakes there was plenty of food and no disaster — as though God had not noticed. Did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind?

God's patience had been mistaken for God's approval. The years of prosperity were not evidence that he was pleased; they were the long stretch in which he sent prophet after prophet saying Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate! Delay is not indifference, and every unpunished season is being remembered.

The LORD could no longer bear your evil deeds and the abominations that you committed. Therefore your land has become a desolation and a waste and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is this day.
