Could no longer bear. The phrase implies that he had borne it for a very long time, and that there was a limit, and that the limit was reached. The desolation they keep pointing at is not the result of the reformation; it is the end of God's forbearance with the very practice they have resumed.

It is because you made offerings and because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD or walk in his law and in his statutes and in his testimonies that this disaster has happened to you, as at this day."

The causation is stated without a gap: It is because. Their reading of history had one word wrong, and Jeremiah corrects that single word. The disaster came because of the offerings, not because they stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said to all the people and all the women, "Hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You and your wives have declared with your mouths, and have fulfilled it with your hands, saying, 'We will surely perform our vows that we have made, to make offerings to the queen of heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her.' Then confirm your vows and perform your vows! Therefore hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the LORD, that my name shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, 'As the Lord GOD lives.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah said to all the people and all the women, "Hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt.

All you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt. The address is almost a definition of what they have become: not Judah in Judah, but Judah in Egypt — a people identified by the place they should not be.

Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You and your wives have declared with your mouths, and have fulfilled it with your hands, saying, 'We will surely perform our vows that we have made, to make offerings to the queen of heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her.' Then confirm your vows and perform your vows!

God quotes their oath back to them, and then says: do it.

Then confirm your vows and perform your vows! There is no sarcasm in it and no bluff. It is the most terrible thing God says in the book, because it is the withdrawal of resistance. They have insisted on their vows for long enough; he stops arguing and lets them keep them.

Scripture knows this judgment elsewhere — God giving people up to what they have chosen. It is not that he has grown indifferent, but that pleading has an end, and being left alone with what you insisted on is the worst answer prayer can receive.

Therefore hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the LORD, that my name shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, 'As the Lord GOD lives.'

And here is the sentence. God swears by my great name that his name will never again be spoken by a Judean in Egypt.

Weigh what is being removed. Not their lives first, but their liturgy — the oath formula As the Lord GOD lives, the ordinary speech of a covenant people. They had gone on using his name while serving the queen of heaven, invoking him as a matter of habit, and he will not have his name in their mouths on those terms. It is possible to lose the right to say God's name while still saying it constantly.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am watching over them for disaster and not for good. All the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by famine, until there is an end of them. And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live, shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs. This shall be the sign to you, declares the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, in order that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for harm: Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I am watching over them for disaster and not for good. All the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by famine, until there is an end of them.

The verb is the one from Jeremiah's first vision. God had shown him an almond branch and said he was watching over his word to perform it (1:12), and the same attentiveness that promised to build and plant in chapter 31 is here watching over them for disaster and not for good.

It is the same eye, the same care, the same refusal to be distracted. That is a sobering thought about the character of God: his watchfulness is not automatically comfort. What it means for you depends on which side of his word you have placed yourself.

And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live, shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.

A few will get home — few in number, the fugitives of verse 14 — and the reason given for their survival is not comfort but demonstration: so that everyone shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.

That is the question the whole book has been asking since the almond branch. Two words had been on offer in Jerusalem for forty years: Jeremiah's and everybody else's. Hananiah said two years; the queen of heaven's devotees said prosperity; the prophets of peace said no disaster would come. Every one of those words had a date on it, and every date passed.

This shall be the sign to you, declares the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, in order that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for harm:

Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life."

The sign is aimed at the precise thing they trusted. They had come to Egypt because Pharaoh's army had once marched north and lifted a siege, and Hophra is the man they were relying on. He will go the way Zedekiah went, and the comparison is spelled out so nobody can miss it: as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.

And history records it. Hophra was overthrown by his own people and killed by a rival some years later, which is exactly into the hand of those who seek his life.

So the last recorded words of Jeremiah to his own people end on a question rather than a curse: whose word will stand, mine or theirs. It is a question with an answer, and the answer is the reason this book exists. Every word spoken against Jerusalem stood; and that means the other words stand too — the everlasting love, the law written on the heart, the sins remembered no more, the shepherd who gathers, the Branch called The LORD is our righteousness. The God who kept the hard half of his word to the letter is the God who has promised the rest of it.

44.title: We Will Not Listen to You
44.overview:
The word comes to the Judeans now settled across Egypt at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis and Pathros. God begins with what they have seen with their own eyes: Jerusalem and the cities of Judah are a desolation, because of offerings made to gods neither they nor their fathers had known. He had persistently sent the prophets pleading with them not to do the thing he hates, and they would not listen or even incline their ear, so his wrath was poured out (vv. 1-6).

He asks why they are committing this evil against themselves, cutting off man and woman, infant and child, doing it again with the works of their hands in the very country they fled to — and lists the evil of fathers, kings, royal wives, themselves and their own wives, none of whom has humbled themselves or feared or walked in his law (vv. 7-10).

So he will set his face against them for harm. Those who set their faces toward Egypt will be consumed there from the least to the greatest, punished as Jerusalem was, with none escaping or returning to the Judah they still intend to go back to — except some fugitives (vv. 11-14).

A great assembly of men and women answers plainly: we will not listen to you. They will keep their vows to the queen of heaven, because while they served her they had plenty and saw no disaster, and since they stopped they have lacked everything; and the women point out that their husbands knew and approved (vv. 15-19).

Jeremiah answers that God did remember those offerings, that he could no longer bear them, and that the desolation came because of the offerings rather than because they ceased. Then God tells them to confirm and perform their vows, and swears by his great name that no man of Judah in Egypt will invoke it again. He is watching over them for disaster; a few will escape home, so that all may know whose word stands. The sign is Pharaoh Hophra, given to those who seek his life as Zedekiah was given to Nebuchadnezzar (vv. 20-30).
44.theology:
God frames idolatry as self-harm — evil committed against yourselves, cutting off your own infants and children — as well as treason against him (v. 7).

Catastrophe does not by itself produce humility. After the city, the temple, the famine and the march, they had still not humbled themselves or feared: suffering reveals the heart rather than changing it (v. 10).

God's patience can be misread as God's approval. The prosperous years were the years of the prophets pleading, and delay is not indifference — he remembered every one of those offerings (vv. 4, 21-22).

Providence can be read carefully and inverted completely. Their timeline was accurate and their verdict was a lie: the disaster came because of the offerings, not because they stopped (vv. 18, 23; Hos 2:5, 8).

Sharing out the blame feels like a defence and works as a confession (v. 19; Num 30:6-8).

The most terrible answer God gives is to stop resisting: confirm your vows and perform them. Being left alone with what you insisted on is the worst reply a prayer can receive (v. 25).

God's watchfulness is not automatically comfort — the same attentiveness that builds and plants can watch for disaster (v. 27; 1:12; 31:28). And the question the book ends on has an answer: because every hard word stood, the promises stand too (v. 28).
44.examples:
Four place names showing a people settling in for good.

Four centuries of preaching distilled to a single Oh.

Refusing even to turn your head toward the word.

A knife described as taken to your own children.

Gods their grandfathers had never heard of.

The one place in Scripture where unbelief simply says: we will not listen.

A whole household baking together for the queen of heaven.

Trouble started when the reform did — an accurate timeline and a false verdict.

Our husbands knew, and never once forbade us.

Then confirm your vows and perform them.

Losing the right to say God's name while still saying it daily.

The Pharaoh they were counting on, going the way of Zedekiah.

45.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch:<sup>3</sup>You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.'<sup>4</sup>Thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up—that is, the whole land.<sup>5</sup>And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD. But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter is dated to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Baruch wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah (v. 1) — the year of the scroll that Jehoiakim burned. God has a word addressed to the scribe by name: Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch (v. 2). And it opens by quoting his own complaint back to him: You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.' (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: God repeats a tired man's private complaint to him, word for word, and it is not a rebuke.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch: You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:

Five verses, addressed to one man, and they are placed here on purpose.

The date takes us back nearly twenty years, to the fourth year of Jehoiakim — the year Baruch sat down and wrote twenty-three years of sermons onto a scroll at Jeremiah's dictation (36:4), and watched the king cut it up and feed it to a brazier. This word belongs to that moment. But the book keeps it until now, so that Jeremiah's words to his own people end not with a nation's refusal but with God bending down to one exhausted assistant.

"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch:

The full prophetic formula — Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel — the same words that introduced oracles to kings, to Babylon, to Egypt and to the nations, is used here to speak to a secretary.

And it is to you, O Baruch. The God who commands the empires has a private message for the man holding the pen, and he uses his name. That is a word for anyone who has served in a supporting role and wondered whether the work registered.

You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.'

God quotes him. Whatever Baruch had said — privately, perhaps only to himself — is repeated back to him in his own words, and there is no reproach in the quotation.

Hear what he was carrying. The LORD has added sorrow to my pain: he is not blaming circumstances but God, openly. I am weary with my groaning — worn out by his own complaining, which is a particular kind of exhaustion. I find no rest.

He had reason. He came from a prominent family — his brother Seraiah was a royal official — and by attaching himself to Jeremiah he had chosen the losing side of every argument in Jerusalem. He wrote out a book and saw it burned. He read it aloud in the temple and had to go into hiding. He was blamed as the sinister influence behind the prophet (43:3). His own prospects were gone and the country was going with them.

And his master had said the same kind of thing: I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot (20:9). The same word for the same tiredness. Serving God faithfully does not exempt a man from being worn out by it, and Scripture records the complaints of both of them without embarrassment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer sets Baruch's grief inside something vastly larger: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up — that is, the whole land (v. 4). Then the question, gentle and searching: And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh. And the promise the chapter ends on: But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: No career, no safety, no acclaim — and your life, wherever you end up.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up—that is, the whole land. And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD. But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up — that is, the whole land.

God's first move is not consolation but perspective, and it is a strange kind of comfort.

Listen to the verbs. Baruch's own scroll had recorded Jeremiah's commission — to pluck up and break down, to build and to plant (1:10). He had written those words with his own hand. Now God takes two of them and applies them to himself: what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up.

And the object is named so there can be no mistake: that is, the whole land. God is dismantling what God made. He is not losing; he is demolishing, deliberately, his own work.

Which reframes Baruch's grief entirely. His pain was real, and it was a small part of something enormous — and, crucially, something God was doing rather than something that was happening to God. The scribe was not watching a disaster; he was watching a purpose.

And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD.

The question goes straight to what was actually wrong, and it is asked without contempt: do you seek great things for yourself?

Somewhere in Baruch's sorrow was an expectation. A man of his background, attached to the true prophet of God, on the right side of the argument, might reasonably have looked for vindication, standing, a future — and God names it and closes it. Seek them not. Not because ambition is always wicked, but because of the timing: I am bringing disaster upon all flesh. This is not the hour for building a career. The whole world is about to be taken apart.

God's way with his weary servants is often this: not a rebuke, not a discussion of their feelings, but a clear-eyed account of what he is doing and an invitation to want less. Jeremiah himself had been answered the same way when he complained — If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? (12:5).

The New Testament says it to everyone. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness (Matt 6:33). The appointed time has grown very short, so live as those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it (1 Cor 7:29-31). And a man who had thrown away far better prospects than Baruch's put it plainly: whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ (Phil 3:7).

But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go."

And here is what he does get, introduced with But.

The phrase is one Jeremiah had shouted across Jerusalem: go out to the Chaldeans and you will have your life as a prize of war (38:2). It was given personally to Ebed-melech for pulling the prophet out of the mud — you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me (39:18). Now the scribe receives it.

It is a soldier's phrase: the one thing you carry off the field. Not the city, not the spoil, not honour — your life, and nothing else. And the promise is unglamorous and exactly calibrated to a man about to be marched into Egypt against his will: in all places to which you may go. God does not promise him a destination he would choose. He promises to be with him in whatever place he ends up.

So the last word to Baruch is: the great things are not for you, and you will live. Reading it from here, we can see what he was given instead of a career. Every word of Jeremiah we possess came through his hand. He wrote the scroll that was burned, and then wrote it again longer (36:32); he took the deed of the field at Anathoth and sealed it in a jar; he was standing there when the new covenant was dictated. He asked for great things and was told not to, and God gave him the book instead — which has outlasted Jehoiakim, Babylon and Egypt, and is being read still.

45.title: A Word for Baruch
45.overview:
Dated to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the year Baruch wrote Jeremiah's words on the scroll that the king later burned, this short chapter records a word addressed to the scribe by name (vv. 1-2).

God begins by quoting Baruch's own complaint back to him: woe is me, the LORD has added sorrow to my pain, I am weary with my groaning and I find no rest (v. 3).

The answer sets that grief inside something far larger. What God built he is breaking down, and what he planted he is plucking up — the whole land. In such an hour Baruch is asked whether he is seeking great things for himself, and told not to, because God is bringing disaster upon all flesh (vv. 4-5).

But one promise is given: God will give him his life as a prize of war, in every place to which he may go (v. 5).
45.theology:
The God who addresses empires has private words for assistants, and he uses their names (v. 2).

Faithful service does not exempt a man from exhaustion. Baruch's weariness is quoted without reproach, in the same language his master had used of himself (v. 3; 20:9).

God comforts by perspective rather than sympathy: what is happening is his own deliberate demolition of his own work, not a disaster overtaking him (v. 4; 1:10).

Ambition is addressed by timing rather than by shame. Seek them not — because this is not the hour, and disaster is coming on all flesh (v. 5; Matt 6:33; 1 Cor 7:29-31; Phil 3:7).

What God promises his servant is the soldier's one prize, his life, and his presence in whatever place the servant ends up rather than a destination of his choosing (v. 5; 38:2; 39:18).
45.examples:
The formula used for kings and empires, spoken to a secretary.

A private complaint quoted back, with no reproach attached.

Worn out by your own groaning.

Writing out a book and watching it cut up and burned.

God demolishing what God built, on purpose.

Do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not.

The one thing a soldier carries off the field.

Asked for a career, given the book instead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Rising Like the Nile, and Fallen at Carchemish
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oracles concerning the nations open at Carchemish (vv. 1-2), where Nebuchadnezzar broke Pharaoh Neco in 605 BC. The poem begins as a mustering order — Harness the horses; mount, O horsemen!, polish the spears, put on the armour (v. 4) — and then breaks off in astonishment: Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and have turned backward, with terror on every side (v. 5). Egypt had said I will rise, I will cover the earth (v. 8), and instead That day is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, a sacrifice held in the north country by the river Euphrates (v. 10). She may go up to Gilead for balm, but In vain you have used many medicines; there is no healing for you (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: An army dressing for victory, and a God holding a sacrifice on the same field.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations. About Egypt. Concerning the army of Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish and which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Prepare buckler and shield, and advance for battle! Harness the horses; mount, O horsemen! Take your stations with your helmets, polish your spears, put on your armor! Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and have turned backward. Their warriors are beaten down and have fled in haste; they look not back— terror on every side! declares the LORD. "The swift cannot flee away, nor the warrior escape; in the north by the river Euphrates they have stumbled and fallen. "Who is this, rising like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge? Egypt rises like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge. He said, 'I will rise, I will cover the earth, I will destroy cities and their inhabitants.' Advance, O horses, and rage, O chariots! Let the warriors go out: men of Cush and Put who handle the shield, men of Lud, skilled in handling the bow. That day is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, to avenge himself on his foes. The sword shall devour and be sated and drink its fill of their blood. For the Lord GOD of hosts holds a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates. Go up to Gilead, and take balm, O virgin daughter of Egypt! In vain you have used many medicines; there is no healing for you. The nations have heard of your shame, and the earth is full of your cry; for warrior has stumbled against warrior; they have both fallen together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations. About Egypt. Concerning the army of Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish and which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:

A new section begins here, and it widens the horizon of the whole book. For forty-five chapters God has dealt with Judah; now come six chapters concerning the nations. The God who judged his own people is not a local deity with jurisdiction over one hill country.

And the date matters: the fourth year of Jehoiakim, 605 BC. That is the year of the scroll (36:1), and Carchemish is the battle that made Babylon the master of the world.

"Prepare buckler and shield, and advance for battle! Harness the horses; mount, O horsemen! Take your stations with your helmets, polish your spears, put on your armor!

The poem opens inside the Egyptian camp, and the voice is a drill sergeant's. Shields up, horses harnessed, helmets on, spears polished. It is all noise and confidence, and it is God who is issuing the orders — which should warn the reader that something ironic is coming.

Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and have turned backward. Their warriors are beaten down and have fled in haste; they look not back — terror on every side! declares the LORD.

The poem breaks mid-parade. Why have I seen it? — the armour was polished and the line has already collapsed.

And the phrase at the end is one Jeremiah had worn as a nickname. Terror on every side was what he cried and what his enemies called him (6:25; 20:3). The thing he had suffered under is now pronounced over the army Judah was trusting in.

Who is this, rising like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge? Egypt rises like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge. He said, 'I will rise, I will cover the earth, I will destroy cities and their inhabitants.'

The image is Egypt's own. The Nile flood was the source of everything she had, and the boast borrows its language: I will rise, I will cover the earth. Three first-person verbs, which is how empires talk.

That day is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, to avenge himself on his foes. The sword shall devour and be sated and drink its fill of their blood. For the Lord GOD of hosts holds a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates.

The battle is renamed. Egypt thought it was a campaign; God calls it a sacrifice, with himself as the one holding it. Isaiah had used the same terrible picture of a sword sated with blood at a sacrifice in Edom (Isa 34:6).

Go up to Gilead, and take balm, O virgin daughter of Egypt! In vain you have used many medicines; there is no healing for you. The nations have heard of your shame, and the earth is full of your cry; for warrior has stumbled against warrior; they have both fallen together."

Gilead was where the balm came from, and Jeremiah had once asked over his own people, Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? (8:22). Judah's wound was called incurable too — and then God said I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal (30:17).

Here the sentence stops at the diagnosis: there is no healing for you. The difference between Judah and Egypt is not the severity of the wound. It is that one of them had a covenant, and a God who heals wounds he inflicted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–19 — Noisy One Who Lets the Hour Go By
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second word concerns Nebuchadnezzar's coming against Egypt itself (v. 13), addressed to the very towns where the Judean refugees had settled — proclaim in Migdol; proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes (v. 14). The mighty ones are face down, and the reason is given: They do not stand because the LORD thrust them down (v. 15), where the ESV notes the Hebrew reads "He does not stand". The mercenaries break for home (v. 16), and Pharaoh is given a new name: Noisy one who lets the hour go by (v. 17). So: Prepare yourselves baggage for exile, O inhabitants of Egypt! (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: A great power renamed as all noise and no timing.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that the LORD spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt: "Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol; proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes; say, 'Stand ready and be prepared, for the sword shall devour around you.' Why are your mighty ones face down? They do not stand because the LORD thrust them down. He made many stumble, and they fell, and they said one to another, 'Arise, and let us go back to our own people and to the land of our birth, because of the sword of the oppressor.' Call the name of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, 'Noisy one who lets the hour go by.' "As I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts, like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea, shall one come. Prepare yourselves baggage for exile, O inhabitants of Egypt! For Memphis shall become a waste, a ruin, without inhabitant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that the LORD spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt: "Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol; proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes; say, 'Stand ready and be prepared, for the sword shall devour around you.'

Read the place names and remember who is living in them. Migdol, Memphis, Tahpanhes — the exact towns where the Judean refugees had settled (44:1). They fled to these cities to escape the sword, and the sword is being proclaimed over the streets they chose.

Why are your mighty ones face down? They do not stand because the LORD thrust them down.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads "He does not stand" — a single champion falling rather than many. Either way the cause is the same, and it is stated without decoration: the LORD thrust them down.

He made many stumble, and they fell, and they said one to another, 'Arise, and let us go back to our own people and to the land of our birth, because of the sword of the oppressor.'

Egypt's army was full of foreign mercenaries, and here they break for home. Hired soldiers fight for pay and leave when the pay is not worth the risk, which is the standing weakness of any strength you have purchased.

Call the name of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, 'Noisy one who lets the hour go by.'

A nickname, and it is devastating. All sound, no timing — a man who blusters while the moment passes him. The refugees in Egypt had staked their lives on this Pharaoh (44:30), and God gives him a name that says he will not turn up.

"As I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts, like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea, shall one come. Prepare yourselves baggage for exile, O inhabitants of Egypt! For Memphis shall become a waste, a ruin, without inhabitant.

Notice the title: the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. In a chapter full of pharaohs and emperors, one King is named.

And the invader will come like Tabor and Carmel — not as a raid but as a landmark, permanent and immovable. So: Prepare yourselves baggage for exile. The country the refugees chose as a refuge is told to pack.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — A Beautiful Heifer and a Biting Fly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The images turn rural and dismissive. A beautiful heifer is Egypt, but a biting fly from the north has come upon her (v. 20); her hired troops are like fattened calves who turned and fled (v. 21); she slips away like a serpent gliding away while woodcutters come with axes against her forest (v. 22), because they are more numerous than locusts (v. 23). Punishment falls on Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods and her kings, upon Pharaoh and those who trust in him (v. 25) — and then, unexpectedly: Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited as in the days of old (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: A superpower reduced to livestock troubled by an insect — and still given an afterward.

verseByVerse.quote: "A beautiful heifer is Egypt, but a biting fly from the north has come upon her. Even her hired soldiers in her midst are like fattened calves; yes, they have turned and fled together; they did not stand, for the day of their calamity has come upon them, the time of their punishment. "She makes a sound like a serpent gliding away; for her enemies march in force and come against her with axes like those who fell trees. They shall cut down her forest, declares the LORD, though it is impenetrable, because they are more numerous than locusts; they are without number. The daughter of Egypt shall be put to shame; she shall be delivered into the hand of a people from the north." The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, said: "Behold, I am bringing punishment upon Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods and her kings, upon Pharaoh and those who trust in him. I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their life, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his officers. Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited as in the days of old, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A beautiful heifer is Egypt, but a biting fly from the north has come upon her. Even her hired soldiers in her midst are like fattened calves; yes, they have turned and fled together; they did not stand, for the day of their calamity has come upon them, the time of their punishment.

The imagery turns to the farmyard, and it is deliberately belittling. Egypt is a beautiful heifer — sleek, well fed, worth looking at — tormented by a biting fly. Anyone who has watched cattle in summer knows the picture: a huge animal made frantic by an insect it cannot reach.

Her professional soldiers are fattened calves, which is what you call an animal being prepared for slaughter rather than for work.

"She makes a sound like a serpent gliding away; for her enemies march in force and come against her with axes like those who fell trees. They shall cut down her forest, declares the LORD, though it is impenetrable, because they are more numerous than locusts; they are without number.

Then three more pictures in quick succession: a snake sliding off through the grass, woodcutters swinging axes, and locusts beyond counting. Egypt's forest is called impenetrable and it comes down anyway.

The daughter of Egypt shall be put to shame; she shall be delivered into the hand of a people from the north."

The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, said: "Behold, I am bringing punishment upon Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods and her kings, upon Pharaoh and those who trust in him.

The list reaches past the politics to the religion — her gods — and then ends on a phrase that is aimed straight at the Judeans reading it: those who trust in him. They had trusted him. They are on the list.

I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their life, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his officers. Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited as in the days of old, declares the LORD.

And then one word that changes the temperature: Afterward.

Egypt will be inhabited again, as in the days of old. This is not an oracle of annihilation. The God who judges the nations has a future for them beyond the judgment, which is a remarkable thing to say about the house of slavery.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–28 — But Fear Not, O Jacob My Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by turning from Egypt to Israel, in words lifted from the Book of Consolation: But fear not, O Jacob my servant, nor be dismayed, O Israel, for behold, I will save you from far away (v. 27). Fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, for I am with you. I will make a full end of all the nations to which I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The oracle against Egypt closes with the exact comfort once spoken to Jacob.

verseByVerse.quote: "But fear not, O Jacob my servant, nor be dismayed, O Israel, for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. Fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, for I am with you. I will make a full end of all the nations to which I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But fear not, O Jacob my servant, nor be dismayed, O Israel, for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid.

The chapter turns, and anyone who has read chapter 30 will recognise every word. This is 30:10-11, repeated almost exactly, dropped here at the end of an oracle against Egypt.

Think about who first needed to hear it. Judeans living in Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes, who had just been told that the sword would come to those streets. They are also told: fear not, O Jacob my servant. The same word that announces Egypt's ruin turns to the exiles trapped inside it and calls them God's servant.

Fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, for I am with you. I will make a full end of all the nations to which I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished."

Fear not twice, because frightened people need it twice. And the ground is a presence, not a change of circumstances: for I am with you.

Then the distinction the whole section rests on. The nations get a full end; Israel does not — but of you I will not make a full end. And the reason is not that Israel behaved better, which this book has spent forty-five chapters disproving. It is covenant, and nothing else.

Nor is the comfort soft. The same sentence promises discipline in just measure and adds I will by no means leave you unpunished. This is a father's measured hand, not an enemy's, and the difference between being disciplined and being ended is the difference between belonging to him and not.

So the first oracle against the nations closes on the strangest note. Egypt is given an afterward; Israel is given a promise; and both come from the same God on the same page. Judgment on the nations is never the last word in this book — not even for the house of slavery, and never for the people he keeps.

46.title: Against Egypt
46.overview:
The oracles concerning the nations begin with Egypt, at the battle of Carchemish in 605 BC. The poem opens as a mustering order — harness the horses, polish the spears — and then breaks off as the line collapses in terror. Egypt had boasted of rising like the Nile to cover the earth; instead the day belongs to the LORD of hosts, who holds a sacrifice by the Euphrates, and Egypt is told that though she fetch balm from Gilead there is no healing for her (vv. 1-12).

A second word concerns Nebuchadnezzar's coming against Egypt itself, proclaimed in Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes — the very towns where the Judean refugees had settled. Her champions are face down because the LORD thrust them down, her mercenaries break for home, and Pharaoh is renamed Noisy one who lets the hour go by. The inhabitants are told to pack their baggage for exile (vv. 13-19).

Egypt is then a beautiful heifer tormented by a biting fly from the north, her hired troops fattened calves that fled, her impenetrable forest felled by woodcutters more numerous than locusts. Punishment comes on Thebes, on Pharaoh, on her gods and kings, and on those who trust in him — and then, unexpectedly, Egypt is promised that afterward she will be inhabited as in the days of old (vv. 20-26).

The chapter closes by turning to Israel in the words of the Book of Consolation: fear not, Jacob my servant, for I am with you; I will make a full end of the nations but not of you, and will discipline you in just measure (vv. 27-28).
46.theology:
The God who judged Judah is not a local deity. The same word that levelled Jerusalem now addresses the nations (v. 1).

Empires talk in the first person — I will rise, I will cover the earth — and God renames their campaigns as his own sacrifice (vv. 8, 10; Isa 34:6).

The difference between Judah and Egypt is not the severity of the wound. Judah's was called incurable and then healed; Egypt's diagnosis stands, because one of them had a covenant (v. 11; 8:22; 30:17).

Strength that has been purchased leaves when the pay is not worth the risk, and a power everyone was counting on can be renamed as all noise and no timing (vv. 16-17; 44:30).

Judgment on the nations is not annihilation. Egypt, of all countries, is given an afterward (v. 26).

Israel is spared a full end by covenant and not by comparative innocence, and the same sentence that comforts promises discipline in just measure — a father's hand rather than an enemy's (vv. 27-28; 30:10-11).
46.examples:
Polishing spears for a battle already lost.

The prophet's own nickname pronounced over the army Judah trusted.

A campaign renamed as God's sacrifice.

Balm fetched from Gilead for a wound that will not close.

The sword proclaimed over the streets the refugees chose.

Mercenaries deciding the wages are not worth it.

A pharaoh renamed: all noise, and the hour gone by.

A sleek heifer driven frantic by one fly.

Fattened calves, which is what you call animals kept for slaughter.

An afterward, promised to the house of slavery.

47.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza.<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. Men shall cry out, and every inhabitant of the land shall wail.<sup>3</sup>At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of their wheels, the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands,<sup>4</sup>because of the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains. For the LORD is destroying the Philistines, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.<sup>5</sup>Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourselves?<sup>6</sup>Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still!<sup>7</sup>How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Waters Rising Out of the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word comes concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza (v. 1), and the invader is water: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it (v. 2). Then the sound of it — the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, rushing chariots, rumbling wheels — and one detail that measures the panic: the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands (v. 3). It is the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, cutting off every helper that remains from Tyre and Sidon, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: A flood out of the north, and fathers too weak to turn round for their own children.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza. "Thus says the LORD: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. Men shall cry out, and every inhabitant of the land shall wail. At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of their wheels, the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands, because of the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains. For the LORD is destroying the Philistines, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza.

Seven verses for a people who had been Israel's tormentors since the judges. Samson, Goliath, the ark carried into Ashdod, Saul's body hung on the wall at Beth-shan — the Philistines are woven through the whole earlier history, and here they are dealt with in a single short poem.

The dating is by an Egyptian raid on Gaza, which places it in the same years as Carchemish. The great powers are moving, and the small nations on the coast road are in the way.

"Thus says the LORD: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. Men shall cry out, and every inhabitant of the land shall wail.

The invader is described as a flood, and the direction is the one this book has used from the beginning: out of the north. The boiling pot tilted from the north in chapter 1; the enemy from the north hung over Judah for twenty-five chapters. The same water that drowned Jerusalem now comes down the coast.

And a flood is the right image for an army of that size. It does not defeat a city so much as cover it — the land and all that fills it — and there is nothing to fight, only something to be submerged by.

At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of their wheels, the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands,

The poem is built out of sound: hooves stamping, chariots rushing, wheels rumbling. You hear the army before you see it.

Then one image that does more than any casualty figure. The fathers look not back to their children. Men running who do not turn round for their own sons and daughters, and the reason given is not cowardice but collapse — so feeble are their hands. Terror had taken the strength out of them before the enemy arrived.

Scripture is not sneering here. It is telling the truth about what overwhelming force does to ordinary people, and the detail is meant to be felt rather than analysed.

because of the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains. For the LORD is destroying the Philistines, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.

Their allies to the north are cut off too: no help will come from Tyre or Sidon, because they will have their own problem.

And the Philistines are called the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor — Caphtor being their old homeland, the place Genesis names in the table of nations (Gen 10:14). They were sea people who had arrived from somewhere else centuries before. God knows where every nation came from, and the word remnant quietly says that they are already the leftovers of something larger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–7 — Sword of the LORD, How Long?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished, and the survivors are asked how long will you gash yourselves? (v. 5). Then the poem turns and pleads with the weapon itself: Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still! (v. 6). And the answer closes the chapter: How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it (v. 7) — where the ESV notes that the Hebrew reads "you" rather than "it".
verseByVerse.theology: Someone begging the sword to stop, and being told who is holding it.

verseByVerse.quote: Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourselves? Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still! How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourselves?

Two of the five Philistine cities are named, and the mourning is described in the forms these people used: heads shaved bare, bodies cut.

The gashing is the same practice the eighty pilgrims from Shechem and Shiloh had been wearing when Ishmael met them on the road (41:5) — and the same that Israel was expressly forbidden: You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead (Deut 14:1). What God prohibited in his own people was the ordinary grammar of grief among their neighbours, and the question how long will you gash yourselves? is not mockery but a comment on futility. Cutting yourself changes nothing.

Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still!

And here the poet does something remarkable: he turns from the victims and speaks to the weapon.

The tone is not triumph. It is the cry of a man who has watched too much of this — Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Go back in your scabbard. Rest. Be still. Jeremiah had wept over his own people's ruin, and he does not gloat over the ruin of Israel's old enemies either. Even the enemies of God's people are pitied by the man who has to announce their fall.

That is a standing rebuke to a certain way of holding the doctrine of judgment. Anyone who can contemplate it without grief has not understood it.

How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it."

The answer comes back, and it is not comfort: the sword cannot rest because it is under orders. The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads "you" where the English has "it", the poet still addressing the weapon directly.

Two verbs settle it. God has given it a charge and appointed it — this is commission, not chaos. The armies rolling down the coast road were not a breakdown of order; they were an assignment, with a named target: Against Ashkelon and against the seashore.

So the shortest oracle in this section makes the point the whole section exists to make. History is not a series of accidents in which the strong happen to eat the weak. There is a sword, and it is the LORD's, and it moves when he gives it a charge and stops when he does not.

And there is one more thing to say, standing where we do. A day came when the sword of the LORD was given a charge and did not fall on Ashkelon or on Judah. It fell on a man in a garden who had asked that it might pass from him, and who put himself in its way — so that the question How long till you are quiet? finally has an answer for everyone who is his.

47.title: Against the Philistines
47.overview:
A short oracle concerning the Philistines, dated by an Egyptian strike on Gaza. The invader is described as waters rising out of the north that will become an overflowing torrent, covering the land, the city and everyone in it, so that men cry out and every inhabitant wails (vv. 1-2).

The poem is built from sound — stamping hooves, rushing chariots, rumbling wheels — and from one image of collapse: fathers who do not look back for their own children, their hands too feeble. The day is coming to destroy all the Philistines and to cut off every remaining helper from Tyre and Sidon, for the LORD is destroying this remnant of the coastland of Caphtor (vv. 3-4).

Baldness has come on Gaza and Ashkelon has perished, and the survivors are asked how long they will go on gashing themselves. Then the poet addresses the weapon itself, pleading with the sword of the LORD to return to its scabbard and be still — and is answered that it cannot rest, because the LORD has given it a charge and appointed it against Ashkelon and the seashore (vv. 5-7).
47.theology:
The enemy from the north that covered Judah is the same flood that covers the coastal plain. God's instruments are not reserved for one nation (v. 2; 1:13-15).

Scripture tells the truth about what overwhelming force does to ordinary people, without sneering: terror empties a father's hands before the enemy arrives (v. 3).

God knows where every nation came from, and calls the Philistines the remnant of Caphtor (v. 4; Gen 10:14).

Pagan grief is futile as well as forbidden — cutting yourself changes nothing (v. 5; Deut 14:1).

The prophet pities even Israel's old tormentors, and asks the sword how long. Anyone who can contemplate judgment without grief has not understood it (v. 6).

History is commission, not chaos: the sword is given a charge and appointed to a named target, and cannot rest until it is done (v. 7; Isa 34:5-6).
47.examples:
Seven verses for the nation that had fought Israel since the judges.

An army described as a flood — nothing to fight, only something to be covered by.

Hearing the wheels before you see the chariots.

Fathers not turning round for their own children.

No help coming from Tyre, which has its own problem.

Cutting yourself for the dead, and changing nothing.

Begging a sword to go back in its scabbard.

A weapon that stops only when the one holding it says so.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oracle opens with town after town falling — Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Horonaim — until the renown of Moab is no more (v. 2). The sound of it is children: Moab is destroyed; her little ones have made a cry (v. 4), and at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping (v. 5). The cause is named: because you trusted in your works and your treasures, you also shall be taken; and Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials (v. 7). No city escapes (v. 8), and the section ends with a hard word on the work itself: Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: A national god carried off into exile alongside the clergy who served him.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Moab. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Woe to Nebo, for it is laid waste! Kiriathaim is put to shame, it is taken; the fortress is put to shame and broken down; the renown of Moab is no more. In Heshbon they planned disaster against her: 'Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!' You also, O Madmen, shall be brought to silence; the sword shall pursue you. "A voice! A cry from Horonaim, 'Desolation and great destruction!' Moab is destroyed; her little ones have made a cry. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; for at the descent of Horonaim they have heard the distressed cry of destruction. Flee! Save yourselves! You will be like a juniper in the desert! For, because you trusted in your works and your treasures, you also shall be taken; and Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials. The destroyer shall come upon every city, and no city shall escape; the valley shall perish, and the plain shall be destroyed, as the LORD has spoken. "Give wings to Moab, for she would fly away; her cities shall become a desolation, with no inhabitant in them. "Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness, and cursed is he who keeps back his sword from bloodshed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning Moab. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Woe to Nebo, for it is laid waste! Kiriathaim is put to shame, it is taken; the fortress is put to shame and broken down; the renown of Moab is no more.

Moab was the nation across the Dead Sea, close kin and old enemy. Genesis records the ugly beginning — Lot's daughter bore a son and called his name Moab (Gen 19:37) — and from then on they are neighbours, sometimes allies, mostly trouble.

The poem moves through their towns like a casualty list, and it is full of proper names for a reason. These were real places with markets and families in them. Judgment in Scripture is rarely abstract.

"A voice! A cry from Horonaim, 'Desolation and great destruction!' Moab is destroyed; her little ones have made a cry. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; for at the descent of Horonaim they have heard the distressed cry of destruction.

The sound that carries is a child's. Her little ones have made a cry — the detail a prophet includes when he is not enjoying his subject.

The ESV notes two things in verse 5: the Hebrew reads "weeping goes up with weeping", and the Septuagint has "heard the cry", comparing Isaiah 15:5. Isaiah had written the same scene a century before, with fugitives climbing the same road: at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping (Isa 15:5). Two prophets, the same hill, the same people stumbling up it.

For, because you trusted in your works and your treasures, you also shall be taken; and Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials.

Here is the indictment: you trusted in your works and your treasures. What you have made and what you have saved. It is the most respectable idolatry there is, and it needs no shrine.

And then the picture that exposes it: Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials. The national god of Moab is deported. A god who has to be carried into captivity by the men who served him is not a god; he is luggage.

"Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness, and cursed is he who keeps back his sword from bloodshed.

A hard verse, and it is spoken to the invading army: do the job God has given you and do not do it carelessly. It is terrible in its context, and the principle beneath it reaches past the battlefield. Work God assigns is not to be done with slackness. Half-hearted obedience is treated here as a serious matter, whatever the task.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab's problem is comfort. Moab has been at ease from his youth and has settled on his dregs; he has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, nor has he gone into exile; so his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed (v. 11). So God will send pourers who will pour him, and empty his vessels and break his jars in pieces (v. 12), and Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel (v. 13). The boast We are heroes and mighty men of war collapses (v. 14), and neighbours are told to grieve: How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Wine left undisturbed keeps its taste; a nation never poured out keeps its sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moab has been at ease from his youth and has settled on his dregs; he has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, nor has he gone into exile; so his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed. "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I shall send to him pourers who will pour him, and empty his vessels and break his jars in pieces. Then Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence. "How do you say, 'We are heroes and mighty men of war'? The destroyer of Moab and his cities has come up, and the choicest of his young men have gone down to slaughter, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. The calamity of Moab is near at hand, and his affliction hastens swiftly. Grieve for him, all you who are around him, and all who know his name; say, 'How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff.' "Come down from your glory, and sit on the parched ground, O inhabitant of Dibon! For the destroyer of Moab has come up against you; he has destroyed your strongholds. Stand by the way and watch, O inhabitant of Aroer! Ask him who flees and her who escapes; say, 'What has happened?' Moab is put to shame, for it is broken; wail and cry! Tell it beside the Arnon, that Moab is laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Moab has been at ease from his youth and has settled on his dregs; he has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, nor has he gone into exile; so his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed.

This is one of the sharpest pictures in the prophets, and it comes out of a winery.

New wine was left to stand so the sediment — the dregs — would settle, and then it was poured off into another jar, and another, leaving the lees behind. Wine that was never decanted kept its strength but also kept everything that should have been removed. It stayed exactly as it was.

That is Moab. At ease from his youth, never conquered, never deported, never shaken — and therefore never changed. His taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed.

Judah had been poured from vessel to vessel until she hardly knew herself. Moab had been left alone on the shelf, and the text treats that as the worse condition. Undisturbed comfort is not the same as God's favour; it can be the reason a nation or a life never becomes anything different.

"Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I shall send to him pourers who will pour him, and empty his vessels and break his jars in pieces.

So God sends pourers. The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads "their" where the English has "his". The decanting Moab never had is coming as an invasion, and this time the jars are broken as well as emptied.

Then Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence.

An even-handed line. Israel's golden calf at Bethel is named in the same breath as Moab's Chemosh, and both are called their confidence. God does not flatter his own people by contrast.

"How do you say, 'We are heroes and mighty men of war'? The destroyer of Moab and his cities has come up, and the choicest of his young men have gone down to slaughter, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts.

The boast is quoted and then answered by events. Note the title again: the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. In a section full of nations and their kings, one King keeps signing the oracles.

Grieve for him, all you who are around him, and all who know his name; say, 'How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff.'

The neighbours are told to mourn, and the words given them are not gloating: How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff. Moab's greatness is acknowledged in the act of lamenting its end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–33 — He Magnified Himself Against the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment runs through a roll-call of towns far and near (vv. 21-24), and the charge is stated: Make him drunk, because he magnified himself against the LORD (v. 26). The particular offence is named — Was not Israel a derision to you?... whenever you spoke of him you wagged your head? (v. 27) — and the root beneath it: the pride of Moab — he is very proud — of his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart (v. 29). Then the voice changes: Therefore I wail for Moab; I cry out for all Moab (v. 31), and the wine ceases from the presses, the shouting is not the shout of joy (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: God pronounces the sentence and then weeps over the country he is sentencing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Judgment has come upon the tableland, upon Holon, and Jahzah, and Mephaath, and Dibon, and Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim, and Kiriathaim, and Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon, and Kerioth, and Bozrah, and all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near. The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken, declares the LORD. "Make him drunk, because he magnified himself against the LORD, so that Moab shall wallow in his vomit, and he too shall be held in derision. Was not Israel a derision to you? Was he found among thieves, that whenever you spoke of him you wagged your head? "Leave the cities, and dwell in the rock, O inhabitants of Moab! Be like the dove that nests in the sides of the mouth of a gorge. We have heard of the pride of Moab— he is very proud— of his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know his insolence, declares the LORD; his boasts are false, his deeds are false. Therefore I wail for Moab; I cry out for all Moab; for the men of Kir-hareseth I mourn. More than for Jazer I weep for you, O vine of Sibmah! Your branches passed over the sea, reached to the Sea of Jazer; on your summer fruits and your grapes the destroyer has fallen. Gladness and joy have been taken away from the fruitful land of Moab; I have made the wine cease from the winepresses; no one treads them with shouts of joy; the shouting is not the shout of joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Judgment has come upon the tableland, upon Holon, and Jahzah, and Mephaath, and Dibon, and Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim, and Kiriathaim, and Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon, and Kerioth, and Bozrah, and all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near.

Eleven towns in four verses, and then the sweep: all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near. The roll-call is slow on purpose. Somebody knew these places.

"Make him drunk, because he magnified himself against the LORD, so that Moab shall wallow in his vomit, and he too shall be held in derision.

The charge is stated at last, and it is not the towns or the treasure: he magnified himself against the LORD. And the punishment fits the image of the chapter — the nation that was never poured out is now made to drink, and ends up in its own vomit. There is nothing dignified in the picture, which is the point about pride.

Was not Israel a derision to you? Was he found among thieves, that whenever you spoke of him you wagged your head?

Here is the specific offence, and it is startling: Moab is being judged for mockery. When Judah fell, Moab laughed and wagged your head. Zephaniah records the same charge — I have heard the taunts of Moab... how they have taunted my people, and the sentence comes in return for their pride (Zeph 2:8, 10).

God had sent the disaster on Judah himself, and he still holds the onlookers accountable for enjoying it. How we speak of another's downfall is noticed.

"Leave the cities, and dwell in the rock, O inhabitants of Moab! Be like the dove that nests in the sides of the mouth of a gorge.

The advice is to go and live like a bird in a cliff face — which is exactly what people did when nothing was left. And the gentleness of the image sits oddly beside the sentence, as though the one pronouncing it is watching a people he does not hate.

We have heard of the pride of Moab — he is very proud — of his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know his insolence, declares the LORD; his boasts are false, his deeds are false.

Five words for the same thing, piled up: pride, loftiness, pride, arrogance, haughtiness. And then God's own assessment underneath the noise — his boasts are false, his deeds are false. The swagger had nothing behind it, and he had always known.

Therefore I wail for Moab; I cry out for all Moab; for the men of Kir-hareseth I mourn.

And then, without warning, the voice breaks.

Therefore I wail for Moab. The therefore should introduce a sentence; it introduces tears. The same God who has just catalogued Moab's arrogance and ordered him made drunk now mourns for him by name, and for the men of one particular town.

More than for Jazer I weep for you, O vine of Sibmah!... Gladness and joy have been taken away from the fruitful land of Moab; I have made the wine cease from the winepresses; no one treads them with shouts of joy; the shouting is not the shout of joy.

Moab was famous for vineyards, and the picture is of harvest silenced. Treading grapes was noisy work, done with singing. Now there is shouting in the presses and it is the wrong kind.

Notice who says I have made the wine cease. He is not grieving over something that happened to him. He is grieving over what he has done, and both are true at once — which is as close as the Old Testament comes to explaining the tears of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–47 — My Heart Moans Like a Flute
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lament deepens: my heart moans for Moab like a flute, and for Kir-hareseth (v. 36), with shaved heads, cut beards, gashed hands and sackcloth everywhere (v. 37), for God has broken Moab like a vessel for which no one cares (v. 38). An eagle spreads its wings against her (v. 40); there is no way out — He who flees from the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare (v. 44) — and the old song is sung again, fire came out from Heshbon (v. 45). Then the last line turns everything: Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days (v. 47).
verseByVerse.theology: Forty-six verses of ruin, and then one word: Yet.

verseByVerse.quote: "From the outcry at Heshbon even to Elealeh, as far as Jahaz they utter their voice, from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah. For the waters of Nimrim also have become desolate. And I will bring to an end in Moab, declares the LORD, him who offers sacrifice in the high place and makes offerings to his god. Therefore my heart moans for Moab like a flute, and my heart moans like a flute for the men of Kir-hareseth. Therefore the riches they gained have perished. "For every head is shaved and every beard cut off. On all the hands are gashes, and around the waist is sackcloth. On all the housetops of Moab and in the squares there is nothing but lamentation, for I have broken Moab like a vessel for which no one cares, declares the LORD. How it is broken! How they wail! How Moab has turned his back in shame! So Moab has become a derision and a horror to all that are around him." For thus says the LORD: "Behold, one shall fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Moab; the cities shall be taken and the strongholds seized. The heart of the warriors of Moab shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains; Moab shall be destroyed and be no longer a people, because he magnified himself against the LORD. Terror, pit, and snare are before you, O inhabitant of Moab! declares the LORD. He who flees from the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For I will bring these things upon Moab, the year of their punishment, declares the LORD. "In the shadow of Heshbon fugitives stop without strength, for fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the house of Sihon; it has destroyed the forehead of Moab, the crown of the sons of tumult. Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh are undone, for your sons have been taken captive, and your daughters into captivity. Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days, declares the LORD." Thus far is the judgment on Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"From the outcry at Heshbon even to Elealeh, as far as Jahaz they utter their voice... And I will bring to an end in Moab, declares the LORD, him who offers sacrifice in the high place and makes offerings to his god.

The cry runs across the whole map, and the religion goes with it. The high places stop, because there is nobody left to climb them.

Therefore my heart moans for Moab like a flute, and my heart moans like a flute for the men of Kir-hareseth. Therefore the riches they gained have perished.

Twice more the lament, and now with an instrument: my heart moans for Moab like a flute. The flute was played at funerals. God says his heart makes the sound of a funeral instrument over a pagan nation.

Isaiah had written the same line with a different instrument — my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth (Isa 16:11) — the same town named in both. Two prophets, a century apart, given the same grief.

"For every head is shaved and every beard cut off. On all the hands are gashes, and around the waist is sackcloth. On all the housetops of Moab and in the squares there is nothing but lamentation, for I have broken Moab like a vessel for which no one cares, declares the LORD.

The mourning rites are the ones we have seen twice already in this book — shaved heads, cut beards, gashed hands (41:5; 47:5). And the vessel image returns one last time: not merely poured out now, but broken... like a vessel for which no one cares.

Terror, pit, and snare are before you, O inhabitant of Moab! declares the LORD. He who flees from the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare.

Three hazards in a row, arranged so that escaping one puts you into the next. It is the picture of a hunt, and it says what the whole chapter has been saying: there is no door out of God's judgment by running faster.

"In the shadow of Heshbon fugitives stop without strength, for fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the house of Sihon; it has destroyed the forehead of Moab... Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh are undone, for your sons have been taken captive, and your daughters into captivity.

These two verses are a quotation. Centuries earlier, when Israel first came through this territory, the old Amorite victory song ran: For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon... Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh! (Num 21:28-29). Jeremiah sings Moab's ancient defeat song back over Moab's final defeat. History rhymes, and God has a long memory for the words.

Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days, declares the LORD." Thus far is the judgment on Moab.

And then, after forty-six verses of ruin, one word: Yet.

I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days. The phrase is the one used of Israel herself (29:14; 30:3). It is spoken over the people of Chemosh, the nation that wagged its head at Jerusalem's funeral, the drunkard in his own vomit.

And it had already begun, quietly, long before. In the years of the judges a Moabite woman had followed her mother-in-law home to Bethlehem and said that Israel's God would be her God; and the neighbourhood women named her son Obed, who was the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:17). The line that runs to the Messiah has Moab in it.

So the closing formula — Thus far is the judgment on Moab — marks a limit in more than one sense. The judgment reaches this far and no further; and the God who wailed over a pagan country while sentencing it had a latter-day mercy in mind for it all along.

48.title: Against Moab
48.overview:
The oracle against Moab moves town by town — Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Horonaim — until Moab's renown is gone, with children crying and fugitives climbing the ascent of Luhith in tears. The cause is that Moab trusted in his works and his treasures, and his god Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and officials. No city escapes, and the invading army is warned not to do the LORD's work slackly (vv. 1-10).

Moab's deeper problem is undisturbed comfort: he has settled on his dregs, never poured from vessel to vessel, so his taste and scent are unchanged. God will send pourers to empty him and break his jars, and he will be ashamed of Chemosh as Israel was ashamed of Bethel. The boast that they are mighty men of war collapses, and neighbours are told to mourn the broken scepter (vv. 11-20).

Judgment covers all his cities. Moab is made drunk because he magnified himself against the LORD — and specifically because he wagged his head at Israel's downfall. His pride, arrogance and haughtiness are catalogued, and his boasts called false. Then the voice breaks into lament: I wail for Moab, and the winepresses fall silent (vv. 21-33).

God's heart moans for Moab like a funeral flute. Heads are shaved, hands gashed, and Moab is broken like a pot nobody wants. Terror, pit and snare are arranged so that escaping one means falling into the next, and the old Amorite song about fire from Heshbon is sung over Moab's end. Then: yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days (vv. 34-47).
48.theology:
Trusting in your works and your treasures is idolatry that needs no shrine, and a god who must be carried into exile by his own clergy is luggage rather than deity (v. 7).

Undisturbed ease is not proof of favour. Wine never decanted keeps its sediment, and a nation never poured out keeps its sin — which makes Moab's untroubled history the worse condition, not the better (v. 11).

God does not flatter his own people by comparison: Bethel and Chemosh are named together as false confidences (v. 13).

Mockery is an offence God prosecutes. He sent Judah's disaster himself and still holds the onlookers accountable for enjoying it (v. 27; Zeph 2:8-10).

The same God pronounces the sentence and weeps over the nation he is sentencing — grieving over what he himself has done (vv. 31-33, 36; Isa 16:11).

There is no escaping judgment by running faster: terror, pit and snare in sequence (v. 44).

The last word over a pagan enemy is restoration in the latter days — and the line to David already ran through a Moabite woman (v. 47; Ruth 4:17).
48.examples:
A casualty list made of real market towns.

A national god deported alongside his priests.

Wine left on the shelf, keeping everything that should have been poured off.

Pourers sent to empty the jars and then break them.

Bethel and Chemosh named in one breath.

Judged for wagging your head at a neighbour's funeral.

A therefore that introduces tears instead of a sentence.

Shouting in the winepresses, and it is the wrong kind.

God's heart making the sound of a funeral flute.

Escaping the pit straight into the snare.

An enemy's old victory song sung over the enemy.

Forty-six verses of ruin, and then: Yet.
