Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad, and his people settled in its cities?<sup>2</sup>Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will cause the battle cry to be heard against Rabbah of the Ammonites; it shall become a desolate mound, and its villages shall be burned with fire; then Israel shall dispossess those who dispossessed him, says the LORD.<sup>3</sup>"Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai is laid waste! Cry out, O daughters of Rabbah! Put on sackcloth, lament, and run to and fro among the hedges! For Milcom shall go into exile, with his priests and his officials.<sup>4</sup>Why do you boast of your valleys, O faithless daughter, who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?'<sup>5</sup>Behold, I will bring terror upon you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, from all who are around you, and you shall be driven out, every man straight before him, with none to gather the fugitives.<sup>6</sup>"But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites, declares the LORD."<sup>7</sup>Concerning Edom. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Is wisdom no more in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom vanished?<sup>8</sup>Flee, turn back, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Dedan! For I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time when I punish him.<sup>9</sup>If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? If thieves came by night, would they not destroy only enough for themselves?<sup>10</sup>But I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hiding places, and he is not able to conceal himself. His children are destroyed, and his brothers, and his neighbors; and he is no more.<sup>11</sup>Leave your fatherless children; I will keep them alive; and let your widows trust in me."<sup>12</sup>For thus says the LORD: "If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, will you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, but you must drink.<sup>13</sup>For I have sworn by myself, declares the LORD, that Bozrah shall become a horror, a taunt, a waste, and a curse, and all her cities shall be perpetual wastes."<sup>14</sup>I have heard a message from the LORD, and an envoy has been sent among the nations: "Gather yourselves together and come against her, and rise up for battle!<sup>15</sup>For behold, I will make you small among the nations, despised among mankind.<sup>16</sup>The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who live in the clefts of the rock, who hold the height of the hill. Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there, declares the LORD.<sup>17</sup>"Edom shall become a horror. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its disasters.<sup>18</sup>As when Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities were overthrown, says the LORD, no man shall dwell there, no man shall sojourn in her.<sup>19</sup>Behold, like a lion coming up from the jungle of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make him run away from her. And I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?<sup>20</sup>Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman: Even the little ones of the flock shall be dragged away. Surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate.<sup>21</sup>At the sound of their fall the earth shall tremble; the sound of their cry shall be heard at the Red Sea.<sup>22</sup>Behold, one shall mount up and fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Bozrah, and the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains."<sup>23</sup>Concerning Damascus: "Hamath and Arpad are confounded, for they have heard bad news; they melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea that cannot be quiet.<sup>24</sup>Damascus has become feeble, she turned to flee, and panic seized her; anguish and sorrows have taken hold of her, as of a woman in labor.<sup>25</sup>How is the famous city not forsaken, the city of my joy?<sup>26</sup>Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed in that day, declares the LORD of hosts.<sup>27</sup>And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad."<sup>28</sup>Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck down. Thus says the LORD: "Rise up, advance against Kedar! Destroy the people of the east!<sup>29</sup>Their tents and their flocks shall be taken, their curtains and all their goods; their camels shall be led away from them, and men shall cry to them: 'Terror on every side!'<sup>30</sup>Flee, wander far away, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Hazor! declares the LORD. For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you and formed a purpose against you.<sup>31</sup>"Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, that dwells securely, declares the LORD, that has no gates or bars, that dwells alone.<sup>32</sup>Their camels shall become plunder, their herds of livestock a spoil. And I will scatter them to all those winds, and there shall be no nation to which those driven out of Elam shall not come.<sup>37</sup>I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life. I will bring disaster upon them, my fierce anger, declares the LORD. I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them,<sup>38</sup>and I will set my throne in Elam and destroy their king and officials, declares the LORD.<sup>39</sup>"But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ammon is charged with squatting on Israel's inheritance: Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad, and his people settled in its cities? (v. 1) — where the ESV notes the name may be read "Or their king". So Israel shall dispossess those who dispossessed him (v. 2), and as with Chemosh, Milcom shall go into exile, with his priests and his officials (v. 3). The taunt is quoted — who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?' (v. 4) — and then, after five verses of ruin: But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: A second national god carried off with his clergy — and a second afterward.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning the Ammonites. Thus says the LORD: "Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad, and his people settled in its cities? Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will cause the battle cry to be heard against Rabbah of the Ammonites; it shall become a desolate mound, and its villages shall be burned with fire; then Israel shall dispossess those who dispossessed him, says the LORD. "Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai is laid waste! Cry out, O daughters of Rabbah! Put on sackcloth, lament, and run to and fro among the hedges! For Milcom shall go into exile, with his priests and his officials. Why do you boast of your valleys, O faithless daughter, who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?' Behold, I will bring terror upon you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, from all who are around you, and you shall be driven out, every man straight before him, with none to gather the fugitives. "But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning the Ammonites. Thus says the LORD: "Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad, and his people settled in its cities?

Ammon was Moab's brother — Lot's other grandson, whose father was named Ben-ammi (Gen 19:38) — and their territory lay east of the Jordan next to Gad's.

The charge is occupation. When Assyria deported the northern tribes, Ammon moved into Gad's towns and stayed. God's questions are those of a landowner: Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? The tribe was gone, but the title deed was not vacant.

The ESV notes that Milcom, the Ammonite god, may also be read "their king" here and in verse 3. Either reading makes the same point: what took Gad's land was a rival claim to lordship.

Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will cause the battle cry to be heard against Rabbah of the Ammonites... then Israel shall dispossess those who dispossessed him, says the LORD.

The reversal is exact — dispossess those who dispossessed him — and notice that God defends the inheritance of a tribe that had already been carried off for its own sins. His discipline of his people does not transfer their birthright to anyone else.

"Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai is laid waste!... For Milcom shall go into exile, with his priests and his officials.

The same sentence passed on Chemosh one chapter earlier (48:7), word for word in structure. Two national gods, two deportations, both needing their own priests to carry them.

Why do you boast of your valleys, O faithless daughter, who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?'

The ESV notes the Hebrew here as "boast of your valleys, your valley flows". What is clear is the confidence: good land, full treasuries, and the question Who will come against me? — which is the sentence every secure nation says just before the answer arrives.

"But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites, declares the LORD."

Five verses of judgment, and then afterward. It is the same pattern as Moab's Yet (48:47) and Egypt's (46:26), and it is becoming the signature of this whole section. God's last word to the nations around Israel is not extinction.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–22 — Though You Make Your Nest as High as the Eagle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom's wisdom fails (v. 7) and her hiding places are opened: But I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hiding places (v. 10). Then a line that reaches past Edom: If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, will you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, but you must drink (v. 12). The pride is named — The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who live in the clefts of the rock, and Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there (v. 16). And the questions nobody can answer: For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: A fortress in a cliff, and a God who asks who exactly is going to summon him.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Edom. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Is wisdom no more in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom vanished? Flee, turn back, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Dedan! For I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time when I punish him. If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? If thieves came by night, would they not destroy only enough for themselves? But I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hiding places, and he is not able to conceal himself. His children are destroyed, and his brothers, and his neighbors; and he is no more. Leave your fatherless children; I will keep them alive; and let your widows trust in me." For thus says the LORD: "If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, will you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, but you must drink. For I have sworn by myself, declares the LORD, that Bozrah shall become a horror, a taunt, a waste, and a curse, and all her cities shall be perpetual wastes." I have heard a message from the LORD, and an envoy has been sent among the nations: "Gather yourselves together and come against her, and rise up for battle! For behold, I will make you small among the nations, despised among mankind. The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who live in the clefts of the rock, who hold the height of the hill. Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there, declares the LORD. "Edom shall become a horror. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its disasters. As when Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities were overthrown, says the LORD, no man shall dwell there, no man shall sojourn in her. Behold, like a lion coming up from the jungle of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make him run away from her. And I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman: Even the little ones of the flock shall be dragged away. Surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate. At the sound of their fall the earth shall tremble; the sound of their cry shall be heard at the Red Sea. Behold, one shall mount up and fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Bozrah, and the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning Edom. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Is wisdom no more in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom vanished?

Edom is Esau, and the rivalry goes back to a womb: Two nations are in your womb... the older shall serve the younger (Gen 25:23). They were famous for shrewdness, and the oracle opens by asking where all that cleverness has gone.

But I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hiding places, and he is not able to conceal himself.

Edom's security was geography — canyons, cliffs and fortresses reached through slot gorges, the region of Petra. I have uncovered his hiding places is the end of that. There is no terrain God does not know.

Leave your fatherless children; I will keep them alive; and let your widows trust in me."

An extraordinary half-verse in the middle of a judgment oracle. To an enemy nation being stripped bare, God says: leave the orphans with me, and let the widows trust me. Even here the character that defends widows and orphans in the law does not switch off.

For thus says the LORD: "If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, will you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, but you must drink.

Here is the deepest sentence in the chapter, and its logic runs on an argument from the greater to the lesser.

The cup is the cup of wrath from chapter 25, which God handed round the nations beginning with Jerusalem (25:15-16). Judah had drunk it — and the phrase used of Judah here is those who did not deserve to drink. Compared with Edom's guilt, God's own people were the less deserving party, and they drank anyway. So how shall Edom escape?

And the sentence reaches further than Edom, because there was one who truly did not deserve the cup and drank it to the bottom. In a garden he prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39). The argument of verse 12 is the argument of the cross read backwards: if the innocent drank, the guilty cannot plead exemption — and because the innocent drank, the guilty who hide in him need not.

The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who live in the clefts of the rock, who hold the height of the hill. Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there, declares the LORD.

The ESV notes that the clefts of the rock may be read "of Sela", the place name behind Petra. And Obadiah has this passage almost word for word: The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock... Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down (Obad 3-4).

Note what deceived them: The horror you inspire. Being feared had convinced them they were safe. A reputation for being dangerous is a poor defence against God.

Behold, like a lion coming up from the jungle of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make him run away from her. And I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?

Three questions, and they are the centre of gravity of the whole section against the nations. Who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?

The second is the sharpest. To summon is to call someone to court. God asks who is going to issue him a summons — and the silence that follows is the answer to every complaint that his judgments are unfair. There is no higher bench to appeal to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Damascus melts — troubled like the sea that cannot be quiet (v. 23) — in anguish and sorrows... as of a woman in labor (v. 24), and God calls her the city of my joy even as he kindles fire in her wall (vv. 25-27). Then the desert tribes: Kedar's tents, curtains and camels taken, with the old cry Terror on every side! (v. 29). Hazor is a nation at ease, that dwells securely... that has no gates or bars, that dwells alone (v. 31) — and that is no protection: Hazor shall become a haunt of jackals, an everlasting waste (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: Walls are no defence, and having no walls at all is no defence either.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Damascus: "Hamath and Arpad are confounded, for they have heard bad news; they melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea that cannot be quiet. Damascus has become feeble, she turned to flee, and panic seized her; anguish and sorrows have taken hold of her, as of a woman in labor. How is the famous city not forsaken, the city of my joy? Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed in that day, declares the LORD of hosts. And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad." Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck down. Thus says the LORD: "Rise up, advance against Kedar! Destroy the people of the east! Their tents and their flocks shall be taken, their curtains and all their goods; their camels shall be led away from them, and men shall cry to them: 'Terror on every side!' Flee, wander far away, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Hazor! declares the LORD. For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you and formed a purpose against you. "Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, that dwells securely, declares the LORD, that has no gates or bars, that dwells alone. Their camels shall become plunder, their herds of livestock a spoil. I will scatter to every wind those who cut the corners of their hair, and I will bring their calamity from every side of them, declares the LORD. Hazor shall become a haunt of jackals, an everlasting waste; no man shall dwell there; no man shall sojourn in her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning Damascus: "Hamath and Arpad are confounded, for they have heard bad news; they melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea that cannot be quiet.

Syria now, and the image is a sea that will not settle. Panic described as water that cannot stop moving is exact: fear has no resting place in it.

Damascus has become feeble, she turned to flee, and panic seized her; anguish and sorrows have taken hold of her, as of a woman in labor. How is the famous city not forsaken, the city of my joy?

The city of my joy. God calls a Gentile capital that. Damascus was ancient and beautiful, and its maker takes pleasure in it even while pronouncing its fall. Anyone who imagines the God of Israel is indifferent to the cities of the nations has not read this verse.

And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad."

Amos had said the same, naming the same dynasty: I will send a fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad (Amos 1:4). The prophets are not improvising.

Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck down... Their tents and their flocks shall be taken, their curtains and all their goods; their camels shall be led away from them, and men shall cry to them: 'Terror on every side!'

Now the Arab tribes of the desert, and the inventory changes accordingly: not walls and gates but tents, curtains, flocks and camels. God's word reaches the nomads as precisely as the capitals, and it names what they actually own.

And there is the phrase again — Terror on every side! — the words that had been Jeremiah's nickname (20:3) and were pronounced over Egypt (46:5), now shouted after camel herds.

"Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, that dwells securely, declares the LORD, that has no gates or bars, that dwells alone.

Hazor's defence was that it had nothing worth attacking: no gates or bars, living alone out in the desert where armies do not go.

Set this beside Moab, whose security was that he had never been poured out, and Edom, whose security was a cliff. Here is a people whose security is obscurity. All three fall. There is no arrangement of walls, wealth or remoteness that functions as a hiding place, and the phrase a nation at ease has been a warning throughout these chapters rather than a compliment.

Hazor shall become a haunt of jackals, an everlasting waste; no man shall dwell there; no man shall sojourn in her."

And note which oracles carry no promise of restoration. Egypt, Moab, Ammon and Elam are all given an afterward; Damascus, Kedar and Hazor are not. God does not owe an explanation for the pattern, and the book does not offer one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elam, far east beyond Babylon, is reached too: Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might (v. 35). God will bring the four winds from the four quarters of heaven and scatter them until there shall be no nation to which those driven out of Elam shall not come (v. 36). He will set my throne in Elam and destroy its king and officials (v. 38). And then the last word of the chapter: But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology: God sets his throne in the farthest country named, and then promises it a future.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might. And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven. And I will scatter them to all those winds, and there shall be no nation to which those driven out of Elam shall not come. I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life. I will bring disaster upon them, my fierce anger, declares the LORD. I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them, and I will set my throne in Elam and destroy their king and officials, declares the LORD. "But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might.

Elam lay beyond Babylon, in what is now south-western Iran — the farthest nation named in the book, a country most Judeans would never see and had no dealings with.

And their strength is identified precisely: the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might. Elamite archers were famous. God names what a nation is actually proud of before he breaks it.

And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven. And I will scatter them to all those winds, and there shall be no nation to which those driven out of Elam shall not come.

Scattering on a scale that reaches everywhere: refugees from this one country will turn up in every nation on earth.

I will terrify Elam before their enemies... I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them, and I will set my throne in Elam and destroy their king and officials, declares the LORD.

I will set my throne in Elam. Not a garrison or a governor — a throne, in the most distant capital in the book. The claim is that the LORD of hosts governs there directly, and that its king sits on borrowed furniture.

"But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam, declares the LORD."

And the chapter ends as the last one did, with a promise rather than a sentence — in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam.

Count the afterwards now: Egypt inhabited as in the days of old (46:26), Moab restored in the latter days (48:47), Ammon restored (49:6), and Elam restored. Four of the nations in these chapters are told that judgment is not the end of their story.

And on a day of Pentecost, when the Spirit fell and the crowd heard the mighty works of God each in his own language, Luke's list of the nationalities present begins: Parthians and Medes and Elamites. The restoration of Elam, promised through a prophet in a besieged city, turns up as men from Elam hearing the gospel in their own tongue.

49.title: Ammon, Edom, and the Nations Around
49.overview:
Ammon is charged with occupying Gad's territory after Israel was deported: has Israel no heir? Rabbah will hear the battle cry, Israel will dispossess those who dispossessed him, and Milcom will go into exile with his priests and officials. Ammon's boast — who will come against me? — is quoted and answered, and then, after five verses of judgment, God promises to restore the fortunes of the Ammonites (vv. 1-6).

Edom's famed wisdom has vanished. God has stripped Esau bare and uncovered his hiding places, though he tells the orphans to be left with him and the widows to trust him. If those who did not deserve to drink the cup had to drink it, Edom will not escape. The pride that deceived her was the horror she inspired; though she nests as high as the eagle among the clefts of the rock, God will bring her down — for who is like him, who will summon him, what shepherd can stand before him? (vv. 7-22).

Damascus melts in panic like a sea that cannot be quiet, and God calls her the city of his joy while kindling fire in her wall. The desert tribes of Kedar lose tents, curtains, flocks and camels to the cry of terror on every side; and Hazor, a nation at ease with no gates or bars, dwelling alone, becomes a haunt of jackals (vv. 23-33).

Elam, the farthest nation named, has its bow broken and is scattered to the four winds until its refugees reach every country. God will set his throne there and destroy its king — and in the latter days will restore its fortunes (vv. 34-39).
49.theology:
God's discipline of his people does not transfer their inheritance to anyone else: those who dispossessed Israel will be dispossessed (vv. 1-2).

A god who needs his own priests to carry him into exile is not a god — said of Milcom as of Chemosh (v. 3; 48:7).

Even mid-judgment God's care for widows and orphans does not switch off, and he says so to an enemy nation (v. 11).

The cup argument runs from the greater to the lesser: if those less deserving drank it, the guilty cannot plead exemption — and because one wholly innocent drank it to the bottom, those who hide in him need not (v. 12; 25:15-16; Matt 26:39).

Being feared is a poor defence. The horror Edom inspired was what deceived her (v. 16; Obad 3-4).

There is no higher court: who is like me, who will summon me, what shepherd can stand before me? (v. 19).

No arrangement of security works — not walls, not wealth, not a cliff, not even obscurity and having no gates at all (vv. 16, 31; 48:11). And God takes pleasure in Gentile cities, calling Damascus the city of his joy (v. 25).

Four nations in these chapters are promised an afterward, and God gives no reason why some are and some are not (vv. 6, 39; 46:26; 48:47).
49.examples:
A landowner asking whether the family really has no heir.

Two national gods, two deportations, both needing porters.

Who will come against me? — said just before the answer arrives.

Leave the orphans with me, said to an enemy being stripped bare.

The innocent drinking first, so the guilty cannot claim exemption.

A reputation for being dangerous, mistaken for safety.

A nest among the stars, and a hand that reaches it.

Who exactly is going to issue God a summons?

An inventory of tents, curtains and camels.

Security by obscurity, and no gates to lose.

A throne set up in the farthest capital in the book.

Elamites at Pentecost, hearing it in their own language.

For this is the vengeance of the LORD: take vengeance on her; do to her as she has done.<sup>16</sup>Cut off from Babylon the sower, and the one who handles the sickle in time of harvest; because of the sword of the oppressor, every one shall turn to his own people, and every one shall flee to his own land.<sup>17</sup>"Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. For who is like me? Who will summon me? verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Babylon Is Taken, Bel Is Put to Shame
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oracle is to be published everywhere — set up a banner and proclaim, conceal it not — with the news: Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed (v. 2). Out of the north a nation has come up against her (v. 3), the phrase that hung over Judah for twenty-five chapters, now turned round. And in the middle of it, Israel and Judah shall come together, weeping as they come, and they shall seek the LORD their God (v. 4), asking the way to Zion and saying Come, let us join ourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten (v. 5). For My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have led them astray (v. 6), and now the call goes out: Flee from the midst of Babylon (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The enemy from the north gets an enemy from the north.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by Jeremiah the prophet: "Declare among the nations and proclaim, set up a banner and proclaim, conceal it not, and say: 'Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed. Her images are put to shame, her idols are dismayed.' "For out of the north a nation has come up against her, which shall make her land a desolation, and none shall dwell in it; both man and beast shall flee away. "In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, the people of Israel and the people of Judah shall come together, weeping as they come, and they shall seek the LORD their God. They shall ask the way to Zion, with faces turned toward it, saying, 'Come, let us join ourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.' "My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have led them astray, turning them away on the mountains. From mountain to hill they have gone. They have forgotten their fold. All who found them have devoured them, and their enemies have said, 'We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD, their habitation of righteousness, the LORD, the hope of their fathers.' "Flee from the midst of Babylon, and go out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be as male goats before the flock. For behold, I am stirring up and bringing against Babylon a gathering of great nations, from the north country. And they shall array themselves against her. From there she shall be taken. Their arrows are like a skilled warrior who does not return empty-handed. Chaldea shall be plundered; all who plunder her shall be sated, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by Jeremiah the prophet:

For fifty chapters Babylon has been the instrument. God called Nebuchadnezzar my servant three times, put the yoke on Judah's neck, and told the nations to submit. Now the instrument is the defendant.

Two chapters, a hundred and ten verses, the longest oracle in the book — because the hardest question this prophet faced was whether God had simply changed sides.

"Declare among the nations and proclaim, set up a banner and proclaim, conceal it not, and say: 'Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed. Her images are put to shame, her idols are dismayed.'

The instruction is to publish it and conceal it not. And notice what falls first: not the walls or the army, but Bel and Merodach, the gods. Isaiah had drawn the same scene — Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts (Isa 46:1). Gods that have to be evacuated by pack animal.

"For out of the north a nation has come up against her, which shall make her land a desolation

Out of the north. That phrase has been a threat since chapter 1 — the boiling pot, the enemy from the north, the flood that covered Judah and the Philistines. Now it points at Babylon. The direction of judgment does not belong to Babylon; it belongs to God, and it turns.

"In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, the people of Israel and the people of Judah shall come together, weeping as they come, and they shall seek the LORD their God. They shall ask the way to Zion, with faces turned toward it, saying, 'Come, let us join ourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.'

In the middle of an oracle against an empire, this. Both houses together — the northern tribes lost for a century and Judah, coming home in one company.

And they come weeping, asking directions: They shall ask the way to Zion. People who had forgotten the road have to be told it, and their faces are turned toward it before their feet arrive. The covenant they ask for is the one promised in chapter 31 — an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten — and it is asked for, not imposed.

"My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have led them astray, turning them away on the mountains.

God's diagnosis of the whole tragedy, in two sentences, and he does not begin with the sheep's stupidity. He begins with the shepherds — the kings, priests and prophets of chapter 23, who scattered my flock (23:2).

The sheep are still called my people, and still called lost. Isaiah puts both halves together and adds the remedy: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned — every one — to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isa 53:6).

"Flee from the midst of Babylon, and go out of the land of the Chaldeans

The same voice that said build houses and plant gardens in Babylon (29:5) now says leave. Obedience is not a fixed posture; it follows the word of God as it moves, and the people who had settled in for seventy years had to be told when the seventy years were up.

John hears that call again over a later Babylon: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues (Rev 18:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–20 — The Hammer Punished, the Flock Restored
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The plunderers who frolic like a heifer in the pasture are told their mother will be shamed and become the last of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert (vv. 11-12). The archers are summoned for she has sinned against the LORD (v. 14), and the rule is stated plainly: this is the vengeance of the LORD: take vengeance on her; do to her as she has done (v. 15). Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions, first by Assyria and now gnawed by Nebuchadnezzar (v. 17) — so God will punish Babylon as I punished the king of Assyria (v. 18), restore Israel to pasture (v. 19), and in that day iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Instruments are not exempt. God punishes the hammer he swung.

verseByVerse.quote: "Though you rejoice, though you exult, O plunderers of my heritage, though you frolic like a heifer in the pasture, and neigh like stallions, your mother shall be utterly shamed, and she who bore you shall be disgraced. Behold, she shall be the last of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert. Because of the wrath of the LORD she shall not be inhabited but shall be an utter desolation; everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds. Set yourselves in array against Babylon all around, all you who bend the bow; shoot at her, spare no arrows, for she has sinned against the LORD. Raise a shout against her all around; she has surrendered; her bulwarks have fallen; her walls are thrown down. For this is the vengeance of the LORD: take vengeance on her; do to her as she has done. Cut off from Babylon the sower, and the one who handles the sickle in time of harvest; because of the sword of the oppressor, every one shall turn to his own people, and every one shall flee to his own land. "Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. First the king of Assyria devoured him, and now at last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has gnawed his bones. Therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing punishment on the king of Babylon and his land, as I punished the king of Assyria. I will restore Israel to his pasture, and he shall feed on Carmel and in Bashan, and his desire shall be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead. In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none, and sin in Judah, and none shall be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Though you rejoice, though you exult, O plunderers of my heritage, though you frolic like a heifer in the pasture, and neigh like stallions, your mother shall be utterly shamed... Behold, she shall be the last of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.

Babylon is pictured as livestock enjoying itself — a heifer kicking up its heels, stallions neighing. The animal imagery of these oracles is consistently deflating: Egypt a heifer troubled by a fly, Moab wine left on its dregs, Babylon a frolicking herd.

And the last of the nations is a deliberate inversion. Babylon was first among the nations; she will be last, and the place will be desert.

Set yourselves in array against Babylon all around, all you who bend the bow; shoot at her, spare no arrows, for she has sinned against the LORD. Raise a shout against her all around... For this is the vengeance of the LORD: take vengeance on her; do to her as she has done.

Here is the ground of the whole chapter, and it answers the question of whether God has changed sides. Babylon is not being punished for defeating Judah — that was God's own doing. She is punished because she has sinned against the LORD, and the measure is do to her as she has done.

An instrument used by God is still accountable for how it behaved in his hand. Babylon went beyond her commission: cruelty, pride, the temple burned, the plundering of God's heritage for pleasure. Being useful to God is not the same as being righteous, and it confers no immunity.

"Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. First the king of Assyria devoured him, and now at last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has gnawed his bones.

Two empires as two lions over one carcass. Gnawed his bones is what is left when the flesh is gone — the second predator working over what the first left behind.

Therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing punishment on the king of Babylon and his land, as I punished the king of Assyria.

The precedent is Assyria. That empire had been God's rod against the north, and it fell — Nineveh gone within living memory. Babylon can read its own future in Assyria's ruins, and so can every power that thinks it is the exception.

I will restore Israel to his pasture, and he shall feed on Carmel and in Bashan... In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none, and sin in Judah, and none shall be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.

The sheep get pasture again — named pasture, Carmel, Bashan, Ephraim, Gilead, the good grazing country.

And then a sentence that goes further than any restoration of land. Iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none. Someone will look for the sin and not find it — not because it was small, but because of the last clause: for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant. This is the sins-remembered-no-more of 31:34, stated as a search that comes up empty.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The attack goes up against the land of Merathaim and the inhabitants of Pekod (v. 21) — names the ESV glosses as "double rebellion" and "punishment". How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken! (v. 23). I set a snare for you and you were taken, O Babylon, and you did not know it (v. 24), for the LORD has opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath (v. 25). Escapees carry word to Zion of vengeance for his temple (v. 28), because she has proudly defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel (v. 29). And the captors refuse to let them go (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: A city named Double Rebellion, caught in a snare it never saw.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the inhabitants of Pekod. Kill, and devote them to destruction, declares the LORD, and do all that I have commanded you. The noise of battle is in the land, and great destruction! How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations! I set a snare for you and you were taken, O Babylon, and you did not know it; you were found and caught, because you opposed the LORD. The LORD has opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath, for the Lord GOD of hosts has a work to do in the land of the Chaldeans. Come against her from every quarter; open her granaries; pile her up like heaps of grain, and devote her to destruction; let nothing be left of her. Kill all her bulls; let them go down to the slaughter. Woe to them, for their day has come, the time of their punishment. "A voice! They flee and escape from the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, vengeance for his temple. "Summon archers against Babylon, all those who bend the bow. Encamp around her; let no one escape. Repay her according to her deeds; do to her according to all that she has done. For she has proudly defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed on that day, declares the LORD. "Behold, I am against you, O proud one, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, for your day has come, the time when I will punish you. The proud one shall stumble and fall, with none to raise him up, and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour all that is around him. "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The people of Israel are oppressed, and the people of Judah with them. All who took them captive have held them fast; they refuse to let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the inhabitants of Pekod. Kill, and devote them to destruction, declares the LORD, and do all that I have commanded you.

Two Babylonian districts, and the ESV explains why these two are named: "Merathaim means double rebellion" and "Pekod means punishment". Real places on the map whose names, heard in Hebrew, spell out the charge and the verdict. The note on devoting also matters — "That is, set apart (devote) as an offering to the Lord (for destruction)" — the old language of holy war, now used against the empire that had carried out God's own judgment.

How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations!

The hammer of the whole earth. Babylon's own oracle will say it more plainly still: You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces (51:20). A tool, and a tool can be broken by the hand that used it.

I set a snare for you and you were taken, O Babylon, and you did not know it; you were found and caught, because you opposed the LORD.

The most chilling verse in the chapter. You did not know it. The snare was set, sprung and closed while the empire went about its business entirely unaware that anything had happened.

That is how judgment usually arrives on the secure — not as a visible siege but as a position already lost before anyone notices. Belshazzar's feast was going on the night the city fell.

The LORD has opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath, for the Lord GOD of hosts has a work to do in the land of the Chaldeans.

God keeps an armoury, and the weapons in it are nations. The invaders massing on the horizon think they are pursuing their own ambitions; they have been taken out of a store.

"A voice! They flee and escape from the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, vengeance for his temple.

Refugees running the other way — out of Babylon toward Zion, carrying news. And the news has a specific object: vengeance for his temple. The burning of that building was not overlooked.

Repay her according to her deeds; do to her according to all that she has done. For she has proudly defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel.

The charge is pride, and the title used is the intimate one: the Holy One of Israel. Babylon had defied not an abstract deity but the God of the people she had plundered.

"Thus says the LORD of hosts: The people of Israel are oppressed, and the people of Judah with them. All who took them captive have held them fast; they refuse to let them go.

They refuse to let them go. The phrase belongs to another story, and any Israelite would hear it: a hard-hearted king who would not release God's people, and a God who took them out anyway. Babylon has made herself Egypt, and the next verse is the response.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause (v. 34). Then a drumbeat of six swords — against officials, wise men, diviners, warriors, horses and treasures — and A drought against her waters, For it is a land of images, and they are mad over idols (vv. 35-38). Wild beasts and ostriches will live there as at Sodom and Gomorrah (vv. 39-40). The king's hands fell helpless at the report (v. 43), and the chapter closes with the questions already asked of Edom: For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? (v. 44).
verseByVerse.theology: The captives do not have a lawyer; they have a Redeemer, and he takes the case himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth, but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon. "A sword against the Chaldeans, declares the LORD, and against the inhabitants of Babylon, and against her officials and her wise men! A sword against the diviners, that they may become fools! A sword against her warriors, that they may be destroyed! A sword against her horses and against her chariots, and against all the foreign troops in her midst, that they may become women! A sword against all her treasures, that they may be plundered! A drought against her waters, that they may be dried up! For it is a land of images, and they are mad over idols. "Therefore wild beasts shall dwell with hyenas in Babylon, and ostriches shall dwell in her. She shall never again have people, nor be inhabited for all generations. As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities, declares the LORD, so no man shall dwell there, and no son of man shall sojourn in her. "Behold, a people comes from the north; a mighty nation and many kings are stirring from the farthest parts of the earth. They lay hold of bow and spear; they are cruel and have no mercy. The sound of them is like the roaring of the sea; they ride on horses, arrayed as a man for battle against you, O daughter of Babylon! "The king of Babylon heard the report of them, and his hands fell helpless; anguish seized him, pain as of a woman in labor. "Behold, like a lion coming up from the thicket of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make them run away from her, and I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Babylon, and the purposes that he has formed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the little ones of their flock shall be dragged away; surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate. At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shall tremble, and her cry shall be heard among the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth, but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon.

The word is Redeemer — the kinsman with the right and the duty to buy back what his relative had lost, the role Jeremiah himself played for a field at Anathoth (32:7). The captives have no standing and no advocate. What they have is a relative with means.

He will surely plead their cause. He does not send a lawyer; he takes the case. Isaiah names him in the same breath: Our Redeemer — the LORD of hosts is his name — is the Holy One of Israel (Isa 47:4).

"A sword against the Chaldeans... and against her officials and her wise men! A sword against the diviners, that they may become fools! A sword against her warriors... A sword against her horses and against her chariots... A sword against all her treasures, that they may be plundered! A drought against her waters, that they may be dried up! For it is a land of images, and they are mad over idols.

Six swords and a drought, hammered out one after another, and the list is a catalogue of everything Babylon trusted: administration, scholarship, divination, army, cavalry, treasury, and the canal system that made the land fertile.

The diviners get a particular sentence — that they may become fools — and the diagnosis underneath it all is blunt: they are mad over idols. Not mistaken. Mad.

"Therefore wild beasts shall dwell with hyenas in Babylon, and ostriches shall dwell in her. She shall never again have people, nor be inhabited for all generations. As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah... so no man shall dwell there.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks in Babylon here. The picture is a ruin with animals in it, measured against the oldest ruin in Scripture — Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24). John sees the same desolation over the last Babylon: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!... a haunt for every unclean bird (Rev 18:2).

"The king of Babylon heard the report of them, and his hands fell helpless; anguish seized him, pain as of a woman in labor.

The image used of Egypt's soldiers (46:5) and Edom's warriors (49:22) now falls on Babylon's king: his hands fell helpless. Every empire in this section ends in the same posture.

"Behold, like a lion coming up from the thicket of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make them run away from her, and I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?

These are the words spoken over Edom a chapter earlier (49:19), repeated without alteration over the superpower. The same three questions do for the greatest nation what they did for the smallest.

I will appoint over her whomever I choose. Within a lifetime the appointment was made, and his name was Cyrus.

At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shall tremble, and her cry shall be heard among the nations."

So the chapter that began with a banner and a proclamation ends with a sound the whole earth hears. And the point of all of it, for the exiles who first read it, was not the satisfaction of seeing an enemy fall. It was that the God who had used Babylon was not owned by Babylon — that the seventy years had an end written into them, that the shepherds who scattered the flock would answer for it, and that the people asking the way to Zion had a Redeemer strong enough to plead their cause against the hammer of the whole earth.

50.title: Against Babylon
50.overview:
The word concerning Babylon is to be published among the nations and not concealed: Babylon is taken, and Bel and Merodach are put to shame. A nation comes up out of the north against her — the very phrase that hung over Judah. In the middle of it, Israel and Judah come home together, weeping, asking the way to Zion and asking to be joined to the LORD in an everlasting covenant; for they had been lost sheep whose shepherds led them astray. So the call goes out to flee from the midst of Babylon (vv. 1-10).

The plunderers who frolicked like cattle are told their mother will become the last of the nations, a desert. Archers are summoned against her because she has sinned against the LORD, and the measure is to do to her as she has done. Israel was a hunted sheep, devoured by Assyria and gnawed by Nebuchadnezzar, so Babylon will be punished as Assyria was; Israel will be restored to good pasture, and iniquity will be sought in her and not found, because God will pardon the remnant (vv. 11-20).

The attack goes up against Merathaim and Pekod — double rebellion and punishment. The hammer of the whole earth is broken; a snare was set and sprung while Babylon never knew; the LORD has opened his armoury, because he has work to do in Chaldea. Escapees carry to Zion the news of vengeance for his temple, for she proudly defied the Holy One of Israel, and her captors refuse to let the people go (vv. 21-33).

Their Redeemer is strong and will plead their cause himself. Six swords fall — on officials, wise men, diviners, warriors, horses, treasures — with a drought on her waters, for she is mad over idols. Wild beasts and ostriches will live in her as in Sodom. The king's hands fall helpless, and the chapter ends with the questions asked of Edom: who is like me, who will summon me, what shepherd can stand before me? (vv. 34-46).
50.theology:
The direction of judgment belongs to God, not to any empire: the enemy from the north that covered Judah is turned on Babylon (v. 3; 1:13-15).

Gods that must be evacuated by pack animal are not gods (v. 2; Isa 46:1).

Being useful to God confers no immunity. Babylon is punished not for defeating Judah, which was God's own doing, but for sinning against the LORD and exceeding her commission — and the hammer can be broken by the hand that swung it (vv. 14-15, 23; 51:20).

God's diagnosis of a scattered people begins with the shepherds rather than the sheep, and the sheep are still called my people (v. 6; 23:1-2; Isa 53:6).

Obedience follows the word as it moves: the God who said settle in Babylon later says flee from it (v. 8; 29:5; Rev 18:4).

Pardon is described as a search that comes up empty — iniquity sought in Israel and none found (v. 20; 31:34).

Judgment on the secure arrives unnoticed: the snare was sprung and Babylon did not know it (v. 24).

The captives have no advocate and no standing; what they have is a Redeemer who takes the case himself (v. 34; Isa 47:4; 32:7).
50.examples:
Fifty chapters as God's instrument, and now the defendant.

Gods loaded onto weary pack animals.

The enemy from the north, pointed the other way.

People who had forgotten the road, asking the way to Zion.

Told to settle in Babylon, and later told to run.

Two empires as two lions over one carcass.

Reading your own future in Nineveh's ruins.

Districts whose names mean Double Rebellion and Punishment.

A snare sprung while the feast carried on.

An armoury in which the weapons are nations.

Diviners sentenced to become fools.

Not a lawyer sent, but a kinsman taking the case.

Spare not her young men; devote to destruction all her army.<sup>4</sup>They shall fall down slain in the land of the Chaldeans, and wounded in her streets.<sup>5</sup>For Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God, the LORD of hosts, but the land of the Chaldeans is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel.<sup>6</sup>"Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life! Be not cut off in her punishment, for this is the time of the LORD's vengeance, the repayment he is rendering her.<sup>7</sup>Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad.<sup>8</sup>Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken; wail for her! Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed.<sup>9</sup>We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. Forsake her, and let us go each to his own country, for her judgment has reached up to heaven and has been lifted up even to the skies.<sup>10</sup>The LORD has brought about our vindication; come, let us declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God.<sup>11</sup>"Sharpen the arrows! The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it, for that is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance for his temple.<sup>12</sup>"Set up a standard against the walls of Babylon; make the watch strong; set up watchmen; prepare the ambushes; for the LORD has both planned and done what he spoke concerning the inhabitants of Babylon.<sup>13</sup>O you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut.<sup>14</sup>The LORD of hosts has sworn by himself: Surely I will fill you with men, as many as locusts, and they shall raise the shout of victory over you.<sup>15</sup>"It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens.<sup>16</sup>When he utters his voice there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses.<sup>17</sup>Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them.<sup>18</sup>They are worthless, a work of delusion; with you I destroy kingdoms;<sup>21</sup>with you I break in pieces the horse and his rider; with you I break in pieces the chariot and the charioteer;<sup>22</sup>with you I break in pieces man and woman; with you I break in pieces the old man and the youth; with you I break in pieces the young man and the young woman;<sup>23</sup>with you I break in pieces the shepherd and his flock; with you I break in pieces the farmer and his team; with you I break in pieces governors and commanders.<sup>24</sup>"I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea before your very eyes for all the evil that they have done in Zion, declares the LORD.<sup>25</sup>"Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, declares the LORD, which destroys the whole earth; I will stretch out my hand against you, and roll you down from the crags, and make you a burnt mountain.<sup>26</sup>No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation, but you shall be a perpetual waste, declares the LORD.<sup>27</sup>"Set up a standard on the earth; Their waves roar like many waters; the noise of their voice is raised,<sup>56</sup>for a destroyer has come upon her, upon Babylon; her warriors are taken; their bows are broken in pieces, for the LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay.<sup>57</sup>I will make drunk her officials and her wise men, her governors, her commanders, and her warriors; they shall sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts.<sup>58</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: The broad wall of Babylon shall be leveled to the ground, and her high gates shall be burned with fire.
