Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Golden Cup That Made the Earth Drunk
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stirs up the spirit of a destroyer against Babylon, against the inhabitants of Leb-kamai (v. 1) — the ESV notes this is "A code name for Chaldea" — and sends winnowers, and they shall winnow her (v. 2). The reason is stated for the exiles' sake: For Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God, the LORD of hosts, but the land of the Chaldeans is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel (v. 5). Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunken (v. 7), and now, astonishingly, someone tries to nurse her: We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed (v. 9). The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, and it is the vengeance for his temple (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The cup that made the world drunk, held all along in a hand that is now setting it down.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will stir up the spirit of a destroyer against Babylon, against the inhabitants of Leb-kamai, and I will send to Babylon winnowers, and they shall winnow her, and they shall empty her land, when they come against her from every side on the day of trouble. Let not the archer bend his bow, and let him not stand up in his armor. Spare not her young men; devote to destruction all her army. They shall fall down slain in the land of the Chaldeans, and wounded in her streets. For Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God, the LORD of hosts, but the land of the Chaldeans is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel. "Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life! Be not cut off in her punishment, for this is the time of the LORD's vengeance, the repayment he is rendering her. Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad. Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken; wail for her! Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. Forsake her, and let us go each to his own country, for her judgment has reached up to heaven and has been lifted up even to the skies. The LORD has brought about our vindication; come, let us declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God. "Sharpen the arrows! Take up the shields! The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it, for that is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance for his temple. "Set up a standard against the walls of Babylon; make the watch strong; set up watchmen; prepare the ambushes; for the LORD has both planned and done what he spoke concerning the inhabitants of Babylon. O you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut. The LORD of hosts has sworn by himself: Surely I will fill you with men, as many as locusts, and they shall raise the shout of victory over you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will stir up the spirit of a destroyer against Babylon, against the inhabitants of Leb-kamai, and I will send to Babylon winnowers, and they shall winnow her, and they shall empty her land

The ESV notes that Leb-kamai is "A code name for Chaldea" — a cipher, letters reversed, the sort of thing written when a document might be read by the wrong people. Jeremiah is writing about an empire from inside its reach.

And the picture is threshing. Winnowers toss grain into the wind so the chaff blows away; God says he will do that to Babylon and empty her land.

For Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God, the LORD of hosts, but the land of the Chaldeans is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel.

Here is the pastoral heart of both chapters, and it answers the question the exiles were actually asking. Not: will Babylon fall? But: has God dropped us?

Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God. They had every appearance of being forsaken — city gone, temple burned, king blinded — and the verse denies it flatly.

Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad.

An image of terrible beauty. Babylon was a golden cup — genuinely magnificent — and she was in the LORD's hand the whole time. He poured her out for the nations to drink, and the drinking drove them mad.

Empires are intoxicating. Their wealth, art and confidence get into the bloodstream of everyone around them, and the cup was never holding itself up.

Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken; wail for her! Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. Forsake her, and let us go each to his own country

And then something unexpected: an attempt at nursing. Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. Somebody fetches medicine for the empire that burned the temple.

We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. The same balm of Gilead offered to Judah (8:22) and denied to Egypt (46:11) is brought to Babylon's bedside, and the verdict is that it did not take. Judgment here is not described as eagerness to destroy, but as a physician's failure declared after the attempt.

The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it, for that is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance for his temple.

The instrument is named a generation before it arrived: the kings of the Medes. Isaiah had said the same — Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them (Isa 13:17) — and Daniel records the night it happened, when Darius the Mede received the kingdom (Dan 5:31).

And the stated motive is a building: the vengeance for his temple. The house Solomon built and the Chaldeans burned is on the charge sheet, which tells you that God does not shrug off what was done to the place where his name was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A creation hymn interrupts the oracle: It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens (v. 15), who brings forth the wind from his storehouses (v. 16). Against that, the idols: every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them (v. 17), a work of delusion (v. 18) — Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob (v. 19). Then the verdict on the empire's whole career: You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces (v. 20), and the repayment for all the evil that they have done in Zion (v. 24), until the destroying mountain becomes a burnt mountain (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: A tool is told what it was, just before it is put down.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens. When he utters his voice there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses. Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them. They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish. Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name. "You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces; with you I destroy kingdoms; with you I break in pieces the horse and his rider; with you I break in pieces the chariot and the charioteer; with you I break in pieces man and woman; with you I break in pieces the old man and the youth; with you I break in pieces the young man and the young woman; with you I break in pieces the shepherd and his flock; with you I break in pieces the farmer and his team; with you I break in pieces governors and commanders. "I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea before your very eyes for all the evil that they have done in Zion, declares the LORD. "Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, declares the LORD, which destroys the whole earth; I will stretch out my hand against you, and roll you down from the crags, and make you a burnt mountain. No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation, but you shall be a perpetual waste, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens. When he utters his voice there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses.

In the middle of a war oracle, a hymn — and it is the same hymn used earlier against the idols of Judah (10:12-13), repeated here against the idols of Babylon.

Three faculties are named: power, wisdom, understanding. And then the weather, described as an operation: mist raised from the ends of the earth, lightning made for the rain, and the wind from his storehouses, as though God keeps weather in a warehouse and brings out what the day requires.

Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them. They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish.

Against that Creator, the craftsman. The contrast is between one who brings forth the wind and one who brings forth a statue, and the fatal lack is named exactly: there is no breath in them. The God who breathed into dust is set beside gods that cannot breathe at all.

Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name.

The portion of Jacob. Israel's share, her allotted inheritance, is a person — and the sentence turns round and says Israel is his: the tribe of his inheritance. Two parties who have each other as their property.

"You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces; with you I destroy kingdoms; with you I break in pieces the horse and his rider... with you I break in pieces the shepherd and his flock; with you I break in pieces the farmer and his team; with you I break in pieces governors and commanders.

Nine times in four verses: with you I break in pieces. It is the rhythm of a hammer, and the list moves from cavalry to civilians to shepherds and ploughmen to the government.

Read as a whole it is God's own account of what Babylon was: You are my hammer and weapon of war. Not a rival kingdom he failed to stop — an implement he swung.

"I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea before your very eyes for all the evil that they have done in Zion, declares the LORD.

And a hammer is accountable. For all the evil that they have done in Zion — the tool exceeded its commission, and the repayment will happen before your very eyes, so the exiles will see it.

"Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, declares the LORD, which destroys the whole earth; I will stretch out my hand against you, and roll you down from the crags, and make you a burnt mountain. No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation, but you shall be a perpetual waste

Babylon sat on a flat plain, so destroying mountain is about stature rather than geology — and the sentence is to be rolled down from the crags and left as a burnt mountain, a slag heap.

Then the detail that finishes it — No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation. Ruined cities were quarries for the next builders. This rubble will not even be worth carting away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nations are summoned — Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz, with horses like bristling locusts (v. 27) — and Babylon's defence collapses from inside: their strength has failed; they have become women; her dwellings are on fire; her bars are broken (v. 30), while One runner runs to meet another to tell the king his city is taken on every side (v. 31). Zion is given words for what was done to her — he has swallowed me like a monster; he has filled his stomach with my delicacies; he has rinsed me out (v. 34) — and God answers: Behold, I will plead your cause and take vengeance for you. I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry (v. 36), until her officers sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology: The city taken while the messengers are still running to say so.

verseByVerse.quote: "Set up a standard on the earth; blow the trumpet among the nations; prepare the nations for war against her; summon against her the kingdoms, Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz; appoint a marshal against her; bring up horses like bristling locusts. Prepare the nations for war against her, the kings of the Medes, with their governors and deputies, and every land under their dominion. The land trembles and writhes in pain, for the LORD's purposes against Babylon stand, to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without inhabitant. The warriors of Babylon have ceased fighting; they remain in their strongholds; their strength has failed; they have become women; her dwellings are on fire; her bars are broken. One runner runs to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to tell the king of Babylon that his city is taken on every side; the fords have been seized, the marshes are burned with fire, and the soldiers are in panic. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden; yet a little while and the time of her harvest will come." "Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me; he has made me an empty vessel; he has swallowed me like a monster; he has filled his stomach with my delicacies; he has rinsed me out. The violence done to me and to my kinsmen be upon Babylon," let the inhabitant of Zion say. "My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea," let Jerusalem say. Therefore thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will plead your cause and take vengeance for you. I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry, and Babylon shall become a heap of ruins, the haunt of jackals, a horror and a hissing, without inhabitant. "They shall roar together like lions; they shall growl like lions' cubs. While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast and make them drunk, that they may become merry, then sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the LORD. I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams and male goats.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Set up a standard on the earth; blow the trumpet among the nations; prepare the nations for war against her; summon against her the kingdoms, Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz; appoint a marshal against her; bring up horses like bristling locusts.

Three obscure northern peoples are named — Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz, from the Armenian highlands — conscripted into the coalition. And the cavalry comes up like bristling locusts: the horsehair crests of massed horsemen seen from a distance, moving like insects over a field.

The warriors of Babylon have ceased fighting; they remain in their strongholds; their strength has failed; they have become women; her dwellings are on fire; her bars are broken.

The collapse is from the inside. They have not been beaten in the field — they have ceased fighting and gone indoors, and then their strength has failed. The bars of the gates are broken and the houses are burning.

One runner runs to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to tell the king of Babylon that his city is taken on every side; the fords have been seized, the marshes are burned with fire, and the soldiers are in panic.

A brilliant piece of reporting: couriers colliding on the road, each carrying worse news to the palace. By the time the king is told, his city is taken on every side. Anyone who has watched an institution fail will recognise the picture — the messages arriving faster than the leadership can hear them.

For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden; yet a little while and the time of her harvest will come."

Back to threshing, and the timing is God's: yet a little while.

"Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me; he has made me an empty vessel; he has swallowed me like a monster; he has filled his stomach with my delicacies; he has rinsed me out.

Now Zion is given a voice, and it is one of the most physical complaints in Scripture. Six verbs of being eaten: devoured, crushed, emptied, swallowed, and then the last indignity — he has rinsed me out, like a jar licked clean and set aside. The ESV notes that the phrase may be read "Or he has expelled me".

God lets his people say exactly how bad it was. There is no instruction here to be measured about it.

Therefore thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will plead your cause and take vengeance for you. I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry,

And the answer to that complaint is not a lecture but an advocate: I will plead your cause.

I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry. Babylon lived by water — the Euphrates and its canal network. Isaiah had put the same promise next to a name: God says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers', and says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose' (Isa 44:27-28).

While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast and make them drunk, that they may become merry, then sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the LORD.

A feast, wine, merriment, and then sleep. Daniel 5 records the night: a banquet, the vessels of the temple used for drinking, writing on the wall, and That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed (Dan 5:30). The cupbearer of the nations was handed a cup of her own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — Go Out of the Midst of Her, My People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How Babylon is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized! (v. 41) — where the ESV notes the Hebrew has "Sheshach, a code name for Babylon". The sea has come up on Babylon; she is covered with its tumultuous waves (v. 42). God will punish Bel in Babylon, and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed (v. 44). Then the summons: Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life (v. 45), with orders not to panic at each year's rumours (v. 46). Then the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, shall sing for joy over Babylon (v. 48). And to the escaped: Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind (v. 50).
verseByVerse.theology: Get out, and take Jerusalem with you in your mind.

verseByVerse.quote: "How Babylon is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations! The sea has come up on Babylon; she is covered with its tumultuous waves. Her cities have become a horror, a land of drought and a desert, a land in which no one dwells, and through which no son of man passes. And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed. The nations shall no longer flow to him; the wall of Babylon has fallen. "Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD! Let not your heart faint, and be not fearful at the report heard in the land, when a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year, and violence is in the land, and ruler is against ruler. "Therefore, behold, the days are coming when I will punish the images of Babylon; her whole land shall be put to shame, and all her slain shall fall in the midst of her. Then the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, shall sing for joy over Babylon, for the destroyers shall come against them out of the north, declares the LORD. Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel, just as for Babylon have fallen the slain of all the earth. "You who have escaped from the sword, go, do not stand still! Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind: 'We are put to shame, for we have heard reproach; dishonor has covered our face, for foreigners have come into the holy places of the LORD's house.' "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will execute judgment upon her images, and through all her land the wounded shall groan. Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortify her strong height, yet destroyers would come from me against her, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"How Babylon is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations! The sea has come up on Babylon; she is covered with its tumultuous waves.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads Sheshach, "a code name for Babylon" — the same cipher used back in chapter 25, where Babylon drank last from the cup she had carried round (25:26). The code name returns for her funeral.

And the praise of the whole earth is not sarcasm. Babylon was admired everywhere, and the tone here is astonishment rather than gloating.

And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed. The nations shall no longer flow to him; the wall of Babylon has fallen.

Bel had swallowed the offerings and tribute of the world, and the temple vessels of Jerusalem with them. God will reach into the idol's mouth and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed — which is exactly what happened when Cyrus counted the bowls back out to a prince of Judah (Ezra 1:7-8).

"Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD! Let not your heart faint, and be not fearful at the report heard in the land, when a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year, and violence is in the land, and ruler is against ruler.

The call again, and now with pastoral care attached. There will be years of rumour before anything happens — a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year — coups, violence, ruler is against ruler. God tells them in advance not to let their hearts faint at the news cycle.

John hears this same summons over the last Babylon: Come out of her, my people (Rev 18:4).

Then the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, shall sing for joy over Babylon, for the destroyers shall come against them out of the north, declares the LORD. Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel

Creation sings. This is not human vindictiveness but the relief of a world that has been groaning — and the ground given is the dead: Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel. The psalmist by the canals had said it in grief, O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed (Ps 137:8), and here God answers him.

"You who have escaped from the sword, go, do not stand still! Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind: 'We are put to shame... for foreigners have come into the holy places of the LORD's house.'

Two instructions for survivors: Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind. Faith at a distance, with a city held in the memory — which is how most of God's people have lived ever since, remembering a place they are not in.

Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortify her strong height, yet destroyers would come from me against her, declares the LORD.

The old ambition of Babel, still running: mount up to heaven. Isaiah had put the boast in the first person — I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high — and given the answer: But you are brought down to Sheol (Isa 14:13-15). Height is no defence when the destroyers come from me.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A voice! A cry from Babylon! (v. 54), for the LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay (v. 56), and The broad wall of Babylon shall be leveled to the ground, and her high gates shall be burned with fire. The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire (v. 58). Then a last acted sign, given to Seraiah the quartermaster travelling to Babylon (v. 59): Jeremiah wrote in a book all the disaster that should come upon Babylon (v. 60), told him to read it all aloud there (v. 61), then tie a stone to it and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates (v. 63) and say, Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more. And the section closes: Thus far are the words of Jeremiah (v. 64).
verseByVerse.theology: A book weighted with a stone, dropped in a river, as the last sermon of his life.

verseByVerse.quote: "A voice! A cry from Babylon! The noise of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans! For the LORD is laying Babylon waste and stilling her mighty voice. Their waves roar like many waters; the noise of their voice is raised, for a destroyer has come upon her, upon Babylon; her warriors are taken; their bows are broken in pieces, for the LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay. I will make drunk her officials and her wise men, her governors, her commanders, and her warriors; they shall sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The broad wall of Babylon shall be leveled to the ground, and her high gates shall be burned with fire. The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire." The word that Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon, in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was the quartermaster. Jeremiah wrote in a book all the disaster that should come upon Babylon, all these words that are written concerning Babylon. And Jeremiah said to Seraiah: "When you come to Babylon, see that you read all these words, and say, 'O LORD, you have said concerning this place that you will cut it off, so that nothing shall dwell in it, neither man nor beast, and it shall be desolate forever.' When you finish reading this book, tie a stone to it and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates, and say, 'Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more, because of the disaster that I am bringing upon her, and they shall become exhausted.'" Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A voice! A cry from Babylon! The noise of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans! For the LORD is laying Babylon waste and stilling her mighty voice.

Stilling her mighty voice. A great city is a noise — markets, processions, armies, temple crowds — and God turns the volume off.

for a destroyer has come upon her, upon Babylon; her warriors are taken; their bows are broken in pieces, for the LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay.

The LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay. It is one of the plainest statements of the doctrine in Scripture, and it is what makes the rest of the book bearable. A world in which the hammer is never put down is a world without justice.

"Thus says the LORD of hosts: The broad wall of Babylon shall be leveled to the ground, and her high gates shall be burned with fire. The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire."

Babylon's walls were among the wonders of the world, wide enough to drive chariots along. They come down.

And the last line is an epitaph for every empire: The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire. Conscripted labour, decades of it, hauling brick for gates that are fuel. Whatever is built without God is built for burning.

The word that Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon, in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was the quartermaster.

A name worth pausing on. Seraiah the son of Neriah — Baruch's brother, from the same family, and the quartermaster, a senior official travelling with the king to Babylon. The family that gave Jeremiah his scribe also gave him a courier into the enemy capital.

Jeremiah wrote in a book all the disaster that should come upon Babylon... And Jeremiah said to Seraiah: "When you come to Babylon, see that you read all these words, and say, 'O LORD, you have said concerning this place that you will cut it off, so that nothing shall dwell in it, neither man nor beast, and it shall be desolate forever.'

So the prophet writes it down again — the man whose first scroll was burned and whose second was longer — and sends it a thousand kilometres to be read aloud in the city it condemns. A private reading, probably to nobody but God and one frightened official standing by a river.

When you finish reading this book, tie a stone to it and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates, and say, 'Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more, because of the disaster that I am bringing upon her, and they shall become exhausted.'"

And there is the last acted sign of his ministry. He had worn a yoke, smashed a flask, buried a loincloth, bought a field and pushed stones into Pharaoh's pavement. Now, by proxy, a book is weighted with a stone and dropped into the Euphrates, and the words are spoken over the ripples: Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more.

Six centuries later a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more" (Rev 18:21). The last book of the Bible repeats the gesture of an old man's courier at a riverbank.

Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.

Five words to close forty years. No account of his death, no grave, no vindication scene — he is last seen in Egypt among people who would not hear him, and the book simply stops recording what he said.

And what he said outlasted every power in it. Jehoiakim burned the first scroll and his line ended; Babylon is a mound in the desert; and the words thrown into the Euphrates with a stone tied to them float still. The man who asked God why he had ever been born (20:18) wrote the sentence about the law written on the heart and the sins remembered no more, and it is being read this morning in languages that did not exist when he dictated it.

51.title: A Stone in the Euphrates
51.overview:
God stirs up a destroyer against Babylon and sends winnowers to empty her land, because Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God while Chaldea is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel. Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand that made the earth drunk; now balm is brought to her and she is not healed, and the LORD has stirred up the kings of the Medes as vengeance for his temple (vv. 1-14).

A creation hymn interrupts: the God who made the earth by his power and brings the wind from his storehouses is set against idols in which there is no breath. Babylon is then told what she was — my hammer and weapon of war, with which God broke nations — and told she will be repaid for the evil done in Zion, rolled down from the crags as a burnt mountain with no stone left worth reusing (vv. 15-26).

Nations are summoned against her. Her warriors stop fighting and shut themselves in, their strength fails, runners collide on the road carrying word that the city is taken on every side. Zion is given words for what Babylon did — devoured, crushed, swallowed, rinsed out — and God answers that he will plead her cause, dry up Babylon's waters, and give her officers a feast that ends in perpetual sleep (vv. 27-40).

Babylon, the praise of the whole earth, is taken; God reaches into Bel's mouth to take back what he swallowed; his people are told to go out of her and not to let their hearts faint at years of rumour; and heaven and earth sing for joy. Survivors are to remember the LORD from far away and let Jerusalem come into their minds, for height is no defence (vv. 41-53).

Her broad wall will be levelled and her gates burned — the nations wearying themselves only for fire. Finally Jeremiah writes it all in a book and sends it with Seraiah the quartermaster to be read aloud in Babylon, then tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates: thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more. Thus far are the words of Jeremiah (vv. 54-64).
51.theology:
The question the exiles were asking was not whether Babylon would fall but whether God had dropped them, and the answer is flat: Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God (v. 5).

Empires are intoxicating, and the cup was always in God's hand rather than holding itself up (v. 7).

Judgment is not eagerness to destroy. Balm was brought and the physician's verdict declared after the attempt: we would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed (v. 9; 8:22; 46:11).

The Creator who brings the wind from his storehouses is set against gods with no breath in them, and Israel's portion is a person rather than a thing (vv. 15-19).

God names what Babylon was — my hammer — and holds the hammer accountable for the evil it did in Zion beyond its commission (vv. 20, 24).

God lets his people say exactly how bad it was, and answers the complaint with an advocate rather than a lecture: I will plead your cause (vv. 34, 36).

Whatever is built without God is built for burning: the nations weary themselves only for fire (v. 58).

A God of recompense who will surely repay is what makes the rest of the book bearable (v. 56).
51.examples:
A code name for an empire, written by a man inside its reach.

A golden cup that made the whole world drunk.

Balm fetched to the bedside of the empire that burned the temple.

Weather kept in storehouses and brought out as needed.

Nine hammer blows in four verses.

Rubble not even worth carting away for foundations.

Couriers colliding on the road with worse news.

A jar licked clean and set aside.

A banquet, and then a sleep nobody wakes from.

Reaching into an idol's mouth for what it swallowed.

Told in advance not to panic at the news each year.

Walls wide enough for chariots, levelled.

A book weighted with a stone, dropped in a river.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The appendix retells the fall in annalist's prose. Zedekiah reigned eleven years and did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done (v. 2), until he cast them out from his presence (v. 3). The siege runs from the tenth month of the ninth year until the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land (v. 6) and a breach was made in the city (v. 7). Zedekiah is overtaken in the plains of Jericho and sentenced at Riblah: The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes (v. 10), and then He put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him in chains, and kept him in prison till the day of his death (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The same account as chapter 39, told again without a word of comment.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done. For because of the anger of the LORD it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon. And in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem, and laid siege to it. And they built siegeworks all around it. So the city was besieged till the eleventh year of King Zedekiah. On the ninth day of the fourth month the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land. Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled and went out from the city by night by the way of a gate between the two walls, by the king's garden, and the Chaldeans were around the city. And they went in the direction of the Arabah. But the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and all his army was scattered from him. Then they captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he passed sentence on him. The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah. He put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him in chains, and the king of Babylon took him to Babylon, and put him in prison till the day of his death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.

The last chapter is an appendix, and it changes voice completely. After fifty-one chapters of poetry, lament, argument and tears, we get the flat prose of a court chronicle, running parallel to the end of 2 Kings.

Somebody thought the facts should be set down plainly, with dates and numbers, after all the preaching. The commentary is over; here is the record.

For because of the anger of the LORD it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

Two causes in one verse, and the order matters. The theological cause first — he cast them out from his presence — and then the political one, Zedekiah's rebellion. The chronicler will give the military details, but he will not let anyone read them as merely military.

And in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem... On the ninth day of the fourth month the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land.

The dating is precise to the day, which is how you write about something you cannot forget. Thirty months between those two dates, and the whole of it summarised in one clause: there was no food.

Jeremiah lived through that on a loaf a day from the bakers' street until the bread ran out (37:21).

Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled and went out from the city by night by the way of a gate between the two walls... But the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho... The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah. He put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him in chains, and the king of Babylon took him to Babylon, and put him in prison till the day of his death.

Everything here has already been told in chapter 39, and it is told again without one word of interpretation. No lament, no reproach, no reference to the offer he refused.

One detail is added that chapter 39 left out: put him in prison till the day of his death. He had been promised that he would not die by the sword but in peace (34:4-5), and this is what that mercy looked like — years in a Babylonian cell, blind, and then a quiet end. God kept the promise exactly, and it was not what anybody would have pictured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–23 — He Burned the House of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A month after the breach Nebuzaradan arrives, and he burned the house of the LORD, and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned down (v. 13). The walls come down, the people are deported, and some of the poorest of the land are left to be vinedressers and plowmen (v. 16). Then a long inventory: the bronze pillars, the stands and the sea broken up and carried off (v. 17), the pots and shovels and snuffers (v. 18), and the measurements — a pillar eighteen cubits high, hollow (v. 21), with ninety-six pomegranates on the sides (v. 23). The bronze of all these things was beyond weight (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: A clerk counting pomegranates on a pillar that is being cut up in front of him.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month—that was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan the captain of the bodyguard, who served the king of Babylon, entered Jerusalem. And he burned the house of the LORD, and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned down. And all the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down all the walls around Jerusalem. And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive some of the poorest of the people and the rest of the people who were left in the city and the deserters who had deserted to the king of Babylon, together with the rest of the artisans. But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and plowmen. And the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD, and the stands and the bronze sea that were in the house of the LORD, the Chaldeans broke in pieces, and carried all the bronze to Babylon. And they took away the pots and the shovels and the snuffers and the basins and the dishes for incense and all the vessels of bronze used in the temple service; also the small bowls and the fire pans and the basins and the pots and the lampstands and the dishes for incense and the bowls for drink offerings. What was of gold the captain of the guard took away as gold, and what was of silver, as silver. As for the two pillars, the one sea, the twelve bronze bulls that were under the sea, and the stands, which Solomon the king had made for the house of the LORD, the bronze of all these things was beyond weight. As for the pillars, the height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits, its circumference was twelve cubits, and its thickness was four fingers, and it was hollow. On it was a capital of bronze. The height of the one capital was five cubits. A network and pomegranates, all of bronze, were around the capital. And the second pillar had the same, with pomegranates. There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; all the pomegranates were a hundred upon the network all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month... Nebuzaradan the captain of the bodyguard, who served the king of Babylon, entered Jerusalem. And he burned the house of the LORD, and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned down.

A month after the walls broke, the fire. And there it is, in six words the earlier account could not bring itself to write: he burned the house of the LORD.

Chapter 39 listed the palace and the houses and the walls and said nothing about the temple. Here the sentence is finally put down, first in the list, and the day is dated. Jewish tradition still fasts on the ninth of Ab for this.

And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive some of the poorest of the people... But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and plowmen.

The poorest are left with the vines and the ploughs — the reversal noted in chapter 39, where those who owned nothing were given fields (39:10). An administrative decision that reads like a verdict.

And the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD, and the stands and the bronze sea that were in the house of the LORD, the Chaldeans broke in pieces, and carried all the bronze to Babylon.

These are the exact items God had named twenty-five chapters earlier, when the popular prophets were promising the temple treasure would be back within two years: the pillars, the sea, the stands (27:19). They would go to Babylon and stay there until the day when I visit them (27:22). Here they go.

As for the two pillars, the one sea, the twelve bronze bulls that were under the sea, and the stands, which Solomon the king had made for the house of the LORD, the bronze of all these things was beyond weight.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks the sea in this verse. What the verse does carry is the name Solomon — four hundred years of it, made by the wisest king Israel had, and now beyond weight as scrap metal.

As for the pillars, the height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits... and its thickness was four fingers, and it was hollow... There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; all the pomegranates were a hundred upon the network all around.

And then the strangest passage in the chapter: a detailed description of the pillars, measured in cubits — the ESV notes "A cubit was about 18 inches or 45 centimeters" — with the thickness of the bronze given in fingers, and the pomegranates counted.

Somebody wrote down how many pomegranates were cast on the capitals of Jachin and Boaz while they were being broken up and loaded onto carts. It is an act of love — the careful recording of a beautiful thing as it is destroyed, so that it would not be as though it had never existed.

Grief keeps inventories. And the God who told them to record it is the God who told them the pillars would come back on a day of his choosing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — So Judah Was Taken Into Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The senior men are rounded up — Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest and the three keepers of the threshold (v. 24), an army commander, seven royal counsellors, a mustering secretary and sixty men of the land (v. 25) — taken to Riblah, and there the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death. Then one flat sentence: So Judah was taken into exile out of its land (v. 27). The deportation figures follow, three of them, totalling all the persons were 4,600 (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: A nation's end recorded as a headcount.

verseByVerse.quote: And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest and the three keepers of the threshold; and from the city he took an officer who had been in command of the men of war, and seven men of the king's council, who were found in the city; and the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the midst of the city. And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. And the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was taken into exile out of its land. This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans; in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem 832 persons; in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Judeans 745 persons; all the persons were 4,600.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest and the three keepers of the threshold; and from the city he took an officer who had been in command of the men of war, and seven men of the king's council, who were found in the city; and the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the midst of the city.

The leadership is collected by function: high priest, deputy priest, three doorkeepers, a general, seven counsellors, the conscription secretary, and sixty ordinary men.

One name is quietly poignant. Zephaniah the second priest is the man who had read Shemaiah's hostile letter aloud to Jeremiah instead of acting on it (29:29), and whom Zedekiah twice sent to ask the prophet for prayer (21:1; 37:3). He was not an enemy. He goes to Riblah with the rest.

And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. And the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was taken into exile out of its land.

So Judah was taken into exile out of its land. One sentence for the end of a nation, and it is the sentence the whole book has been warning about since a young man saw an almond branch.

This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans; in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem 832 persons; in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Judeans 745 persons; all the persons were 4,600.

Three deportations, counted. And the totals are small — 4,600, probably heads of households rather than every person, but small in any reckoning.

That is what a remnant looks like on paper. Not a nation, a number; and a number low enough to be written in one line. Everything God had promised about restoration, the everlasting covenant, the Branch and the law written on the heart now rested on four thousand six hundred deportees and some vinedressers left behind.

God's purposes have often been carried by numbers that look like nothing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thirty-seven years later the book turns. Evil-merodach graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison (v. 31) — where the ESV notes the Hebrew idiom is "lifted up the head of". He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon (v. 32). So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king's table (v. 33), with an allowance according to his daily needs, until the day of his death (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: The book of the weeping prophet ends with a pardoned son of David eating dinner.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison. And he spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon. So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king's table, and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king, according to his daily needs, until the day of his death, as long as he lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison.

And now, after everything, the book lifts.

Thirty-seven years is most of a lifetime. Jehoiachin is the Jeconiah of chapter 22, the young king carried off in 597 whom God had told to be written down as childless, with none of his offspring on David's throne (22:30), and the good figs of chapter 24 went into exile with him. He has been in a Babylonian prison ever since.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew idiom behind graciously freed is "lifted up the head of" — the phrase used of a man whose face is raised out of shame into favour. Somebody lifted the head of the last king of Judah.

And he spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon. So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king's table, and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king, according to his daily needs, until the day of his death, as long as he lived.

Four things happen, and every one of them is a picture of grace.

He is spoken kindly to — the first kind words recorded to a king of Judah in this book. He is given a seat above the seats of the kings, honoured above other captive royalty for no stated reason. He put off his prison garments and was dressed otherwise. And he ate at the king's table every day of his life, on a regular allowance suited according to his daily needs.

Nothing is said about Jehoiachin deserving it. He had done what was evil; he had been in that cell thirty-seven years; and a new emperor, for reasons of his own, raised his head, changed his clothes and sat him down to dinner. It is what happens to every sinner God pardons — summoned out of a cell, robes exchanged, seated at a table, and fed daily for life.

And there is more here than a picture. The book ends this way because the line of David is alive. The house that was supposed to be finished has a living heir eating in Babylon, and Matthew's genealogy runs straight through him: Jeconiah, and then the generations to Joseph the husband of Mary (Matt 1:11-12).

So the last verse of the weeping prophet is an allowance of food for a pardoned king. No temple yet, no city yet, no Branch yet — but a son of David out of prison, at a table, with bread given him according to his daily needs, which is exactly how his greater Son would later teach his people to ask for it.

Everything else in these fifty-two chapters came true to the letter: the siege, the famine, the breach, the blinded king, the burned house, the counted pomegranates, the seventy years. On the strength of that accuracy, the rest of what he wrote stands — an everlasting love, a heart given rather than demanded, a righteous Branch, a name over the city that reads The LORD is our righteousness, and sins that God has undertaken to remember no more.

52.title: A King at the Table
52.overview:
The closing appendix retells the fall in the flat prose of a chronicle. Zedekiah did what was evil, and because of the LORD's anger he cast them out from his presence; Zedekiah rebelled, the siege came, and after thirty months the famine left no food in the city. The wall was breached, the king fled by night, was overtaken in the plains of Jericho and sentenced at Riblah: his sons killed before his eyes, his own eyes put out, and prison in Babylon till the day of his death (vv. 1-11).

A month later Nebuzaradan burned the house of the LORD, the palace and every great house, broke down the walls, and deported the people — leaving some of the poorest as vinedressers and plowmen. The bronze pillars, the stands and the sea were broken up and carried to Babylon, along with every vessel, and the chapter records the pillars' height, the thickness of the bronze, and the ninety-six pomegranates on the capitals (vv. 12-23).

The chief priest, the second priest, the doorkeepers, a commander, seven royal counsellors, the mustering secretary and sixty men of the land were taken to Riblah and executed. So Judah was taken into exile out of its land, and the three deportations are counted: 4,600 persons in all (vv. 24-30).

Then, in the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile, Evil-merodach freed him from prison, spoke kindly to him, gave him a seat above the other captive kings, and let him put off his prison garments and dine at the royal table every day of his life, with a daily allowance until his death (vv. 31-34).
52.theology:
The record puts the theological cause before the political one: God cast them out from his presence, and then Zedekiah rebelled. The military facts are never to be read as merely military (v. 3).

God keeps his promises exactly, and not as we would picture them. Zedekiah was promised he would not die by the sword, and it meant years blind in a cell and then a quiet end (v. 11; 34:4-5).

The sentence chapter 39 could not write is finally written here, and dated: he burned the house of the LORD (v. 13).

Grief keeps inventories. Somebody counted the pomegranates on Solomon's pillars while they were being cut up, so that a beautiful thing would not vanish as though it had never been — and the God who let them be taken had promised their return (vv. 21-23; 27:19-22).

A remnant on paper is a number small enough to fit in one line, and God's purposes have often been carried by numbers that look like nothing (v. 30).

The book ends in pure grace: a head lifted, kind words, robes exchanged, a seat above others, and daily bread for life, with nothing said about deserving (vv. 31-34) — and the Davidic line alive in Babylon, running on to Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:11-12).
52.examples:
Poetry for fifty-one chapters, and then a court clerk's prose.

Dated to the day, because nobody could forget it.

Thirty months of siege, summarised as: there was no food.

The six words the earlier account could not bring itself to write.

The poorest left behind with the vines and the ploughs.

Four hundred years of Solomon's bronze, weighed as scrap.

Counting pomegranates on a pillar being loaded onto a cart.

A nation's end recorded as 4,600 persons.

An idiom that means somebody lifted his head.

Prison garments put off, and a seat above the other kings.

Bread given according to his daily needs.
